In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

O Lord, make it easy. The exegesis (tafsir) of Surat al-Ma'idah, with Allah's power and might.

It is Medinan by consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement). It is narrated that it was revealed when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from al-Hudaybiyah. Al-Naqqash reported from Abu Salamah that he said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from al-Hudaybiyah, he said: "O Ali, did you realize that the Surah of al-Ma'idah has been revealed to me, and what an excellent benefit it is?"

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is a fabricated hadith (hadith mawdu'). It is not lawful for a Muslim to believe it. As for saying "the Surah of al-Ma'idah, and what an excellent benefit it is," we do not transmit it from anyone, but it is a fine statement.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This, in my view, does not resemble the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ).

It is also narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "The Surah of al-Ma'idah is called in the kingdom of Allah 'the Deliverer': it delivers its companion from the hands of the angels of punishment."

Some of this surah was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada'), and some was revealed in the year of the Conquest (of Makkah), namely the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:2], and so on.

Every part of the Qur'an revealed after the Prophet's migration (hijrah) is Medinan, whether it was revealed in Madinah or during a journey. What is classed as Makkan is only that which was revealed before the migration.

Abu Maysarah said: "al-Ma'idah" is among the last things revealed. There is no abrogated (mansukh) ruling in it, and it contains eighteen obligations (fara'id) not found elsewhere. They are: ﴿the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and what a beast of prey has eaten﴾ [5:3]; ﴿what is sacrificed on stone altars, and that you seek decision by arrows﴾; ﴿what the hunting animals you have trained have caught for you﴾ [5:4]; ﴿the food of those who were given the Scripture﴾ [5:5]; ﴿and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [5:5]; the completion of purification, ﴿when you rise to prayer﴾ [5:6]; ﴿the thief, male and female﴾ [5:38]; ﴿do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [5:95], up to His words ﴿the Mighty, the Possessor of retribution﴾ [5:95]; and ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah, or ham﴾ [5:103]. And His words, the Exalted: ﴿The testimony between you when death approaches one of you﴾ [5:106], and so on.

I say: The nineteenth obligation is His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when you call to prayer﴾ [5:58]. The call to prayer (adhan) is mentioned in the Qur'an only in this surah. As for what comes in the Surah of al-Jumu'ah, it is specific to Friday, whereas in this surah it is general for all prayers.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited the Surah of al-Ma'idah during the Farewell Pilgrimage and said: "O people, the Surah of al-Ma'idah is among the last things revealed, so make lawful its lawful things and make unlawful its unlawful things." A similar report from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) is transmitted as a statement of her own (mawquf).

Jubayr ibn Nufayr said: I entered upon 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), and she said: "Do you recite the Surah of al-Ma'idah?" I said: "Yes." She said: "It is among the last that Allah revealed, so whatever you find in it of lawful, make it lawful, and whatever you find in it of unlawful, make it unlawful."

al-Sha'bi said: Nothing was abrogated from this surah except His words: ﴿Nor the sacred month, nor the offerings﴾ [5:2], and so on.

Some scholars said: From it was abrogated ﴿or two others from among other than you﴾ [5:106].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill (awfu) the contracts. Lawful to you are the animals of grazing livestock, except what is recited to you, but not while you are hunting game while in the state of ihram. Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills.﴾ [5:1]

In it are seven issues (masa'il).

The first: His words, the Exalted, ﴿O you who have believed﴾. 'Alqamah said: Everything in the Qur'an that begins "O you who have believed" is Medinan, and "O mankind" [4:1] is Makkan. This is a general rule, and it has been discussed earlier (see vol. 1, p. 229).

This verse is one whose eloquence and abundance of meanings, despite the brevity of its words, become evident to everyone who has insight into speech. It contains five rulings:

The first: the command to fulfill contracts.
The second: the permission of the animals of grazing livestock.
The third: the exception of what is recited after this.
The fourth: the exception concerning the state of ihram regarding game.
The fifth: what the verse requires regarding the permissibility of hunting for one who is not in ihram.

Al-Naqqash related that the companions of al-Kindi said to him: "O wise man, produce for us something like this Qur'an." He said: "Yes! I will produce something like part of it." He then secluded himself for many days, then came out and said: "By Allah, no one can do this, nor can anyone bear it. I opened the mushaf and the Surah of al-Ma'idah came out. I looked, and behold, it speaks of fulfilling promises and forbids breaking them, makes a general permission, then makes an exception after an exception, then informs of His power and wisdom in two lines. No one can produce this except in volumes."

The second: His words, ﴿awfu﴾ (fulfill). It is said: wafa and awfa are two dialects (lughatan). Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?﴾ [9:111], and He said: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled﴾ [53:37]. And the poet said: [The poet is Tufayl al-Ghanawi. Qila'as al-najm are the twenty stars which the Dabaran drove in the speech of the Pleiades, as the Arabs claim.]

As for Ibn Tawq, he fulfilled his covenant,
just as the driver of the star-camels fulfilled them.

So he combined the two dialects.

﴿Al-'uqud﴾ (the contracts): al-'uqud are bonds; their singular is 'aqd. It is said: "I tied the pledge and the rope" (aqadtu al-'ahd wa al-habl), and "I tied the chain" ['aqadtu al-ghull] [The text in the origins reads 'asal, and in the margin of al-Jamal citing al-Qurtubi it reads "I tied the chain".]. It is used for abstract meanings and for physical things. al-Hutay'ah said:

A people who, when they make a contract with their neighbor,
tie the 'inaj and tie above it the karab.

['Inaj: a thread or strap tied to the bottom of a bucket and then fastened to its handle. Karab: the rope tied around the bucket after the mannin, which is the first rope. If the mannin breaks, the karab remains. It has also been said otherwise. These are images the poet coined to illustrate their fulfillment of covenants.]

Therefore Allah, glorified is He, commanded fulfilment of the contracts (ʿuqūd). Al-Ḥasan said: By this He means the contracts of obligation (ʿuqūd al-dayn), which are what a person binds upon himself, such as sale and purchase, hiring and renting, marriage, divorce, sharecropping, reconciliation, transfer of ownership, granting of options, manumission, arrangement of freedom upon death (tadbīr), and other such matters, so long as these are not outside the Sharīʿah. Likewise, what a person binds upon himself for Allah of acts of worship, such as the Ḥajj, fasting, i'tikāf, night prayer, and vows (nadhr), and what resembles these of the acts of worship of the religion of Islam. As for vowing something permissible (mubāḥ), it is not binding by the consensus of the Muslim community, said Ibn al-ʿArabī. Then it was said: the verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book, [saying], "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187] [[See vol. 4, p. 304.]]. Ibn Jurayj said: It is specific to the People of the Book, and it was revealed concerning them. It was also said: It is general, and this is the sound view, for the word "believers" encompasses the believers among the People of the Book, because between them and Allah there is a contract regarding the discharge of the trust concerning what is in their Book about the matter of Muḥammad ﷺ, [[In z: "and it encompasses the nation of Muḥammad ﷺ." In the marginal notes of al-Jamal on al-Qurtubi: "and they are from the nation of Muḥammad." Etc. I say: meaning the nation of response (ijābah)... corrected by its editor.]] for they are commanded with this in His saying, "Fulfil the contracts," and in other places. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Fulfil the contracts" means: concerning what He has made lawful, what He has made unlawful, what He has enjoined, and what He has set as limits, in all matters. Mujāhid and others said likewise. Ibn Shihāb said: I read the letter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which he wrote to ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm when he sent him to Najrān, and at its beginning was: "This is a declaration to the people from Allah and His Messenger: 'O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts,'" and he wrote the verses in it up to His saying: "Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning" [al-Māʾidah: 4]. Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning is: fulfil the contract of Allah upon you, and your contracts with one another. All of this returns to the view of generality, which is the sound position in this matter. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Muslims are bound by their conditions," and he said: "Every condition that is not in the Book of Allah is void, even if it is a hundred conditions." Thus he clarified that the condition or contract that must be fulfilled is that which agrees with the Book of Allah, i.e., the religion of Allah; if something in it is found to contradict this, it is rejected, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected." Ibn Isḥāq reported: Groups of the Quraysh gathered in the house of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān, for his nobility and lineage, and they made a pact and covenant that they would not find anyone wronged in Makkah, from its people or others, without standing with him until his grievance was restored to him. The Quraysh named that alliance the Alliance of the Virtuous (Ḥilf al-Fuḍūl), and it is concerning it that the Messenger ﷺ said: "I witnessed in the house of [ʿAbd Allāh] [[From j and z.]] ibn Judʿān an alliance that I would not love to have in exchange for red camels, and if I were called to it in Islam I would respond." This alliance is the intended meaning in his saying, upon him be peace: "Any alliance that existed in the Jāhiliyyah, Islam has only strengthened it," because it agrees with the Sharīʿah, since it commands seeking redress from the wrongdoer. As for their corrupt covenants and false contracts based on oppression and raids, Islam has demolished them, and praise be to Allah. Ibn Isḥāq said: Al-Walīd ibn ʿUtbah wronged al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī concerning a property of his, by virtue of al-Walīd's authority, for he was the governor of Madīnah. Al-Ḥusayn said to him: "I swear by Allah that you will do me justice regarding my right, or I will take up my sword, then I will stand in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then I will call for the Alliance of the Virtuous." ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr said: "And I swear by Allah that if he calls me, I will take up my sword, then I will stand with him until he obtains his right, or we all die." It reached al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and he said the same, and it reached ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Taymī and he said the same. When this reached al-Walīd, he did him justice.

The third matter: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle﴾. The address is to everyone who has committed to faith in its proper form and completeness. The Arabs had customs regarding livestock: the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah, the waṣīlah and the ḥām, whose explanation will come. So this verse was revealed abolishing those imaginary superstitions and corrupt, false opinions. The meaning of "beasts of cattle" (bahīmat al-anʿām) has been differed over. The word bahīmah is the name for every quadruped; it was so named because of its ambiguity (ibhām) in terms of the deficiency of its speech, understanding, lack of discernment and intellect; from this comes "a closed door" (bāb mubham), i.e., shut, "a dark night" (layl bahīm), and "bahmah" for a brave man about whom it is not known from where he may be attacked. And "al-anʿām" are camels, cattle and sheep; they were so named for the gentleness of their walking [[In al-Mufradāt of al-Rāghib: the naming of camels by this is because they are the greatest blessing among them, and they are not called anʿām unless camels are among the whole group.]], Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits﴾ [al-Naḥl: 5], up to His saying: ﴿and they carry your loads﴾ [al-Naḥl: 7] [[See vol. 10, pp. 68 and 152.]], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And of the cattle are those for carrying and those for flesh﴾ [al-Anʿām: 142], meaning the large and the small; then He explained them, saying: ﴿eight pairs﴾ [al-Anʿām: 143] up to His saying: ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133]. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿And He made for you from the hides of cattle shelters which you find light on the day of your travel and the day of your residence, and from their wool, fur and hair﴾ [al-Naḥl: 80] [[See vol. 10, pp. 68 and 152.]]: "from their wool" meaning sheep; "their fur" meaning camels; "their hair" meaning goats. These are three proofs indicating that the name anʿām includes these kinds: camels, cattle and sheep. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan. Al-Harawī said: When it is said al-naʿam, it refers to camels alone. Al-Ṭabarī said: Some people said "beasts of cattle" means their wild kinds, such as gazelles, wild cattle, wild asses and others. Others besides al-Ṭabarī reported this from al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ, Qatādah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, as if He had said: "The cattle are made lawful for you," so the genus was attributed to a more specific part of it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is a good view, because the anʿām are the eight pairs, and whatever is added to them of the rest of the animals is called anʿām together with them; and the predator, such as the lion and every animal with fangs, is outside the limit of the anʿām. Thus "beasts of cattle" are the grazing quadrupeds. I say: On this view, animals with hooves would be included, since they are grazing and not predatory; but this is not so, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the cattle — He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits﴾ [al-Naḥl: 5], then He joined to them His saying: ﴿and the horses, mules and donkeys﴾ [al-Naḥl: 8]. Since He resumed their mention and coordinated them with the cattle, this indicates that they are not among them, and Allah knows best. It was also said: "beasts of cattle" is whatever is not game (ṣayd), because game is called wild (waḥsh), not beast (bahīmah); and this returns to the first view. It is narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar that he said: "Beasts of cattle" are the fetuses that come out at slaughter from the wombs of their mothers, so they are eaten without slaughter (dhakāh). This was also said by Ibn ʿAbbās, though there is weakness in it, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, and there is nothing in fetuses that is excepted. Mālik said: The slaughter of the slaughtered animal is slaughter for its fetus if it was not found alive and its hair had grown and its form was complete; but if its form was not complete and its hair had not grown, it is not eaten unless it is found alive and then slaughtered. If they hastened to slaughter it and it died on its own, it was said: it is slaughtered (dhakī); and it was said: it is not slaughtered. More elaboration on this will come, Allah willing.

The fourth matter: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, i.e., what is read to you in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3], and from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Every predator with fangs among beasts of prey is unlawful" [[The narration of Muslim and al-Nasāʾī: "Every predator with fangs among beasts of prey, its eating is unlawful."]]. If it is said: What is recited to us is the Book, not the Sunnah, we say: Every Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is from the Book of Allah, and the evidence for this is two matters. The first: the hadith of the laborer ("I will judge between you two by the Book of Allah"), and stoning is not explicitly stated in the Book of Allah. The second: the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd: "And why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed, and it is in the Book of Allah," and so on. It will come in Surah al-Ḥashr [[See vol. 18, p. 17.]]. "Except what is recited to you" may mean what is recited to you now, or "what is recited to you" later, in future time, upon the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; and this would be evidence for the permissibility of delaying clarification (al-bayān) beyond a time when there is no need for immediate necessity.

The fifth matter: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿not hunting while you are in the state of iḥrām﴾, i.e., whatever is game is lawful when not in iḥrām but not in iḥrām, and whatever is not game is lawful in both states. The grammarians differed over whether "except what is recited to you" is an exception or not. The Basrans said: It is an exception from "beasts of cattle," and "not lawful to hunt" is another exception from it too; so both exceptions are from "beasts of cattle," and the excepted item is: except what is recited to you, except game while you are in iḥrām, unlike His saying: ﴿Indeed, We were sent to a criminal people, except the family of Lot﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 58–59] [[See vol. 10, p. 36.]], as will come. It was also said: It is an exception from what follows it of the exception, so it becomes equivalent to His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Indeed, We were sent to a criminal people﴾. If that were so, hunting would be permitted in iḥrām, because it would be excepted from the prohibition, since His saying "except what is recited to you" would be excepted from the permission; and this view is invalid. So its meaning is: "Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, not making lawful game while you are in the state of iḥrām, except what is recited to you, apart from game." It is also permissible that its meaning be: "Fulfil the contracts, not making lawful game, and lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you." Al-Farrāʾ permitted that "except what is recited to you" be in the nominative position as a substitution (badal), on the basis that it is conjoined with "illā" just as it is conjoined with "lā"; but the Basrans do not permit this except with an indefinite noun or what approximates it among the names of genera, as in: "The people came, except Zayd." The accusative, according to him, is because "not making lawful game" is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl) of the element in "fulfil" [[the wāw in ʾawfū]]. Al-Akhfash said: "O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts, not making lawful game." Others said: It is a state (ḥāl) of the kāf and mīm in "for you" (lakum), and the estimate is: "Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, not making lawful game." Then it was said: The making lawful may refer to people, i.e., do not make game lawful while in iḥrām; and it may refer to Allah, exalted is He, i.e., I have made lawful for you the beast except what is game at the time of iḥrām, as you say: "I have made such-and-such lawful for you, not permitting it for you on Friday." If you say it refers to people, then the meaning is: "not making game lawful," and the nūn was dropped for lightness.

The sixth matter: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you are in the state of ḥurum﴾, meaning being in iḥrām for Ḥajj and ʿUmrah. It is said: "a man ḥarām and a people ḥurum" when they have entered into iḥrām for Ḥajj; and from this is the saying of the poet [[He is al-Muḍarrib ibn Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr.]]:
I said to her: "Turn back to me, for indeed I am in iḥrām, and I am, after that, a man of sense."

Meaning: "muhrim" (one who has entered the state of ihram, i.e., one who is saying the talbiyah). This state is called ihram because of what the one who enters it makes forbidden to himself, such as women, perfume, and other things. It is also said: "ahram" means he entered the Haram (the sacred precinct), and so the game of the Haram is likewise forbidden.

Al-Hasan, Ibrahim and Yahya ibn Thabbat read "hurm" with a sukun on the ra', and this is a Tamimi dialect, in which they say "rusl" for "rusul" (messengers), "kutb" for "kutub" (books), and similar.

Seventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah decrees what He wills﴾, serves to strengthen these legal rulings that differ from the familiar rulings of the Arabs. That is, "you, O Muhammad, who hear of the abrogation of those rulings of theirs that you were accustomed to, take heed, for He who owns everything ﴿decrees what He wills﴾ ﴿none can repel His command﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 41]. He legislates what He wills as He wills."

[[See vol. 9, p. 334.]]

**Question 1**

﴿O you who believe, do not violate the sacred rites of Allah﴾. This is addressed to true believers, meaning: do not transgress the limits of Allah in any matter. The word *sha'a'ir* (sacred rites or symbols of Allah) is the plural of *sha'ira* on the pattern *fa'ila*. Ibn Faris said: "The singular is also said to be *sha'ara*, and this is the better form." A *sha'ira* is a camel offered as a sacrifice (*badana*). *Ishar* (marking) means cutting its hump until blood flows from it, so that it is known to be an offering. *Ishar* means informing through a visible sign. From the same root comes *mash'ar* (a landmark), plural *mashaʿir*, which are the places marked with signs. It also gives *shi'r* (poetry), because it is the kind of speech that stirs feeling (*shu'ur*). It gives *sha'ir* (poet), because he perceives by his acuteness what others do not. It gives *sha'ir* (barley), named for the hair (*sha'ra*) on its head.

According to one view, the *sha'a'ir* are the animals marked to be offered to the House of Allah. According to another, they are all the rites of the Hajj. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said: "Al-Safa, al-Marwa, the offerings, and the camels are all among the sha'a'ir." The poet said:

*We fight them generation after generation, and you see them as sacred offerings through which one draws near (to Allah).*

The polytheists used to perform Hajj, ʿUmrah, and make offerings, and the Muslims wished to raid them. So Allah revealed: "Do not violate the sacred rites of Allah." ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah said: "The sha'a'ir of Allah are everything Allah has commanded and forbidden." Al-Hasan said: "They are the whole religion of Allah," as in His words: ﴿That, and whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾ [al-Hajj 22:32], meaning the religion of Allah.

I say: this view is the preponderant one, and it is to be preferred over others because of its generality.

The scholars differed concerning the marking of the offering. This is **Question 2**. The majority permitted it. They then differed as to which side should be marked. Al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Abu Thawr said it should be on the right side. This is also reported from Ibn ʿUmar. It is established from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) marked his she-camel on the right side of her hump. Muslim and others narrated it, and this is the sound report. It is also reported that he marked a camel on the left side, but Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: "In my view this is a munkar (rejected) report from Ibn ʿAbbas. The sound one is the hadith of Muslim from Ibn ʿAbbas, and nothing else is authentic from him." *Safhat al-sanam* means its side, and *sanam* is the top of the back.

Another group said it should be on the left side. This is the view of Malik, who said: "There is no harm in marking the right side." Mujahid said: "On whichever side one wishes," and Ahmad held this in one of his two positions. Abu Hanifa prohibited all of this and said: "It is torture of an animal." The hadith refutes him. Moreover, it is like branding, by which ownership is known, as already mentioned. Ibn al-ʿArabi went to great lengths in rejecting and denying Abu Hanifa's position when he saw no marking. He said: "It is as if he has never heard of this sacred rite in the Sharia! It is more famous than that among the scholars."

I say: what I have seen stated in the books of the Hanafi scholars is that marking is disliked according to Abu Hanifa. According to Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, it is neither disliked nor recommended, but permissible, because marking is a form of informing, so it is a sunnah in the position of garlanding. Yet since it is a wound and mutilation, it is forbidden. Since it combines sunnah and innovation, it was made permissible. Abu Hanifa's argument is that marking is mutilation, and that it is forbidden because it is torture of an animal, so it is disliked. What was reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was only at the beginning, when the Arabs plundered every property except what was designated as an offering, and they knew the offering only by marking. Then this ceased when the excuse was removed. This is how it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Al-Shaykh al-Imam Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, may Allah have mercy on him, is reported to have said: "It is possible that Abu Hanifa disliked the marking practiced by people of his time, which was excessive cutting in a way that feared spreading (infection) (*sirayah*)." *Sirayah* is a term of the jurists: the wound spreads to the soul, meaning its pain persists until death results from it, as is clear from *al-Misbah*. As for what does not exceed the limit, doing it as it was done in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is good. This is also what Abu Jaʿfar al-Tahawi mentioned.

This is the Hanafi scholars' excuse for Abu Hanifa regarding the hadith that came concerning marking. They had heard it, it reached them, and they knew it. They said: "According to the view that it is disliked, no one becomes a muhrim (one in the state of ihram) by it, because performing a disliked act is not counted among the rites."

**Question 3**: His words, ﴿nor the sacred month﴾. This is a singular noun denoting the category, covering all the sacred months. They are four: one single month and three consecutive months. Their explanation comes in *Bara'a* (Surah 9). The meaning is: do not make them lawful for fighting or raiding, and do not postpone them, for postponing them is making them lawful. This is what they used to do through *al-nasi'* (intercalation). Likewise His words, ﴿nor the offerings, nor the garlands﴾, meaning do not make them lawful. It is by omitting a noun: that is, *nor the owners of the garlands*. He forbade making the offerings lawful in general, and then mentioned the garlanded ones specifically, as emphasis and to stress the sanctity of garlanding.

**Question 4**: His words, ﴿nor the offerings, nor the garlands﴾. *Al-hadyu* is what is brought as a gift to the House of Allah, whether a camel, a cow, or a sheep. Its singular forms are *hadyah*, *hadiyyah*, and *hadyun*. Whoever says that the intended meaning of the sha'a'ir is the rites says: He mentioned the offerings as an indication of their particular status. Whoever says that the sha'a'ir are the offerings says: The sha'a'ir are what has been marked, that is, made known by the flowing of blood from its hump, while the offering is what has not been marked, and for which garlanding is sufficient.

It was also said: the difference is that the sha'a'ir are the camels among the livestock, while the offering includes cows, sheep, garments, and everything that is given as a gift. The majority said: "Hadi" is general for everything by which one draws near to Allah, whether slaughtered animals or charities. From this is the saying of the Prayer and Peace be upon him: "The one who goes early to Friday prayer is like one who brings a camel as an offering," to the end, "like one who brings an egg as an offering." He called it an offering. Calling the egg an offering has no meaning except that he meant charity. Likewise the scholars said: if someone says, "I make my garment an offering," he must give it in charity. However, the general term refers only to one of the three categories: camels, cows, and sheep, and driving them to the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and slaughtering them there. This is taken from the established usage of the Sharia in His words: ﴿But if you are prevented, then (send) what offering is feasible﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:196], meaning a sheep. He also said: ﴿judged by two just men among you as an offering reaching the Kaʿbah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:95], and: ﴿So whoever enjoys ʿUmrah to Hajj, then (let him give) what offering is feasible﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:196]. The least of it, according to the jurists, is a sheep. Malik said: "If someone says, 'my garment is an offering,' he should make its value an offering."

*Al-qala'id* (garlands) are what people used to hang around the necks of the offerings as a safeguard for them. It is by omission of a noun, meaning *nor the owners of the garlands*. Then it was abrogated (*nusikha*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Two verses of al-Ma'idah were abrogated: the verse about the garlands, and His words: ﴿If they come to you, then judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:42]. As for the garlands, the command to kill the polytheists wherever they are and in whatever month they are, abrogated it. As for the other, His words abrogated it: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:49], as will come."

It was also said: the intended meaning of *al-qala'id* is the garlands themselves. Then it is a prohibition against taking the bark (*lihaʾ*) of the trees of the Sacred Precinct so that one may wear it as a garland seeking security. This was said by Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, and Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir. And Allah knows best.

The reality of the offering is whatever is given without any return being mentioned with it. The jurists agreed that whoever says, "For Allah upon me is an offering," must send its price to Makkah. As for the garlands, they are whatever is hung on the humps and necks of the offerings as a sign that it belongs to Allah, the Glorified, whether a shoe or something else. This is an Abrahamic practice that remained in the Jahiliyyah, and Islam confirmed it. It is the practice for cows and sheep. ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Once the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent sheep as an offering to the House, and he garlanded them." Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it. To this view went a group of scholars: al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and Ibn Habib. Malik and the people of opinion (Ahl al-Ra'y) rejected it, as if the hadith about garlanding sheep had not reached them. Or it reached them, but they rejected it because al-Aswad alone narrated it from ʿAʾishah. So the position that accepts it is preferable. And Allah knows best.

As for cows, if they have humps they are marked like camels. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar, and Malik agreed with it. Al-Shafiʿi said: "They are garlanded and marked absolutely, without distinction." Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "They are garlanded but not marked." This view is more sound, since cows have no hump, and they resemble sheep more than camels. And Allah knows best.

**Question 5**: They agreed that whoever garlands a camel with the intention of ihram and drives it becomes a muhrim. Allah said: ﴿Do not violate the sacred rites of Allah﴾ up to His words, ﴿Then hunt﴾. He did not mention ihram, but when He mentioned garlanding, it was understood that it has the status of ihram.

**The sixth issue:** If someone sends a sacrificial animal (hady) ahead but does not travel with it himself, he does not thereby become a muhrim (one in the state of ihram). This is based on the hadith of 'A'isha, who said: "I myself braided the garlands of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ sacrificial animals with my own hands. Then he garlanded them with his own hands and sent them with my father, and nothing became forbidden to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Allah had made lawful for him until the sacrificial animal was slaughtered." Related by al-Bukhari. This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and the majority of scholars. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said the sender becomes a muhrim. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Whoever sends a sacrificial animal, what is forbidden to the pilgrim becomes forbidden to him until the animal is slaughtered." Related by al-Bukhari. This is the position of Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Khattabi reports it from the proponents of opinion (ashab al-ra'y). They argued from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: "I was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when he tore his shirt at the collar and pulled it off over his feet. The people looked at the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: 'I was commanded regarding my camels that I sent, that they be garlanded and marked at such-and-such a place. I put on my shirt and forgot, and I did not want to take my shirt off over my head.'" He had sent his camels and remained in Madina. In its chain is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Ata' ibn Abi Lubaba [[In al-Tahdhib: (Ibn bint Abi Lubaba).]], and he is weak. If someone garlands a sheep and sets out with it, the Kufans said he does not become a muhrim, because garlanding a sheep is neither prescribed (masnun) nor among the rites (sha'a'ir), since a wolf may threaten it and it may not reach the Haram, unlike camels, which are left to drink water, graze on trees, and reach the Haram. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, said: "I braided their garlands from wool that I had." 'Ihn' means dyed wool, and from it is the saying of Allah: ﴿and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ [al-Qari'a: 5] [[See vol. 20, p. 165.]].

**The seventh issue:** It is not permitted to sell or give away the sacrificial animal once it has been garlanded or marked, because it has become obligatory. If the one who made it obligatory dies, it is not inherited from him, and it is carried out for its purpose. This is unlike the udhiyya (sacrificial animal on Eid), which according to Malik is not made obligatory except by slaughter alone, unless one makes it obligatory by words. If he makes it obligatory by words before slaughter, saying: "I have made this sheep an udhiyya," it becomes specified, and if it is lost and he finds it on the days of sacrifice or after them, he must slaughter it, and it is not permitted for him to sell it. If he bought another udhiyya in its place, he slaughters both, according to Ahmad and Ishaq. Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no replacement for it if it strays or is stolen, since replacement applies only to what is obligatory." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "If it strays, it has been fulfilled." If someone dies on the day of sacrifice before sacrificing, his udhiyya is inherited from him like the rest of his property, unlike the hady. Ahmad and Abu Thawr said: "It is slaughtered in every case." Al-Awza'i said: "It is slaughtered, unless he has a debt that can be paid only from that udhiyya, in which case it is sold to pay his debt." If he dies after slaughtering it, his heirs do not inherit it from him, and they may do with it, in eating and charity, what he was entitled to do, but they may not divide its meat as an inheritance. If the udhiyya develops a defect before slaughter, its owner must replace it, unlike the hady. This is the summary of Malik's school. It has been said that for the hady too the owner must replace it, but the first view is more correct. And Allah knows best.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿nor those making for the Sacred House﴾, meaning those intending it, from their saying "amamtu kadha," meaning "I headed for such-and-such." Al-A'mash read: "wa-la amm al-bayt al-haram" (in the genitive construction), like the saying: "ghayra muhilli al-sayd" [al-Ma'ida: 1]. The meaning is: do not prevent the disbelievers who intend the Sacred House for the sake of worship and devotion. On this basis it has been said that whatever is in these verses of prohibition concerning a polytheist, or of respecting his garland, or his intending the House, is all abrogated (mansukh, meaning naskh, abrogation) by the verse of the sword in His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5] and His saying: ﴿So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawba: 28]. Thus the polytheist is not enabled to perform Hajj, and he is not given safe conduct during the sacred months, even if he brings a sacrificial animal, garlands it, and performs Hajj. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and said by Ibn Zayd, as will be mentioned. Others said: the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated, muhkam meaning a clear ruling not subject to abrogation), and it concerns Muslims, since Allah forbade frightening those among the Muslims who intend His House. The prohibition is general, covering the sacred month and other times, but He singled out the sacred month for mention, to honor and exalt it. This accords with the view of 'Ata', for the meaning is: do not violate the signs of Allah, which are His commands and prohibitions and what people know of them, so do not violate them. For this reason Abu Maysara said: "It is muhkam." Mujahid said: "Of it, only 'the garlands' was abrogated, for a man used to garland himself with some bark of the Haram [[That is, the bark of the trees of the Haram.]] and he would not be approached, so that was abrogated." Ibn Juraij said: "This verse is a prohibition against cutting off the roads of the pilgrims." Ibn Zayd said: "The verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in Makka. Some polytheists came to perform Hajj and 'Umra, and the Muslims said: 'O Messenger of Allah, these are only polytheists, and we will not leave them unless we raid them.' So the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿nor those making for the Sacred House﴾." It was also said: this happened because of Shurayh ibn Dhuba'a al-Bakri [[In MS. z: al-Kindi, and in Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: it was revealed concerning al-Khutam, whose name was Shurayh ibn Dhuba'a al-Kindi.]], who was called al-Hutam. The troops of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ seized him while he was on his 'umra, and this verse was revealed, then this ruling was abrogated as we mentioned. Al-Hutam lived to see the apostasy of Yamama and was killed as an apostate. It is reported from his story that he came to the Prophet ﷺ in Madina and left his horses outside Madina, and said: "To what are you calling people?" He said: "To the testimony that there is no god but Allah, establishing prayer, and giving zakat." He said: "Good, but I have leaders whom I do not decide any matter without, and perhaps I will become Muslim and bring them with me." The Prophet ﷺ had said to his companions: "A man will enter upon you who speaks with the tongue of a devil." Then he left from his presence, and the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, said: "He entered with the face of a disbeliever and left with the back of a treacherous man, and this man is not a Muslim." Then he passed by the livestock (sarh) of Madina [[Sarh: grazing livestock.]] and drove them off. They pursued him but could not catch him, so he went away saying:

"The night has wrapped them with a driver, al-Hutam [[A man hutam and hutama is one who has little mercy on livestock, crushing some of them against others.]]...
He is not a camel herdsman, nor a shepherd,
Nor a butcher upon a chopping block [[Al-wadm: anything on which meat is placed, of wood or mat, to protect it from the ground.]]...
They slept soundly, while the son of Hind did not sleep.
A youth like an arrow [[Al-zalam (with the zay open or closed): an arrow-shaft, plural al-azlam, which are the arrows the people of the Jahiliyya used to draw lots with.]] keeps watch over them...
Thick of the two calves, broad of the foot [[Khadlaj al-saqayn: large of them.]] [[Khaffaq al-qadam: broad of the instep.]]"

When the Prophet ﷺ went out in the year of al-Qadiyya [[Al-qadiyya: the making up of the 'umra from which he was prevented.]], he heard the talbiya of the pilgrims of Yamama and said: "This is al-Hutam and his companions." He had garlanded what he had plundered from the livestock of Madina and sent it as an offering to Makka [[In MSS. j and z: the Ka'ba.]], so they set out in pursuit of him, and the verse was revealed, meaning: do not violate what has been marked for Allah, even if they are polytheists. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned this.

**The ninth issue:** On the basis that the verse is muhkam, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not violate the signs of Allah﴾ requires completing the matters of the rites. For this reason the scholars said: if a man enters into Hajj and then invalidates it, he must complete all the actions of Hajj, and it is not permitted for him to leave any of them, even if his Hajj is invalid. Then he must make up (qada') the Hajj in the second year. Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi said: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿nor the sacred month﴾ is abrogated by His saying: "And fight the polytheists all together" [al-Tawba: 36] [[See vol. 8, p. 136.]], and His saying: "nor the offerings nor the garlands" is muhkam and not abrogated. So everyone who garlands the offering and intends ihram becomes a muhrim, and it is not permitted for him to exit ihram, by the evidence of this verse. These rulings are linked to one another, some of them abrogated and some not abrogated.

**The tenth issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord and good pleasure﴾. Most of the exegetes said about it: its meaning is that they seek bounty and profits in trade, and along with that they seek His good pleasure in their assumption and hope. It was said: among them were those who sought trade, and among them were those who through Hajj sought the good pleasure of Allah, even though they would not attain it. Among the Arabs there were some who believed in a reward after death and that they would be resurrected, and it is not improbable that they would receive some kind of lightening of the Fire. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this verse is an act of winning over the Arabs by Allah, may He be exalted, and an act of gentleness toward them, so that their souls would be at ease, people would mingle, they would come to the season and listen to the Qur'an, faith would enter their hearts, and the proof would stand before them as it had. This verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, and then Allah abrogated all of that after a year, in the year nine, when Abu Bakr performed Hajj and people were proclaimed the Surah "Bara'a" (al-Tawba).

**The eleventh issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you are released from ihram, then hunt﴾ is a command of permission, by the consensus of people, lifting what had been forbidden by ihram. Many scholars reported this, but it is not correct. Rather, the form "af'al" (imperative) that comes after a prohibition retains its original meaning of obligation. This is the view of al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib and others, because the factor requiring obligation is present, and the prior prohibition is not fit to be an obstacle. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. Here "uqtulu" is obligatory, because what is meant is jihad. Permission was understood there, and in similar cases such as His saying: "When the prayer is concluded, then disperse" [al-Jumu'a: 10] and "When they have purified themselves, then approach them" [al-Baqara: 222], it is understood from consideration of meaning and consensus, not from the form of the command. And Allah knows best.

**The twelfth issue:** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not let the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress﴾. "Yajrimannakum" means "do not let it drive you," according to Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, and this is the view of al-Kisa'i and Abu al-'Abbas. It is transitive to two objects, as one says: "jaramani kadha 'ala bughdika," meaning "it drove me to it." The poet said [[He is Abu Asma' ibn al-Durayba; it is also said he is 'Utayba ibn 'Afif. "Tu'ina" (with the ta' open) because he is addressing Karz al-'Uqayli and lamenting him. Before the verse: "O Karz, you have killed in Fars a hero who, when the warriors feared and recoiled..." Karz had struck Abu 'Uyayna, who is Hisn ibn Hudhayfa ibn Badr al-Fazari (al-Lisan).]]:

"Indeed I struck Abu 'Uyayna with a blow
That drove Fazara, after it, to be angry."

Al-Akhfash said: that is, "wa-la yuhiqqannakum" (nor let it bring you into dire straits). Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: the meaning of "la yajrimannakum" is: do not let the hatred of a people earn for you, so that you exceed the truth into falsehood and justice into injustice. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you," and this matter has already been discussed. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqara: 194], and it has already been fully discussed [[See vol. 2, p. 356 and what follows.]]. It is said: "Fulan is the jarima of his family," meaning their earner, so "al-jarima" and "al-jarim" mean the earner. "Ajrama fulan" means he acquired sin, and from this is the saying of the poet [[He is Abu Khurash al-Hudhali, describing an eagle, likening his horse to it. "Nahid" is the eaglet, and "al-nabq" is the highest place on a mountain.]]:

"A jarima, a fledgling eagle at the summit of a crag,
You see it gathering the bones it has collected like a crucifix."

Its meaning is "one who earns sustenance." *Al-ṣalīb* is the fat (*al-wadak*: the grease of meat). This is the root meaning of the pattern *j-r-m*. Ibn Fāris said: it is said *jaramma* and *ajrama*. *Lā jaram* is equivalent to your saying *lā budda* ("there is no escaping") and *lā maḥāla* ("without doubt"). Its origin is from *jaramma*, meaning "he earned." Someone said:

*Fazāra* earned, after this, that they would be angry.

Another said:

O you who complain of ʿUkl, and what they earned
from killing and disgrace among the tribes.

It is also said: *jarama yajrimu jarman*, meaning "he cut." Al-Rummānī, ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā, said: this is the original meaning. *Jaramma* in the sense of "he inclined toward something" is because he has cut himself off from other things. *Jaramma* in the sense of "he earned" is because he has committed himself to earning. *Jaramma* in the sense of "it is due" is because the right is cut off for its holder. Al-Khalīl said: ﴿Without doubt, for them is the Fire﴾ (16:62) means ﴿It is certainly due that for them is the punishment﴾. Al-Kisāʾī said: *jaramma* and *ajrama* are two dialectal forms with one meaning, namely "he earned."

Ibn Masʿūd read *yajrimannakum* with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ*. The meaning is likewise: "let it not earn for you." The Basrans do not recognize the *ḍamma*; they say only *jaramma*.

*Al-shanaʾān* is hatred. It is also read with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* and with a *sukūn* on it. It is said: *shanitu al-rajula ashnaʾuhu shanʾan*, *shanaʾatan*, *shanaʾānan*, and *shanʾānan* with a *jazm* on the *nūn*. All of these forms mean "when I hated him." The meaning is: let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you, earn for you (the license) to transgress. The intended sense is your hatred of a people, so the verbal noun is attributed to its object.

Ibn Zayd said: when the Muslims were barred from the House in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyya, some polytheists passed by them intending ʿumra. The Muslims said: "We will bar them as their companions barred us." Then this verse was revealed. The meaning is: do not transgress against these people, and do not bar them. ﴿Because they barred you﴾ (*an ṣaddūkum*), with a *fatḥa* on the hamza, is the object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*, the object indicating the reason), meaning "because they barred you."

Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read *in ṣaddūkum* with a *kasra* on the hamza. This is the choice of Abū ʿUbayd. It is also narrated from al-Aʿmash: *in yaṣuddūkum*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: *in* here is conditional, meaning "if such an act occurs in the future." The first reading is more suitable in meaning.

Al-Naḥḥās said: as for *in ṣaddūkum* with a *kasra* on *in*, the eminent scholars of grammar, hadith, and reasoning reject this reading for several reasons. Among them: the verse was revealed in the year of the Conquest, in the eighth year (AH), whereas the polytheists barred the Muslims in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyya, in the sixth year. So the barring occurred before the verse. If it is read with a *kasra*, it can only refer to what comes after it, as you say: "Do not give So-and-so anything if he fights you." This applies only to the future. If you read it with a *fatḥa*, it refers to the past. Therefore, on this basis, only *an ṣaddūkum* is permissible. Furthermore, even if this hadith were not authentic, the *fatḥa* would still be required, because His saying ﴿Do not violate the rites of God﴾ to the end of the verse indicates that Mecca was in their hands, and that they were not forbidden from this except when they were able to bar people from the Sacred House. Therefore, from this, the *fatḥa* on *an* is required, because it refers to what has passed.

(*An taʿtadū*) is in the accusative position, because it is the object, meaning: the hatred of a people must not drive you to transgression (*al-iʿtidāʾ*). Abū Ḥātim and Abū ʿUbayd rejected reading *shanʾān* with a *sukūn* on the *nūn*, because verbal nouns of this pattern come with a vowel. Others disagreed with them and said: this is not a verbal noun, but an active participle on the pattern of *kaslān* and *ghaḍbān*.

The thirteenth matter: His saying, ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾. Al-Akhfash said: this is a new sentence separated from the beginning of the speech. It is a command to all creation to cooperate in righteousness and piety, meaning: let some of you help one another, urge one another toward what God Almighty has commanded and act upon it, and refrain from what God has forbidden and abstain from it. This agrees with what has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The one who points to good is like the one who does it." It has also been said: "The one who points to evil is like the one who commits it."

Then it was said: *al-birr* and *al-taqwā* are two words with one meaning, and the repetition with different wording is for emphasis and intensification, since every act of righteousness is piety and every piety is righteousness. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: there is some looseness in this. The customary meaning of these two words is that *al-birr* covers what is obligatory and what is recommended, while *al-taqwā* is the observance of what is obligatory. If one is put in place of the other, that is by figurative usage.

Al-Māwardī said: God, glory be to Him, urged cooperation in righteousness and linked it with piety, because piety contains the pleasure of God Almighty, and righteousness contains the pleasure of people. Whoever combines the pleasure of God Almighty and the pleasure of people has completed his happiness and his blessing has become general.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandād said in his book *Aḥkām*: cooperation in righteousness and piety takes several forms. It is obligatory for the scholar to help people with his knowledge, teaching and giving legal rulings to them. The wealthy help with their wealth, and the brave with their courage in the way of God. The Muslims should be mutually supportive like one hand, [as in the text in Z: "teaching and giving legal rulings to them", and in it: "like one hand, their blood is equal and their protection is extended by the least of them, and they are a hand against others."] It is required to turn away from the transgressor, to withhold support from him, and to turn him back from what he is doing. Then He forbade, saying:

﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾. This is the ruling that follows from crimes (*al-jarāʾim*) [interpreted "sin" as in Ibn ʿAṭiyya], and from *al-ʿudwān*, which is the oppression of people. Then He commanded piety, and threatened with a general threat, saying: ﴿And fear God; indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾

There are twenty-seven [[As in the manuscripts; the correct number is twenty-seven.]] issues (masa'il) in it.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾. Its discussion has already passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 216 and what follows.]].

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the strangled animal﴾ (al-munkhaniqah) is the one that dies by strangulation, which is the stopping of breath, whether a human does this to it or it happens to it by a rope, between two pieces of wood, or the like. Qatadah mentioned that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to strangle sheep and other animals, and when they died they ate them. Ibn Abbas mentioned something similar.

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the beaten to death﴾ (al-mawqudhah). The mawqudhah is the animal that is struck or hit with a stone or a stick until it dies without dhakah (ritual slaughter), according to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. It is said of the verb: waqadhahu, yaqidhuhu, waqdhan, and it is waqidh. Al-waqdh is the severity of striking; and so-and-so is waqidh, meaning badly beaten. Qatadah said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to do that and eat it. Al-Dahhak said: They used to strike the cattle with wood for their idols until they killed them, and then ate them. From this is the animal killed by a pellet from a bow (al-maqtulah bi-qaws al-bunduq). Al-Farazdaq said:

*A she-camel that raises her forelegs to kick, kicking her young with her hind leg,*
*Milked with the thumb and fingers, [the teats] of the front udder of the young she-camels.* [[Al-shaghgharah: the she-camel that raises her forelegs to kick. Al-fatr: milking with the forefinger and middle finger, using the tip of the thumb as an aid. The two front teats of the udder are the qadimān, plural qawadim. Young she-camels are milked fatran because one cannot milk them by the usual method due to the shortness of the hind teats, since they are young.]]

In Sahih Muslim, from Adi ibn Hatim, he said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, I shoot game with the mi'radh [[Al-mi'radh: an arrow shot without feathers, and it mostly strikes with the side of its shaft rather than its point.]] and hit it." He said: "If you shoot with the mi'radh and it pierces [[Kharaqa al-sahm: the arrow went through the target; the meaning is that it passed through and made the blood flow, because it may kill by its side, which is not permitted.]], then eat it; but if it strikes it with its side, do not eat it." In another narration: "For it is then waqidh (beaten to death)."

Abu Umar said: The scholars, past and present, have differed regarding hunting with the bunduq (pellet), the stone, and the mi'radh. Whoever holds that it is waqidh does not permit it except for what is reached while its dhakah is still possible, according to what is narrated from Ibn Umar. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Thawri and al-Shafi'i. The people of Syria differed with them on this. Al-Awza'i said regarding the mi'radh: Eat it whether it pierced or did not pierce. Abu al-Darda', Fadalah ibn Ubayd, Abdullah ibn Umar and Makhul used to see no harm in it. Abu Umar said: This is how al-Awza'i related it from Abdullah ibn Umar, but what is known from Ibn Umar is what Malik related from Nafi' from him. The basis in this chapter, and what is acted upon, and the proof for whoever adopts it, is the hadith of Adi ibn Hatim, in which: "What it strikes with its side, do not eat, for it is only waqidh."

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the fallen﴾ (al-mutaraddiyah). The mutaraddiyah is the one that falls from a height to a lower place and dies, whether that was from a mountain or into a well or the like. It is a form from al-radda, which means destruction, whether it fell by itself or was thrown down by another. If the arrow strikes the game and it falls from a mountain to the ground, it is also forbidden, because it may have died from the impact and the fall, not from the arrow. From this is the hadith: "If you find it drowned in water, do not eat it, for you do not know whether the water killed it or your arrow." Muslim related it. The Jahiliyyah used to eat the fallen animal, and they did not regard as carrion except what died of illness or the like without a known cause. As for these causes, they regarded them as dhakah. So the Law restricted dhakah to a specific manner, as will be explained, and all of these remained carrion. This is all of the clear (muhkam) and agreed-upon matter. Likewise the gored animal (al-nativah) and the animal partly eaten by a predator, whose life ended through goring and eating.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the gored﴾ (al-nativah). Al-nativah is a form (fa'ilah) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ulah). It is the sheep gored by another or by something else, and it dies before it is slaughtered. Some people interpreted al-nativah in the sense of al-natihah (the one that gores), because two sheep may gore each other and both die. It was said: the text says nativah and not nativ; the rule for fa'il is that the feminine ending is not mentioned, as one says: kaff khadib (a dyed hand) and lihyah dahin (an oiled beard). But the ha' is mentioned here, because the ha' is only dropped from fa'ilah when it is an adjective for a named noun, as one says: shah nativ (a gored sheep) and imra'ah qatil (a slain woman). If you do not mention the noun, you add the ha', so you say: I saw the slain woman of so-and-so, and this is the gored one of the flock (hadhihi nativat al-ghanam). For if you did not mention the ha' and said: I saw the slain man of so-and-so, it would not be known whether it was a man or a woman. Abu Maysarah read: "wal-manthuhah."

**The sixth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what the predator has eaten﴾. It means everything that a beast with fangs and claws has preyed upon, such as the lion, the panther, the fox, the wolf, the hyena and the like; all of these are predators (siba'). It is said: Fulan sabaa Fulanan, meaning he bit him with his tooth; and sabahu, meaning he disparaged him and attacked him. There is an implied ellipsis in the speech, meaning: and what the predator ate of it, because what the predator has eaten has perished. Some Arabs restrict the name al-sab' to the lion. When a predator seized a sheep and it escaped from it, the Arabs would eat it; and likewise if it ate part of it. This was said by Qatadah and others. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywah read "al-sab'" with a sukun on the ba', which is a dialect of the people of Najd. Hassan said concerning Utbah ibn Abi Lahab:

*Whoever returns to his family this year, the one eaten by the predator will not be among those who return.* [[Trans. note: a line of verse, rendered as above.]]

Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-akilatu al-sab'" (and the eaten of the predator), and Abdullah ibn Abbas read: "wa-akilu al-sab'" (and the eaten of the predator).

**The seventh issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except what you have slaughtered﴾. It is in the accusative as a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), according to the majority of scholars and jurists. It refers to everything from the above-mentioned that still has life when its dhakah is reached, since dhakah acts upon it, because the exception ought to be directed to what precedes in the speech, and it is not to be made disconnected (munqati') except by a proof that must be accepted. Ibn Uyaynah, Shurayk and Jarir related from al-Rukayn ibn al-Rabi' from Abu Talhah al-Asadi, who said: I asked Ibn Abbas about a wolf that attacked a sheep and tore open its belly until its intestines spilled out, and I reached its dhakah and slaughtered it. He said: Eat it, but do not eat what has spilled out of its intestines. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: The Sunnah regarding the sheep is as Ibn Abbas described, for although its intestines came out, it is still alive, and the place of dhakah in it is intact. One only looks at the time of slaughter to see whether it is alive or dead, and one does not look at whether such an animal could survive. Likewise the sick animal. Ishaq said: Whoever opposes this has opposed the Sunnah of the majority of the Companions and the general body of scholars. [[In the source: "al-qasab" appears in a variant; the Arabic text has "al-qusb" for intestines.]] I say: This is also the view of Ibn Habib, reported from the companions of Malik, and it is the view of Ibn Wahb and the more well-known position in the school of al-Shafi'i. Al-Muzani said: I recall another view of al-Shafi'i, that it is not eaten if the predator or the fall has reached a point where no life remains in it. This is the view of the people of Madinah and the well-known opinion of Malik, and it is what Abd al-Wahhab mentioned in his Talqin, and it is reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, which Malik mentioned in his Muwatta'. This is also the view of Isma'il al-Qadi and the Baghdadi Malikis. On this view the exception is disconnected (munqati'), meaning: these things were forbidden to you, but what you have slaughtered is not what was forbidden.

Ibn al-Arabi said: Malik's opinion on these matters varies. It is related from him that only what was slaughtered with a valid dhakah may be eaten. What is in the Muwatta' is that if one slaughters it while its breath is still flowing and it is still moving, then let him eat it. This is the correct view from what he wrote with his own hand and read to people from every land throughout his life, so it takes precedence over the rare narrations. Our scholars have stated generally that the school's position is the permissibility of slaughtering a sick animal even if it is near death, as long as some life remains in it. I wonder what difference there is between a remnant of life from illness and a remnant of life from a predator, if the reasoning is consistent and the thinking is free from doubt! Abu Amr said: They have all agreed that for a sick animal whose life is not expected to return, its slaughter is a dhakah for it if life is present at the time of slaughter, which is known from it by the movement of its foreleg, hind leg, tail, or the like. And they agreed that if it has reached the state of death throes and does not move a foreleg or a hind leg, there is no dhakah for it. By analogy it should likewise be that the ruling for the fallen animal and what is mentioned with it in the verse is the same. [[From the editor's note in the source: the passage is followed by "and Allah knows best" in the manuscripts; see variants in j, z and k.]] And Allah knows best.

**The eighth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You have slaughtered﴾ (dhakkaytum). In the speech of the Arabs, dhakah means slaughter; so said Qutrub. Ibn Sidah said in al-Muhkam: The Arabs say: "The dhakah of the fetus is the dhakah of its mother." Ibn Atiyyah said: This is only a hadith. And dhakka the animal means he slaughtered it, and from this is the poet's saying:

*It is slaughtered by the spears.* [[Al-asal here: spears and arrows.]]

I say: The hadith to which he refers was related by al-Daraqutni from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, Abu Hurayrah, Ali and Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The dhakah of the fetus is the dhakah of its mother." The majority of the people of knowledge hold this, except what is reported from Abu Hanifah, that he said: If the fetus comes out from its mother's belly dead, it is not permissible to eat it, because the dhakah of one soul cannot be the dhakah of two souls. Ibn al-Mundhir said: In the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "The dhakah of the fetus is the dhakah of its mother," there is evidence that the fetus is other than the mother. Abu Hanifah says: If a pregnant slave woman is freed, her fetus is freed along with her, and this implies that its dhakah is the dhakah of its mother, because if it is permissible for the freeing of one to be the freeing of two, it is permissible for the dhakah of one to be the dhakah of two. Moreover, the report from the Prophet (ﷺ), what came from his Companions, and what most people hold, make the opinion of any individual unnecessary.

qā'il [. The scholars are unanimous that when a fetus is born alive, the slaughter of its mother is not a slaughter for it. They differ when the mother is slaughtered while a fetus is in her womb. Malik and all his companions said: its slaughter is the slaughter of its mother, if its form has been completed and its hair has grown. This applies whether it is born dead or born with a remnant of life in it. It is nonetheless recommended that it be slaughtered if it comes out moving; if it dies on its own before they reach it, it may be eaten.

Ibn al-Qasim said: I sacrificed a ewe, and when I slaughtered it, its young began to kick in its belly. I ordered them to leave it until it died in its belly. Then I ordered them to split open its belly, and it was taken out. I slaughtered it, blood flowed from it, and I told my family to roast it.

'Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: when the fetus has hair (ash'ara), its slaughter is the slaughter of its mother.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Among those who said "its slaughter is the slaughter of its mother" without mentioning whether it had hair or not were 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (raḍiya Allāhu 'anhu), Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq.

Al-Qadi Abu al-Walid al-Baji said: It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The slaughter of the fetus is the slaughter of its mother, whether it has hair or not." However, it is a weak hadith. The view of Malik is the most sound of the opinions, and it is the view on which the majority of jurists of the cities are agreed. And success is from Allah.

The ninth point: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you have slaughtered (dhakkaytum)﴾. Linguistically, dhakāh (slaughter, completion) originally means completion, and from it comes the completion of a tooth's growth. A mature horse that has reached its full age is called mudhakkan, the one that comes after the completion of its qurūḥ [[qaraḥa al-faras qurūḥan: when its teeth are complete; this happens only at about five years.]] by one year, and that is the completion of the attainment of strength. It is said: dhakka yudhakkī (to slaughter properly). The Arabs say: "The race of the mudhakkiyāt is a contest (ghilāb)." [[The meaning: the race of the horses that have reached full maturity is a contest in which each strives to outdo the other.]] Dhakā' means keenness of heart (ḥiddat al-qalb). The poet [[He is Zuhayr.]] said:

"It prefers him, when they strive for it, the completion of his tooth and his keenness (dhakā')."

Dhakā' means quickness of understanding. Its verb is dhakiya yadhkā dhakan. Al-dhakwah is that by which fire is kindled, and I kindled (adhkaytu) the war and the fire, meaning I lit them. Dhukā' is a name of the sun, because it kindles like fire, and the dawn is "the son of Dhukā'" because it comes from its light. So the meaning of "dhakkaytum" is: you attained its slaughter in full. Dhakkaytu al-dhabīḥah, udhakkīhā, is derived from tatyīb (perfuming); it is said: a fragrant smell (rā'iḥah dhakiyyah). An animal whose blood has been made to flow has thereby been made good (ṭuyyiba), because drying (al-tajfīf) quickly comes to it. In the hadith of Muhammad ibn 'Ali (raḍiya Allāhu 'anhumā): "The slaughter of the earth is its drying (yabsuhā)." He means its purification from impurity. So slaughter (al-dhakāh) in the sacrificed animal is for its purification and permissibility for eating; thus the drying of the earth after impurity was made a purification for it, and the permissibility of prayer upon it is in the position of slaughter for the slaughtered animal. This is the view of the people of Iraq.

Having established this, know that in the Law, slaughter is an expression for the flowing of blood and the cutting of the two jugular veins (awdāj) in the slaughtered animal, and for naḥr (throat-piercing) in the animal that is to be sacrificed by nahr, and for 'aqr (wounding) in the animal that cannot be reached, together with the intention of directing it to Allah and mentioning His name over it, as will be explained.

The tenth point: The scholars differ regarding what makes slaughter valid. The position of the majority of scholars is that anything that cuts the awdāj and makes the blood flow is one of the instruments of slaughter, except the tooth and the bone. On this, the reports are mutawātir, and the jurists of the cities have said so. As for the tooth and the nail, which are prohibited in slaughter, they are the ones that are not removed, because that would become strangling (khanq). Likewise Ibn 'Abbas said: "That is strangling." As for the removed ones, if they cut the awdāj, slaughter with them is permissible according to them. A group disliked the tooth, the nail and the bone in every case, whether removed or not, among them Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i), al-Hasan (al-Basri) and al-Layth ibn Sa'd. It has been related from al-Shafi'i too. Their proof is the apparent meaning of the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, we are going to meet the enemy tomorrow and we do not have knives (mudā)" — in one narration — "so shall we slaughter with flint (al-līṭ)?"

In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Nafi', from a man from the Ansar, from Mu'adh ibn Sa'd or Sa'd ibn Mu'adh: a slave girl of Ka'b ibn Malik was herding sheep for him at Sala' [[al-Sal': a crack in the mountain.]] and one of the sheep was injured. She caught up with it and slaughtered it with a stone. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about that, and he said: "There is no harm in it; eat it."

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud: "Shall we slaughter with the marwah [[al-marwah: a white, shining stone from which something like a knife is made.]] and a split of wood (shiqqat al-'aṣā)?" [[In j, w and k: shu'bah.]] He said: "Hasten and quicken (arin) [[arin: hasten. Al-Nawawi said: arin (with fatḥah on the hamzah, kasrah on the rā', and sukūn on the nūn) and it is narrated with sukūn on the rā' and kasrah on the nūn, and arinī (with sukūn on the rā' and an added yā'). Al-Khattabi said: arin is on the pattern of a'jil and has the same meaning; it is from briskness and lightness, meaning hasten its slaughter so that it does not die by strangulation.]] the blood, and mention the name of Allah over it, and eat. Not the tooth and the nail. I will tell you: as for the tooth, it is a bone, and as for the nail, it is the knife of the Abyssinians." The hadith was recorded by Muslim.

It has been related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he said: "Whatever is slaughtered with a reed-split (al-līṭah), a wood-splinter (al-shaṭīr) or a sharp stone (al-ẓirar) is lawful and slaughtered." Al-līṭah is a split of a cane, and slaughter and throat-cutting can be done with it. Al-shaṭīr is a split of a stick, and slaughter can be done with it because it has a fine edge. Al-ẓirar is a split of a stone with which slaughter is possible but nahr is not. The reverse is the shiẓāẓ [[al-shiẓāẓ: a stick with a sharpened end that is inserted into the two handles of the two saddlebags to join them when they are loaded on a camel.]] with which nahr is done, because it is like the tip of a spearhead, and slaughter cannot be done with it.

The eleventh point: Malik and a group said: slaughter is not valid except by cutting the throat (ḥulqūm) and the two jugulars (wadajān). Al-Shafi'i said: it is valid by cutting the throat and the windpipe (marī), and it does not require the two jugulars, because they are the passage of food and drink, and with them there is no life, and that is the purpose of death. Malik and others considered death in a manner by which the meat becomes good (yaṭīb) and the lawful meat is distinguished from the unlawful, which comes out by cutting the awdāj. This is the position of Abu Hanifah, and the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij indicates it in his saying: "what makes the blood flow." The Baghdadis related from Malik that he requires cutting four: the throat, the two jugulars and the windpipe. This is the view of Abu Thawr [[In k: Ibn Abi Thawr.]], but the well-known view is what has preceded, and it is the view of al-Layth. Then our companions differed regarding whether cutting one of the two jugulars and the throat constitutes slaughter or not, on two views.

The twelfth point: The scholars are agreed that if the slaughter is made in the throat below the glottis (al-ghalṣamah), slaughter is complete. They differ regarding what is done if it is slaughtered above it and passes it toward the body (jāzahā ilā al-badan [[In j, w and k: ḥāzahā.]]), whether that is slaughter or not, on two views. It has been related from Malik that it is not eaten. Likewise, if it is slaughtered from the back of the neck, and the cut is completed, the blood flows, and the throat and the two jugulars are cut, it is not eaten according to him. Al-Shafi'i said: it is eaten, because the purpose has been achieved. This is built on a principle: that although the purpose of slaughter is the flowing of blood, there is in it an aspect of worship (ta'abbud). The Prophet (ﷺ) slaughtered at the throat and sacrificed by nahr at the labbah [[al-labbah: the hollow above the chest, where camels are sacrificed by nahr.]], and he said: "Slaughter is only at the throat and the labbah," thereby clarifying its place and specifying its location. He also said, explaining its benefit: "What makes the blood flow and the name of Allah is mentioned over it, then eat." So when that is neglected, and it is not done with intention, condition or a specific attribute, its share of worship is removed, and so it is not eaten for that reason. And Allah knows best.

The thirteenth point: They differed regarding one who lifted his hand before completing the slaughter and then returned immediately and completed the slaughter. It was said: it suffices him. It was said: it does not suffice him. The first is more sound, because he wounded it and then slaughtered it afterward while its life was still fully present in it.

The fourteenth point: It is recommended that only one whose condition is pleasing should slaughter. Anyone who is capable of it and brings it in accordance with its sunnah, whether male or female, adult or non-adult, is permitted to slaughter if he is a Muslim or a People of the Book (kitābī). The slaughter of a Muslim is more excellent than the slaughter of a kitābī. A nusuk (sacrifice) is slaughtered only by a Muslim. If a kitābī slaughters a nusuk, there is disagreement about it, and it is not permitted according to the madhhab in the approved view, though Ashhab permitted it.

The fifteenth point: Whatever has become wild (istawḥasha) from the domestic animal (al-insī), its slaughter is not permitted except by what is permitted for the slaughter of the domestic animal, according to the view of Malik and his companions, Rabi'ah and al-Layth ibn Sa'd. Likewise the one that has fallen into a well: slaughter in it is only between the throat and the labbah, according to the sunnah of slaughter. Some people of Madina and others differed in these two issues. In this chapter is the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij, which has already been mentioned, and its completion after his saying "the Abyssinians' knife" is: he said: "We obtained plunder of camels and sheep, and a camel bolted from them. A man shot it with an arrow and held it back. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'These camels have wild ways (awābid) like the wild animals of the wilderness. So if any of them overcomes you, do with it this way'" — in one narration — "then eat it." Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said likewise. Al-Shafi'i said: The Prophet's (ﷺ) authorising this act is evidence that it is a slaughter. He argued with what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from Abu al-'Ushara, from his father, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, is slaughter only at the throat and the labbah?" He said: "If you had stabbed it in its thigh, it would have sufficed you." Yazid ibn Harun said: "It is a sound hadith," and it pleased Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he related it from Abu Dawud [[In z: Abu Dawud related it. But in al-Tahdhib: Abu Dawud said: Ahmad ibn Hanbal heard it from me.]], and he advised those of the ḥuffāẓ who came to him to write it down. Abu Dawud said: This applies only to the one that has fallen and the one that has become wild. Ibn Habib interpreted this hadith as referring to what has fallen into a pit, so that its slaughter cannot be reached except by stabbing it at a place other than the slaughter-place; this is a view he held alone against Malik and his companions. Abu 'Umar said: The view of al-Shafi'i is more apparent among the scholars, and that it is eaten by what the wild animal is eaten by, based on the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij. It is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. By analogy: since the wild animal, when it is subdued, is not lawful except by what makes the domestic animal lawful, because it has become subdued, so analogically, when a domestic animal has become wild or has come to be in the sense of the wild animal in its refusal, it should be lawful by what makes the wild animal lawful.

I say: Our scholars have answered the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij by saying: the Prophet's (ﷺ) "domination" over the animal applies only to its restraint (ḥabs), not to its slaughter (dhakāh). This is what the hadith requires and what its apparent meaning indicates, since he said, "so it restrained it," and did not say, "the arrow killed it." Also, the animal is controllable in most circumstances, so the rare case is not taken into account, and this applies only to hunting. The hadith explicitly states that the arrow restrained the animal, and once it became restrained it became controllable, so it may not be eaten except by slaughter or by cutting the throat (naḥr). And Allah knows best.

As for the hadith of Abu al-'Ushara, al-Tirmidhi said about it: "It is a gharib hadith (a narration transmitted by a single narrator at some point in its chain). We do not know it except through the hadith of Hammad ibn Salamah, and we do not know of any hadith from Abu al-'Ushara from his father other than this one. They differed about the name of Abu al-'Ushara: some said his name is Usama ibn Qihtim, and it is said his name is Yasar ibn Barz, and it is said Balz, and it is said his name is 'Utarid, and he was attributed to his grandfather." So this is an unknown chain (sanad majhul) with no proof in it. Even if its authenticity were granted, as Yazid ibn Harun said, it would still not be a proof, because its implication would be permitting slaughter in any body part absolutely, both in the controllable and the uncontrollable cases, and no one holds this for the controllable case.
