Then, as for the hair that extends beyond the chin and falls down from the beard, Sahnun related from Ibn al-Qasim: "I heard Malik being asked: 'Have you heard some of the scholars say that the beard is part of the face, so the water must flow over it?' He said: 'Yes, and running the fingers through it in ablution is not something people do,' and he criticized the one who did it." Ibn al-Qasim also mentioned from Malik: "The one performing ablution should move the outer part of his beard without inserting his hand into it." He said: "It is like the toes of the two feet."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam said: "Running the fingers through the beard is obligatory in ablution and in ghusl (full washing)." Abu ʿUmar said: "It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he ran his fingers through his beard during ablution, from several routes, all of which are weak." Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned that the jurists agreed that running the fingers through the beard is not obligatory in ablution, except for something related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, his saying: "What is the matter with a man who washes his beard before it grows, and when it grows he does not wash it, and what is the matter with the beardless man who washes his chin, while the bearded man does not wash it?" Al-Tahawi said: "Tayammum requires wiping the skin before the hair grows on the face; then this obligation falls away after it, according to all of them. Likewise, ablution." Abu ʿUmar said: "Whoever makes washing the whole beard obligatory regards it as part of the face, because the face is derived from confronting, and Allah has commanded washing the face with an unrestricted command that did not single out the bearded man from the beardless. Therefore, washing it is obligatory by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, because it is a substitute for the skin."

I say: Ibn al-'Arabi chose this opinion and said: "I also hold it, because it is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to wash his beard. Al-Tirmidhi and others transmitted it, so the ambiguous is clarified by the action." Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ishaq that whoever deliberately leaves off passing water through his beard must repeat (the ablution). Al-Tirmidhi related from Uthman ibn Affan that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pass his fingers through his beard. He said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith." Abu 'Umar said: Whoever does not make it obligatory to wash what hangs down from the beard holds that the original thing commanded to be washed is the skin, so what appears above the skin must be washed, and what hangs down from the beard has nothing beneath it that must be washed, so washing the beard is a substitute for it.

They also differed concerning washing what lies beyond the sideburn (al-'idhar) up to the ear. Ibn Wahb related from Malik that he said: "What is behind the temple (al-sudgh), which is behind the hair of the beard down to the chin, is not part of the face." Abu 'Umar said: I know of no jurist of the major cities who said what Ibn Wahb related from Malik. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: "The whiteness between the sideburn and the ear is part of the face, and washing it is obligatory." Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said something similar. It was also said that washing it is recommended. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The sound view, in my opinion, is that washing it is obligatory only for the beardless youth, not for the one whose sideburn has grown" [[ 'udhr al-ghulam: the growth of hair on his sideburns.]]. I say: This is also the view of al-Qadi 'Abd al-Wahhab, and the cause of the disagreement is whether confrontation (al-muwajahah) applies to it or not. And Allah knows best.

Because of this ambiguity they differed over whether the command to wash the face includes the inside of the nose and the mouth. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq and others held that this is obligatory in both ablution and bathing, except that Ahmad said: whoever omits sniffing water (al-istinshaq) in his ablution must repeat it, but whoever omits rinsing the mouth (al-madmadah) need not repeat. The majority of jurists said: both are sunnah in ablution and bathing, because the command applies only to the outward and not to the inward, and the Arabs call "face" only that which is faced directly. Moreover, Allah the Exalted did not mention them in His Book, the Muslims did not make them obligatory, and there is no consensus on them, while obligations are established only through these channels. This meaning has already been discussed in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 212 and what follows.]]. As for the eyes, all people agree that the inside of the eyes need not be washed, except what is related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, that he used to pour water into his eyes. Washing them is dropped only because of the harm and hardship involved in it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: For this reason, when 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar became blind, he used to wash his eyes, since he was no longer harmed by it.

Once this ruling about the face is established, it is necessary to wash a part of the head together with the face without a fixed limit, just as, on the view that the whole head must be wiped, it is necessary to wipe a part of the face along with it that is not fixed in measure. This rests on a principle of the foundations of jurisprudence: "What the obligatory cannot be completed without is itself obligatory." And Allah knows best.

Fourth: The majority of scholars hold that ablution requires intention (niyyah), based on his words (peace be upon him): "Actions are only by intentions." Al-Bukhari said: Thus faith, ablution, prayer, zakat, pilgrimage, fasting and the rulings are all included in it. Allah the Exalted said: "Say, each acts according to his manner (shakilatihi)" [[Al-Isra' 17:84]], meaning according to his intention. The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "But there is jihad and intention." Many Shafi'is said: there is no need for intention, and this is the view of the Hanafis. They said: intention is obligatory only in the obligations which are intended for their own sake and have not been made a cause for something else. As for what is a condition for the validity of another act, it is not obligatory by the mere arrival of the command, unless accompanied by an indication, and purification is a condition, for whoever is not required to pray is not obligated to perform the obligatory purification, like the menstruating woman and the woman in postnatal bleeding. Our scholars and some Shafi'is argued with the words of Allah the Exalted: "When you rise to prayer, wash your faces" [[Al-Ma'idah 5:6]]. Since the act of washing is obligatory, intention is a condition for the validity of the act, because the obligation comes from Allah the Exalted, so the doing of what Allah commanded should be obligatory. If we say that intention is not obligatory for him, then it is not obligatory for him to intend to perform what Allah commanded. It is known that one who bathes for cooling or for some other purpose has intended to fulfil the obligation. It is also sound in a hadith that ablution expiates sins; had it been valid without intention, it would not expiate. And Allah the Exalted said: "They were only commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion" [[Al-Bayyinah 98:5]].

Fifth: Ibn al-'Arabi said: Some of our scholars said: whoever goes out to the river with the intention of bathing is sufficient, even if his intention lapses on the way; but if he goes out to the bathhouse and his intention lapses along the way, the intention is nullified. Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: On this basis the shallow muftis built that the intention for prayer is to be derived from the two opinions, and they cited a text from one who does not distinguish between assumption and certainty, that it is permissible for intention to precede the takbir in it. Woe to Allah, and woe to the worlds, from a community that wished to be muftis and mujtahids, yet Allah did not grant them success nor guide them aright! Know, may Allah have mercy on you, that the intention in ablution is disputed among scholars as to whether it is obligatory, and Malik's own opinion on it varied. When it descends from the level of consensus, it is allowed to precede it in some places. But as for prayer, none of the imams differed about it, and it is a principal and intended act. How can the principal intended act, agreed upon, be made to bear on the subordinate disputed branch? Is this anything but extreme stupidity! As for fasting, the Law removed the hardship in it, since its beginning occurs at a time of heedlessness, by requiring the intention to precede it.

Sixth: His words, exalted is He: "and your hands up to the elbows" [[Al-Ma'idah 5:6]]. People differed over whether the elbows are included in the limit. Some said: yes, because what comes after "ila" (up to), when it is of the same kind as what precedes it, is included in it; this was said by Sibawayh and others, and this has been explained earlier in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 327.]]. It was also said: the elbows are not included in the washing. Both reports are transmitted from Malik: the second is that of Ashhab, and the first is the view on which most scholars rely, and it is the sound one, because of what al-Daraqutni related from Jabir, that the Prophet (ﷺ) when he performed ablution used to turn the water around his elbows. Some have said that "ila" here means "ma'a" (with), as in the saying: "al-dawd ila al-dawd ibil" (a few camels added to a few become many), meaning with the herd [[This proverb means: the little added to the little becomes much. The dawd is a herd of camels from three to nine; it was also said from three to ten, from three to fifteen, and other things were said.]]. This does not need to be resorted to, as we have explained in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 10.]]. Moreover, among the Arabs "yad" applies to the fingertips up to the shoulder, and likewise "rijl" applies to the toes up to the root of the thigh, so the elbow falls under the name "hand." If the meaning were "with the elbows," it would add nothing. Since He said "ila," He excluded the elbow's limit from washing, and the elbows remained to be washed up to the nail. This is a sound statement, consistent with the principles both linguistically and in meaning. Ibn al-'Arabi said: No one understood the crux of this question except Qadi Abu Muhammad, for he said: His words "ila al-marafiq" are a limit for what is left unwashed of the hands, not for what is washed; therefore the elbows are included in the washing.

I say: Since "yad" and "rijl" extend in language as we have mentioned, Abu Hurayrah used to carry the ablution up to his armpit and his leg, saying: "I heard my close friend (ﷺ) say: the adornment (al-hilyah) of the believer reaches as far as the ablution reaches." Qadi 'Iyad said: People are agreed against this, and that one should not exceed the limits of ablution, because of his words (peace be upon him): "Whoever exceeds has transgressed and wronged." Others said: this act was his own view, something he held alone, and he did not relate it from the Prophet (ﷺ); he derived it only from his words (peace be upon him): "You are the radiant ones, with white marks (al-gurr al-muhajjalun)" [[al-Gurr, plural of aghurr, from ghurrah, whiteness of the face: meaning the whiteness of their faces by the light of ablution on the Day of Resurrection.]], and from his words: "the adornment reaches," as mentioned.

Seventh: His words, exalted is He: "and wipe your heads" [[Al-Ma'idah 5:6]]. It was mentioned in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 238 and what follows.]] that the word "masḥ" (wiping) is a shared term. As for "ra's" (head), it refers to the whole that people know by necessity, and among it is the face. When Allah the Mighty and Majestic mentioned it in ablution and specified the face for washing, the rest of it remained for wiping; and if He had not mentioned washing, it would have been necessary to wipe all of it, including the part covered with hair of the head, what the eyes, nose and mouth are on. Malik indicated the obligation of wiping the head by what we have mentioned, for he was asked about one who leaves part of his head in ablution, and he said: "Do you see, if he leaves washing part of his face, would it suffice him?" By what we have mentioned, it is clarified that the ears are part of the head, and their ruling is the ruling of the head, contrary to al-Zuhri, who said: they are part of the face and are washed with it; and contrary to al-Sha'bi, who said: what faces forward of them is part of the face and their outer side is part of the head. This is also the view of al-Hasan and Ishaq, and Ibn Abi Hurayrah related it from al-Shafi'i. The explanation of their evidence will come. The head is called "ra's" for its height and for the growth of hair on it, as in "ra's al-jabal" (the peak of the mountain). We say that "ra's" is a name for a collection of members because of the poet's words:
"When they carry off my head, and most of me is in the head, and the rest of me is left at the meeting place, there."

Eighth: The scholars differed over the measure of wiping it, in eleven opinions: three from Abu Hanifa, two from al-Shafi'i, and six from our scholars. Of these the sound one is one only, which is the obligation of covering the whole, for the reason we have mentioned. The scholars agreed that whoever wipes his whole head has done well and fulfilled what is required of him. The "ba'" (in "bi-ru'usikum") is emphatic and superfluous, not for partiality; the meaning is "wipe your heads." It was said: its presence is fine, as its presence in tayammum in His words "then wipe your faces" [[Al-Nisa' 4:43]]; had its meaning been partiality, it would have conveyed it in that place, and this is decisive. It was also said: it was added to convey a wonderful meaning, which is that washing in language requires something washed with, while wiping in language does not require something wiped with. So had He said "wa-msahu ru'usakum" it would have sufficed to wipe with the hand passing over the head without anything; therefore the "ba'" was added to convey "something wiped with," which is water, as if He had said: "and wipe your heads with water." This is eloquent in the language in two ways: either by inversion (al-qalb), as Sibawayh cited:
"Like the feathers' edges of a dove on its cheeks, and you wiped its gums with powdered antimony" [[The verse is by Khufaf ibn Nadbah al-Sulami, describing the lips of a woman, likening them to the edges of a dove's feathers in thinness and delicacy, their roundness. He meant her gums tending to dark red, as if wiped with antimony, and 'asf al-ithmid is what is crushed of it.]]
The gums are what is wiped with the powder of antimony, so the wording is inverted. Or it is by sharing in the action and equality in its attribution, as in the words of the poet [[The verse is by al-Akhtal satirizing Jarir; al-qanafidh are hedgehogs, an animal proverbial for its night-wandering; al-haddaj is one who staggers in his walk. The meaning: the clan of Jarir are like hedgehogs in their night movement for theft and debauchery.]]:
"Like hedgehogs staggering, having reached Najran, or their shame has reached Hajar."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 6 (part 3 of 8):

This is what our scholars (ʿulamaʾunā) said regarding the meaning of the bāʾ (the letter "bi" in "bi-ruʾusikum"). Al-Shafiʿi said: The saying of Allah, the Exalted, "wamsahu bi-ruʾusikum" (and wipe over your heads) may mean wiping part of the head or wiping all of it. The Sunnah then showed that wiping part of it suffices, namely that the Prophet ﷺ wiped over his forelock (nāṣiyah). In another place he said: If it is said that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "fa-msahu bi-wujuhikum" (then wipe your faces) in tayammum (dry ablution), could part of the face suffice in it? It is said to him: Wiping the face in tayammum is a substitute for washing it, so one must wipe over the entire area that is washed. Wiping the head is the original act, so this is the difference between them. Our scholars answered the hadith by saying: Perhaps the Prophet ﷺ did that because of an excuse, especially since this action of his ﷺ took place during a journey, and travel is a place of excuses, of haste and of shortening, and of omitting many obligations because of hardships and dangers. Moreover, he did not confine himself to the forelock, but wiped over the turban (ʿimāmah). Muslim narrated it from the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shuʿbah. Had wiping the whole head not been obligatory, he would not have wiped over the turban. And Allah knows best.

The Ninth issue: The majority of scholars hold that a single wiping that is complete and comprehensive suffices. Al-Shafiʿi said: One wipes one's head three times. This is narrated from Anas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and ʿAtaʾ. Ibn Sirin used to wipe twice. Abu Dawud said: The authentic hadiths of Uthman all indicate that wiping the head is once, for they mentioned the washing (of the limbs) three times, and in them they said: "and he wiped his head," without mentioning a number.

The Tenth issue: They differed about where one should begin the wiping. Malik said: One begins with the front of the head, then takes both hands to the back of it, then returns them to the front, following the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Zayd, which Muslim narrated. This is also the view of al-Shafiʿi and Ibn Hanbal. Al-Hasan ibn Hayy used to say: One begins with the back of the head, following the hadith of al-Rubayyiʿ bint Muʿawwidh ibn ʿAfraʾ. This hadith is disputed in its wording, and it revolves around ʿAbdullah ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAqil, who is not considered a reliable memoriser (ḥāfiẓ) by them. Abu Dawud narrated it from the transmission of Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal from ʿAbdullah from al-Rubayyiʿ. Ibn ʿAjlan narrated from him, from al-Rubayyiʿ: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed ablution with us and wiped the whole head, from the hairline on every side, with the hair laid flat, not moving the hair from its position. This description was also narrated from Ibn Umar, and that he used to begin from the middle of his head. The most authentic thing in this chapter is the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Zayd. Everyone who permits wiping only part of the head means that part at the front of the head. It is narrated from Ibrahim and al-Shaʿbi that both of them said: Whatever part of your head you wipe suffices for you. Umar wiped only the top of the head (yāfūkh). There is consensus (ijmaʿ) on the recommendation of wiping with both hands together, and on the validity of wiping with one hand. They differed about one who wipes with a single finger until he covers what he considers sufficient of the head. The well-known view is that this suffices, and this is the opinion of Sufyan al-Thawri. Sufyan said: If he wipes his head with one finger, it suffices him. It was also said: This does not suffice, because it departs from the Sunnah of wiping and looks like play, unless it is due to the necessity of illness, in which case there should be no disagreement about its validity. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: Wiping the head does not suffice with fewer than three fingers. They differed about returning the hands over the hair of the head: is it an obligation (farḍ) or a Sunnah? Given the consensus that the first wiping is obligatory by the Qur'an, the majority hold that returning is a Sunnah. It was also said: it is obligatory.

The Eleventh issue: If a person performing ablution washes his head instead of wiping it, Ibn al-ʿArabi said: We know of no disagreement that this suffices him, except what Imam Fakhr al-Islam al-Shashi informed us in a lesson, from Abu al-ʿAbbas ibn al-Qassar of their companions, who said: It does not suffice him. This is a corrupt intrusion into the doctrine of the Dawudis, who follow the apparent meaning (of texts), which nullifies the Sharia, the very thing Allah censured in His saying: "They know only an outward appearance of the life of this world" (Rum 7), and His saying: "Or an outward appearance of speech?" (Ra'd 33). Otherwise, this one who washed has done what he was commanded and something more. If it is said: This is an addition that goes beyond the wording that is to be worshipped by, we say: It does not go beyond its meaning, which is conveying the act to the place. Likewise, if he wiped his head and then shaved it, he does not have to repeat the wiping.

The Twelfth issue: As for the two ears, they are part of the head according to Malik, Ahmad, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and others. Then they differed about renewing the water. Malik and Ahmad said: He takes fresh water for them, other than the water with which he wiped the head, following what Ibn Umar did. Al-Shafiʿi said the same regarding renewing the water, and said: They are a Sunnah in their own right, neither from the face nor from the head, since the scholars agree that one does not shave the hair upon them during the Hajj. The view of Abu Thawr on this is like that of al-Shafiʿi. Al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa said: They are wiped together with the head with one water. This view was narrated from a group of the early generations, from among the Companions and the Successors. Dawud said: If he wipes his ears, that is good; otherwise there is nothing upon him, since they are not mentioned in the Qur'an. It is said to him: The name "head" includes them, as we have explained. Authentic hadiths in the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, Abu Dawud and others have come that the Prophet ﷺ wiped their outer and inner surfaces, and inserted his fingers into their ear canals. The fact that they are not mentioned in the Book only indicates that they are not obligatory, like washing the face and hands, and the Sunnah of wiping them is established by the Sunnah. The people of knowledge dislike that one performing ablution leave off wiping his ears, and they regard him as having abandoned one of the Sunnahs of the Prophet ﷺ, but they do not require him to repeat the ablution, except Ishaq, who said: If he leaves off wiping his ears, it does not suffice him. Ahmad said: If he leaves them deliberately, I would like him to repeat. It is narrated from ʿAli ibn Ziyad, one of the companions of Malik, that he said: Whoever deliberately leaves a Sunnah of the ablution or the prayer must repeat. This view is weak according to the jurists, and its proponent has no predecessor and no share of sound reasoning. Had it been so, one would not know the obligatory obligation (farḍ) from other things. And Allah knows best.

Those who said: They (the ears) are from the face argued by what is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he used to say in his prostration: "My face prostrates to the One who created it, shaped it, and split open its hearing and sight." He attributed hearing to the face, so it is established that they have the ruling of the face. In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from the hadith of Uthman: "He washed their inner and outer surfaces once, then washed his feet," then said: "Where are those who ask about ablution? This is how I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ perform ablution." Those who said that the outer surface is washed with the face, and the inner surface is wiped with the head, argued that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded washing the face and commanded wiping the head; so whatever of the ears faces you must be washed, because it is part of the face, and whatever does not face you must be wiped, because it is part of the head. This is refuted by the reports that the Prophet ﷺ used to wipe the outer and inner surfaces of his ears, from the hadiths of Ali, Uthman, Ibn Abbas, al-Rubayyiʿ and others. Those who said: They are from the head argued by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of al-Sunabihi: "When he wipes his head, the sins come out of his head, until they come out from his ears." The hadith was narrated by Malik.

The Thirteenth issue: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your feet﴾. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisaʾi read "wa-arjulakum" with the accusative (naṣb). Al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated from Nafiʿ that he read "wa-arjulukum" with the nominative (rafʿ), which is the reading of al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash Sulayman. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Hamzah read "wa-arjulikum" with the genitive (khafḍ). According to these readings, the Companions and the Successors differed. Whoever reads with the accusative makes the governing verb "fa-ghsilu" (wash), and holds that the obligation for the feet is washing, not wiping. This is the view of the majority and the general body of scholars, and it is what is established from the action of the Prophet ﷺ, and what is required from his saying in more than one hadith. He saw some people performing ablution while their heels were visible, so he called out at the top of his voice: "Woe to the heels from the Fire! Perfect your ablution." Then Allah defined the limit of the two (feet) by saying: "up to the ankles" (kaʿbayn), just as He said regarding the hands "up to the elbows" (marāfiq), which indicates the obligation of washing them. And Allah knows best. Whoever reads with the genitive makes the governing element the preposition bāʾ (i.e., "wipe with" applied to the feet). Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The scholars agreed on the obligation of washing them, and I know of no one who rejected this except al-Tabari among the jurists of the Muslims, and the Rafidah (Shiʿa) among others. Al-Tabari relied on the reading with the genitive.

I say: It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Ablution is two washings and two wipings." It is also narrated that al-Hajjaj gave a sermon at al-Ahwaz and mentioned ablution, saying: "Wash your faces and your hands, wipe your heads and your feet, for there is nothing of the son of Adam closer to filth than his feet, so wash their undersides, their upper surfaces and their heels." Anas ibn Malik heard that and said: "Allah has spoken the truth and al-Hajjaj has lied. Allah, the Exalted, said: 'And wipe your heads and your feet.'" He (Anas) said: When he wiped his feet, he would moisten them. It is also narrated from Anas that he said: "The Qur'an was revealed with wiping, and the Sunnah with washing." Ikrimah used to wipe his feet and said: "There is no washing for the two feet; only wiping was revealed concerning them." ʿAmir al-Shaʿbi said: "Jibril descended with wiping. Do you not see that in tayammum, what is washed is wiped, and what is wiped is dropped?" Qatadah said: "Allah prescribed two washings and two wipings." Ibn Jarir al-Tabari held that their obligation is a choice between washing and wiping, and he treated the two readings like the two narrations.

The commentary of al-Nahhas says: Among the best of what has been said on this is that both wiping and washing are obligatory. Wiping is obligatory according to the reading of whoever reads with the genitive (*khafd*), and washing is obligatory according to the reading of whoever reads with the accusative (*nasb*). The two readings are like two verses.

Ibn Atiyya said: A group among those who read with the genitive held that wiping the feet is in fact washing.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: This is the correct view, for the word *mash* (wiping) is homonymous. It is used with the meaning of wiping and also with the meaning of washing. Al-Harawi said: Al-Azhari informed us, from Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Dari, from Abu Hatim, from Abu Zayd al-Ansari, who said: In the speech of the Arabs, *mash* can mean washing and can mean wiping. From this usage it is said of a man who performed ablution and washed his limbs: "He has *tamassaha*" (he has wiped himself). It is also said: "God wipes away what is upon you," meaning He washes you and purifies you from sins. Since it is established from the Arabs' usage that *mash* can mean washing, the view of those who say that the intended meaning of the genitive reading is washing is preferred, given the accusative reading, which admits of no ambiguity, and given the great number of established reports about washing, and the threats against neglecting to wash the feet, in sound reports too numerous to count, compiled by the imams.

Moreover, wiping of the head was placed among the parts to be washed to indicate the order, since the head is the object before the two feet. The sense is: "Wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and your feet up to the ankles, and wipe your heads." When the head was the object before the two feet, it was mentioned before them in the recitation, God knows best, not because the two feet share the same ruling as the head, given its precedence over them in the description of purification.

Asim ibn Kulayb narrated from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: Al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may God have mercy on them both, recited in front of Ali "*wa-arjulikum*" (with the genitive). Ali heard this, and he was judging between people, so he said: "*wa-arjulakum*" (with the accusative). This is a case of inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in speech.

Abu Ishaq narrated from al-Harith, from Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: Wash the feet up to the ankles.

It is similarly narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas that they recited "*wa-arjulakum*" with the accusative.

It has been said: The genitive in the feet came only as a restriction on wiping them, but only when they are wearing socks (*khuffan*). We received this restriction from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), since it is not authentically reported from him that he wiped his feet except while they were wearing socks. So he (ﷺ) explained by his action the state in which the foot is washed and the state in which it is wiped. This is good.

If it is said: The wiping over socks has been abrogated by the surah of al-Ma'ida. Ibn Abbas said this, and Abu Hurayra and Aisha rejected wiping, and Malik denied it in one report from him. The answer: When one person negates something and another affirms it, the negator has no proof. A large number of the Companions and others affirmed wiping over socks. Al-Hasan said: Seventy men from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) told me that they wiped over their socks. It is also established by a sound transmission from Hammam, who said: Jarir urinated, then performed ablution and wiped over his socks. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) urinated, then performed ablution and wiped over his socks. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: This hadith used to please them, because Jarir's acceptance of Islam came after the revelation of al-Ma'ida. This is an explicit text that refutes what they mentioned and what they argued from, namely the report of al-Waqidi from Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far from his father, that Jarir embraced Islam on the sixteenth of Ramadan, and that al-Ma'ida was revealed in Dhu al-Hijja on the Day of Arafat. This report is not established, due to its weakness. Only the verse "*Today I have perfected for you your religion*" was revealed on the Day of Arafat, as has been previously mentioned.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: I hold the hadith of Jarir about wiping over socks in high regard, because his Islam came after the revelation of al-Ma'ida. As for what is reported from Abu Hurayra and Aisha, may God be pleased with them both, it is not authentic. As for Aisha, she did not have knowledge of it, and for that reason she referred the questioner to Ali, may God be pleased with him, and sent him to him, saying: "Ask him, for he used to travel with the Messenger of God (ﷺ)," and the hadith continues.

As for Malik, what is reported from him of denial is a rejected report that is not authentic. The authentic position is what he said at his death to Ibn Nafi': "I used to take the purity (ablution) for myself personally, and I do not see that one who wipes is negligent regarding what is obligatory upon him." Ahmad ibn Hanbal interpreted in this way what Ibn Wahb narrated from him, that he said: "I do not wipe, neither at home nor on a journey." Ahmad said: Just as it is reported from Ibn Umar that he ordered them to wipe their socks, but he himself took them off and washed, and said: "Ablution has been made beloved to me." Something similar is reported from Abu Ayyub. Ahmad, may God be pleased with him, said: Whoever leaves wiping in the manner that Ibn Umar, Abu Ayyub and Malik left it, I do not denounce him for it, and we pray behind him, and we do not blame him, unless he abandons it and does not regard it as valid, as the people of innovation do, in which case one does not pray behind him. [And God knows best.]

It has been said: The phrase "*wa-arjulakum*" is conjoined to the wording (*lafz*) and not the meaning (*ma'na*). This too indicates washing, since what is considered is the meaning and not the wording. The genitive was used only by attraction (*jiwar*), as the Arabs do. This occurs in the Qur'an and elsewhere. God, the Exalted, said: "*Flames of fire and copper (nuhas) will be sent against you both*" (al-Rahman: 35), in the genitive, because *nuhas* means smoke, according to the reading of Ibn Kathir. [See vol. 17, p. 168.] He also said: "*Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, on a preserved tablet*" (al-Buruj: 21-22), in the genitive. [See vol. 19, p. 296.] Imru' al-Qays said:

*"An elder of men, wrapped in a striped cloak"* (kabir unasin fi bijadin muzammali)

[Verse opening: "Our father was among the twists of his locks..." The *bijad* is a striped cloak, and *muzammal* means one wrapped in garments. The meaning is that the rain-laden cloud covered him up to his head, like an old man in a striped cloak.]

He genitived *muzammal* by attraction, although *muzzammil* (the wrapped one) is a man and its case-ending (*i'rab*) is the nominative.

Zuhayr said:

*"Time has played with them and changed them after me, the sweeping winds of dust and rain"* (la'iba al-zamanu biha wa ghayyaraha ba'di sawafi al-mauri wal-qatri)

[*Sawafi* is the plural of *safiya*, a strong wind that sweeps up dust, i.e. blows it away; *al-mur* is dust.]

Abu Hatim said: The correct form was *al-qatr* in the nominative, but he put it in the genitive by attraction to *al-mur*, as the Arabs say: "This is the hole of a ruined lizard," where they genitive it, though it is in the nominative. This is the view of al-Akhfash and Abu Ubayda. Al-Nahhas rejected it and said: This view is a great error, because attraction is not a form in speech that may be used as a basis for analogy. It is an error, and its parallel is *al-iqwa'* (the faulty rhyme of a poem with a mismatched vowel).

I (al-Qurtubi) say: What decisively settles the matter, that the obligatory duty for the feet is washing, is what we have already mentioned, and what is established from his statement, upon him be blessings and peace: "Woe to the heels and the soles of the feet from the Fire." He warned us by mentioning the Fire [this is the wording in al-Jim, Z and K; it is the narration of Ahmad] for violating the intent of God, the Mighty and Majestic. It is well known that no one is punished with the Fire except one who abandons an obligation. It is also well known that wiping is not characterized by thoroughness, and there is no disagreement among those who hold wiping of the feet that this applies to their upper surfaces, not their soles. Thus this hadith demonstrates the invalidity of the view of those who hold wiping, since in their view there is no room for wiping the soles, and that is attained only by washing, not wiping.

There is another proof from consensus (*ijma'*, the scholarly agreement of the community): They have agreed that whoever washes his feet has fulfilled what is obligatory upon him, while they differed concerning whoever wipes his feet. Certainty lies in what they agreed upon, not in what they differed about.

The majority transmitted, from every generation to every generation, from their Prophet (ﷺ), that he used to wash his feet in his ablution once, twice, and three times until he cleaned them. This alone suffices as proof for washing, along with what we have explained. It has thus become clear and evident that the reading with the genitive, whose intended meaning is washing and not wiping, is as we have mentioned, and that the governing element of "*wa-arjulakum*" is His saying "*fa-righsilu*" (so wash). The Arabs sometimes conjoin one thing to another by a verb that applies to only one of them. You say: "I ate the bread and the milk," meaning "and I drank the milk." From this is the saying of the poet:

*"I fed her chaff and cool water"* (ʿalaftuha tibnan wama'an baridan)

[A well-known rajaz verse whose composer is unknown. The second half of the line is "until her eyes, with their tears streaming, were scattered." Some cited a first half for it and gave the verse as follows: "When I unsaddled the rider from her and she came to water, I fed her chaff and cool water."]

Another said:

*"And I saw your husband in the battle, girding on a sword and a spear"* (wa ra'aytu zawjaki fil-waghi mutaqqiliden sayfan wa rumha)

[As it stands in the original sources. In *Khizanat al-Adab* and *Kitab Sibawayh* it is: "Would that your husband had gone forth..." etc.]

Another said [the verse is by Labid, and *al-Lisan* reports it in the entries *jalla* and *tifl* as follows:]

*"He rose over the branches of the ayhaqan, and its gazelles and ostriches gave birth in the two Jalhatain"* (fa'ala furu'a al-ayhaqani wa atfalat bil-jalhatayni zibauha wa na'amuha)

[...the gazelles and ostriches gave birth...]

Another said:

*"A drinker of milk, dates and aqit"* (sharrabu albanin wa tamrin wa aqitin)

The estimate: "I fed her straw and gave her water." And "wearing a sword and carrying a spear." And "her gazelles gave birth on both sides of the valley, and her ostriches hatched their young." The ostrich does not give birth to young (ṭufl) but hatches eggs (yufrikh). "Aṭfalat" means that she had young. "Al-Jalhatān" means the two sides of the valley. "One who drinks milk and eats dates." So the words "and wipe your heads and your feet" are joined by conjunction to the washing, in line with the meaning, and what is intended is washing. And Allah knows best.

**The Fourteenth Issue:** As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿to the ankles﴾. Al-Bukhari narrated: Musa told me, he said: Wuhayb informed us, from Amr, that is Ibn Yahya, from his father, who said: I witnessed Amr ibn Abi Hasan ask Abdullah ibn Zayd about the ablution of the Prophet (ﷺ). He called for a tawr [a vessel from which one drinks, or a basin, a bowl, or a pot like a cooking pot, made of brass or stone] of water. He performed ablution for them as the Prophet (ﷺ) had performed ablution. He poured water from the tawr over his hand and washed his hands three times. Then he put his hand into the tawr, rinsed his mouth, sniffed water into his nose, and blew it out three handfuls. Then he put his hand in and washed his face three times. Then he put his hands in and washed his arms up to the elbows three times [in Sahih al-Bukhari: he washed his hands up to the elbows twice]. Then he put his hand in, wiped his head, moving them forward and backward once. Then he washed his feet up to the ankles. This hadith is evidence that the "bi" in His saying "wipe your heads" is extra, since he said "fa-masaha ra'sahu" (and he wiped his head) and did not say "bi-ra'sihi." It also shows that wiping the head is done once. This is clarified in the Sahih of Muslim, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd, in explanation of his saying "moving them forward and backward." He began with the front of his head, then took them back to his nape, then brought them back to the place where he had begun.

The scholars differed concerning "the ankles." The majority hold that they are the two protruding bones on either side of the foot. Al-Asma'i denied the view of people that the ankle is on the top of the foot. He stated this in (al-Sihah), and it is narrated from Ibn al-Qasim, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan also held it. Ibn Atiyya said: I do not know of anyone who made the limit of ablution at this point. However, Abd al-Wahhab in (al-Talqin) gave a statement on this matter which contains confusion and ambiguity. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: I know of no one who disagrees that the ankles are the two bones at the joint of the leg. Al-Tabari narrated from Yunus, from Ashhab, from Malik, who said: The two ankles to which washing is obligatory are the two bones attached to the leg, adjacent to the heel, and the ankle is not on the upper surface of the foot. [The addition is from Ibn Atiyya.] I say: This is the correct view linguistically and according to the Sunnah, for "al-ka'b" in the speech of the Arabs derives from elevation, and from it the Ka'bah is named. "Ka'abat al-mar'ah" means her breast became prominent. "Ka'b al-qanah" means its segment, and the segment between each two knots is a ka'b. It is also used figuratively for nobility and glory. From this is the hadith [this is the hadith of Qayla bint Makhrama al-Anbariyya, who emigrated to the Prophet (ﷺ) with Huraith ibn Hassan seeking companionship; see (al-Isabah fi Tamyiz al-Sahabah)]: "By Allah, your ankle will always be high." As for the Sunnah, there is his saying (ﷺ), narrated by Abu Dawud from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir: "By Allah, you must straighten your rows, or Allah will cause discord between your hearts." He said: So I saw a man attach his shoulder to his companion's shoulder, his knee to his companion's knee, and his ankle to his companion's ankle. The heel (al-'aqib) is the back of the foot beneath the tendon, and the tendon (al-'urquub) is the joint where the leg and foot meet. From this is the hadith: "Woe to the heels from the Fire," meaning if they are not washed, as he said: "Woe to the heels and the soles of the feet from the Fire."

**The Fifteenth Issue:** Ibn Wahb said, from Malik: No one is required to interlace (takhlil) the toes of their feet in ablution or in ghusl, and there is no good in harshness or excess. Ibn Wahb said: Interlacing the toes of both feet is recommended, and it is necessary to do so for the fingers of both hands. Ibn al-Qasim said, from Malik: Whoever does not interlace the toes of his feet, there is nothing upon him. Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn al-Qasim, from Malik, concerning one who performed ablution in a river and moved his feet: it is not sufficient for him until he washes them with his hands. Ibn al-Qasim said: If he is able to wash one foot with the other, it suffices him. I say: The correct view is that nothing is sufficient for them except washing what is between them, just as the rest of the foot is washed, since that is part of the foot, just as what is between the fingers is part of the hand. There is no consideration of spreading the fingers of the hands versus joining the toes of the feet, for a person is commanded to wash the whole foot just as he is commanded to wash the whole hand. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he performed ablution he would rub the toes of his feet with his little finger, and it is established that he (peace and blessings be upon him) washed his feet, and this implies generality. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him), in the last part of his life, used to rub the toes of his feet with his little finger or with some of his fingers, due to a hadith that Ibn Wahb narrated to him from Ibn Lahi'a and al-Layth ibn Sa'd, from Yazid ibn Amr al-Ghifari, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli [with a dammah on the letter ha' and the ba'], from al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad al-Qurashi, who said: I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performing ablution and interlacing between the toes of his feet with his little finger. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said to me: This is good, and I have never heard it until just now. Ibn Wahb said: I heard him later asked about interlacing the fingers in ablution, and he commanded it. Hudhayfa narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Interlace between your fingers, lest the Fire interlace them." This is an explicit threat against leaving off interlacing, so what we have said is established. And Allah is the Granter of success.

**The Sixteenth Issue:** The wording of the verse requires continuity (muwalat) between the parts of the body, which means the one performing ablution follows each act with the next until the end, without delay between its parts and without separating them by an act not part of it. The scholars differed on this. Ibn Abi Salama and Ibn Wahb said: This is one of the obligations of ablution, whether forgotten or deliberate, so whoever separates the parts of his ablution, deliberately or forgetfully, his ablution is not valid. Ibn Abd al-Hakam said: It suffices him, whether forgetful or deliberate. Malik said in (al-Mudawwanah) and in the book of Muhammad: Continuity is not obligatory, and al-Shafi'i held the same. Malik and Ibn al-Qasim said: If he separates them deliberately, it does not suffice him, but it suffices him if forgetful. Malik, in the narration of Ibn Habib, said: It suffices him in the washed parts but not in the wiped parts. These are five opinions built upon two principles. The first: Allah, Exalted is He, gave an absolute command, "continue or separate," and the intention is only that washing occur in all the parts when standing up to pray. The second: They are acts of worship with different pillars, so continuity is required in them as in prayer, and this is more sound. And Allah knows best.

**The Seventeenth Issue:** The wording of the verse also includes the sequence (tartib), and this has been differed over. Al-Abhari said: Sequence is a sunnah. The apparent position of the school is that reversing the order for the forgetful is valid. Concerning the deliberate, it was said: It is valid, and he sequences in the future. Abu Bakr al-Qadi and others said: It is not valid, because he is playing around. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and all his companions, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr also said it. Abu Mus'ab, a companion of Malik, held it and mentioned it in his abridgment, and he reported it from the people of Medina, with Malik among them, that whoever puts his hands before his face in ablution and does not perform ablution in the order of the verse must repeat the prayer he prayed with that ablution. Malik, in most of his narrations and the most famous of them, held that "wa" (and) does not require succession and does not indicate order. His companions said the same, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Muzani, and Dawud ibn Ali. Ilkiya al-Tabari said: The apparent meaning of His saying, "wash your faces and your hands," indicates sufficiency whether one separates, joins, or follows in order, according to the sound view of al-Shafi'i's school, and it is the view of the majority of scholars. [In the manuscript z: "of our scholars."] Abu Umar [Ibn Abd al-Barr] said: However, Malik recommends that he renew the ablution in succession for the prayer he will perform, and he does not regard this as obligatory for him. This is the summary of his school. Ali ibn Ziyad narrated from Malik, who said: Whoever washed his forearms, then his face, then remembered on the spot, should repeat washing the forearms, and if he did not remember until he had prayed, he must repeat both the ablution and the prayer. Ali said: Then he said afterward: He does not repeat the prayer, but he repeats the ablution for what he will undertake. The cause of the disagreement is what some said: "fa" (then) requires sequence in His saying "fa-ghsilu" (so wash), since it is a response to a condition and links the conditioned to the condition, so it requires sequence in everything. It was answered: It only requires beginning with the face, since it is the response and consequence of the condition. It would require sequence in all parts only if the response of the condition were one meaning. When the response consists of several clauses, you need not care with which you begin, since what is sought is achieving them all. It was said: Sequence comes only from the "wa." This is not so, for you say: "Zayd and 'Amr fought (taqatala)," and "Bakr and Khalid quarreled (takhasama)." Its appearance in the mufa'alah form removes it from sequence. The correct position is that sequence is derived from four aspects. The first: that one begins with what Allah began with, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said when he performed Hajj: "We begin with what Allah began with." The second: from the consensus of the early generations, for they used to observe sequence. The third: from the comparison of ablution to prayer. The fourth: from the constant practice of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in this. Those who permitted this argued by consensus that there is no sequence in washing the parts in the state of major impurity (janabah), and likewise washing the parts of minor ablution, because the meaning in that is washing, not the order of beginning. It was narrated from Ali that he said: "I do not mind, once I have completed my ablution, with which of my limbs I began." And from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud he said: "There is no harm in beginning with your feet before your hands." Al-Daraqutni said: This is a mursal report and is not established, and the more correct view is that sequence is obligatory. And Allah knows best.

**The Eighteenth Issue:** If occupation with ablution causes the time of prayer to pass, then according to most scholars one does not perform tayammum. Malik permits tayammum in such a case, because tayammum was originally legislated to preserve the time of prayer, and were it not for this, it would be obligatory to delay the prayer until water is found. The majority argued with His saying, "if you find no water, then perform tayammum." This person does find water, so the condition for the validity of tayammum is absent, and therefore he does not perform tayammum.

**Nineteenth:** Some scholars have used this verse to argue that removing impurity (*najasah*) is not obligatory, because He said, ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾, and did not mention *istinja'* (cleansing after relieving oneself), but mentioned *wudu'* (ablution). If removing it were obligatory, it would have been the first thing mentioned. This is the view of the companions of Abu Hanifa, and it is a narration from Ashhab from Malik. Ibn Wahb said, quoting Malik, that removing it is obligatory whether one remembers it or forgets it, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Ibn al-Qasim said that removing it is obligatory when one remembers it and drops away when one forgets it. Abu Hanifa said that removing impurity is obligatory when it exceeds the size of the al-Baghli dirham [[Al-Damiri mentioned a type of currency called the al-Baghliyyah, and said: the head of a mule (baghl) struck it for Umar ibn al-Khattab with a Kisrawi die.]], meaning the large one that is in the shape of the mithqal, by analogy with the mouth of the usual excretory passage, which is excused. The correct view is the narration of Ibn Wahb, because the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the two people in the graves: (They are being punished, and they are not being punished for a great matter. As for one of them, he used to go about spreading slander; as for the other, he did not guard himself against his urine.) And one is only punished for abandoning an obligation. There is no proof in the apparent wording of the Qur'an, because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, only explained from the verse of ablution the manner of ablution specifically, and He did not address removing impurity or anything else.

**Twentieth:** The verse also indicates wiping over the leather socks (*masḥ 'ala al-khuffayn*), as we have explained. Malik has three narrations on this matter. Denying it absolutely, as the Kharijites say; this narration is rejected and is not sound. This has already been mentioned.

**Second:** One wipes while traveling but not while resident, because most of the reports about wiping are concerning travel. The hadith of the refuse heap indicates the permissibility of wiping while resident. Muslim transmitted it from the hadith of Hudhayfah, who said: I saw myself and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ walking together, and he came to a refuse heap [[The sabatah is the place where dust and what is swept from houses is thrown. Its attribution to the people is an attribution of specification, not of ownership, since it was unclaimed open land.]] of a people behind a wall, and he stood as one of you stands and urinated. I withdrew from him, but he gestured to me, so I came and stood at his heel until he finished. In another narration he added: Then he performed ablution and wiped over his leather socks. Similar to it is the hadith of Shurayh ibn Hani', who said: I came to Aisha asking her about wiping over the leather socks, and she said: Go to the son of Abu Talib and ask him, for he used to travel with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So we asked him, and he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made it three days and their nights for the traveler, and one day and one night for the resident. This is the third narration: one wipes whether resident or traveling, and its mention has already preceded.

**The twenty-first issue:** According to Malik, the traveller wipes over the leather socks (khuff) without any time limit. This is also the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd. Ibn Wahb said: I heard Malik say, "The people of our city have no time limit for this." Abu Dawud related, from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Imara, that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I wipe over the two leather socks?" He said: "Yes." He said: "For a day?" He said: "For a day." He said: "And two days?" He said: "And two days." He said: "And three [days]?" [The addition is from Abu Dawud.] He said: "Yes, and as long as you wish." In another narration: "Yes, and as long as it seems fit to you." Abu Dawud said: its chain has been disputed, and it is not strong. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifa) and al-Tabari said: the resident wipes for one day and night, and the traveller for three days, based on the hadith of Shurayh and what is similar to it. It is related from Malik in his letter to Harun or to one of the caliphs, but his companions rejected it.

**The twenty-second issue:** Wiping is, according to all of them, for one who put on his two socks in a state of ritual purity (wudu'). This is based on the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, that he said: "I was with the Prophet ﷺ one night on a journey," – the hadith – in which: "I bent down to take off his two socks, and he said: 'Leave them, for I put them on in a state of purity,' and he wiped over them." Asbagh held that this purity is the purity of tayammum (dry ablution), and this is based on his view that tayammum removes ritual impurity (hadath). Dawud deviated and said: the meaning of "purity" here is only purity from impurity (najasah). So if his feet are clean of impurity, wiping over the two socks is permissible. The reason for the disagreement is the shared use of the term "purity" (tahara).

**The twenty-third issue:** According to Malik, wiping over the sock is permissible even if it has a slight tear. Ibn Khuwiz Mandad said: its meaning is that the tear does not prevent benefiting from it or wearing it, and that such a sock may be walked in. Al-Layth, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i and al-Tabari agreed with this view of Malik. It is related from al-Thawri and al-Tabari that they permitted wiping over a torn sock entirely. Al-Awza'i said: one wipes over the sock and over what appears of the foot, and this is the view of al-Tabari. Abu Hanifa said: if what appears of the foot is less than three fingers, one wipes; but one does not wipe if three [fingers] are exposed. This is a limit that requires a textual basis (tawqif). It is known that the socks of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and of the other Successors were not free from a slight tear, and that this is overlooked by the majority of them. It is related from al-Shafi'i that if the tear is at the front of the foot, wiping over it is not permissible. Al-Hasan ibn Hayy said: one wipes over the sock if what appears of it is covered by the sock-sleeve (jawrab); but if any part of the foot appears, one does not wipe. Abu Umar said: this is according to his view on wiping over two thick socks (jawrabayn), and this is the view of al-Thawri, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad.

**The twenty-fourth issue:** Wiping over two socks (jawrab) is not permissible according to Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i unless they are leather-soled (mujallad). This is one of Malik's two views. He also has another view, that wiping over two socks is not permissible even if they are leather-soled. In Abu Dawud's book, from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed wudu' and wiped over the two socks and the sandals (na'layn). Abu Dawud said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi would not narrate this hadith, because what is known from al-Mughira is that the Prophet ﷺ wiped over the two leather socks. This hadith is also related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari from the Prophet ﷺ, but it is neither strong nor connected (muttasil). Abu Dawud said: Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Mas'ud [In the original: Ibn Mas'ud; the correction is from Abu Dawud's book], al-Bara' ibn Azib, Anas ibn Malik, Abu Umama, Sahl ibn Sa'd and Amr ibn Hurayth also wiped over the socks, and this is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them all.

I say: as for wiping over sandals (na'layn), Abu Muhammad al-Darimi related in his Musnad: Abu Nu'aym told us, Yunus informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Abd Khayr [his name was "Abd Shar," which the Prophet ﷺ changed (al-Isabah)], who said: "I saw Ali perform wudu' and wipe over his sandals, and he made the wiping wide. Then he said: 'Had I not seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ do as you have seen me do, I would have thought that the soles of the feet are more deserving of wiping than their upper surfaces.'" Abu Muhammad al-Darimi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this hadith is abrogated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: "wipe your heads and your feet to the ankles." I say: Ali's statement, "I would have thought that the soles of the feet are more deserving of wiping than their upper surfaces," is similar to what he said concerning wiping over the two socks. Abu Dawud recorded it from him, saying: "If religion were by opinion, the sole of the sock would be more deserving of wiping than its top, but I have seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wipe over the top of his two socks." Malik and al-Shafi'i said, concerning one who wipes the tops of his socks without their soles, that this suffices him; but Malik said: whoever does this must repeat [the prayer] within the time. Whoever wipes the soles of the socks without their tops, it does not suffice him, and he must repeat [the prayer] within the time and after it. All the companions of Malik said likewise, except one view related from Ashhab, that he said: the soles and tops of the socks are equal, and whoever wipes their soles without their tops must repeat only within the time. It is related from al-Shafi'i that he said wiping the soles without the tops suffices him, but the well-known position of his school is that whoever wipes the soles and limits himself to them does not suffice, and he is not a wiper. Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: one wipes the two tops of the socks without their soles; this is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq and a group. The preferred view according to Malik, al-Shafi'i and their followers is wiping both the upper and lower surfaces. This is also the view of Ibn Umar and Ibn Shihab, based on what Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni related from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, who said: "I performed wudu' for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the expedition of Tabuk, and he wiped the top and bottom of the sock." Abu Dawud said: it is related that Thawr did not hear this hadith from Raja' ibn Haywa.

**The twenty-fifth issue:** The scholars differed concerning one who removed his socks after having wiped over them, with three views. The first: he washes his feet in that same place, and if he delays, he begins wudu' again. This is said by Malik and al-Layth, and likewise al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and their companions. It is related from al-Awza'i and al-Nakha'i, but they did not mention "in that same place." The second: he begins wudu' again. This is said by al-Hasan ibn Hayy, and it is related from al-Awza'i and al-Nakha'i. The third: he has nothing to do, and he prays as he is. This is said by Ibn Abi Layla and al-Hasan al-Basri, and it is a narration from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, may Allah be pleased with them all.

**The twenty-sixth issue:** The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves﴾. The meaning of janabah has already been discussed in "al-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, p. 204]. "Fa-tahharu" [purify yourselves] is a command to perform ghusl (full washing) with water. For this reason, Umar and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, held that one in janabah never performs tayammum, but leaves the prayer until he finds water. Most people said: rather, this phrase refers to one who finds water. The janabah state is mentioned again later in the rulings for one who lacks water, with the words: "or you have touched women," and "touching" (mulamasah) here means intercourse. It is authentically reported from Amr ibn Mas'ud [sic; the reference is to Ibn Mas'ud] that they both returned to what the people held, and that the one in janabah performs tayammum. The hadith of Imran ibn Husayn is an explicit text on this, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a man standing apart who had not prayed with the people, and he said: "O so-and-so, what prevented you from praying with the people?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have become junub and there is no water." He said: "Upon you is the clean earth (sa'id), for it suffices you." Related by al-Bukhari.

**The twenty-seventh issue:** The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you are sick, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself (al-ghaʼit)﴾. This was discussed fully in "al-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, p. 212]. Here we add a juristic (usuli) question that we omitted there, namely the specification of a general term by what is customary and predominant. The word "al-ghaʼit" is a metaphor for the impurities coming out of the two passages, as we explained in "al-Nisa'." It is therefore general, but most of our scholars restricted it to the usual impurities that come out in the usual manner. So if something unusual comes out, such as pebbles or worms, or if the usual comes out in the manner of incontinence or illness, none of that nullifies wudu'. They resorted to the wording because whenever a word becomes firmly established for its referent by a predominant usage, that predominant meaning comes first to the listener's understanding upon hearing the word unqualified, and other things the word was originally applied to become remote from the mind, so they are no longer understood by it. The situation is like that of the word "dabbah" (animal): when it is used without qualification, the mind goes first to four-legged animals, and an ant does not come to the hearer's mind, so it is not intended or evidently understood by that word. The opponent says: it does not follow from the priority of the predominant that the rare is not intended, for the word's coverage of both is equal by its original imposition, and this indicates that the speaker intends both. The first view is more correct, and its completion is in the books of usul.

**The twenty-eighth issue:** The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿or you have touched women﴾. Ubayda related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "kissing is part of touching, and everything short of intercourse is touching." Likewise Ibn Umar said, and Muhammad ibn Yazid chose this view, saying: "because He mentioned in the beginning of the verse what is obligatory upon one who has had intercourse, in His words: 'and if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves.'" Abdullah ibn Abbas said: "lams, mass and ghashy" mean intercourse, but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, uses euphemism. Mujahid, concerning the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72], said: "when they mention marriage, they refer to it indirectly." The discussion of this topic has been fully covered in "al-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, pp. 223, 228ff.], and praise be to Allah.

**The twenty-ninth issue:** The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿but you find no water﴾. It has already been stated in "al-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, pp. 223, 228ff.] that its absence applies to one who is healthy and present, such as one who is imprisoned or tied up. Concerning such a person, who finds neither water nor earth and fears the time will run out, the jurists differed on the ruling in four views. The first: Ibn Khuwiz Mandad said: the sound view according to the school of Malik is that he does not pray and has nothing to make up. He said: the people of Madina related it from Malik, and he said: this is the sound view of the school. Ibn al-Qasim said: he prays and repeats (the prayer). This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Ashhab said: he prays and does not repeat. Asbagh said: he neither prays nor makes up [the prayer].

And Abu Hanifa said the same (ﷺ no). [[As in the manuscripts. This is probably a discredited opinion of Abu Hanifa, since he does not hold that no prayer must be made up. He only said that the prayer should be delayed. The preponderant view in his school is the view of his two companions, that one who lacks both water and dust prays a formal prayer (salat sawriyya) and repeats it when he is able.]] Abu Umar Ibn Abd al-Barr said: I do not know how Ibn Khuwayz Mandad came to make the sound position in the school what he mentioned, when the majority of the early scholars, the common body of jurists, and a group of the Maliki scholars hold otherwise. I think he followed the apparent meaning of the hadith of Malik in his words: "and they were not with water," and it does not mention that they prayed. This is no proof. Hisham ibn Urwa reported from his father, from Aisha, concerning this hadith, that they prayed without ablution and did not mention repetition. A group of jurists took this view. Abu Thawr said: this is the analogical position (al-qiyas).

I say: al-Muzani relied, in what Ilkiya al-Tabari reported, on the story of the necklace from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, when it was lost, and that the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) whom he sent to search for the necklace prayed without tayammum or wudu', and they informed him of this. Then the verse of tayammum was revealed, and he did not object to their doing it without wudu' or tayammum. Since tayammum was not yet prescribed, they prayed without any purity at all. From this al-Muzani said: and no repetition is required. This is a clear text on the permissibility of prayer without purity absolutely, when reaching water or dust is impossible.

Abu Umar said: it should not be taken to refer to one who is unconscious, because the unconscious person is overcome in his mind, whereas this person retained his mind. Ibn al-Qasim and the rest of the scholars said: prayer is obligatory for him as long as his mind is intact. When the obstacle is removed, he performs wudu' or tayammum and prays. There are two reports from al-Shafi'i. The well-known one from him is that he prays as he is and then repeats. Al-Muzani said: if he is confined and cannot reach clean dust, he prays and repeats. This is also the view of Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, al-Thawri and al-Tabari. Zufar ibn al-Hudhayl said: one confined in a settled area does not pray even if he finds clean dust. This follows from his own principle, for he does not permit tayammum in a settled area, as has already been mentioned.

Abu Umar said: whoever says he prays as he is and repeats when he is able to purify himself has taken precaution regarding the prayer without purity. They said: the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Allah does not accept a prayer without purity," applies to one who is able to obtain purity. As for one who is not able, it is not so, because the time is an obligation and he is able to pray within the time as he is, and then repeat. Thus he has taken precaution regarding both the time and the purity together.

Those who said he does not pray relied on the apparent meaning of this hadith. This is the view of Malik, Ibn Nafi' and Asbagh. They said: whoever lacks both water and dust does not pray, and if the time of prayer passes he does not make it up, because the non-acceptance of the prayer for lack of its conditions shows that he is not addressed by it in the state where its conditions are lacking, so nothing is established on his responsibility, and therefore he does not make it up. This was said by others than Abu Umar. On this view, purity is a condition of obligation (shart al-wujub).

The thirtieth matter concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿then make tayammum with clean earth﴾. The disagreement about the earth (al-sa'id) has already passed in "al-Nisa'," and the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn clearly supports what Malik says. For if "earth" (al-sa'id) meant dust, the Prophet, peace be upon him, would have said to the man: "Take the dust, for it will suffice you." But when he said: "Take the earth (al-sa'id)," he referred him to the surface of the ground. And Allah knows best. [[See vol. 5, pp. 236, 238 onward.]] ﴿Then wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾: the discussion of this has already passed in "al-Nisa'," so reflect on it there.

The thirty-first matter: when our discussion of the verses reaches this point, know that the scholars have spoken about the virtue of wudu' and purity, and this is the conclusion of the chapter. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Purity (al-tuhur) [[Al-tuhur, with a damma, means purification, and with a fatha means water, like wudu' and wudu'. Sibawayh said: al-tahur with a fatha is used both for water and for the verbal noun, so the hadith may be read with fatha or damma. (Al-Nihaya of Ibn al-Athir.)]] is half of faith." Muslim reported it from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, and its discussion has already passed in "al-Baqara." Ibn al-Arabi said: wudu' is a foundation of religion and of the purity of Muslims, and especially for this community among all nations. It has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed wudu' and said: "This is my wudu' and the wudu' of the prophets before me and the wudu' of Abraham." But this is not authentic. Another said: this is not in conflict with his saying, peace be upon him: "You have a mark (sima) that others do not have," for they used to perform wudu'. What was specially granted to this community is the radiance (al-gurra) and the white marks (al-tahjil), not wudu' itself. These are a favour from Allah, the Exalted, by which He singled out this community, as an honour for it and for its Prophet (ﷺ), like its other virtues over the other nations, just as He preferred its Prophet (ﷺ) with the praised station (al-maqam al-mahmud) and other things over the other prophets. And Allah knows best.

Abu Umar [[In the (ج/و) manuscript: Ibn Umar, which is a scribal error.]] said: it is possible that the prophets performed wudu' and thereby gained the radiance and the white marks, while their followers did not perform wudu', as has come from Moses, peace be upon him, who said: "My Lord, I find a community all of whose members are like the prophets, so make them my community." He was told: "That is the community of Muhammad." This is in a long hadith. Salim ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he heard a man relate that he saw in a dream that people had been gathered for reckoning, then the prophets were called, each prophet with his community, and that he saw each prophet with two lights walking between them, and for whoever followed him from his community one light by which he walked, until Muhammad (ﷺ) was called. Then the hair of his head and face was all light, which everyone who looked at him could see, and for whoever followed him from his community there were two lights like the lights of the prophets. Ka'b said to him, while he did not realise it was a dream: "Who told you this hadith, and what is your knowledge of it?" He informed him that it was a dream. Then Ka'b adjured him by Allah, besides whom there is no god: "Did you truly see what you describe in your dream?" He said: "Yes, by Allah, I saw that." Ka'b said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul" (or he said: "By Him who sent Muhammad with the truth") "this is truly the description of Ahmad and his community, and the description of the prophets in the Book of Allah. What you describe is in the Torah." He reported it in the book "al-Tamhid." Abu Umar said: it has been said that all the other nations used to perform wudu', and Allah knows best, but I do not know this from any sound route.

Muslim reported from Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Muslim servant, or the believer [[This is the narrator's doubt, and likewise his words: "with the water or with the last drop of water." (al-Nawawi)]], performs wudu' and washes his face, every sin that his eyes looked upon goes out from his face with the water or with the last drop of water. When he washes his hands, every sin his hands seized goes out from his hands with the water or with the last drop of water. When he washes his feet, every sin his feet walked to goes out with the water or with the last drop of the water, until he comes out pure from sins." The hadith of Malik from Abd Allah al-Sunabihi is complete [[The hadith is reported by Malik in the Muwatta'.]]. The correct name is Abu Abd Allah, not Abd Allah, and this is one of Malik's errors. His name is Abd al-Rahman ibn Usayla, a major Syrian Successor (tabi'i) who lived to the beginning of the caliphate of Abu Bakr. Abu Abd Allah al-Sunabihi said: I came as a migrant to the Prophet (ﷺ) from Yemen. When we reached al-Juhfa, we met a rider and said to him: "What is the news?" He said: "We buried the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) three days ago."

These hadiths, and what is similar to them from the hadith of Amr ibn Abasa and others, show you that their meaning is that wudu' is prescribed as an act of worship to wipe away sins, and this requires that it depend on a lawful intention, because it was prescribed to erase sin and to raise ranks with Allah, the Exalted.

The thirty-second matter concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not desire to place upon you any hardship﴾, that is, any constriction in religion. Its evidence is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 99.]] (al-Hajj: 78). The "min" (of "min harajin") is superfluous, so that the meaning is: "that He may place upon you hardship."

﴿but He desires to purify you﴾: that is, from sins, as we mentioned from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and al-Sunabihi. It has also been said: from minor impurity (hadath) and major impurity (janaba). It has been said: so that you may deserve the description of purity by which the people of obedience are described. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read "li-yutahhirakum" (with a different form), and the meaning is the same, as one says: najjahu and anjahu (both meaning he saved him).

﴿and to complete His favour upon you﴾: that is, by permitting tayammum in illness and travel. It has also been said: by making the laws clear. It has also been said: by forgiving sins, and in a report: "The completion of the favour is entering Paradise and being saved from the Fire."

﴿that you may be grateful﴾: that is, so that you may thank His favour and thereby devote yourselves to His obedience.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 5, verse 7:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember the favour of God upon you, and His covenant which He made with you﴾. It has been said that this is the covenant mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: "And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam..." (Al-A'raf 7:172). This was said by Mujahid and others. Although we have not mentioned it, the Truthful One (al-Sadiq, i.e. the Prophet ﷺ) has informed us of it, so it is permissible that we be commanded to fulfil it. [[See vol. 7, p. 313.]]

It has also been said that this is an address to the Jews, to preserve what was taken from them in the Torah (al-Tawrah). However, the view held by the majority of commentators (al-mufassirun), such as Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi, is that it refers to the pledge and covenant that took place between them and the Prophet ﷺ to hear and obey, in ease and in hardship, when they said: "We hear and we obey." This is what took place on the night of al-Aqabah and under the tree. God attributed it to Himself, as He said: "Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you pledge allegiance only to God" (Al-Fath 48:10). [[See vol. 16, pp. 267 and 274. In manuscripts K, J and H: "the pledge of the tree."]]

They pledged allegiance (bayah, a pledge of allegiance) to the Messenger of God ﷺ at al-Aqabah that they would protect him from whatever they protect themselves, their women and their children from, and that he and his companions would migrate to them. The first to pledge allegiance to him was al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, who had in that night the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud) in securing the Messenger of God ﷺ and binding the matter firmly. He was the one who said: "By Him who sent you with the truth, we shall protect you from what we protect our azr (izar, i.e. our wives and families, referred to by the term 'waist-wrapper'). So pledge to us, O Messenger of God, for by God we are sons of wars and people of the ring (or armour); we inherited it generation after generation." This well-known report is in the Sirah (biography) of Ibn Ishaq. [[Azr means our women and families; they are referred to by this euphemism. It has also been said that he meant ourselves. See Sirat Ibn Hisham, vol. 1, p. 293, Europe edition.]] The mention of the pledge of al-Ridwan will come in its proper place. [[See vol. 16, pp. 267 and 274. In manuscripts K, J and H: "the pledge of the tree."]]

This is connected to His saying, may He be exalted: "O you who believe, fulfil the contracts" (Al-Ma'idah 5:1), so they fulfilled what they had said. May God reward them on behalf of their Prophet and on behalf of Islam with good, and may God be pleased with them and make them pleased.

His saying: ﴿And fear God﴾, that is, by disobeying Him. Indeed, He is Knowing of everything.

O you who believe, be steadfast in upholding justice for Allah's sake, bearing witness with fairness... (the verse) — its meaning has already been explained in Surat an-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 410]. The meaning is: "I have perfected My blessing upon you, so be steadfast for Allah," that is, for the sake of Allah's reward; so stand up for His right, and bear witness to the truth without leaning toward your relatives or wronging your enemies.

(And do not let the hatred of a people) prompt you to abandon justice and prefer transgression over the truth. This verse is evidence that the ruling of an enemy against his enemy in the matter of Allah is binding, and that his testimony against him is valid, because He commanded justice even toward one whom you hate. Had his ruling against him, or his testimony, been impermissible while hating him, there would be no sense in the command to be just toward him.
