The verse also indicates that a disbeliever's unbelief does not prevent justice being done toward him, and that retaliation against them should be limited to what is due in fighting and enslavement, and that mutilating them is not permissible even if they kill our women and children and grieve us thereby; we may not kill them by mutilation intending to inflict grief and sorrow upon them. Abdullah ibn Rawahah alluded to this in his well-known verse in the famous story [it is so in all the manuscripts, and there appears to be a lacuna. The story intended is, Allah knows best, what happened to Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; see ar-Rawd al-Unf, vol. 2, p. 82]. This is the meaning of the verse. The meaning of "and do not let the hatred of a people" has been discussed earlier at the beginning of this surah [see p. 44 of this part].

It is read as "wa la yujrimannakum" (with a dammah). Al-Kisa'i said: both are dialects of the same meaning. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "la yujrimannakum" is "do not bring you into sin (jurm)," just as you say, "atham-ani," meaning "he brought me into sin (ithm)."

The meaning of "that is nearer to piety" is: so that you may fear Allah. It was also said: so that you may fear the Fire.

The meaning of "for them is forgiveness and a great reward" is that Allah said concerning the believers: "for them is forgiveness and a great reward," meaning that the minds of creatures cannot grasp its reality, as He said: "No soul knows what is hidden for them of the delight of the eyes" [see vol. 14, p. 103] (as-Sajdah 17). When Allah says "a great reward," "a noble reward," and "a large reward" (Yasin 11; Hud 11), who then can estimate its measure? Since a promise is a kind of speech, it is well-formed to introduce the lam in His saying "for them is forgiveness," though it occupies an accusative position, because it stands in the place of the thing promised, meaning: He promised them that they would have forgiveness, or promised them forgiveness. However, the clause occupies the place of a single noun, as the poet said [it is 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Kilabi]:

We found the righteous have a reward... and gardens and springs of salsabil.

The position of the clause is accusative, and therefore what is conjoined to it is in the accusative. It was also said that it is in the nominative position, with the object of promise omitted, as if it were: "for them is forgiveness and a great reward in what He promised them." This meaning is attributed to al-Hasan.

(And those who disbelieve) — it was revealed concerning the Banu an-Nadir. It was said: concerning all disbelievers.

O you who believe, be steadfast in upholding justice for Allah's sake, bearing witness with fairness... (the verse) — its meaning has already been explained in Surat an-Nisa' [see vol. 5, p. 410]. The meaning is: "I have perfected My blessing upon you, so be steadfast for Allah," that is, for the sake of Allah's reward; so stand up for His right, and bear witness to the truth without leaning toward your relatives or wronging your enemies.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 11:

His saying, Exalted is He: (O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands toward you) said: A group said: It was revealed concerning the act of the Bedouin at the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa', when he drew (ikhtarata, to draw out of its sheath) the sword of the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Who will protect you from me, O Muhammad?" As has preceded in "al-Nisa'" [see vol. 5, p. 372].

In al-Bukhari: the Prophet ﷺ called the people, and they gathered while he was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ, and he did not punish him [i.e., he did not punish the Bedouin, in order to win over the disbelievers].

Al-Waqidi and Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned that he embraced Islam.

Some people mentioned that he struck his head against the trunk of a tree until he died.

In al-Bukhari, concerning the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa', the name of the man is Ghawrath ibn al-Harith (with a dotted ghayn, vowelled with a fatha, and the waw after it silent, followed by a raa' and a thaa' with three dots). Some have vowelled the ghayn with a damma, but the first is more sound.

Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris al-Razi and Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Waqidi mentioned that his name was Du'thur ibn al-Harith, and mentioned that he embraced Islam as has preceded.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq related [in other manuscripts: "and related"] that his name was Amr ibn Jihash, and he was a brother of the Banu al-Nadir. Some have mentioned that the story of Amr ibn Jihash is other than this story. And Allah knows best.

Qatadah, Mujahid and others said: It was revealed concerning a people of the Jews to whom the Prophet ﷺ came seeking their help regarding blood money, so they determined to kill him ﷺ, but Allah protected him from them.

Al-Qushayri said: A verse may be revealed concerning one incident and then its mention is revealed again to recall what preceded.

"That they extend their hands toward you" means with harm, "so He restrained their hands from you" means He prevented them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 5, verse 12:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah certainly took the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised from among them twelve chiefs﴾. On this there are three issues.

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Atiyyah said: These verses, which contain the report of their breaking the covenants of Allah, strengthen the view that the preceding verse about the restraining of hands was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir. The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) differed about the manner in which these chiefs (*nuqaba'*) were raised, though there is consensus that the *naqib* is the leader of a people, the one who takes charge of their affairs and investigates (*yunaqqibu*) them and their interests. The *naqqab* is the great man who is over the people in this manner, and from this it was said of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that "he was indeed a *naqqab*." So the *nuqaba'* are the guarantors, the singular being *naqib*, and he is the witness and surety of his people. It is said: *naqaba 'alayhim* (he became their chief/guarantor), and *huwa hasan al-naqibah*, meaning he has a good disposition. *Al-naqb* and *al-nuqb* mean a path through a mountain. It is said he is called *naqib* because he knows the inner matters of the people and recognises their virtues (*manaqib*), and he is the way to knowing their affairs. Others said: the *nuqaba'* are the trustees over their people. All of these are close to one another. The *naqib* is of greater rank than the *'arif* (overseer). 'Ata' ibn Yasar said: "The bearers of the Qur'an are the *'urafa'* (overseers) of the people of Paradise," which al-Darimi mentioned in his *Musnad*.

Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on him, and others said: These *nuqaba'* were senior men from each tribe, each of whom took responsibility for his tribe, that they would believe and fear Allah. Something similar was the case of the *nuqaba'* at the Night of 'Aqabah, when seventy men and two women pledged allegiance. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) chose twelve men from the seventy and named them *nuqaba'*, following the example of Musa (peace be upon him).

Al-Rabi' and al-Suddi and others said: The *nuqaba'* from the Children of Israel were only sent as trustees to scout the giants (*al-jabbarin*) and to test their strength and power. They set out to examine the condition of those who were there, and to inform (Musa) of what they observed, so that he might consider the campaign against them. They discovered among the giants a great power, as will be mentioned, and they thought that they had no means to face it. So they agreed among themselves to conceal this from the Children of Israel and to inform Musa (peace be upon him) alone. When they returned to the Children of Israel, ten of them betrayed (the agreement). They informed their relatives and those whom they trusted with their secret, so the news spread until the affair of the Children of Israel became crooked, and they said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 24).

**The second issue:** In the verse there is evidence for the acceptance of the report of a single transmitter (*khabar al-wahid*) concerning matters that a person needs and must be informed of, from among his religious and worldly needs. Rulings are built upon it, and lawful and unlawful matters are attached to it. A similar principle also appears in Islam. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Hawazin: "Return until your overseers (*'urafa'*) bring your matter to us." Al-Bukhari transmitted it.

**The third issue:** In it there is also evidence for the employment of a spy (*jasus*). *Al-tajassus* means searching out information. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Basbasah as a spy (*'ayn*),[[This was in the Battle of Badr. It is said he was the son of 'Amr al-Ansari, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) sent to seek news of the caravan of Abu Sufyan.]] which Muslim transmitted. The ruling on the spy will come in *al-Mumtahanah*,[[See vol. 18, p. 53.]] Allah willing.

As for the names of the chiefs of the Children of Israel, Muhammad ibn Habib mentioned their names in *al-Muhabbar*,[[Abu Hayyan said in *al-Bahr*: Muhammad ibn Habib mentioned in *al-Muhabbar* the names of these chiefs whom Musa chose in this account, in wordings whose letters and vowels cannot be fixed. Others mentioned them, differing in most respects from what Ibn Habib mentioned, and these too cannot be fixed. In the margin of al-Tabari: there has been distortion and disagreement among the history books regarding the names of the tribes and their chiefs, so let it be verified.]] and said: From the tribe of Ruwil: Sham'un ibn Rakub; from the tribe of Sham'un: Shawqut ibn Huri; from the tribe of Yahudha: Kalib ibn Yuqana; from the tribe of the Sahir: Yawghul ibn Yusuf; from the tribe of Ifraythim ibn Yusuf: Yusha' ibn al-Nun; from the tribe of Binyamin: Yalazha ibn Ruqu; from the tribe of Zabulun: Karabil ibn Suda; from the tribe of Manshа ibn Yusuf: Kadi ibn Susha; from the tribe of Dan: 'Ama'il ibn Kasal; from the tribe of Shir: Sturur ibn Mikha'il; from the tribe of Naftali: Yuhanna ibn Waqushah; and from the tribe of Kadhkawal: Ibn Mukha. The two believers among them were Yusha' and Kalib. Musa (peace be upon him) invoked against the others, so they perished, cursed, as al-Mawardi said.

As for the chiefs of the Night of 'Aqabah, they are mentioned in the *Sirah* of Ibn Ishaq.[[See Ibn Hisham's *Sirah*, vol. 1, p. 297, European edition.]] Let them be consulted there.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah said: Indeed I am with you. If you establish prayer…﴾ (the verse). Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: He said that to the chiefs. Others said he said it to all the Children of Israel. The *inna* is pronounced with a kasrah because it begins a sentence (*mubtada'ah*). *Ma'akum* is in the accusative because it is an adverb of place (*zarf*), meaning with help and support. Then he begins: ﴿If you establish prayer﴾ up to his saying ﴿I will surely remove from you your misdeeds﴾, meaning: if you do that. The *lam* in *la'in* is the *lam* of emphasis and its meaning is an oath; likewise in *la'ukaffiranna 'ankum* and *la'udkhilannakum*. It was said: the meaning is "if you establish prayer, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds," and this contains another condition for his saying *la'ukaffiranna*, that is: if you do that, I will surely remove. It was also said: his saying *la'in aqamtum al-salah* is the response (*jaza'*) to his saying *inni ma'akum* and a condition for his saying *la'ukaffiranna*. *Al-Ta'zir* means honouring and revering. Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

*And how many a noble man among them, generous, and a lion who is honoured in the assembly.*

That is, he is magnified and revered. *Al-Ta'zir* also means striking short of the prescribed punishment (*hadd*), and repelling. You say: *'azzartu fulanan* when you disciplined him and turned him back from wrongdoing. So his saying *'azzartumuhum* means: you repelled their enemies from them.

﴿And you lend Allah a goodly loan﴾ means charities. He did not say *iqradan* (the verbal noun), and this is one of the cases where the form *qard* is used instead of the verbal noun, as in His saying ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾,[[See vol. 18, p. 305.]] and ﴿So his Lord accepted her with a goodly acceptance﴾,[[See vol. 4, p. 69.]] which has already been mentioned. Then it was said: *hasanan* means good, with which your souls are content. It was said: they seek thereby the face of Allah. It was said: lawful. It was said: *qardan* is a noun, not a verbal noun.

﴿Then whoever disbelieves after that among you﴾ means after the covenant.

﴿Has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ means he has missed the direct path. And Allah knows best.

**"فَبِما نَقْضِهِمْ مِيثاقَهُمْ"** (﴿So for their breaking of their covenant﴾). That is, "فَبِما" (*fa-bi-ma*) is extra (*za'idah*) for emphasis, according to Qatadah and the rest of the scholars. This is because it reinforces the speech, making it firmer in the soul through the beauty of its arrangement and through the increase in emphasis. As the poet said:

*Lishay'in ma yusawwadu man yasud*
(For some reason, whoever becomes a leader is made a leader.)

So the emphasis by means of an added particle is like emphasis by repetition.

**"لَعَنَّاهُمْ"** (﴿We cursed them﴾). Ibn Abbas said: "We punished them with the jizyah (poll tax)." Al-Hasan and Muqatil said: "With transformation (into apes and swine)." Ata' said: "We removed them far away." *Al-la'n* (cursing) is removal and expulsion from mercy.

**"وَجَعَلْنا قُلُوبَهُمْ قاسِيَةً"** (﴿and We made their hearts hard﴾). That is, hard and unyielding, not understanding good nor doing it. *Al-qasiyah* and *al-ʿatiyah* have the same meaning.

Al-Kisa'i and Hamzah read **"قَسِيَّةً"** (*qasiyyah*) with a doubled *ya'* and without an *alif*. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab. *Al-ʿam al-qasiyy* means a severe year without rain. It is also said that it comes from *al-darahim al-qasiyyat*, meaning counterfeit, debased dirhams. On this view, the meaning of *qasiyyah* is that it is not pure faith; there is hypocrisy in it. Al-Nahhas said: "This is a good opinion, because it is said: *dirham qasiyy* when it is mixed with copper or something else." It is said: *dirham qasiyy* (with a light *sin* and a doubled *ya'*), on the pattern of *shaqiyy*, meaning counterfeit. Abu Ubayd mentioned this and recited:

*Laha sawahilu fi summi as-salami kama*
*sah al-qasiyyatu fi aydi as-sayarifi*
(For it there are neighings amid the hard rocks, as the counterfeit coins cry out in the hands of the money-changers.)

[[The verse is by Abu Zayd al-Ta'i. *Al-sawahil* (plural of *al-sahilah*) is a verbal noun on the pattern *fa'ilah*, meaning *al-sahil*, which is a sound.]]

It describes the impact of the *al-masahi* [[*al-masahi* (plural of *al-misha*) is an iron shovel.]] on the stones. Al-Asma'i and Abu Ubayd said: "*Dirham qasiyy* seems to be an arabicised form of *qashi*." Al-Qushayri said: "This is far-fetched, because there is nothing in the Qur'an that is not from the language of the Arabs. Rather, *al-dirham al-qasiyy* comes from *al-qaswah* (hardness) and *al-shiddah* (severity), because a coin whose stamp is faint becomes hard and solid."

Al-A'mash read **"قَسِيَةٌ"** (*qasiyah*) with a light *ya'*, on the pattern *fa'ilah* like *ʿamiyah* and *shajiyah*, from *qasa yaqsi*, not from *qasa yaqsu*. The rest of the readers read it on the pattern *fa'ilah*, and this is the choice of Abu Ubayd. They are two dialectal forms, like *al-ʿaliyyah* and *al-ʿaliyah*, and *al-zakiyyah* and *al-zakiyah*.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "The best view is that *qasiyyah* means *qasiyah* (hard), except that *fa'iliyah* is more intensive than *fa'ilah*." So the meaning is: We made their hearts coarse and averse to faith and to being guided to obey Me, because these people were not described with anything of faith, so their hearts would not be described as having faith mixed with disbelief, like counterfeit dirhams mixed with adulteration. The reciter said:

*Qad qasawti wa qasat li-dati*
(You have become hard, and my contemporaries have become hard.)

**"يُحَرِّفُونَ الْكَلِمَ عَنْ مَواضِعِهِ"** (﴿they distort words from their places﴾). That is, they interpret it in other than its real interpretation, and they convey that to the common people. It is also said: the meaning is that they change its letters. *"Yuharrifuna"* is in the accusative position, meaning: We made their hearts hard, distorting [their words].

Al-Sulami and al-Nakha'i read **"الْكَلَامَ"** (*al-kalam*, with an *alif*). This is because they changed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

**"وَنَسُوا حَظًّا مِمَّا ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ"** (﴿and they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of﴾). That is, they forgot the covenant of God which the prophets took from them, to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and to explain his description.

**"وَلا تَزالُ تَطَّلِعُ"** (﴿and you will not cease to discover﴾). That is, and you, O Muhammad, still now keep coming upon "a treachery from them" (﴿treachery﴾). *Al-khaʾinah* is treachery, said Qatadah. This is permissible in the language, and it is like their saying *qa'ilah* meaning *qaylulah* (noon nap). It is also said that it is an adjective of an omitted noun, and the implied phrase is "a treacherous group." *Khaʾinah* may also be used for a single person, as one says *rajul nassabah* and *allamah* (a man who is very knowledgeable about genealogies). On this view, *khaʾinah* is for intensification. One says *rajul khaʾinah* when you exaggerate in describing him with treachery. The poet said:

*Haddathta nafsaka bil-wafa'i wa lam takun*
*lil-ghadri khaʾinatan mughalla al-isbaʿi*
(You told yourself of faithfulness, but you were not one who betrays with the finger-cut thief.)

Ibn Abbas said: "*ʿAla khaʾinah*" means disobedience. It is also said: lying and wickedness. Their treachery was their breaking of the covenant between them and the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and their supporting the polytheists in fighting the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as on the day of the Confederates and other occasions, and from their intention to kill him and revile him.

**"إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْهُمْ"** (﴿except a few of them﴾). Those did not betray, so this is an exception from the *ha'* and *mim* in "khaʾinatin minhum" (a treachery from them).

**"فَاعْفُ عَنْهُمْ وَاصْفَحْ"** (﴿so pardon them and overlook﴾). There are two views on its meaning. The first: pardon them and overlook, as long as there is a covenant between you and them, and they are *ahl al-dhimmah* (the protected non-Muslim subjects under a covenant). The other view is that it is *mansukh* (abrogated) by the verse of the sword [[*Mansukh* means abrogated, that is, a ruling replaced by a later ruling.]]. It is also said that it is abrogated by His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 31.]] (al-Anfal 8:58).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 5, verses 14–16**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾, meaning: concerning monotheism and belief in Muhammad ﷺ, since it is written in the Gospel (al-Injil).

(But they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of) and that portion is belief in Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. That is, they did not act upon what they had been commanded, and they made their desires and their distortion (al-tahrif) a cause for disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ. The meaning of "We took their covenant" is like your saying, "I took from Zayd his garment and his dirham." This was said by al-Akhfash. The proper position of "alladhina" (those who) is after "akhadna" (We took) and before "al-mithaq" (the covenant), so the construction becomes: "We took from those who said, 'We are Christians,' their covenant," because it stands in the position of the second object of "akhadna." According to the Kufans, its estimated form is: "And from those who said, 'We are Christians,' is the one whose covenant We took," so the pronouns "ha'" and "mim" return to the omitted "man" (whoever). According to the first opinion, they return to "alladhina." The grammarians do not permit "akhadna mithaqahum min alladhina qalu inna nasara" (We took their covenant from those who said, "We are Christians"), nor "ala'yanaha labistu min al-thiyab" (the softest of garments I wore), lest a pronoun precede its noun. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 17:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary," have certainly disbelieved.﴾ Its explanation and the discussion concerning it have already been given at the end of "al-Nisa'" [[See p. 21 and what follows in this part.]]. The disbelief of the Christians, according to the implication of this statement, lay only in their saying, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary," in the manner of affirming it as a creed (al-dayunah bihi), for if they had said it by way of quotation while rejecting it, they would not have disbelieved.

(Say: "Who then has any power against Allah?") That is, against the command of Allah. "Yamliku" (has power) here means "yaqdiru" (is able), from their saying "malaktu 'ala fulanin amrahu," meaning "I gained power over him." That is: who is able to prevent anything from that? Allah the Exalted thereby informs that if the Messiah were a god, he would have been able to repel what befalls him or others. Yet he caused his mother to die and was not able to repel death from her. So if He destroys him as well, who will repel that from him or turn it back?

(And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them.) The Messiah and his mother are between them, two created, bounded, confined beings, and whatever is encompassed by limit and end is not fit for divinity. He said "wa ma baynahuma" (whatever is between the two) and did not say "wa ma baynahunna," because He intended the two kinds and the two categories, as the poet al-Ra'i said:

Two came at night, so those are my worries I bring near, [[al-hamahim: meaning worries.]]
young she-camels [[qulus (plural of qalus): young female camels.]] fertile like bows and barren [[hawal (plural of ha'il): a she-camel that was mated but did not conceive; it was also said to be one that carries for a year, two years, or several years.]]

He said "taraqa" (came), then said "fatilka hamahimi" (those are my worries) in the feminine dual.

(He creates what He wills.) The creation of Jesus from a mother without a father is a sign for His servants.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 18:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Jews and the Christians said, "We are the children of Allah and His beloved."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) warned a group of the Jews of punishment, and they said, "We do not fear, for we are the children of Allah and His beloved." So the verse was revealed. Ibn Ishaq said: Nu'man ibn Ada, Bahri ibn 'Amr and Sha's ibn 'Adi came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They spoke with him and he spoke with them, and he called them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and warned them of His retribution. They said, "What are you frightening us with, O Muhammad? We are the children of Allah and His beloved, as the Christians say." So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed concerning them: "And the Jews and the Christians said, 'We are the children of Allah and His beloved.' Say, 'Why then does He punish you for your sins?'" to the end of the verse. Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah and 'Uqbah ibn Wahb said to them: "O company of Jews, fear Allah! By Allah, you know that he is the Messenger of Allah, and you used to mention him to us before his mission and describe him to us by his attributes." Rafi' ibn Huraymilah and Wahb ibn Yahudha said: "We did not say this to you, and Allah has not sent down any Book after Musa, nor has He sent any bringer of good tidings or warner after him." So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "O People of the Book, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you after a gap in the messengers..." to His saying: "And Allah is over all things Competent."

Al-Suddi said: The Jews claimed that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Israel, peace be upon him, that "Your firstborn is of the firstborn sons." Others said: The Christians said, "We are the children of Allah," because in the Gospel there is a narration from 'Isa: "I go to my Father and your Father."

It was also said: the meaning is, "We are the children of the messengers of Allah," and so it is an elision of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf).

In sum: they regarded themselves as having a special merit, so He refuted their claim by saying (Why then does He punish you for your sins?). They could not avoid one of two positions. Either they say, "He punishes us," and it is said to them: "Then you are not His children and beloved, for the beloved does not punish his beloved, and you acknowledge His punishment; this is evidence of your lie." This is what the dialecticians call the proof by reductio (burhan al-khulf). Or they say, "He does not punish us," and so they deny what is in their books and what their messengers brought, and they permit sins while acknowledging the punishment of the sinners among them; and for this reason they hold to the rulings of their books.

It was also said: the meaning of "yu'adhdhibukum" is "'adhdhabakum," which is in the past sense: why did He transform you into apes and swine? And why did He punish those before you among the Jews and Christians with various kinds of punishment, when they were like you? Because Allah, glory be to Him, does not argue against them with something that had not yet occurred, for they might say, "We will not be punished tomorrow"; rather He argues against them with what they already knew.

Then He said: (Rather, you are human beings among those He created), i.e., like the rest of His creatures; He will call you to account for obedience and disobedience, and will recompense each for what he did.

(He forgives whom He wills) i.e., those among the Jews who repent.

(And He punishes whom He wills) those who die upon it.

(And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth) so there is no partner who opposes Him.

(And to Him is the final return) i.e., the affair of the servants returns to Him in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Scripture, indeed there has come to you Our Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

(Making clear to you) the cutting off of their argument, so that they will not say tomorrow, "No messenger came to us."

(After a lapse in the messengers) meaning a cessation (sukun). It is said: fatara al-shay' (the thing lapsed), meaning it became still (sakana). It was also said: "after a lapse" means after a break between the prophets. This is related from Abu 'Ali and a group of the people of knowledge, and al-Rummani reported it. He said: The root meaning of fatrah is the cessation of an action from the diligence that it had been carried out with, from their saying: fatara 'an 'amalihi (he slackened in his work) and fattartuhu 'anhu (I made him slacken from it). From this is: fatara al-ma' (the water lost its heat) when it ceased from being hot and became cold. And a woman with fatirat al-taraf (a languid glance) means one whose sharpness of gaze has ceased. The languor of the body is like the languor of water. And al-fitr is the span between the index finger and the thumb when you spread them apart. The meaning is that a period passed for the messengers before him.

The scholars differed over the length of that lapse. Muhammad ibn Sa'd mentioned in the book "al-Tabaqat", from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Between Musa ibn 'Imran and 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon them both, there were one thousand and seven hundred [[According to the well-known report. In the原 texts: one thousand and nine hundred.]] years, and there was no lapse between them, and that there were sent between them one thousand prophets from the Children of Israel, besides those sent from other than them. And between the birth of 'Isa and the Prophet (ﷺ) there were five hundred and sixty-nine years, in the first of which three prophets were sent. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When We sent to them two, and they denied them, so We strengthened them with a third﴾ [Ya-Sin: 14]. The one who was strengthened with them was Shim'un, and he was one of the disciples (al-hawariyyun). The lapse in which Allah sent no messenger was four hundred and thirty-four years.

Al-Kalbi mentioned that between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, there were five hundred and sixty-nine years, and between them there were four prophets, one of whom was from the Arabs, from the Banu 'Abs, and he was Khalid ibn Sinan. Al-Qushayri said: Such a matter is not known except through a truthful report.

Qatadah said: Between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, there were six hundred years. This was also said by Muqatil, al-Dahhak and Wahb ibn Munabbih, except that Wahb added twenty years. And from al-Dahhak also: four hundred and some thirty years.

Ibn Sa'd mentioned from 'Ikrimah, who said: Between Adam and Nuh there were ten centuries, all of them upon Islam. Ibn Sa'd said: Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Waqid al-Aslami informed us, from more than one person, who said: Between Adam and Nuh there were ten centuries, and a century is one hundred years; and between Nuh and Ibrahim there were ten centuries, and between Ibrahim and Musa ibn 'Imran there were ten centuries, a century being one hundred years. This is what lies between Adam and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, in centuries and years. And Allah knows best.

(Lest you should say) meaning, lest, or out of dislike that you should say; it is in a position of accusative (nasb). "There has not come to us any bearer of good tidings" meaning one who gives glad tidings. "Nor any warner" meaning one who warns. It is permissible to read "min bashir wa la nadhir" according to the position (of the grammatical structure), and the addition of (min) in the subject is for emphasis in negating the coming (Ruh al-Ma'ani).

Ibn 'Abbas said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah and 'Uqbah ibn Wahb said to the Jews: "O assembly of Jews, fear Allah, for by Allah you indeed know that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and you used to mention him to us before his mission and describe him with his attributes." They said: "Allah did not send down any book after Musa, nor did He send after him any bearer of good tidings or warner." So the verse was revealed.

(And Allah is over all things Competent) over sending whomever He wills of His creation. It was also said: Competent over fulfilling what He gave glad tidings of and warned against.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 3):

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you"﴾ are a clarification from Allah the Exalted that their forefathers rebelled against Musa and disobeyed him, and so did these (people) against Muhammad (ﷺ). This is a consolation for him. That is, "O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you, and remember the story of Musa." It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Kathir that he recited "Ya qawmu udhkuru" with a ḍamma on the mim (qawmu), and likewise whatever resembles it, and its implied meaning is "O you people" (yā ayyuhā al-qawm).

(When He placed among you prophets) "anbiya'" is not declined (lam yanṣarif), because it has the feminine alif (alif al-ta'nith).

(And made you kings) That is, you control your own affairs, and no conqueror overpowers you in them, after you had been slaves of Pharaoh, subdued. So He rescued you from him by drowning (him). Thus they are "kings" in this sense. Al-Suddi and al-Husayn and others explained it in this manner. Al-Suddi said: each one of them was king over himself, his family and his property. Qatadah said: He only said "and made you kings" because we used to hear that they were the first of the children of Adam to be served (by others). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is weak, because the Copts used to employ the Children of Israel, and the apparent matter regarding the children of Adam is that some of them would subjugate others from the time they multiplied and spread; the nations only differed in the meaning of "possession" (tamlik) alone. It was also said: He made you people of dwellings who may not be entered upon except with permission. Its meaning is narrated from a group of the scholars. Ibn 'Abbas said: If a man does not let anyone enter his house except with his permission, then he is a king. And from al-Hasan and also Zayd ibn Aslam: whoever has a house, a wife and a servant is a king. This is also the view of Abdullah ibn 'Amr, as in Sahih Muslim, from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, when a man asked him, "Are we not among the poor emigrants?" Abdullah said to him, "Do you have a wife you return to?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Do you have a dwelling you live in?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then you are among the wealthy." He said, "But I have a servant." He said, "Then you are among the kings." Ibn al-'Arabi said: The benefit of this is that if a man is obligated to expiate (kaffarah) and he owns a house and a servant, he sells them for the expiation and it is not permissible for him to fast, because he is able to free a slave, and kings do not expiate by fasting, nor are they described as incapable of manumission. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: He made them kings through the manna, the quails, the rock and the clouds, that is, they were served like kings. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning the servant and the dwelling, and this was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah, who added the wife. Zayd ibn Aslam said likewise, except that he said, as is known from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever has a house, or said a dwelling, to which he returns, and a wife and a servant who serves him, then he is a king." Al-Nahhas mentioned it. It is also said: whoever is independent of others is a king. This is like what the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wakes up secure in his dwelling, healthy in his body, and has his food for the day, it is as if the whole world has been gathered for him."

The words of Allah the Exalted: (And gave you) that is, bestowed upon you (what He had not given to anyone of the worlds). According to the majority of the commentators the address is from Musa to his people, and this is the apparent sense of the speech. Mujahid said: the "giving" refers to the manna, the quails, the rock and the clouds. It was also said: the multitude of prophets among them, and the signs that came to them. It was also said: hearts free from rancour and deceit. It was also said: the lawfulness of spoils of war and benefiting from them. I say: this view is rejected, for spoils of war were not made lawful to anyone except this Ummah, as is established in the Sahih, and its explanation will come, Allah willing. This statement of Musa was a preparation of their souls so that they would be strengthened and would take up the matter of entering the land of the tyrants with strength, and would proceed in that with the authority of one whom Allah has honoured and elevated. The meaning of "of the worlds" is "of the worlds of your time," according to al-Hasan. Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik said: the address is to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is a departure from the apparent meaning of the speech, one that is not fitting in this way. And the reports are consistent that Damascus is the seat of the tyrants. And "the holy" (al-Muqaddasah) means "the purified." Mujahid said: "the blessed," and blessing is purification from drought, hunger and the like. Qatadah said: it is al-Sham (Greater Syria). Mujahid said: it is Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and what surrounds it. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: it is Jericho (Ariha'). Al-Zajjaj said: Damascus, Palestine, and some say Jordan. Qatadah's view encompasses all of this.

(Which Allah has prescribed for you) That is, He ordained your entry into it and promised you its entry and its dwelling as yours. When the Children of Israel left Egypt, He commanded them to fight the people of Jericho in the lands of Palestine, but they said: "We have no knowledge of those lands." So, by the command of Allah, He sent twelve chieftains (nuqaba'), one from each tribe, to spy out the news, as was mentioned earlier. They saw its inhabitants, the tyrants of the 'Amalaqah, who were of enormous bodies, to the extent that it is said that one of them saw these chieftains, took them in his sleeve together with some fruit he had brought from his orchard, and came with them to the king, scattered them before him and said: "These people intend to fight us." The king said to them: "Go back to your companion and tell him our news," as mentioned earlier. It was also said: when they returned they took a cluster of grapes from that land; some said one man carried it, and some said the twelve chieftains carried it together. I say: this is more plausible, for it is said that when they reached the tyrants they found that two of them could enter into the sleeve of one of them, and that a single cluster of one of them could be carried only by five of them on a pole, and that half a pomegranate, once its seeds were removed, could hold five or four persons. (Al-Alusi said: these reports, in my view, are like the reports of 'Uj ibn 'Unuq, and they are a fabricated tale.)

I say: there is no contradiction between this and the first account, for that tyrant who took them in his sleeve, and it is said in his lap, was 'Uj ibn 'Unaq, who was the tallest of them in stature and the greatest in form, as will be mentioned later, Allah willing. The height of the rest of them was six and a half cubits according to Muqatil. Al-Kalbi said: the height of each man of them was eighty cubits, and Allah knows best. When they spread the report, all except Yusha' and Kalib ibn Yuqina refused, and the Children of Israel refused to fight. They were punished with the wandering (al-tih) for forty years, until those disobedient ones died and their children grew up, and they fought the tyrants and overcame them.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not turn back on your heels﴾ That is, do not turn back from my obedience and from what I have commanded you concerning fighting the tyrants. It was also said: do not turn back from obedience to Allah to disobedience to Him, and the meaning is one.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed in it are a people of tyrants"﴾ That is, huge of body and tall, as was mentioned before. It is said: "a jabbarah palm" meaning a tall palm. The jabbar is the one who magnifies himself and refuses humiliation and poverty. Al-Zajjaj said: the jabbar among human beings is the insolent one, who compels people to do what he wishes, so its root in this sense is from ijbar, which is coercion, for he compels others to what he desires, and "ajbarahu" means "he compelled him." It was also said: it is derived from setting a bone (jabr al-'azm), so the original meaning of jabbar in this sense is the one who sets right his own affairs, then it came to be used for everyone who draws benefit to himself, whether rightly or wrongly. It was also said that setting a bone reverts to the meaning of compulsion. Al-Farra' said: I have not heard fa''al from af'ala except in two words: jabbar from ajbar, and darrak from adraka. Then it was said: these were remnants of 'Ad. It was also said: they were of the descendants of 'Is ibn Ishaq, and they were of the Romans, and with them was 'Uj al-A'naq, whose height was three thousand and three hundred and thirty-three cubits, as said by Ibn 'Umar. [[In manuscripts J, H, K and Z: "three thousand and twenty thousand"... etc.]] He used to seize the clouds, that is, pull them down with his staff and drink from them, and he would take the fish from the bottom of the sea and roast it in the sun's heat by raising it up to the sun, then eat it. He was present at the flood of Nuh (peace be upon him), but the water did not reach beyond his knees, and his lifespan was three thousand six hundred years. It is said that he uprooted a rock the size of Musa's army in order to crush them with it, but Allah sent a bird which pecked at it, and it fell on his neck and felled him. Musa (peace be upon him), whose height was ten cubits, and his staff was ten cubits, went out and leapt up into the sky ten cubits, and he struck only his ankle while he was fallen, and he killed him. It was also said: rather he struck him in the vein beneath his ankle, and he fell and died, and he landed upon the Nile of Egypt, and so it became a bridge for them for a year. Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, Makki and others mentioned this meaning with varying wording. Al-Kalbi said: 'Uj was a descendant of Harut and Marut, when they lay with a woman and she conceived. And Allah knows best. [[Al-Qurtubi's note: all that the author mentions in this place of the Isra'iliyyat (narratives from Jewish and Christian sources) is not to be relied upon.]]

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And we will never enter it until they leave it﴾ meaning the city of Iliya', and it is said Jericho, until they hand it over to us without fighting. It was also said: they said this out of fear of the tyrants, and did not intend disobedience, for they said: "If they leave it, then we will enter."

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Two men from among those who feared said﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and others said: they were Yusha' and Kalib ibn Yuqina, and it is said Ibn Qaniya, and they were of the twelve chieftains. And "who feared" means of the tyrants. Qatadah said: they feared Allah the Exalted. Al-Dahhak said: they were two men who were in the city of the tyrants, upon the religion of Musa, so the meaning of "feared" in this view is that they feared the 'Amaliqah by nature, lest they discover their faith and afflict them, but they trusted in Allah. It was also said: they feared the weakness and cowardice of the Children of Israel. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr read "yukhafun" with a ḍamma on the ya', and this strengthens the view that they were not of the people of Musa.

(Upon whom Allah had bestowed favour) That is, with Islam, or with certainty and righteousness.

(ادْخُلُوا عَلَيْهِمُ الْبابَ فَإِذا دَخَلْتُمُوهُ فَإِنَّكُمْ غالِبُونَ) ﴿Enter upon them through the gate, and when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious.﴾ Said the two men to the Children of Israel: "Let not the great size of their bodies terrify you, for their hearts are filled with fear of you. Their bodies are large but their hearts are weak." They knew that if they entered through that gate, victory would be theirs. It is also possible that the two men said this out of confidence in God's promise. Then they said: (وَعَلَى اللَّهِ فَتَوَكَّلُوا إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ) ﴿And upon God rely, if you are believers﴾, meaning, believing in Him, for He will help you.

Then it was said, according to the first opinion: when the two men said this, the Children of Israel wanted to stone them, and they said: "We believe you both, and we will abandon the word of ten [of them]!" Then they said to Moses: (إِنَّا لَنْ نَدْخُلَها أَبَداً مَا دامُوا فِيها) ﴿Indeed, we will never enter it as long as they are within it.﴾ This was obstinacy, a refusal to fight, and despair of victory.

Then they showed ignorance of the attributes of the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, when they said: "So go, you and your Lord" (فَاذْهَبْ أَنْتَ وَرَبُّكَ). They described Him with going and moving, whereas God is exalted above that. This indicates that they were anthropomorphists (mushabbihah), which is the meaning of the statement of al-Hasan, for he said: "This is disbelief in God on their part," and this is the most apparent meaning of the words. It was also said: the meaning is that the help of your Lord for you is more deserved than our help, and His fighting with you, if you are His messenger, is more fitting than our fighting. On this interpretation, their words were disbelief, because they doubted his prophethood. It was also said that the meaning is: "Go, you, and fight, and let your Lord help you." It was also said: by "Lord" they meant Aaron, who was older than Moses, and Moses used to obey him. In sum, they transgressed by their words, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾, that is, do not grieve over them.

(إِنَّا هاهُنا قاعِدُونَ) ﴿Indeed, we are sitting here﴾, meaning, we will not move and we will not fight. It is permissible to read "qā'idūn" as "qā'idīn" in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), since the speech was complete before it.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I possess none except myself and my brother"﴾, because he was obeyed by him. It was also said the meaning is: "I possess none except myself," then he began anew and said, "and my brother," meaning: my brother also possesses none except himself. So "my brother" according to the first view is in the accusative position, conjoined to "myself," and according to the second view is in the nominative position. If you wish, you may conjoin it to the subject of "inna," which is the ya' (my), meaning: "I and my brother possess only ourselves." And if you wish, you may conjoin it to the pronoun in "amliku" (I possess), as if he said: "Neither I nor my brother possess except ourselves."

(فَافْرُقْ بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَ الْقَوْمِ الْفاسِقِينَ) ﴿So part between us and the defiant people﴾. It is asked: in what way did he ask God to separate him from these people? There are several answers. First: by that which indicates their distance from the truth and their departure from rectitude in the disobedience they committed, and for this reason they were cast into the wandering (tīh). Second: by requesting distinction, meaning, distinguish us from their community and their entirety, and do not join us with them in punishment. It was also said the meaning is: judge between us and them by Your protecting us from the disobedience with which You tested them. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Therein is made distinct every precise matter﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:4], meaning, is decided. And He did so when He caused them to die in the wandering. It was also said: he meant only in the Hereafter, that is, make us among the people of Paradise and do not make us with them in the Fire. As evidence for the distinction that indicates separation in conditions, the poet said:

يَا رَبِّ فَافْرُقْ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنِي ... أَشَدَّ مَا فَرَّقْتَ بَيْنَ اثنين

"O Lord, part him from me, with the strongest parting You have ever made between two."

Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, that he read: "fāfriq" with a kasra on the rā'.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land."﴾ God answered his supplication and punished them with the wandering for forty years. The root meaning of tīh in the language is bewilderment; it is said: tāha yatīhu tīhan and tawhan when he was bewildered, and tayyahtuhu and tawwahtuhu (I caused him to wander), with yā' and wāw, the yā' being more common. "Al-arḍ al-tayhā'" is the land in which one cannot find the way, and "arḍ tīh" and "tayhā'" are used. From this, another said:

تِيهٌ أَتَاوِيهُ عَلَى السُّقَّاطِ

[This is from al-'Ajjaj, describing an unknown land with no signs by which one may be guided. "Atāwīh" means things of wandering, and "al-saqqāṭ" refers to whoever falls upon them, those who are unpatient and do not find the way. The verse's first half is: "wa-basṭahu bi-sa'at al-basāṭ" (and its spreading out with the breadth of the plain), and al-basāṭ means the wide place of the earth. It was also said this verse is: "wa-baldatin ba'īdat al-niyāṭ, majhūlatin taghtāl khaṭw al-khāṭī" (and a town far in its distances, unknown, stealing the step of the walker).]

Another said:

بِتَيْهَاءَ قَفْرِ وَالْمَطِيُّ كَأَنَّهَا ... قَطَا الْحَزَنِ قَدْ كَانَتْ فِرَاخًا بُيُوضُهَا

"In a barren wandering waste, while the mounts were like the sand-grouse of the rough ground whose eggs had been hatched into chicks."

They used to travel within a few parasangs, said to be about six parasangs, the whole day and night, so they would wake up where they had gone to sleep and would sleep where they had woken up. Thus they were wanderers with no settled home. It has been disputed whether Moses and Aaron were with them. It was said: no, because the wandering was a punishment, and the years of the wandering were according to the number of days of the calf, so each day was matched with a year. And He said: ﴿So part between us and the defiant people﴾. It was also said: they were with them, but God made the matter easy for them both, just as He made the fire cool and safe for Abraham.

The meaning of "muḥarramah" (forbidden) is that they are prevented from entering it, as one says: God forbade your face to the Fire, and I forbade you entry into the house. It is a prohibition of prevention, not a legal prohibition, according to most of the exegetes, as the poet said:

جَالَتْ لِتَصْرَعَنِي فَقُلْتُ لَهَا اقْصُرِي ... إِنِّي امْرُؤٌ صَرْعِي عَلَيْكِ حَرَامُ

"She charged to throw me down, so I said to her: 'Hold back, for I am a man whose being thrown down by you is forbidden.'"

That is, I am a horseman, so you cannot throw me. Abu 'Ali said: it may be a prohibition of worship (taʿabbud). It is asked: how is it possible for a large group of intelligent people to walk within a few parasangs and not find the way out? The answer, according to Abu 'Ali: this may happen by God turning the land on which they were, when they slept, and returning them to the place from which they had started. It may also happen by other means of confusion and obstacles preventing them from leaving, by way of a miracle outside the normal course.

"Arba'īn" (forty) is a time-adverb for the wandering, according to al-Hasan and Qatadah, who said: none of them entered it. On this view, the pause is at "'alayhim" (upon them). Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said: "arba'īna sanatan" (forty years) is a time-adverb for the prohibition, so the pause on this view is at "arba'īna sanatan." On the first view, only their children entered it, as Ibn 'Abbas said, and none of them remained except Yusha' (Joshua) and Kaleb (Caleb). Thus Yusha' went out with their offspring to that city and conquered it. On the second view, whoever remained of them after forty years entered it.

It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Moses and Aaron died in the wandering. Another said: God gave prophethood to Yusha' and commanded him to fight the tyrants (al-jabbārīn). In that period the sun was held back for him until he entered the city. In that period, the one in whose possession the embezzlement (ghulūl) was found was burned. The custom was that when they took spoils, a white fire would descend from heaven and devour the booty, and this was a sign that it had been accepted. If there was embezzlement in it, the fire did not consume it, and the beasts and wild animals came and ate it. Then the fire descended and did not consume what they had taken. He said: "Indeed, among you is embezzlement. Let every tribe pledge allegiance to me." So each tribe pledged to him, and the hand of one man from them stuck to his hand. He said: "Among you is embezzlement. Let every man among you pledge to me." So they pledged to him man by man, until the hand of one man stuck to his hand. He said: "The embezzlement is with you," and he brought out something like the head of a cow made of gold [like a pot, or like its image, of gold, which he had concealed and hidden], and the fire descended and consumed the spoils. It was a white fire like silver, having a rustling (ḥafīf), that is, a sound like the sound of a tree and the wing of a bird, as they relate. They mentioned that the embezzler and his property were burned in a ravine that is now called Ghawr 'Ajiz, known by the name of the embezzler, whose name was 'Ajiz.

I say: From this is derived the punishment of the embezzler among those before us, and its ruling has already been discussed [in our community's law]. As for clarifying what is ambiguous in the name of the prophet and the embezzler in the authentic hadith from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "A prophet among the prophets went out to fight..." The hadith was recorded by Muslim, and in it he said: "He fought and drew near to the town [the wording of al-Bukhari is 'fa-dana min al-qarya,' and perhaps what is here implies an omitted object, meaning he brought his armies and his forces close to it]." (al-Nawawi)

(٤). That is, I will keep it from moving for a time, until the conquest by day is made easy for me.]] "At the time of the afternoon prayer, or near it," he said to the sun, "You are commanded and I am commanded. O God, hold it back for me," and it was held back for him until God granted him the conquest. He said: They gathered what they had seized as booty, and the fire came to consume it, but it refused to eat it. He said: "Among you there is embezzlement (ghulul). Let one man from every tribe pledge allegiance to me." They pledged allegiance to him. He said: Then a man's hand stuck to the hand of two or three men, and he said: "Among you is the embezzlement." And he mentioned something similar to what came before.

Our scholars said: The wisdom in holding back the sun for Yusha' (Joshua) when he fought the people of Ariha (Jericho), and when he was overlooking its conquest on the evening of Friday, and his fear that the sun would set before the conquest, is that if it had not been held back for him, fighting would have become forbidden for him because of the Sabbath, and their enemy would have known it, and would have used the sword against them and destroyed them. So that was a sign for him, specific to him, after his prophethood had been established by the report of Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, according to what is said. And God knows best.

In this hadith the Prophet, peace be upon him, says: "Spoils of war were not made lawful for anyone before us." That is because God, exalted and majestic, saw our weakness and our incapacity, so He made them lawful for us. This refutes the view of those who, in interpreting His words, "and has given you what He has not given to anyone among the worlds" (﴿وَآتاكُمْ مَا لَمْ يُؤْتِ أَحَداً مِنَ الْعالَمِينَ﴾), said that it means the making lawful of spoils and benefiting from them.

Among those who said that Musa, peace be upon him, died in the wandering (al-tih, the desert wilderness) was 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi, and he added: and Harun (Aaron). They had gone out in the wandering to one of the caves, and Harun died, so Musa buried him and returned to the Children of Israel. They said: "What became of Harun?" He said: "He died." They said: "You are lying, but you killed him out of love for us, for he was beloved among the Children of Israel." So God, exalted, revealed to him: "Set out with them to his grave, for I will raise him up, so that he may tell them that he died a natural death and that you did not kill him." So he set out with them to his grave and called out, "O Harun!" and he came out of his grave shaking his head, and said: "Am I your killer?" He said: "No, but I died." He said: "Return to your resting place," and he went back.

Al-Hasan said: Musa did not die in the wandering. Others said: Musa conquered Ariha, and Yusha' was at its vanguard, and he fought the tyrants who were there. Then Musa entered it with the Children of Israel, and he remained there as long as God willed him to remain. Then God took him to Himself, and no one of creation knows his grave. Al-Tha'labi said: This is the most sound of the opinions.

I say: Muslim transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Angel of Death was sent to Musa, peace be upon him. When he came to him, he slapped him and gouged out his eye. He returned to his Lord and said: "You sent me to a servant who does not want death." He said: God returned his eye to him and said: "Go back to him and tell him: let him place his hand on the back of a bull, and for every hair his hand covers he will have a year." He said: "O Lord, and then what?" He said: "Then death." He said: "Then now." So he asked God to bring him near to the Holy Land, a stone's throw away. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "If I had been there, I would have shown you his grave beside the road, under the red sand hill." So this is our Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who knew his grave and described its place, and saw him there standing and praying, as in the hadith of the Night Journey (al-Isra'). However, it is possible that God hid it from all creatures other than him, and did not make it known among them, and perhaps that was so that it would not be worshipped. And God knows best. By "the road" is meant the road to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). In some narrations it occurs as "beside Mount Sinai" (al-Tur) instead of "the road."

The scholars differed in interpreting Musa's slapping the eye of the Angel of Death and gouging it out, on several views. Among them: that it was an imagined eye and not a real one. This is false, because it leads to the conclusion that what the prophets see of the forms of angels has no reality. Among them: that it was a figurative eye, and that he gouged it out with the proof (hujja), and this is metaphor, not reality. Among them: that he, peace be upon him, did not recognize the Angel of Death, and that he saw a man who had entered his house without permission, intending to take his soul, so he defended himself, slapped his eye and gouged it out, and defending oneself in such a case is obligatory by every possible means. This is a good view, because it is literal regarding the eye and the slap. This was said by the Imam Abu Bakr ibn Khuzayma. However, it was objected to on the basis of what is in the hadith, namely that when the Angel of Death returned to God, exalted, he said: "O Lord, You sent me to a servant who does not want death." Had Musa not recognized him, the statement from the Angel of Death would not have been accurate. Also, his words in the other narration, "Answer your Lord," indicate that he introduced himself. And God knows best. Among them: that Musa, peace be upon him, had a quick temper; when he became angry, smoke rose from his qalansuwa (a cap worn on the head), and the hair of his body raised his robe, and the quickness of his anger was the cause of his slapping the Angel of Death. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This, as you see, is not so, for the prophets are protected from such things occurring from them at the beginning, in contentment or anger.

Among them, and it is the sound one of these views: that Musa, peace be upon him, recognized the Angel of Death, and that he came to take his soul, but he came as one who is certain that he had been commanded to take his soul without choice. Musa had what our Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, had stated explicitly: that God does not take the soul of a prophet until He informs him. So when he came to him in a manner other than the one he had been told, he hastened, with his nobility and strength of character, to discipline him, and he slapped him and gouged out his eye, as a test for the Angel of Death, since he had not explicitly offered him the choice. Among what indicates the soundness of this is that when the Angel of Death returned to him and gave him the choice between life and death, he chose death and submitted. And God, in His unseen knowledge, is most wise and most knowing. This is the most sound of what has been said about the death of Musa, peace be upon him.

The commentators have mentioned in this matter stories and reports, of whose soundness God alone knows, and the sound reports suffice without them. Musa's age was one hundred and twenty years. It is related that Yusha' saw him after his death in a dream and said to him: "How did you find death?" He said: "Like a sheep being skinned while still alive." This is correct in meaning. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said in the sound hadith: "Indeed death has agonies (sakarat)," as we have explained in the book "al-Tadhkira."

As for His words, ﴿فَلا تَأْسَ عَلَى الْقَوْمِ الْفاسِقِينَ﴾ (So do not grieve over the defiant people), that means: do not be sad. Al-asa is grief; asiya, ya'sa, asan means he grieved. He said [the poet]:

They say, "Do not perish from grief, and bear it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 3):

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you"﴾ are a clarification from Allah the Exalted that their forefathers rebelled against Musa and disobeyed him, and so did these (people) against Muhammad (ﷺ). This is a consolation for him. That is, "O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you, and remember the story of Musa." It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Kathir that he recited "Ya qawmu udhkuru" with a ḍamma on the mim (qawmu), and likewise whatever resembles it, and its implied meaning is "O you people" (yā ayyuhā al-qawm).

(When He placed among you prophets) "anbiya'" is not declined (lam yanṣarif), because it has the feminine alif (alif al-ta'nith).

(And made you kings) That is, you control your own affairs, and no conqueror overpowers you in them, after you had been slaves of Pharaoh, subdued. So He rescued you from him by drowning (him). Thus they are "kings" in this sense. Al-Suddi and al-Husayn and others explained it in this manner. Al-Suddi said: each one of them was king over himself, his family and his property. Qatadah said: He only said "and made you kings" because we used to hear that they were the first of the children of Adam to be served (by others). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is weak, because the Copts used to employ the Children of Israel, and the apparent matter regarding the children of Adam is that some of them would subjugate others from the time they multiplied and spread; the nations only differed in the meaning of "possession" (tamlik) alone. It was also said: He made you people of dwellings who may not be entered upon except with permission. Its meaning is narrated from a group of the scholars. Ibn 'Abbas said: If a man does not let anyone enter his house except with his permission, then he is a king. And from al-Hasan and also Zayd ibn Aslam: whoever has a house, a wife and a servant is a king. This is also the view of Abdullah ibn 'Amr, as in Sahih Muslim, from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, when a man asked him, "Are we not among the poor emigrants?" Abdullah said to him, "Do you have a wife you return to?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Do you have a dwelling you live in?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then you are among the wealthy." He said, "But I have a servant." He said, "Then you are among the kings." Ibn al-'Arabi said: The benefit of this is that if a man is obligated to expiate (kaffarah) and he owns a house and a servant, he sells them for the expiation and it is not permissible for him to fast, because he is able to free a slave, and kings do not expiate by fasting, nor are they described as incapable of manumission. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: He made them kings through the manna, the quails, the rock and the clouds, that is, they were served like kings. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning the servant and the dwelling, and this was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah, who added the wife. Zayd ibn Aslam said likewise, except that he said, as is known from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever has a house, or said a dwelling, to which he returns, and a wife and a servant who serves him, then he is a king." Al-Nahhas mentioned it. It is also said: whoever is independent of others is a king. This is like what the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wakes up secure in his dwelling, healthy in his body, and has his food for the day, it is as if the whole world has been gathered for him."

The words of Allah the Exalted: (And gave you) that is, bestowed upon you (what He had not given to anyone of the worlds). According to the majority of the commentators the address is from Musa to his people, and this is the apparent sense of the speech. Mujahid said: the "giving" refers to the manna, the quails, the rock and the clouds. It was also said: the multitude of prophets among them, and the signs that came to them. It was also said: hearts free from rancour and deceit. It was also said: the lawfulness of spoils of war and benefiting from them. I say: this view is rejected, for spoils of war were not made lawful to anyone except this Ummah, as is established in the Sahih, and its explanation will come, Allah willing. This statement of Musa was a preparation of their souls so that they would be strengthened and would take up the matter of entering the land of the tyrants with strength, and would proceed in that with the authority of one whom Allah has honoured and elevated. The meaning of "of the worlds" is "of the worlds of your time," according to al-Hasan. Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik said: the address is to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is a departure from the apparent meaning of the speech, one that is not fitting in this way. And the reports are consistent that Damascus is the seat of the tyrants. And "the holy" (al-Muqaddasah) means "the purified." Mujahid said: "the blessed," and blessing is purification from drought, hunger and the like. Qatadah said: it is al-Sham (Greater Syria). Mujahid said: it is Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and what surrounds it. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: it is Jericho (Ariha'). Al-Zajjaj said: Damascus, Palestine, and some say Jordan. Qatadah's view encompasses all of this.

(Which Allah has prescribed for you) That is, He ordained your entry into it and promised you its entry and its dwelling as yours. When the Children of Israel left Egypt, He commanded them to fight the people of Jericho in the lands of Palestine, but they said: "We have no knowledge of those lands." So, by the command of Allah, He sent twelve chieftains (nuqaba'), one from each tribe, to spy out the news, as was mentioned earlier. They saw its inhabitants, the tyrants of the 'Amalaqah, who were of enormous bodies, to the extent that it is said that one of them saw these chieftains, took them in his sleeve together with some fruit he had brought from his orchard, and came with them to the king, scattered them before him and said: "These people intend to fight us." The king said to them: "Go back to your companion and tell him our news," as mentioned earlier. It was also said: when they returned they took a cluster of grapes from that land; some said one man carried it, and some said the twelve chieftains carried it together. I say: this is more plausible, for it is said that when they reached the tyrants they found that two of them could enter into the sleeve of one of them, and that a single cluster of one of them could be carried only by five of them on a pole, and that half a pomegranate, once its seeds were removed, could hold five or four persons. (Al-Alusi said: these reports, in my view, are like the reports of 'Uj ibn 'Unuq, and they are a fabricated tale.)

I say: there is no contradiction between this and the first account, for that tyrant who took them in his sleeve, and it is said in his lap, was 'Uj ibn 'Unaq, who was the tallest of them in stature and the greatest in form, as will be mentioned later, Allah willing. The height of the rest of them was six and a half cubits according to Muqatil. Al-Kalbi said: the height of each man of them was eighty cubits, and Allah knows best. When they spread the report, all except Yusha' and Kalib ibn Yuqina refused, and the Children of Israel refused to fight. They were punished with the wandering (al-tih) for forty years, until those disobedient ones died and their children grew up, and they fought the tyrants and overcame them.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not turn back on your heels﴾ That is, do not turn back from my obedience and from what I have commanded you concerning fighting the tyrants. It was also said: do not turn back from obedience to Allah to disobedience to Him, and the meaning is one.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed in it are a people of tyrants"﴾ That is, huge of body and tall, as was mentioned before. It is said: "a jabbarah palm" meaning a tall palm. The jabbar is the one who magnifies himself and refuses humiliation and poverty. Al-Zajjaj said: the jabbar among human beings is the insolent one, who compels people to do what he wishes, so its root in this sense is from ijbar, which is coercion, for he compels others to what he desires, and "ajbarahu" means "he compelled him." It was also said: it is derived from setting a bone (jabr al-'azm), so the original meaning of jabbar in this sense is the one who sets right his own affairs, then it came to be used for everyone who draws benefit to himself, whether rightly or wrongly. It was also said that setting a bone reverts to the meaning of compulsion. Al-Farra' said: I have not heard fa''al from af'ala except in two words: jabbar from ajbar, and darrak from adraka. Then it was said: these were remnants of 'Ad. It was also said: they were of the descendants of 'Is ibn Ishaq, and they were of the Romans, and with them was 'Uj al-A'naq, whose height was three thousand and three hundred and thirty-three cubits, as said by Ibn 'Umar. [[In manuscripts J, H, K and Z: "three thousand and twenty thousand"... etc.]] He used to seize the clouds, that is, pull them down with his staff and drink from them, and he would take the fish from the bottom of the sea and roast it in the sun's heat by raising it up to the sun, then eat it. He was present at the flood of Nuh (peace be upon him), but the water did not reach beyond his knees, and his lifespan was three thousand six hundred years. It is said that he uprooted a rock the size of Musa's army in order to crush them with it, but Allah sent a bird which pecked at it, and it fell on his neck and felled him. Musa (peace be upon him), whose height was ten cubits, and his staff was ten cubits, went out and leapt up into the sky ten cubits, and he struck only his ankle while he was fallen, and he killed him. It was also said: rather he struck him in the vein beneath his ankle, and he fell and died, and he landed upon the Nile of Egypt, and so it became a bridge for them for a year. Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, Makki and others mentioned this meaning with varying wording. Al-Kalbi said: 'Uj was a descendant of Harut and Marut, when they lay with a woman and she conceived. And Allah knows best. [[Al-Qurtubi's note: all that the author mentions in this place of the Isra'iliyyat (narratives from Jewish and Christian sources) is not to be relied upon.]]

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And we will never enter it until they leave it﴾ meaning the city of Iliya', and it is said Jericho, until they hand it over to us without fighting. It was also said: they said this out of fear of the tyrants, and did not intend disobedience, for they said: "If they leave it, then we will enter."

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Two men from among those who feared said﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and others said: they were Yusha' and Kalib ibn Yuqina, and it is said Ibn Qaniya, and they were of the twelve chieftains. And "who feared" means of the tyrants. Qatadah said: they feared Allah the Exalted. Al-Dahhak said: they were two men who were in the city of the tyrants, upon the religion of Musa, so the meaning of "feared" in this view is that they feared the 'Amaliqah by nature, lest they discover their faith and afflict them, but they trusted in Allah. It was also said: they feared the weakness and cowardice of the Children of Israel. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr read "yukhafun" with a ḍamma on the ya', and this strengthens the view that they were not of the people of Musa.

(Upon whom Allah had bestowed favour) That is, with Islam, or with certainty and righteousness.

(ادْخُلُوا عَلَيْهِمُ الْبابَ فَإِذا دَخَلْتُمُوهُ فَإِنَّكُمْ غالِبُونَ) ﴿Enter upon them through the gate, and when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious.﴾ Said the two men to the Children of Israel: "Let not the great size of their bodies terrify you, for their hearts are filled with fear of you. Their bodies are large but their hearts are weak." They knew that if they entered through that gate, victory would be theirs. It is also possible that the two men said this out of confidence in God's promise. Then they said: (وَعَلَى اللَّهِ فَتَوَكَّلُوا إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ) ﴿And upon God rely, if you are believers﴾, meaning, believing in Him, for He will help you.

Then it was said, according to the first opinion: when the two men said this, the Children of Israel wanted to stone them, and they said: "We believe you both, and we will abandon the word of ten [of them]!" Then they said to Moses: (إِنَّا لَنْ نَدْخُلَها أَبَداً مَا دامُوا فِيها) ﴿Indeed, we will never enter it as long as they are within it.﴾ This was obstinacy, a refusal to fight, and despair of victory.

Then they showed ignorance of the attributes of the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, when they said: "So go, you and your Lord" (فَاذْهَبْ أَنْتَ وَرَبُّكَ). They described Him with going and moving, whereas God is exalted above that. This indicates that they were anthropomorphists (mushabbihah), which is the meaning of the statement of al-Hasan, for he said: "This is disbelief in God on their part," and this is the most apparent meaning of the words. It was also said: the meaning is that the help of your Lord for you is more deserved than our help, and His fighting with you, if you are His messenger, is more fitting than our fighting. On this interpretation, their words were disbelief, because they doubted his prophethood. It was also said that the meaning is: "Go, you, and fight, and let your Lord help you." It was also said: by "Lord" they meant Aaron, who was older than Moses, and Moses used to obey him. In sum, they transgressed by their words, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾, that is, do not grieve over them.

(إِنَّا هاهُنا قاعِدُونَ) ﴿Indeed, we are sitting here﴾, meaning, we will not move and we will not fight. It is permissible to read "qā'idūn" as "qā'idīn" in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), since the speech was complete before it.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I possess none except myself and my brother"﴾, because he was obeyed by him. It was also said the meaning is: "I possess none except myself," then he began anew and said, "and my brother," meaning: my brother also possesses none except himself. So "my brother" according to the first view is in the accusative position, conjoined to "myself," and according to the second view is in the nominative position. If you wish, you may conjoin it to the subject of "inna," which is the ya' (my), meaning: "I and my brother possess only ourselves." And if you wish, you may conjoin it to the pronoun in "amliku" (I possess), as if he said: "Neither I nor my brother possess except ourselves."

(فَافْرُقْ بَيْنَنا وَبَيْنَ الْقَوْمِ الْفاسِقِينَ) ﴿So part between us and the defiant people﴾. It is asked: in what way did he ask God to separate him from these people? There are several answers. First: by that which indicates their distance from the truth and their departure from rectitude in the disobedience they committed, and for this reason they were cast into the wandering (tīh). Second: by requesting distinction, meaning, distinguish us from their community and their entirety, and do not join us with them in punishment. It was also said the meaning is: judge between us and them by Your protecting us from the disobedience with which You tested them. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Therein is made distinct every precise matter﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:4], meaning, is decided. And He did so when He caused them to die in the wandering. It was also said: he meant only in the Hereafter, that is, make us among the people of Paradise and do not make us with them in the Fire. As evidence for the distinction that indicates separation in conditions, the poet said:

يَا رَبِّ فَافْرُقْ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنِي ... أَشَدَّ مَا فَرَّقْتَ بَيْنَ اثنين

"O Lord, part him from me, with the strongest parting You have ever made between two."

Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, that he read: "fāfriq" with a kasra on the rā'.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land."﴾ God answered his supplication and punished them with the wandering for forty years. The root meaning of tīh in the language is bewilderment; it is said: tāha yatīhu tīhan and tawhan when he was bewildered, and tayyahtuhu and tawwahtuhu (I caused him to wander), with yā' and wāw, the yā' being more common. "Al-arḍ al-tayhā'" is the land in which one cannot find the way, and "arḍ tīh" and "tayhā'" are used. From this, another said:

تِيهٌ أَتَاوِيهُ عَلَى السُّقَّاطِ

[This is from al-'Ajjaj, describing an unknown land with no signs by which one may be guided. "Atāwīh" means things of wandering, and "al-saqqāṭ" refers to whoever falls upon them, those who are unpatient and do not find the way. The verse's first half is: "wa-basṭahu bi-sa'at al-basāṭ" (and its spreading out with the breadth of the plain), and al-basāṭ means the wide place of the earth. It was also said this verse is: "wa-baldatin ba'īdat al-niyāṭ, majhūlatin taghtāl khaṭw al-khāṭī" (and a town far in its distances, unknown, stealing the step of the walker).]

Another said:

بِتَيْهَاءَ قَفْرِ وَالْمَطِيُّ كَأَنَّهَا ... قَطَا الْحَزَنِ قَدْ كَانَتْ فِرَاخًا بُيُوضُهَا

"In a barren wandering waste, while the mounts were like the sand-grouse of the rough ground whose eggs had been hatched into chicks."

They used to travel within a few parasangs, said to be about six parasangs, the whole day and night, so they would wake up where they had gone to sleep and would sleep where they had woken up. Thus they were wanderers with no settled home. It has been disputed whether Moses and Aaron were with them. It was said: no, because the wandering was a punishment, and the years of the wandering were according to the number of days of the calf, so each day was matched with a year. And He said: ﴿So part between us and the defiant people﴾. It was also said: they were with them, but God made the matter easy for them both, just as He made the fire cool and safe for Abraham.

The meaning of "muḥarramah" (forbidden) is that they are prevented from entering it, as one says: God forbade your face to the Fire, and I forbade you entry into the house. It is a prohibition of prevention, not a legal prohibition, according to most of the exegetes, as the poet said:
