Among them, and it is the sound one of these views: that Musa, peace be upon him, recognized the Angel of Death, and that he came to take his soul, but he came as one who is certain that he had been commanded to take his soul without choice. Musa had what our Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, had stated explicitly: that God does not take the soul of a prophet until He informs him. So when he came to him in a manner other than the one he had been told, he hastened, with his nobility and strength of character, to discipline him, and he slapped him and gouged out his eye, as a test for the Angel of Death, since he had not explicitly offered him the choice. Among what indicates the soundness of this is that when the Angel of Death returned to him and gave him the choice between life and death, he chose death and submitted. And God, in His unseen knowledge, is most wise and most knowing. This is the most sound of what has been said about the death of Musa, peace be upon him.

The commentators have mentioned in this matter stories and reports, of whose soundness God alone knows, and the sound reports suffice without them. Musa's age was one hundred and twenty years. It is related that Yusha' saw him after his death in a dream and said to him: "How did you find death?" He said: "Like a sheep being skinned while still alive." This is correct in meaning. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said in the sound hadith: "Indeed death has agonies (sakarat)," as we have explained in the book "al-Tadhkira."

As for His words, ﴿فَلا تَأْسَ عَلَى الْقَوْمِ الْفاسِقِينَ﴾ (So do not grieve over the defiant people), that means: do not be sad. Al-asa is grief; asiya, ya'sa, asan means he grieved. He said [the poet]:

They say, "Do not perish from grief, and bear it."

**Question one:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth﴾, and the rest of the verse. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that Allah alerts that the injustice of the Jews, and their breaking of covenants and pacts, is like the injustice of the son of Adam to his brother. The meaning is: if these Jews intend to treat you treacherously, O Muhammad, they have already killed the prophets before you, and Qabil (Cain) killed Habil (Abel), and evil is ancient. That is, remind them of this story, for it is a true account and not like the fabricated traditions. In this there is a rebuke for those who oppose Islam and a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ).

The scholars differed concerning the two sons of Adam. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: they were not his own sons. They were two men from the Children of Israel, through whom Allah struck the example to demonstrate the envy of the Jews. There was enmity between them, so they drew near (to God) with two offerings, and offerings were only (accepted) among the Children of Israel. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is an error. How could anyone among the Children of Israel be ignorant of the manner of burial, so that he would have to imitate the crow? The correct view is that they were his own sons. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes, and it was said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and others. They are Qabil and Habil. The offering of Qabil was a bundle of grain-stalks, because he was a farmer, and he chose it from the worst of his crops. Then he found in it a good ear, so he rubbed it and ate it. The offering of Habil was a ram, because he was a herdsman, which he took from his best flock. "So it was accepted," and it was raised up to Paradise, and it kept grazing there until the Sacrificed One, upon him be peace, was ransomed with it. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others.

When the offering of Habil was accepted, because he was a believer, Qabil said to him out of envy, (claiming) that he was an unbeliever: "Will you walk upon the earth while people see you as better than me?" "I will surely kill you." It was also said that the cause of this offering was that Hawwa (Eve), upon her be peace, used to bear, with every pregnancy, a male and a female, except Shith (Seth), upon him be peace, whom she bore alone in place of Habil, as will come later. His name was Hibat Allah (Gift of God), because Jibril, upon him be peace, said to Hawwa when she bore him: "This is the gift of God to you in place of Habil." Adam was one hundred and thirty [[In (j) and (w): eighty.]] years old on the day Shith was born. Adam used to marry a male from one birth to a female from the other birth, and a man could not marry his twin sister. So with Qabil she bore a beautiful sister named Iqlimiya, and with Habil she bore a sister who was not like that, named Liyudha. When Adam wished to marry them, Qabil said: "I have more right to my sister." Adam commanded him, but he did not obey, and he rebuked him, but he did not desist. So they agreed to make offerings. This was said by a group of exegetes, among them Ibn Mas'ud. It is also related that Adam was present at that. And Allah knows best.

It has been related on this subject from Ja'far al-Sadiq that Adam did not marry his daughter to his son, and that if Adam had done so, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have shunned it, and the religion of Adam was no different from the religion of the Prophet (ﷺ). Also (it is related) that when Allah sent Adam and Hawwa down to the earth and brought them together, Hawwa bore a daughter, whom he named ʿAnaq, and she transgressed, and she was the first to transgress upon the face of the earth. So Allah gave power over her to someone who killed her. Then she bore Qabil to Adam, then she bore him Habil. When Qabil reached maturity, Allah manifested to him a jinn-female from the offspring of the jinn, called Jamalah, in the form of a human female, and Allah revealed to Adam to marry her to Qabil, and he married her to him. When Habil reached maturity, Allah sent down to Adam a hur (a celestial maiden) [[In (j) and (w): hawra' (a woman with large dark eyes).]] in the form of a human female, and created for her a womb. Her name was Bazlah. When Habil looked at her, he loved her. So Allah revealed to Adam to marry Bazlah to Habil, and he did so. Qabil said: "O my father, am I not older than my brother?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then I had more right to what you did with him than he did!" Adam said to him: "My son, Allah has commanded me to do that, and bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills." He said: "No, by Allah, rather you preferred him over me." Adam said: "Then offer an offering, and whichever of you has his offering accepted will have more right to the bounty."

I say: this account from Ja'far, I do not think it is sound. The correct view is what we have mentioned, that he used to marry a boy of one birth to a girl of the other birth. The evidence for this from the Book is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate and dispersed from both of them many men and women﴾ [An-Nisa: 1]. This is almost explicit. Then that was abrogated [naskh, abrogation], as has been explained earlier in Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 62 onwards.]]. The total of what Hawwa bore was forty, male and female, in twenty births. The first of them was Qabil and his twin Iqlimiya, and the last of them was Abd al-Mughith. Then Allah blessed the offspring of Adam. Ibn Abbas said: Adam did not die until his children and the children of his children reached forty thousand.

As for what has been related from Ja'far—that she bore a daughter and that she transgressed—it is said: with whom did she transgress? With a jinn who came down to her? Such a matter requires a sound transmission that removes all excuse, and that is absent. And Allah knows best.

**Question two:** In Habil's saying ﴿He said: Allah only accepts from the righteous﴾ there is an omitted statement before it, because when Qabil said to him, "I will surely kill you," he said: "Why would you kill me when I have committed no crime, and I am not at fault in Allah's acceptance of my offering? Indeed, I was fearful of Him, and I was upon the clear path of truth, and Allah only accepts from the righteous." Ibn Atiyyah said: the meaning of piety here is guarding against shirk (associating partners with Allah), by the consensus of Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah). Whoever guards against it while being a monotheist, his deeds whose intention is true are accepted. As for one who guards against shirk and sins, he has the highest rank of acceptance and of being sealed with mercy. This is known from the report of Allah the Exalted, not because it is obligatory upon Allah by reason. Adi ibn Thabit and others said: the offering of the pious of this community is prayer. I say: this is specific to one type of worship. Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, said: Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him. My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely protect him. I do not hesitate about anything I am going to do as I hesitate about taking the soul of the believer, who dislikes death, and I dislike to harm him."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 28–29:

There are two issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand toward you to kill you﴾ (the verse). That is, if you intend to kill me, I do not intend to kill you; this is a form of submission on his part. In a report: "When strife occurs, be like the better of the two sons of Adam." Abu Dawud related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: I said, "O Messenger of God, if someone enters my house and stretches his hand toward me to kill me?" He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Be like the better of the two sons of Adam," and he recited this verse: "If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me..." Mujahid said: The obligation upon them at that time was that no one should draw a sword, and that one should not defend himself against one who intends to kill him. Our scholars said: This is among the things for which worship may be enjoined, but in our law it is permissible to repel (an aggressor) by consensus. There is disagreement over whether that is obligatory for him, and the more correct view is that it is obligatory, because of what it contains of forbidding wrongdoing. Among the Hashwiyya there are people who do not permit the one who is attacked to defend himself, and they argued with the hadith of Abu Dharr [hadith of Abu Dharr: see Ahkam al-Jassas, vol. 1, p. 402, Istanbul edition, where the hadith is given in full], and the scholars interpreted it as refraining from fighting during strife and restraining the hand at times of doubt, as we have explained in the book "al-Tadhkira." Abdullah ibn Amr and the majority of people said: Habil was physically stronger than Qabil, but he refrained. Ibn Atiyya said: This is the more apparent view, and from here it is strengthened that Qabil was a sinner, not an unbeliever, because if he were an unbeliever there would be no sense in refraining here. The sense of refraining in this case is that the one who refrains refuses to fight a monotheist, and is content to be wronged so that he will be recompensed in the Hereafter; and 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, did something similar. It was also said: The meaning is, I do not intend to kill you, but I intend to repel you from myself. On this view it was said: He was asleep, and Qabil came and crushed his head with a stone, as will be mentioned. Repelling a person from one who intends to wrong him is permissible even if it results in the death of the aggressor. It was also said: If you begin by killing me, I will not begin killing. It was also said: He meant, if you stretch your hand toward me unjustly, I am not one who does wrong; indeed I fear God, Lord of the worlds.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I want you to bear my sin and your sin﴾. It was said: its meaning is that of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." It was said: O Messenger of God, this is the killer, so what about the killed? He said: "Indeed he was eager to kill his companion." Habil meant: I am not eager to kill you, so the sin that would have fallen upon me had I been eager to kill you, you would bear along with your sin in killing me. It was also said: the meaning of "my sin" is the sin that is specific to me for what I have neglected, i.e., it is taken from my bad deeds and cast upon you because of your wronging me, and you bear your sin in killing me. This is supported by his saying, peace be upon him: "On the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer and the wronged will be brought, and good deeds will be taken from the wrongdoer and added to the good deeds of the wronged, until he is given his due; but if he has no good deeds, some of the wronged one's bad deeds will be taken and cast upon him." Muslim related it in meaning, and it has been mentioned earlier. It is also supported by His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 330]. This is clear and there is no difficulty in it. It was also said: the meaning is, I want that you not bear my sin and your sin, as He said: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you﴾ [An-Nahl 16:15], meaning lest it shake with you. And His saying: ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [An-Nisa 4:176], meaning lest you go astray, with "not" omitted. I say: This is weak, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing." Thus it is established that the sin of killing is incurred. For this reason most scholars said: the meaning is that you return with the sin of my killing and your sin that you committed before killing me. Al-Tha'labi said: This is the view of the majority of commentators. It was also said: it is an interrogative, meaning, "Do I want...?" in the sense of denial, like His saying: ﴿And that is a blessing﴾ [vol. 13, p. 93], meaning, "Is that a blessing?" This is because the intention to kill is disobedience. [Related by al-Qushayri.] Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan was asked: How can a believer want his brother to incur sin and enter the Fire? He said: The intention arose only after he stretched his hand toward him to kill him, and the meaning is: If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I will refrain from that, desiring reward. He was asked: Then why did he say "my sin and your sin," and what sin does he have if he is killed? He said: There are three answers. The first: that you bear the sin of my killing and the sin of your wrongdoing for which my sacrifice was not accepted; this view is related from Mujahid. The second: that you bear the sin of killing me and the sin of your aggression against me, since one may incur sin by aggression even if he does not kill. The third: that if he stretches his hand toward him he incurs sin, and he saw that if he refrains from that, his sin returns upon his companion. This is like your saying: "The wealth is between him and Zayd," meaning the wealth is between them; so the meaning is "that you bear our sin." The root of "baa'" is returning to the mabaa'a, which is the dwelling place. ﴿And they returned with wrath from God﴾ [al-Baqara 2:61], meaning they returned. It has been discussed fully in al-Baqara [vol. 1, p. 430]. The poet said [he is Jabir ibn Jubayr al-Taghlibi]:

Will not kings refrain from us, and fear
Our sanctities? Blood will not return for blood.

[This is how it is related in the book of Sibawayh, where he cites it as evidence for the jussive "yaba'" in answer to an interrogative, and said in its commentary: the sense is "refrain from us, blood will not return for blood," i.e., if they refrain from us and do not kill any of us, no one will be killed in return for another. It is related differently in al-Lisan.]

That is, blood does not return for blood in retaliation.

﴿So you would be among the companions of the Fire﴾ is evidence that at that time they were under obligation, and the promise and threat applied to them. It has been argued from Habil's saying to his brother Qabil, "So you would be among the companions of the Fire," that he was an unbeliever, because the phrase "companions of the Fire" occurs in the Qur'an only with reference to unbelievers. This is rejected here by what we have mentioned from the scholars regarding the interpretation of the verse. The meaning of "among the companions of the Fire" is the duration of your being in it. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 28–29:

There are two issues in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand toward you to kill you﴾ (the verse). That is, if you intend to kill me, I do not intend to kill you; this is a form of submission on his part. In a report: "When strife occurs, be like the better of the two sons of Adam." Abu Dawud related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: I said, "O Messenger of God, if someone enters my house and stretches his hand toward me to kill me?" He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Be like the better of the two sons of Adam," and he recited this verse: "If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me..." Mujahid said: The obligation upon them at that time was that no one should draw a sword, and that one should not defend himself against one who intends to kill him. Our scholars said: This is among the things for which worship may be enjoined, but in our law it is permissible to repel (an aggressor) by consensus. There is disagreement over whether that is obligatory for him, and the more correct view is that it is obligatory, because of what it contains of forbidding wrongdoing. Among the Hashwiyya there are people who do not permit the one who is attacked to defend himself, and they argued with the hadith of Abu Dharr [hadith of Abu Dharr: see Ahkam al-Jassas, vol. 1, p. 402, Istanbul edition, where the hadith is given in full], and the scholars interpreted it as refraining from fighting during strife and restraining the hand at times of doubt, as we have explained in the book "al-Tadhkira." Abdullah ibn Amr and the majority of people said: Habil was physically stronger than Qabil, but he refrained. Ibn Atiyya said: This is the more apparent view, and from here it is strengthened that Qabil was a sinner, not an unbeliever, because if he were an unbeliever there would be no sense in refraining here. The sense of refraining in this case is that the one who refrains refuses to fight a monotheist, and is content to be wronged so that he will be recompensed in the Hereafter; and 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, did something similar. It was also said: The meaning is, I do not intend to kill you, but I intend to repel you from myself. On this view it was said: He was asleep, and Qabil came and crushed his head with a stone, as will be mentioned. Repelling a person from one who intends to wrong him is permissible even if it results in the death of the aggressor. It was also said: If you begin by killing me, I will not begin killing. It was also said: He meant, if you stretch your hand toward me unjustly, I am not one who does wrong; indeed I fear God, Lord of the worlds.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I want you to bear my sin and your sin﴾. It was said: its meaning is that of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." It was said: O Messenger of God, this is the killer, so what about the killed? He said: "Indeed he was eager to kill his companion." Habil meant: I am not eager to kill you, so the sin that would have fallen upon me had I been eager to kill you, you would bear along with your sin in killing me. It was also said: the meaning of "my sin" is the sin that is specific to me for what I have neglected, i.e., it is taken from my bad deeds and cast upon you because of your wronging me, and you bear your sin in killing me. This is supported by his saying, peace be upon him: "On the Day of Resurrection the wrongdoer and the wronged will be brought, and good deeds will be taken from the wrongdoer and added to the good deeds of the wronged, until he is given his due; but if he has no good deeds, some of the wronged one's bad deeds will be taken and cast upon him." Muslim related it in meaning, and it has been mentioned earlier. It is also supported by His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [see vol. 13, p. 330]. This is clear and there is no difficulty in it. It was also said: the meaning is, I want that you not bear my sin and your sin, as He said: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you﴾ [An-Nahl 16:15], meaning lest it shake with you. And His saying: ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [An-Nisa 4:176], meaning lest you go astray, with "not" omitted. I say: This is weak, because of his saying, peace be upon him: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing." Thus it is established that the sin of killing is incurred. For this reason most scholars said: the meaning is that you return with the sin of my killing and your sin that you committed before killing me. Al-Tha'labi said: This is the view of the majority of commentators. It was also said: it is an interrogative, meaning, "Do I want...?" in the sense of denial, like His saying: ﴿And that is a blessing﴾ [vol. 13, p. 93], meaning, "Is that a blessing?" This is because the intention to kill is disobedience. [Related by al-Qushayri.] Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan was asked: How can a believer want his brother to incur sin and enter the Fire? He said: The intention arose only after he stretched his hand toward him to kill him, and the meaning is: If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I will refrain from that, desiring reward. He was asked: Then why did he say "my sin and your sin," and what sin does he have if he is killed? He said: There are three answers. The first: that you bear the sin of my killing and the sin of your wrongdoing for which my sacrifice was not accepted; this view is related from Mujahid. The second: that you bear the sin of killing me and the sin of your aggression against me, since one may incur sin by aggression even if he does not kill. The third: that if he stretches his hand toward him he incurs sin, and he saw that if he refrains from that, his sin returns upon his companion. This is like your saying: "The wealth is between him and Zayd," meaning the wealth is between them; so the meaning is "that you bear our sin." The root of "baa'" is returning to the mabaa'a, which is the dwelling place. ﴿And they returned with wrath from God﴾ [al-Baqara 2:61], meaning they returned. It has been discussed fully in al-Baqara [vol. 1, p. 430]. The poet said [he is Jabir ibn Jubayr al-Taghlibi]:

Will not kings refrain from us, and fear
Our sanctities? Blood will not return for blood.

[This is how it is related in the book of Sibawayh, where he cites it as evidence for the jussive "yaba'" in answer to an interrogative, and said in its commentary: the sense is "refrain from us, blood will not return for blood," i.e., if they refrain from us and do not kill any of us, no one will be killed in return for another. It is related differently in al-Lisan.]

That is, blood does not return for blood in retaliation.

﴿So you would be among the companions of the Fire﴾ is evidence that at that time they were under obligation, and the promise and threat applied to them. It has been argued from Habil's saying to his brother Qabil, "So you would be among the companions of the Fire," that he was an unbeliever, because the phrase "companions of the Fire" occurs in the Qur'an only with reference to unbelievers. This is rejected here by what we have mentioned from the scholars regarding the interpretation of the verse. The meaning of "among the companions of the Fire" is the duration of your being in it. And God knows best.

This passage has four issues. The first is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So his soul facilitated for him the killing of his brother﴾. That is, his soul made the matter appealing and easy for him, encouraged him, and presented to him that killing his brother was easy and simple [for him]. It is said: "ṭāʿa al-shayʾu yaṭūʿu," meaning it became easy and submissive. "Ṭawwaʿahu fulān lahu" means he made it easy for him. Al-Harawi said: "ṭawwaʿat" and "aṭāʿat" have the same meaning; one says "ṭāʿa lahu kadhā" when he came to it willingly. It is also said that his soul complied with him in killing his brother, so the preposition was dropped and the noun became accusative.

It is narrated that he did not know how to kill him, so Iblis came with a bird, or another animal, and began to smash its head between two stones, so that Qabil would imitate him, and he did so. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, Mujahid and others. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud said: he found him sleeping and smashed his head with a stone. This happened at Thawr, a mountain in Makkah, as Ibn ʿAbbas said. It is also said: at the ascent of Hira, related by Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Jaʿfar al-Sadiq said: in Basra, at the site of the Great Mosque. Habil was twenty years old when Qabil killed him.

It is said that Qabil knew killing by his nature, because a person, even if he has not seen killing, knows by his nature that the soul is mortal and can be destroyed. So he took a stone and killed him in the land of India. Allah knows best. When he had killed him, he regretted it and sat weeping by his head. Then two ravens came, fought, and one killed the other. Then it dug a hole for it and buried it. So the killer did the same with his brother. The word "sawʾah" is intended to mean the private parts. It is also said it means the corpse of the slain. Then he fled to the land of ʿAdan in Yemen. Iblis came to him and said: "The fire only consumed your brother's offering because he worshipped fire. So set up a fire for yourself too, which will belong to you and your descendants." So he built a fire-temple, and he is said to be the first to worship fire. Allah knows best.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that when he killed him, while Adam was in Makkah, the trees became withered, the foods changed, the fruits turned sour, the waters became brackish, and the earth became dusty. Adam, upon him be peace, said: "An event has occurred on the earth." So he went to India, and found that Qabil had killed Habil. It is also said that it was Qabil who went to Adam. When he reached him, he said: "Where is Habil?" He said: "I do not know. As if you had appointed me to guard him." Adam said to him: "Did you do it? By Allah, his blood cries out. O Allah, curse the land that drank the blood of Habil." It is narrated that from that time no land has drunk blood.

Then Adam remained a hundred years without laughing, until an angel came to him and said: "May Allah keep you alive, O Adam, and make you cry." He said: "What is it that makes me cry?" [The angel] said: "Make you laugh." This was said by Mujahid and Salim ibn Abi al-Jaʿd. When thirty years had passed from the life of Adam, and that was five years after the killing of Habil, he begot Shith, and his name means "the gift of Allah," that is, a successor in place of Habil. Muqatil said: before Qabil killed Habil, the beasts of prey and the birds used to be familiar with Adam. When Qabil killed Habil they fled; the birds flew into the air, the wild animals went to the wilderness, and the beasts of prey went to the thickets. It is narrated that when Adam's situation changed, he said:

"The lands and those upon them have changed, so the face of the earth is dusty and ugly.
Every taste and colour has changed, and the cheerfulness of the beautiful face has diminished."

This is in many verses, which al-Thaʿlabi and others mentioned. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: thus the verse is, with "bashāshatan" in the accusative and without tanwin. Al-Qushayri and others said: Ibn ʿAbbas said: Adam did not compose poetry, and Muhammad and all the prophets are equal in forbidding poetry. But when Habil was killed, Adam lamented him in Syriac, and it is an elegy in the Syriac language, which he bequeathed to his son Shith, saying: "You are my executor, so preserve this speech from me so that it may be inherited." It was preserved until the time of Yaʿrub ibn Qahtan, who translated it into Arabic and made it into poetry. [Editor's note: Al-Alusi said: some scholars of Arabic mentioned that in that poem there is a fault in grammar, or irregular rhyme, or a poetic license, and it is better not to attribute it to Yaʿrub as well, because of its obvious weakness. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: it is also narrated with "bashāshatan" in the accusative without tanwin, as a specification, and "al-wajh al-malīḥ" in the nominative, and this is not a grammatical error.]

The second issue: It is narrated from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was asked about Tuesday, and he said: "It is the day of blood, in which Hawwa menstruated, and in which the son of Adam killed his brother." It is established in Sahih Muslim and others, from ʿAbdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing." This is a clear statement of the reason. On this basis, Iblis bears a share of the sin of everyone who disobeys by refusing to prostrate, because he was the first to disobey in that way. Likewise, everyone who introduces into the religion of Allah what is not permitted, of innovations (bidaʿ) and desires (ahwāʾ). The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, and whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." This is a clear text on good and evil. He ﷺ also said: "The thing I fear most for my community is the misguiding leaders." All this is explicit and a sound text regarding the meaning of the verse. This applies so long as the doer has not repented of that sin. Adam, upon him be peace, was the first to disobey by eating what he had been forbidden, and no part of the burden of those who disobeyed by eating or drinking what was forbidden, from those after him, falls upon him, by consensus (ijmaʿ), because Adam repented of that and Allah accepted his repentance, so he became like one who did not commit it. Another view: he ate forgetfully, according to the correct opinion among the sayings, as we explained in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 306; this is what befits prophetic infallibility]. The forgetful person is neither sinful nor held accountable.

The third issue: This verse contains an explanation of the state of the envious person, to the point that his envy may drive him to destroy himself by killing the person closest to him in kinship, most intimately bound to him by blood, and most deserving of his kindness and of protecting him from harm.

The fourth issue: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and so he became one of the losers﴾, that is, of those who lost their good deeds. Mujahid said: one of the killer's legs was tied by its shin to its thigh from that day until the Day of Resurrection, and his face is turned toward the sun wherever it turns; in summer he has a pen of fire around him, and in winter a pen of ice around him. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: if this is sound, then it is part of his loss which the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿and so he became one of the losers﴾ include; otherwise, loss includes the loss of this world and the Hereafter. I say: Perhaps this is his punishment according to the view that he was a disobedient person and not an unbeliever, so the meaning of "and so he became one of the losers" is: in this world. Allah knows best.

There are five issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿Then God sent a raven scratching in the earth﴾. Mujahid said: God sent two ravens, and they fought until one of them killed the other; then it dug and buried it. This son of Adam was the first person to be killed. It was also said that the raven scratched the earth to hide its food (ṭu'm, i.e. its food) so that it could retrieve it when needed, since it is the raven's habit to do this, and so Qabil was prompted to conceal his brother. It is related that when Qabil killed Habil, he put him in a bag and carried him on his neck for a hundred years; this is what Mujahid said. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik [in some manuscripts: from Muhammad] that he carried him for one year, and this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. It was also said: until the corpse became putrid (arwaḥa, i.e. it stank), and he did not know what to do with it, until he was guided by the raven, as has been mentioned.

There is a report from Anas who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Allah has favoured the son of Adam with three things after three: with the wind after the spirit, for were it not that the wind comes after the spirit, no intimate would bury another intimate; and with the worm in the corpse, for were it not that the worm falls upon the corpse, the kings would hoard it, and it would be better for them than dirhams and dinars; and with death after old age, for a man grows old until he becomes weary of himself, and his family, his children and his relatives become weary of him, so death is more concealing for him."

Some said: Qabil knew how to bury, but he left his brother in the open out of contempt for him, so God sent a raven scratching the ground over Habil so that it would bury him. At that, he said: "Woe is me! Am I incapable of being like this raven, and of concealing my brother's nakedness?" and he became one of the regretful. This was when he saw God's honouring of Habil by sending the raven to him until it concealed him. That regret was not repentance. It was also said that his regret was over losing him, not over killing him; and if it was over killing him, he had not fulfilled its conditions; or he regretted but his regret did not persist. Ibn 'Abbas said: Had his regret been over killing him, the regret would have been repentance on his part.

It is said that Adam and Hawwa' came to his grave and wept over him for days.

Then Qabil was once on the peak of a mountain when a bull gored him, and he fell to the foot of the mountain with his veins torn apart. It is said that Adam invoked a curse upon him, and the earth swallowed him up. It is also said that Qabil became lonely after killing Habil and stayed in the wilderness, and he could only find food from wild animals; whenever he caught one, he would strike it severely (waqdh, i.e. a severe blow) until it died, and then he would eat it. Ibn 'Abbas said: So the mawqudhah (an animal killed by a blow) was forbidden from the time of Qabil son of Adam, and he was the first of the children of Adam to be driven to the Fire. This is God's words: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who led us astray of the jinn and mankind﴾ [Fussilat: 29], [the verse]. Iblis is the head of the disbelievers among the jinn, and Qabil is the head of sin among mankind, as will be explained in the commentary on Ḥā-Mīm Fuṣṣilat, God willing. It has also been said that regret at that time was not repentance. God knows best about all this, and He is most wise.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that Habil was the first dead person among the children of Adam; for this reason the custom of burial was unknown. Al-Tabari likewise related from Ibn Ishaq, from some people of knowledge, what is in the books of the ancients.

His words "yabḥathu" mean that it searches the earth with its beak and stirs it up. From this the sūrah of Barā'ah was called "al-Buḥūth" (the Searching ones), because it searched out the hypocrites (the vowel of the bāʾ is pronounced with a ḍammah, being the plural of baḥth; Ibn al-Athir said: I saw in al-Fa'iq the sūrah called "al-Buḥūth" with a fatḥah on the bāʾ; if this is correct, it is fa'ūl from the forms of intensification, and it would be an instance of a noun being qualified by its adjective). From this is the saying of the poet:

"If people cover me, I cover myself from them, / and if they search me, among them I am a searched-out subject" [Ibn 'Atiyyah's version; the manuscripts read: "I was among them, a subject of investigation"].

And in the proverb: "Do not be like one who searches on the blade" (al-bāḥith 'alā al-shafrah). The poet said:

"She was like an evil she-goat that stood on her leg / toward a buried knife, stirring it up."

The second issue: God sent the raven as wisdom, so that the son of Adam would see how to bury, and this is the meaning of God's words: ﴿Then He caused him to die and assigned him a grave﴾ [Abasa: 21]. Thus the raven's act of burial became a lasting sunnah among creation, an obligation upon all people as a communal duty (fard kifayah): if some of them perform it, the obligation is lifted from the rest. Those most entitled to it are the nearest relatives who are closest to the deceased, then the neighbours, then all Muslims. As for the disbelievers, Abu Dawud related from 'Ali who said: I said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Your uncle, the erring old man, has died." He said: "Go and cover your father with earth, then do not do anything new until you come to me." So I went and buried him, then came to him, and he ordered me, so I washed, and he prayed for me.

The third issue: it is recommended that the grave be spacious and well made, for what Ibn Majah related from Hisham ibn 'Amir (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Dig, and make it spacious, and make it good." It is also related from al-Adra' al-Sulami who said: I came one night to guard the Prophet (ﷺ), and there was a man whose recitation was loud. The Prophet (ﷺ) went out, and I said: "O Messenger of Allah, this man is showing off [from riya', ostentation; it seems the Prophet (peace be upon him) turned away from his speech to indicate that it was wrong, and later explained that the matter was contrary to what he claimed]." He said: Then he died in Madinah, and they finished preparing him and carried his bier. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Be gentle with him; Allah is gentle with him, for he loved Allah and His Messenger." He said: And he attended his grave and said: "Make room for him; may Allah make room for him." Some of his companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, you have grieved for him?" He said: "Indeed, for he loved Allah and His Messenger." [Added from Ibn Majah.] It was related by Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, from Zayd ibn al-Hubab, from Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id.

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Al-Adra' al-Sulami related one hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), and from him related Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Maqburi, and [unclear in the text] Hisham ibn 'Amir ibn Umayyah ibn al-Hasḥas ibn 'Amir ibn Ghanm ibn 'Adi ibn al-Najjar al-Ansari. He was called Shihab in the Jahiliyyah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) changed his name and called him Hisham. His father 'Amir was martyred at the Battle of Uhud. Hisham settled in Basra and died there. This is mentioned in the Kitab al-Sahabah.

The fourth issue: it is said that the lahd (a niche dug into the side of the grave) is better than the shaq (a trench with a central channel), for it is what Allah chose for His Messenger (ﷺ). When the Prophet (ﷺ) died, there were two men in Madinah, one of whom made a lahd and the other did not. They said: "Whichever of them comes first, let him do his work." The one who made a lahd came and dug a lahd for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Malik mentioned this in the Muwatta' from Hisham ibn 'Urwah from his father, and Ibn Majah related it from Anas ibn Malik and 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with them both). The two men were Abu Talhah and Abu 'Ubaydah; Abu Talhah made a lahd, and Abu 'Ubaydah made a shaq. The lahd is to dig in the side of the grave if the soil is firm; the deceased is placed in it, then bricks are laid over it, then earth is poured over. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said in his final illness: "Make a lahd for me, and set up the bricks over me as was done for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Related by Muslim. Ibn Majah and others related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The lahd is for us, and the shaq is for others."

The fifth issue: Ibn Majah related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab who said: I attended Ibn 'Umar at a funeral, and when he placed it in the lahd he said: "In the name of Allah, and in the way of Allah, and upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." When he began to level the bricks over the lahd, he said: "O Allah, protect her from Satan and from the punishment of the grave. O Allah, lift the earth from her two sides, raise her spirit, and receive her from You with pleasure." I said: "O Ibn 'Umar, is this something you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or did you say it by your own opinion?" He said: "If I were to speak by opinion!... Rather, it is something I heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It is also related from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over a funeral, then went to the grave of the deceased and threw earth over it from the direction of the head three times.

These are the rulings that relate to the meaning of the verse.

The word "yā waylatā" (woe is me) is originally "yā waylatī", then the yā' was replaced by an alif. Al-Hasan recited it according to the original with a yā': "yā waylatī". The first is more eloquent, because omitting the yā' in the vocative is more common. It is a word that the Arabs use at the time of destruction, said Sibawayh. Al-Asma'i said: "Waylun" means distance (bu'd). Al-Hasan recited "a-'ajiztu" with a kasrah on the jīm. Al-Nahhas said: This is an irregular dialect; one says "'ajizat al-mar'ah" only when her buttocks become large, and "'ajiztu 'an al-shay'" means "I was unable to do the thing," with the verbal noun "'ajz" and "ma'jizah" and "ma'jazah." And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 32:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Because of that﴾, i.e., because of the consequence of that killer and his offence. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., because of his crime. It is said: "ajala al-rajulu 'ala ahlihi sharran, ya'julu ajlan, idha jana" (the man committed evil against his family, i.e., he committed a crime), like "akhadha, ya'khudhu, akhdhan." Al-Khinnawt [[Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to Khuwwat ibn Jubayr, and so does al-Lisan. The line is in the Diwan of Zuhayr. In manuscripts j, z, k, h: dhat baynihim.]] said:

"And the people of a good tent, among whom I was,
They fought over a matter, and I am its 'ajil (the one who bears its consequence)."

That is, its perpetrator (jani). It is also said: "I am its jarr (one who drags it) upon them." 'Adi ibn Zayd said:

"Indeed, God has favoured you
Above him who tightens his loins (ahka'a) with a waistcloth."

Its root meaning is "jarr" (dragging), and from it comes "al-ajal" (the term), because it is a time to which the first contract is dragged. From it also comes "al-ajil," the opposite of "al-'ajil" (the immediate), and it has the sense of a matter being dragged to it, something previously determined. From it also comes "ajal" meaning "na'am" (yes), because it is submission to what has been dragged to it. From it also comes "al-ijl" [[In the originals: al-ajal, which is a plural.]] for a herd of wild cattle, because some of them are dragged along by others, as al-Rummani said. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' Abu Ja'far read: "min ijli dhalika" with a kasra on the nun and the hamza omitted, and this is a dialect. The original is "min ajli dhalika," so the kasra of the hamza was placed on the nun and the hamza was dropped. Then it was said: it is permissible that his saying "min ajli dhalika" be connected to his saying "min al-nadimin" (Al-Ma'idah 5:31), so the pause is on "min ajli dhalika." It is also permissible that it be connected to what follows it, which is "kataba-na" (We prescribed). Then "min ajli" is the beginning of a statement, and the completion is "min al-nadimin." Most people hold this view, meaning: because of the cause of this incident, We prescribed. He singled out the Children of Israel for mention, although nations before them had also prohibited killing a soul, because they were the first nation for whom the threat concerning killing souls was prescribed in writing, whereas before that it had been an unrestricted command. So the matter was made more severe for the Children of Israel through the Book, in accordance with their transgression and their shedding of blood. The meaning of "without a soul" is: without his having killed a soul, thereby deserving execution. God has prohibited killing in all the sacred laws except for three cases: disbelief after belief, or adultery after marriage (ihsan), or killing a soul unjustly and aggressively. "Or corruption in the land" means polytheism (shirk); it is also said: highway robbery. Al-Hasan read "aw fasadan" with a fatha, on the presumption of an omitted verb indicated by the beginning of the statement, the estimate being "or he caused corruption." The evidence for it is His saying: "whoever kills a soul without a soul," because it is among the greatest corruption. The common reading is "fasadin" with a kasra, meaning "or without corruption."

(Whoever kills a soul... as if he had killed all mankind) The words of the exegetes have varied regarding the arrangement of this comparison, because the punishment for one who kills all people is greater than for one who kills a single person. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the meaning is, whoever kills a prophet or a just leader, it is as if he killed all people; and whoever keeps him alive by strengthening his arm and supporting him, it is as if he gave life to all people. He also said: the meaning is, whoever kills one soul and violates its sanctity, he is like one who kills all people; and whoever refrains from killing one soul, preserves its sanctity and spares it out of fear of God, he is like one who gives life to all people. He also said: the meaning is, "as if he killed all people" in the sight of the one killed, and whoever keeps him alive and rescues him from destruction, it is as if he gave life to all people in the sight of the one rescued. Mujahid said: the meaning is that whoever deliberately kills a believing soul, God makes his recompense Hell, is angry with him, curses him, and prepares for him a great punishment; it is as if he said: even if he killed all people, he would not add to that (i.e., he would not add to that punishment, as in al-Tabari); and whoever does not kill, people are preserved from him. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul incurs the retaliation and legal requital that would be incurred by one who kills all people. He said: "whoever gives it life," i.e., whoever pardons the one against whom killing is due; al-Hasan also said this, i.e., it is pardon after the ability to exact retaliation. It is also said: the meaning is that whoever kills a soul, all the believers are his opponents, because he has wronged everyone; and whoever gives it life, it is as if he gave life to all people, i.e., it is obligatory on all to thank him. It is also said: the guilt of killing one is made the guilt of killing all, and He may judge as He wills. It is also said: this was specific to the Children of Israel, as a severity upon them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: in general, the comparison, as is said, is total, and the one who violates in one case is regarded in the same light as the violator of all; an example is two men who swore upon two trees that they would not eat any of their fruit; one of them ate one fruit from his tree, and the other ate all the fruit of his tree; both have equally broken the oath. It is also said: the meaning is that whoever deems one killing lawful has deemed all killing lawful, because he has denied the Sharia. In His saying, may He be exalted, "and whoever gives it life" (wa man ahyaha), there is a figurative usage, for it is an expression for refraining and rescuing from destruction; otherwise, giving life in its true sense, which is bringing into existence, belongs only to God, may He be exalted. This giving of life is like the saying of the accursed Nimrod: "I give life and cause death" (al-Baqarah 2:258), so he called refraining "giving life." Then God informed about the Children of Israel that the messengers came to them with clear proofs, and that most of them were transgressors beyond the limit and abandoners of God's command.

The passage contains fifteen issues. The first: the scholars differ about the occasion of revelation of this verse. The majority view is that it was revealed concerning the 'Uraniyyin (the people of 'Urayna). The imams narrated, and the wording is that of Abu Dawud, from Anas ibn Malik that a group from 'Ukl [ 'Ukl (with a dammed 'ayn and a sukun on the kaf): a well-known tribe] - or he said from 'Urayna - came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and were stricken by the climate of Madinah [ i.e., the illness of the belly (jawa) befell them when it persisted, because its air did not suit them and they found it unwholesome. (al-Nihayah) of Ibn al-Athir.]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that they be given milch camels, and ordered them to drink from their urine and their milk. They set off, and when they recovered they killed the shepherd of the Prophet (ﷺ) and drove off the camels. News of them reached the Prophet (ﷺ) early in the day, and he sent after them. When the day had risen high they were brought to him. He ordered that their hands and feet be cut off, and that their eyes be branded [ to blind someone's eyes: to gouge them out (fa'a'ha)], and they were thrown into al-Harrah [ al-Harrah (with a fatha on the ha and a shadda on the ra): land outside Madinah with black stones] where they asked for water but were not given any. Abu Qilabah said: "These are people who stole, killed, disbelieved after their faith, and waged war against Allah and His Messenger."

In another narration: he ordered nails to be heated, and he branded their eyes with them, and cut off their hands and feet, and did not cauterise their stumps [ hasm al-'irq: cutting a vein and then cauterising it so that its blood does not flow].

In another narration: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a qafah [ al-qafah (plural of qa'if): one who follows tracks] in pursuit of them, and they were brought back. He said: Allah, Blessed and Exalted, then revealed concerning that: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is..." [the verse].

In another narration, Anas said: "I saw one of them biting the earth with his mouth from thirst until they died." In al-Bukhari, Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah said in his narration: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me with a group of Muslims until we overtook them, and they had already reached the outskirts of their land [ in one manuscript: "we had reached"]. We brought them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Jarir said: They kept saying "water," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Fire."

The historians and biographers have related that they cut off the hands and feet of the shepherd and planted thorns in his eyes until he died, and he was brought into Madinah dead. His name was Yasar, and he was a Nubian. This act was committed by apostates in the sixth year after the Hijrah.

In some narrations from Anas: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) burned them with fire after he had killed them.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak that the verse was revealed concerning a people from the People of the Book who had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke the covenant, cut off the highway, and spread corruption in the land.

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger" up to His saying "Forgiving, Merciful" - this verse was revealed concerning the polytheists. Whoever among them was seized [ in the Musannaf of Abu Dawud: repented, instead of "was seized"] before he came under power, that did not prevent the punishment (hadd) that befell him from being carried out upon him.

Among those who said the verse was revealed concerning the polytheists are 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan. But this view is weak, because it is refuted by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and by the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "Islam wipes away what was before it," related by Muslim. The first view is the correct one, because of the explicit texts of the established hadiths on this matter.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the companions of ra'y (opinion) said: the verse was revealed concerning those who went out from among the Muslims, cutting the highway and striving on the earth with corruption. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The statement of Malik is correct." Abu Thawr, arguing for this view, said: "In the verse there is evidence that it was revealed concerning non-polytheists, namely His saying, may His praise be exalted: 'except those who repent before you gain power over them.' And they have agreed that when polytheists fall into our hands and then embrace Islam, their blood is made inviolable. This shows that the verse was revealed concerning the people of Islam."

Al-Tabari related from some scholars that this verse abrogated (nasakha) the action of the Prophet (ﷺ) towards the 'Uraniyyin, so the matter was confined to these prescribed penalties [ naskh (abrogation): the removal of a earlier ruling by a later revealed ruling].

Muhammad ibn Sirin narrated: "This was before the hudud (prescribed punishments) were revealed," meaning the hadith of Anas, mentioned by Abu Dawud.

Some people, including al-Layth ibn Sa'd, said: what the Prophet (ﷺ) did to the delegation of 'Urayna was abrogated, since mutilation (tamthil) of an apostate is not permissible. [ In one manuscript the text reads "lam yajuz" (was not permissible) instead.]

Abu al-Zinad said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cut off the hands of those who stole his camels and branded their eyes with fire, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rebuked him for that, and Allah revealed concerning it: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is that they be killed or crucified..." [the verse]. Abu Dawud related it. Abu al-Zinad said: "When they were admonished and forbidden from mutilation, they did not return to it."

It is related from a group that this verse does not abrogate that act, because it occurred against apostates. Especially since it is established in Sahih Muslim, and in the Sunan of al-Nasa'i and others, that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) only branded the eyes of those people because they had branded the eyes of the shepherds, so that was retaliation (qisas) [ qisas: retaliation in kind]. And this verse concerns the believing muharib." [ In some manuscripts: "The Prophet (ﷺ)".]

I say: This is a good view, and it is the meaning of what Malik and al-Shafi'i held. That is why Allah said: "except those who repent before you gain power over them." It is known that the rulings for disbelievers do not differ in that punishment is removed from them by repentance after they have power over them, just as it falls away before they have power over them. The apostate deserves to be killed by the apostasy itself, apart from hirabah (waging war); he is not banished, his hand and foot are not cut off, and he is not left free, but he is killed if he does not embrace Islam, and he is not crucified either. This shows that what the verse includes is not what is meant for the apostate.

And He said concerning disbelievers: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. And He said concerning the muharibun: "except those who repent," and so on, and this is clear.

According to what we established at the beginning of the chapter, there is no problem, no blame, and no reproach, for it is the requirement of the Book. Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿Whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. "So they mutilated, and they were mutilated in return." However, it is possible that the reproach, if it is authentic, concerned the excess in killing, which is their branding with heated nails and leaving them thirsty until they died. And Allah knows best.

Al-Tabari related from al-Suddi that the Prophet (ﷺ) had branded the eyes of the 'Uraniyyin, and that he had intended that, and then the verse was revealed forbidding it. This view is very weak, for the established reports state that branding occurred, and in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: "He ordered nails to be heated, and he branded their eyes with them."

There is no disagreement among the scholars that the ruling of this verse applies to muharibun from among the people of Islam, even if it was revealed concerning apostates or Jews.

In His saying, exalted be He: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger" there is an metaphor (isti'arah) and figurative usage (majaz), since Allah, glory be to Him and exalted be He, is not fought against or overcome, because of His attributes of perfection and because of the transcendence due to Him above opposites and equals. The meaning is: they wage war against the friends (awliya') of Allah. He expressed His own might by speaking of His friends, to magnify the harm done to them, just as He spoke of Himself in reference to the poor and weak in His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], to urge compassion towards them. A similar example in the authentic Sunnah is: "I asked you for food, but you did not feed me." It was related by Muslim, and it has been mentioned before in al-Baqarah.

**The second issue:** The scholars differed about who deserves the name *muharib* (one who wages war, a highway brigand). Malik said: "The *muharib* in our view is one who attacks people in a city or in open country, overpowering them regarding their persons and property, without a stirred-up quarrel [[نارت نائرة في الناس: هاجت هائجة. ("a quarrel was stirred up among the people": it was agitated.)]], without a blood-feud [[الذحل: الثأر. (dhahl: vengeance.)]], and without enmity."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Reports from Malik on this question differ. He once affirmed that *hirabah* (armed robbery, waging war) occurs in the city and once denied it." A group said: "The ruling on this in the city, in houses, on roads, and in the dwellings of desert people and villages is the same, and their limits are one. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "So it is, because each falls under the name *muharabah*, the Book is general, and no one may exclude a group from the verse without evidence." Another group said: "*Muharabah* does not occur in the city; it occurs only outside the city. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, Ishaq, and al-Nu'man."

The *mughtal* (one who kills by stealth) is like the *muharib*: he is one who schemes to kill a person in order to take his property, even if he does not brandish a weapon, but enters his house or accompanies him on a journey and gives him poison, so that he dies. He is executed as a *hadd* (a fixed punishment prescribed by God), not as *qisas* (retaliation).

**The third issue:** They differed about the ruling for the *muharib*. One group said: "He is punished according to his act. Whoever terrorizes the road and takes property, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides. If he takes property and kills, his hand and foot are cut off, then he is crucified. If he kills and does not take property, he is killed. If he neither takes property nor kills, he is exiled." This is related from Ibn Abbas, and reported from Abu Mijlaz, al-Nakha'i, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, and others.

Abu Yusuf said: "If he takes property and kills, he is crucified and killed on the wood." Al-Layth said: "With a spear, while crucified." Abu Hanifa said: "If he kills, he is killed. If he takes property without killing, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides. If he takes property and kills, the ruler has a choice: if he wishes, he cuts off his hand and foot, and if he wishes, he does not cut and kills him and crucifies him." [[في ك: لم يقطع وصلبه. (In K: "he does not cut and crucifies him.")]] Abu Yusuf said: "Killing covers everything." The view of al-Awza'i is similar.

Al-Shafi'i said: "If he takes property, his right hand is cut off and cauterized, then his left foot is cut off and cauterized, and he is released, because this crime exceeds theft by being *hirabah*. If he kills, he is killed. If he takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified." It is reported from him that he said: "He is crucified for three days." He also said: "If he attends [the banditry] and increases [its numbers], and is feared, and serves as a support for the enemy, he is imprisoned."

Ahmad said: "If he kills, he is killed. If he takes property, his hand and foot are cut off, like the view of al-Shafi'i."

Some people said: "It is not fitting to crucify him before killing him, so that he is prevented from prayer, eating, and drinking." It is related from al-Shafi'i: "I dislike that he be killed while crucified, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade mutilation (*muthla*)."

Abu Thawr said: "The imam has a choice according to the apparent meaning of the verse." Malik said the same, and this is related from Ibn Abbas. It is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Nakha'i, all of whom said: "The imam has a choice in ruling against the *muharibun*. He rules against them with whichever of the punishments God has enjoined: killing, crucifixion, amputation, or exile, according to the apparent meaning of the verse." Ibn Abbas said: "Whatever in the Qur'an is 'or' (*aw*), its addressee has a choice."

This view is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse. The adherents of the first view, who said that *aw* indicates sequence, though they differed, are found to combine two penalties in their views: they say, "He is killed and then crucified," some say, "He is crucified and then killed," and some say, "His hand and foot are cut off and he is exiled." But the verse is not like that, nor is that the meaning of *aw* in the language, said al-Nahhas.

The first group argued with what al-Tabari reported from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked Jibril (peace be upon him) about the ruling on the *muharib*, and he said: 'Whoever terrorizes the road and takes property, cut off his hand for the taking and his foot for the terrorizing. Whoever kills, kill him. Whoever combines these, crucify him.'" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Exile remains only for the one who terrorizes, and the terrorizer is under the ruling of the killer. Nevertheless, Malik considers taking the lighter punishment and penalty to be preferable (*istihsan*)." [[الاستحسان: (istihsan) a legal principle of choosing a preferable ruling for reasons of equity.]]

**The fourth issue:** Concerning Allah's words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾, its meaning has been disputed. Al-Suddi said: "It means that he is pursued perpetually with horsemen and on foot until he is captured and the *hadd* of God is applied to him, or he flees out of the abode of Islam from those who pursue him." This is related from Ibn Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, Malik ibn Anas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and al-Zuhri. Al-Rummani related it in his book.

It is related from al-Shafi'i that they are taken out from one city to another and pursued so that the *hadd* may be applied to them. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd and al-Zuhri also said this.

Malik also said: "He is banished from the town in which he committed this to another and is imprisoned there, like the fornicator."

The Kufans said: "Their exile is imprisonment. He is exiled from the breadth of the world to its narrowness, so that when he is imprisoned, it is as if he has been exiled from the earth except for the place where he stays." They argued with the words of some prisoners:

*We went out of the world while we were of its people,*
*so we are neither among the dead within it nor the living.*
*When the jailer comes to us one day for some need,*
*we marvel and say: this one has come from the world.*

Makhul related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was the first to imprison people in prisons, and he said: "I imprison him until I know his repentance, and I do not exile him from one town to another, lest he harm them."

The apparent meaning of "the land" in the verse is the land of the calamity. People in ancient times avoided the land in which they had committed sins, and from this comes the hadith of the one who killed ninety-nine souls, who (*nā'a bi-sadrihi*) [[الحديث: هو حديث الذي قتل تسعا وتسعين نفسا. وناء بمعنى نهض، ويحتمل أنه بمعنى بعد. (This is the hadith of the man who killed ninety-nine souls. *Nā'a* means "rose up," and it may also mean "departed.")]] leaned forward with his chest toward the Holy Land.

If this *muharib* is feared, and it is thought that he will return to *hirabah* or corruption, the imam should imprison him in the town to which he is exiled. If he is not feared, and it is thought that he will not return to a crime, he is released. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is clearly the school of Malik: he is exiled and imprisoned wherever he is exiled. This is based on the most likely assumption that he is dangerous." Al-Tabari favored this view and it is clear, because exiling him from the land of the calamity is the text of the verse, and imprisoning him afterward depends on the fear of him. If he repents and his condition is understood, he is released.

**The fifth issue:** Allah's words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾: the root of *nafy* (exile, expulsion) is destruction. From it comes *ithbāt* (affirmation) and *nafy* (negation). *Nafy* means destruction by annihilation. From the same root comes *nafāya* (the worthless remnant of goods), and *nafy* (the spray that flies off water from the bucket). The *rājiz* (rhymed-verse poet) said [[هو الأخيل. (He is al-Akhyal.)]]:

*As if his two flanks, from the spray of water,*
*were the places where birds have alighted upon the smooth rock.*

[[جاء في (اللسان) مادة نفى أن الصحيح (كأن متني) لان بعده (من طول إشرافي على الطوى). ومتنا الظهر مكتنفا الصلب عن يمين وشمال من عصب ولحم. والصفي (بضم الصاد وكسرها) جمع صفا مقصور، وصفا جمع صفاة وهي الحجر؟ الصلد الضخم الذي لا ينبت شيئا. وفسر بأنه شبه الماء وقد وقع على ظهر المستقى بذرق الطائر على الصفي. (In *Lisan al-'Arab*, under the root n-f-y, it is stated that the correct reading is *ka'anna matnayh*, because after it comes *min tūli ishrāfī 'alā l-ṭawā* ("from the length of my looking down over the well"). The two *matnān* are the two sides of the back flanking the spine, of sinew and flesh, on the right and left. *Al-ṣafī* (with *ḍamma* or *kasra* on the *ṣād*) is the plural of *ṣafā* (the short form), and *ṣafā* is the plural of *ṣafāh*, meaning a stone; *al-ṣaldu* is a large one that grows nothing. It has been explained that he likened the water, which fell on the back of the one drawing water, to the droppings of a bird on the stone.)]]

The sixth point: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: The property taken by the muharib (highway robber) is not subject to a minimum value (nisab) as it is for the thief. It has been said that the nisab in this matter is a quarter dinar. Ibn al-'Arabi said: al-Shafi'i and the Ashab al-Ra'y (the jurists of opinion) said: No one among the highwaymen is to have his hand cut off unless he took an amount for which the hand of a thief is cut off. Malik said: He is judged by the ruling of the muharib, and this is the correct view. God Almighty specified, through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, the cutting of the hand for theft at a quarter dinar, but He specified nothing for hirabah. Rather, He mentioned the recompense of the muharib. This requires that they be given the full recompense for waging war, even over a single grain. Moreover, this is analogy of one principle upon another, which is itself disputed, and it is the analogy of the higher to the lower and of the lower to the lowest, which is the reverse of analogy. How can the muharib be analogized to the thief, when the thief seeks to snatch property and flees if he is noticed? If a thief enters armed seeking property, and he is prevented or confronted and fights over it, then he is a muharib and is judged by the ruling of the muharib.

Qadi Ibn al-'Arabi said: During my days of judging among people, someone brought me a thief who had entered a house with a knife, holding it to the heart of the owner who was asleep, while his companions were taking the man's property. I judged them by the ruling of the muharibun. So understand this from the foundation of the religion, and rise to the height of knowledge, away from the lowland of the ignorant.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: al-yafa' (the height) is the top of a mountain, and from it comes the expression ghulam yafa'a, meaning a boy who has risen toward puberty. al-hadid is the pit at the bottom of a valley. So said the lexicographers.

The seventh point: There is no disagreement that in hirabah whoever kills is himself killed, even if the victim was not an equal (mukafa'a) of the killer. al-Shafi'i has two opinions. The first is that equality is taken into account, because it is a killing, so equality is taken into account in it as in qisas (retribution). This view is weak, because the killing here is not merely a killing, but a general corruption through terror and the seizure of property. God said: ﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is that they be killed﴾. So He commanded the implementation of the hudud (fixed penalties) upon the muharib when he combines two things: waging war and striving to cause corruption on earth. He did not single out a noble from a lowly person, nor an exalted person from a base one.

The eighth point: If muharibun go out and fight a caravan, and some of them kill while others do not, then all of them are killed. al-Shafi'i said that only the one who killed is killed. This too is weak, for whoever attends the attack is a partner in the spoils, even if not all of them killed. It is agreed among us that the ridf (the one who stands behind to support), namely the lookout (talai'ah), is to be killed, so the muharib is more deserving of this.

The ninth point: When muharibun terrorize the road and cut off the way, it is obligatory upon the imam to fight them without first calling on them to submit, and it is obligatory upon the Muslims to cooperate in fighting them and in restraining them from harming Muslims. If they flee, none of the fleeing ones is pursued unless he has killed and taken property. If that is the case, he is pursued so that he may be seized and the penalty due for his crime may be carried out against him. None of them may finish off a wounded person (yudaffif, to put an end to one who is wounded) unless he himself has killed. If they are captured and property belonging to a specific person is found in their possession, it is returned to him or to his heirs. If no owner can be found, it is placed in the bayt al-mal (public treasury). Whatever property they destroyed belonging to anyone, they must compensate for it. There is no blood money (diyah) for those they killed if they are overpowered before repentance.

If they repent and come forward as penitents, which is the tenth point: the imam has no authority over them, and what was a hadd (fixed penalty) owed to God falls from them. They are held accountable for the rights of human beings, so retaliation is taken from them for killing and for wounds, and they must pay for the property and blood they destroyed to the heirs of the victims. It is permissible for the victims' heirs to pardon them or to waive the claim, as with other offenders apart from the muharibun. This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and the Ashab al-Ra'y. Whatever property was in their possession is taken, and they pay the value of what they consumed, because that is ghasb (usurpation), so their possession of it is not permitted. It is returned to its owners, or the imam keeps it until its owner is known.

Some of the Companions and the Successors said: Property is demanded only from what was found in his possession, and nothing is demanded for what he consumed. al-Tabari mentioned this from Malik through the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from him. This is also the apparent practice of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) regarding Harithah ibn Badr al-Ghudani, for he was a muharib who repented before he was overpowered, so 'Ali wrote him a public written decree releasing him from the claims of property and blood.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: The reports from Malik differ concerning a muharib upon whom the hadd has been carried out but from whom no property was found. Is he pursued for a debt equal to what he took, or is it dropped from him just as it is dropped from the thief? The Muslim and the dhimmi are equal in this matter.

**Eleventh:** The scholars have agreed that the ruler (al-sultan) is the guardian (wali) over whoever wages war (yuharib). If a muharib (one who wages armed banditry, see below) kills the brother or father of a man while engaged in this hirabah, then the one seeking blood-retaliation has no say in the matter of the muharib, and the pardon of the blood-guardian is not permitted. The one who carries out the punishment is the imam (head of state). They treated this as being in the same category as one of the hudud (prescribed punishments) of God, exalted is He.

I say: This is a collection of rulings concerning the muharibin, whose gems we have gathered and whose pearls we have brought together. Among the strangest things said in explaining it is:

**Twelfth:** The interpretation of Mujahid of it. Mujahid said: "What is meant by hirabah in this verse is adultery (al-zina) and theft (al-sariqa)." This is not correct, for God, glorified is He, has made clear in His Book and through the tongue of His Prophet that the thief's hand is cut off, and that the adulterer is flogged and exiled if he is unmarried (bikr), and stoned if he is married (thayyib muhsan). The ruling on the muharib in this verse differs from that, unless he intends to terrify the road by displaying weapons, aiming to overpower people's chastity (furuj). This is the most vile form of hirabah and worse than taking property, and it falls within the meaning of His saying: ﴿And they strive upon the earth to cause corruption﴾.

**Thirteenth:** Our scholars said: The robber (al-liss) is adjured by God, exalted is He. If he desists, he is left alone; if he refuses, he is fought. If you kill him, it is a worst kind of killing, and his blood is unpunished (hadar). Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayra that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, what do you think if someone attacks my property?" He said: "Then adjure him by God." He said: "If they refuse me?" He said: "Then adjure him by God." He said: "If they refuse me?" He said: "Then adjure him by God." He said: "If they refuse me?" He said: "Then fight, and if you are killed, you are in Paradise, and if you kill, you are in the Fire."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also reported it, though without mention of the adjuration, from Abu Hurayra, who said: A man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, what do you think if a man comes wanting to take my property?" He said: "Then do not give him your property." He said: "What do you think if he fights me?" He said: "Then fight him." He said: "What do you think if he kills me?" He said: "Then you are a martyr." He said: "What if I kill him?" He said: "He is in the Fire."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It has been related from a group of the people of knowledge that they held that fighting robbers and repelling them from their lives and property is permissible. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatada, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and al-Nu'man, and the common body of the people of knowledge say this: a man may fight in defence of himself, his family and his property when wrongful aggression is intended, based on the reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) which did not restrict it to one time over another or one situation over another, except for the ruler. The people of hadith are almost unanimous that whoever cannot protect his self and property except by rising against the ruler and fighting him, he should not fight him or rebel against him, based on the reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that enjoin patience with what comes from them of oppression and injustice, and that they should not be fought or rebelled against as long as they establish the prayer.

I say: Our school (madhhab) has differed on whether, when a robber seeks something light such as a garment or food, they should be given it or fought. This disagreement is built on a principle: is the command to fight them because it is changing a wrong (taghyir munkar), or is it from the category of repelling harm (daf' al-darar)? On this basis also the disagreement about calling them to desist before fighting is built. And God knows best.

**Fourteenth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾. This is due to the heinousness of hirabah and the magnitude of its harm. Hirabah is grave in harm because it cuts off the path of earning among people, since most and the greatest of livelihoods is trade, whose pillar and foundation is travel through the land, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of God's bounty﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 20) [See vol. 19, p. 50]. When the road is made fearful, people stop travelling and are obliged to stay in their houses, so the door of trade is closed to them and their earnings are cut off. Therefore God prescribed severe hudud for highwaymen (qutta' al-tariq), and that disgrace in this world is a deterrent to them from their evil deeds and an opening of the door of trade, which He permitted to His servants for those of them who want it, and He promised for it a great punishment in the Hereafter.
