This sin may be considered as standing outside the general category of sins and excepted from the hadith of 'Ubada, in the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Whoever commits any of these and is punished for it in this world, that is his expiation (kaffara)." [The addition [lahu] is from Ibn 'Atiyya.] And God knows best. It is also possible that the disgrace applies to the one who is punished, and the punishment of the Hereafter to the one who escapes punishment in this world, and this sin is treated like other sins. There is no eternity in the Fire for a believer, as has been stated before, but its punishment is magnified because of the magnitude of the sin, and then he is brought out either by intercession or by a handful (of God's mercy). Moreover, this threat is conditional in its execution upon God's will, as in His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ (al-Nisa': 116) [See vol. 5, p. 385]. Yet fear prevails over them in proportion to the threat and the greatness of the disobedience. [This is as it stands in the original and in Ibn 'Atiyya's tafsir. What is in al-Bahr is: "This threat, like others, is restricted by God's will; He may forgive this sin, but in the threat there is fear for the one threatened, that the threat will be executed." This is clearer.]

**Fifteenth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who repent before you have power over them﴾. He, mighty and majestic, excepted those who repent before they are overpowered, and informed that their right (of punishment) is dropped from them by His saying: ﴿Then know that God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. As for retaliation (qisas) and the rights of human beings, these are not dropped. As for one who repents after being overpowered, the apparent meaning of the verse is that repentance does not benefit him, and the hudud are established upon him as previously explained. There is a view of al-Shafi'i that every hadd is dropped by repentance, but the sound position in his school is that whatever involves a human right, whether retaliation or other, is not dropped by repentance made before one has power over him. It was also said: the exception intended is the polytheist who repents and believes before he is overpowered, so the hudud are dropped from him. This is weak, because if he believes after being overpowered he is also not killed, by consensus. It was also said: the hadd is not dropped from the muharibin after they have been overpowered, and God knows best, because they are suspected of lying in their repentance and of feigning it when the hand of the imam reaches them; or because once they are overpowered they are in a position to be made an example of, so their repentance is not accepted, like one who is caught up in punishment among the nations before us, or one who has reached the death-rattle (al-gharghara) and then repents. As for when their repentance precedes their being overpowered, there is no suspicion, and it benefits them, as will be explained in Surat Yunus [See vol. 8, p. 383]. As for drinkers, fornicators and thieves who repent, reform, and whose condition is known, and who are then brought before the imam, it is not proper for him to apply the hadd to them; but if they are brought to him and say "we have repented," they are not left alone, and in this state they are like muharibin who have been overpowered. And God knows best.

The passage contains fifteen issues. The first: the scholars differ about the occasion of revelation of this verse. The majority view is that it was revealed concerning the 'Uraniyyin (the people of 'Urayna). The imams narrated, and the wording is that of Abu Dawud, from Anas ibn Malik that a group from 'Ukl [ 'Ukl (with a dammed 'ayn and a sukun on the kaf): a well-known tribe] - or he said from 'Urayna - came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and were stricken by the climate of Madinah [ i.e., the illness of the belly (jawa) befell them when it persisted, because its air did not suit them and they found it unwholesome. (al-Nihayah) of Ibn al-Athir.]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that they be given milch camels, and ordered them to drink from their urine and their milk. They set off, and when they recovered they killed the shepherd of the Prophet (ﷺ) and drove off the camels. News of them reached the Prophet (ﷺ) early in the day, and he sent after them. When the day had risen high they were brought to him. He ordered that their hands and feet be cut off, and that their eyes be branded [ to blind someone's eyes: to gouge them out (fa'a'ha)], and they were thrown into al-Harrah [ al-Harrah (with a fatha on the ha and a shadda on the ra): land outside Madinah with black stones] where they asked for water but were not given any. Abu Qilabah said: "These are people who stole, killed, disbelieved after their faith, and waged war against Allah and His Messenger."

In another narration: he ordered nails to be heated, and he branded their eyes with them, and cut off their hands and feet, and did not cauterise their stumps [ hasm al-'irq: cutting a vein and then cauterising it so that its blood does not flow].

In another narration: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a qafah [ al-qafah (plural of qa'if): one who follows tracks] in pursuit of them, and they were brought back. He said: Allah, Blessed and Exalted, then revealed concerning that: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is..." [the verse].

In another narration, Anas said: "I saw one of them biting the earth with his mouth from thirst until they died." In al-Bukhari, Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah said in his narration: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent me with a group of Muslims until we overtook them, and they had already reached the outskirts of their land [ in one manuscript: "we had reached"]. We brought them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Jarir said: They kept saying "water," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Fire."

The historians and biographers have related that they cut off the hands and feet of the shepherd and planted thorns in his eyes until he died, and he was brought into Madinah dead. His name was Yasar, and he was a Nubian. This act was committed by apostates in the sixth year after the Hijrah.

In some narrations from Anas: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) burned them with fire after he had killed them.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak that the verse was revealed concerning a people from the People of the Book who had a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but they broke the covenant, cut off the highway, and spread corruption in the land.

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger" up to His saying "Forgiving, Merciful" - this verse was revealed concerning the polytheists. Whoever among them was seized [ in the Musannaf of Abu Dawud: repented, instead of "was seized"] before he came under power, that did not prevent the punishment (hadd) that befell him from being carried out upon him.

Among those who said the verse was revealed concerning the polytheists are 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan. But this view is weak, because it is refuted by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and by the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "Islam wipes away what was before it," related by Muslim. The first view is the correct one, because of the explicit texts of the established hadiths on this matter.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the companions of ra'y (opinion) said: the verse was revealed concerning those who went out from among the Muslims, cutting the highway and striving on the earth with corruption. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The statement of Malik is correct." Abu Thawr, arguing for this view, said: "In the verse there is evidence that it was revealed concerning non-polytheists, namely His saying, may His praise be exalted: 'except those who repent before you gain power over them.' And they have agreed that when polytheists fall into our hands and then embrace Islam, their blood is made inviolable. This shows that the verse was revealed concerning the people of Islam."

Al-Tabari related from some scholars that this verse abrogated (nasakha) the action of the Prophet (ﷺ) towards the 'Uraniyyin, so the matter was confined to these prescribed penalties [ naskh (abrogation): the removal of a earlier ruling by a later revealed ruling].

Muhammad ibn Sirin narrated: "This was before the hudud (prescribed punishments) were revealed," meaning the hadith of Anas, mentioned by Abu Dawud.

Some people, including al-Layth ibn Sa'd, said: what the Prophet (ﷺ) did to the delegation of 'Urayna was abrogated, since mutilation (tamthil) of an apostate is not permissible. [ In one manuscript the text reads "lam yajuz" (was not permissible) instead.]

Abu al-Zinad said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cut off the hands of those who stole his camels and branded their eyes with fire, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rebuked him for that, and Allah revealed concerning it: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is that they be killed or crucified..." [the verse]. Abu Dawud related it. Abu al-Zinad said: "When they were admonished and forbidden from mutilation, they did not return to it."

It is related from a group that this verse does not abrogate that act, because it occurred against apostates. Especially since it is established in Sahih Muslim, and in the Sunan of al-Nasa'i and others, that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) only branded the eyes of those people because they had branded the eyes of the shepherds, so that was retaliation (qisas) [ qisas: retaliation in kind]. And this verse concerns the believing muharib." [ In some manuscripts: "The Prophet (ﷺ)".]

I say: This is a good view, and it is the meaning of what Malik and al-Shafi'i held. That is why Allah said: "except those who repent before you gain power over them." It is known that the rulings for disbelievers do not differ in that punishment is removed from them by repentance after they have power over them, just as it falls away before they have power over them. The apostate deserves to be killed by the apostasy itself, apart from hirabah (waging war); he is not banished, his hand and foot are not cut off, and he is not left free, but he is killed if he does not embrace Islam, and he is not crucified either. This shows that what the verse includes is not what is meant for the apostate.

And He said concerning disbelievers: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. And He said concerning the muharibun: "except those who repent," and so on, and this is clear.

According to what we established at the beginning of the chapter, there is no problem, no blame, and no reproach, for it is the requirement of the Book. Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿Whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. "So they mutilated, and they were mutilated in return." However, it is possible that the reproach, if it is authentic, concerned the excess in killing, which is their branding with heated nails and leaving them thirsty until they died. And Allah knows best.

Al-Tabari related from al-Suddi that the Prophet (ﷺ) had branded the eyes of the 'Uraniyyin, and that he had intended that, and then the verse was revealed forbidding it. This view is very weak, for the established reports state that branding occurred, and in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: "He ordered nails to be heated, and he branded their eyes with them."

There is no disagreement among the scholars that the ruling of this verse applies to muharibun from among the people of Islam, even if it was revealed concerning apostates or Jews.

In His saying, exalted be He: "Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger" there is an metaphor (isti'arah) and figurative usage (majaz), since Allah, glory be to Him and exalted be He, is not fought against or overcome, because of His attributes of perfection and because of the transcendence due to Him above opposites and equals. The meaning is: they wage war against the friends (awliya') of Allah. He expressed His own might by speaking of His friends, to magnify the harm done to them, just as He spoke of Himself in reference to the poor and weak in His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], to urge compassion towards them. A similar example in the authentic Sunnah is: "I asked you for food, but you did not feed me." It was related by Muslim, and it has been mentioned before in al-Baqarah.

**The second issue:** The scholars differed about who deserves the name *muharib* (one who wages war, a highway brigand). Malik said: "The *muharib* in our view is one who attacks people in a city or in open country, overpowering them regarding their persons and property, without a stirred-up quarrel [[نارت نائرة في الناس: هاجت هائجة. ("a quarrel was stirred up among the people": it was agitated.)]], without a blood-feud [[الذحل: الثأر. (dhahl: vengeance.)]], and without enmity."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Reports from Malik on this question differ. He once affirmed that *hirabah* (armed robbery, waging war) occurs in the city and once denied it." A group said: "The ruling on this in the city, in houses, on roads, and in the dwellings of desert people and villages is the same, and their limits are one. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "So it is, because each falls under the name *muharabah*, the Book is general, and no one may exclude a group from the verse without evidence." Another group said: "*Muharabah* does not occur in the city; it occurs only outside the city. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, Ishaq, and al-Nu'man."

The *mughtal* (one who kills by stealth) is like the *muharib*: he is one who schemes to kill a person in order to take his property, even if he does not brandish a weapon, but enters his house or accompanies him on a journey and gives him poison, so that he dies. He is executed as a *hadd* (a fixed punishment prescribed by God), not as *qisas* (retaliation).

**The third issue:** They differed about the ruling for the *muharib*. One group said: "He is punished according to his act. Whoever terrorizes the road and takes property, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides. If he takes property and kills, his hand and foot are cut off, then he is crucified. If he kills and does not take property, he is killed. If he neither takes property nor kills, he is exiled." This is related from Ibn Abbas, and reported from Abu Mijlaz, al-Nakha'i, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, and others.

Abu Yusuf said: "If he takes property and kills, he is crucified and killed on the wood." Al-Layth said: "With a spear, while crucified." Abu Hanifa said: "If he kills, he is killed. If he takes property without killing, his hand and foot are cut off from opposite sides. If he takes property and kills, the ruler has a choice: if he wishes, he cuts off his hand and foot, and if he wishes, he does not cut and kills him and crucifies him." [[في ك: لم يقطع وصلبه. (In K: "he does not cut and crucifies him.")]] Abu Yusuf said: "Killing covers everything." The view of al-Awza'i is similar.

Al-Shafi'i said: "If he takes property, his right hand is cut off and cauterized, then his left foot is cut off and cauterized, and he is released, because this crime exceeds theft by being *hirabah*. If he kills, he is killed. If he takes property and kills, he is killed and crucified." It is reported from him that he said: "He is crucified for three days." He also said: "If he attends [the banditry] and increases [its numbers], and is feared, and serves as a support for the enemy, he is imprisoned."

Ahmad said: "If he kills, he is killed. If he takes property, his hand and foot are cut off, like the view of al-Shafi'i."

Some people said: "It is not fitting to crucify him before killing him, so that he is prevented from prayer, eating, and drinking." It is related from al-Shafi'i: "I dislike that he be killed while crucified, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade mutilation (*muthla*)."

Abu Thawr said: "The imam has a choice according to the apparent meaning of the verse." Malik said the same, and this is related from Ibn Abbas. It is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-Nakha'i, all of whom said: "The imam has a choice in ruling against the *muharibun*. He rules against them with whichever of the punishments God has enjoined: killing, crucifixion, amputation, or exile, according to the apparent meaning of the verse." Ibn Abbas said: "Whatever in the Qur'an is 'or' (*aw*), its addressee has a choice."

This view is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse. The adherents of the first view, who said that *aw* indicates sequence, though they differed, are found to combine two penalties in their views: they say, "He is killed and then crucified," some say, "He is crucified and then killed," and some say, "His hand and foot are cut off and he is exiled." But the verse is not like that, nor is that the meaning of *aw* in the language, said al-Nahhas.

The first group argued with what al-Tabari reported from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked Jibril (peace be upon him) about the ruling on the *muharib*, and he said: 'Whoever terrorizes the road and takes property, cut off his hand for the taking and his foot for the terrorizing. Whoever kills, kill him. Whoever combines these, crucify him.'" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Exile remains only for the one who terrorizes, and the terrorizer is under the ruling of the killer. Nevertheless, Malik considers taking the lighter punishment and penalty to be preferable (*istihsan*)." [[الاستحسان: (istihsan) a legal principle of choosing a preferable ruling for reasons of equity.]]

**The fourth issue:** Concerning Allah's words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾, its meaning has been disputed. Al-Suddi said: "It means that he is pursued perpetually with horsemen and on foot until he is captured and the *hadd* of God is applied to him, or he flees out of the abode of Islam from those who pursue him." This is related from Ibn Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, Malik ibn Anas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and al-Zuhri. Al-Rummani related it in his book.

It is related from al-Shafi'i that they are taken out from one city to another and pursued so that the *hadd* may be applied to them. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd and al-Zuhri also said this.

Malik also said: "He is banished from the town in which he committed this to another and is imprisoned there, like the fornicator."

The Kufans said: "Their exile is imprisonment. He is exiled from the breadth of the world to its narrowness, so that when he is imprisoned, it is as if he has been exiled from the earth except for the place where he stays." They argued with the words of some prisoners:

*We went out of the world while we were of its people,*
*so we are neither among the dead within it nor the living.*
*When the jailer comes to us one day for some need,*
*we marvel and say: this one has come from the world.*

Makhul related that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was the first to imprison people in prisons, and he said: "I imprison him until I know his repentance, and I do not exile him from one town to another, lest he harm them."

The apparent meaning of "the land" in the verse is the land of the calamity. People in ancient times avoided the land in which they had committed sins, and from this comes the hadith of the one who killed ninety-nine souls, who (*nā'a bi-sadrihi*) [[الحديث: هو حديث الذي قتل تسعا وتسعين نفسا. وناء بمعنى نهض، ويحتمل أنه بمعنى بعد. (This is the hadith of the man who killed ninety-nine souls. *Nā'a* means "rose up," and it may also mean "departed.")]] leaned forward with his chest toward the Holy Land.

If this *muharib* is feared, and it is thought that he will return to *hirabah* or corruption, the imam should imprison him in the town to which he is exiled. If he is not feared, and it is thought that he will not return to a crime, he is released. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is clearly the school of Malik: he is exiled and imprisoned wherever he is exiled. This is based on the most likely assumption that he is dangerous." Al-Tabari favored this view and it is clear, because exiling him from the land of the calamity is the text of the verse, and imprisoning him afterward depends on the fear of him. If he repents and his condition is understood, he is released.

**The fifth issue:** Allah's words ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾: the root of *nafy* (exile, expulsion) is destruction. From it comes *ithbāt* (affirmation) and *nafy* (negation). *Nafy* means destruction by annihilation. From the same root comes *nafāya* (the worthless remnant of goods), and *nafy* (the spray that flies off water from the bucket). The *rājiz* (rhymed-verse poet) said [[هو الأخيل. (He is al-Akhyal.)]]:

*As if his two flanks, from the spray of water,*
*were the places where birds have alighted upon the smooth rock.*

[[جاء في (اللسان) مادة نفى أن الصحيح (كأن متني) لان بعده (من طول إشرافي على الطوى). ومتنا الظهر مكتنفا الصلب عن يمين وشمال من عصب ولحم. والصفي (بضم الصاد وكسرها) جمع صفا مقصور، وصفا جمع صفاة وهي الحجر؟ الصلد الضخم الذي لا ينبت شيئا. وفسر بأنه شبه الماء وقد وقع على ظهر المستقى بذرق الطائر على الصفي. (In *Lisan al-'Arab*, under the root n-f-y, it is stated that the correct reading is *ka'anna matnayh*, because after it comes *min tūli ishrāfī 'alā l-ṭawā* ("from the length of my looking down over the well"). The two *matnān* are the two sides of the back flanking the spine, of sinew and flesh, on the right and left. *Al-ṣafī* (with *ḍamma* or *kasra* on the *ṣād*) is the plural of *ṣafā* (the short form), and *ṣafā* is the plural of *ṣafāh*, meaning a stone; *al-ṣaldu* is a large one that grows nothing. It has been explained that he likened the water, which fell on the back of the one drawing water, to the droppings of a bird on the stone.)]]

The sixth point: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: The property taken by the muharib (highway robber) is not subject to a minimum value (nisab) as it is for the thief. It has been said that the nisab in this matter is a quarter dinar. Ibn al-'Arabi said: al-Shafi'i and the Ashab al-Ra'y (the jurists of opinion) said: No one among the highwaymen is to have his hand cut off unless he took an amount for which the hand of a thief is cut off. Malik said: He is judged by the ruling of the muharib, and this is the correct view. God Almighty specified, through the tongue of His Prophet ﷺ, the cutting of the hand for theft at a quarter dinar, but He specified nothing for hirabah. Rather, He mentioned the recompense of the muharib. This requires that they be given the full recompense for waging war, even over a single grain. Moreover, this is analogy of one principle upon another, which is itself disputed, and it is the analogy of the higher to the lower and of the lower to the lowest, which is the reverse of analogy. How can the muharib be analogized to the thief, when the thief seeks to snatch property and flees if he is noticed? If a thief enters armed seeking property, and he is prevented or confronted and fights over it, then he is a muharib and is judged by the ruling of the muharib.

Qadi Ibn al-'Arabi said: During my days of judging among people, someone brought me a thief who had entered a house with a knife, holding it to the heart of the owner who was asleep, while his companions were taking the man's property. I judged them by the ruling of the muharibun. So understand this from the foundation of the religion, and rise to the height of knowledge, away from the lowland of the ignorant.

I (al-Qurtubi) say: al-yafa' (the height) is the top of a mountain, and from it comes the expression ghulam yafa'a, meaning a boy who has risen toward puberty. al-hadid is the pit at the bottom of a valley. So said the lexicographers.

The seventh point: There is no disagreement that in hirabah whoever kills is himself killed, even if the victim was not an equal (mukafa'a) of the killer. al-Shafi'i has two opinions. The first is that equality is taken into account, because it is a killing, so equality is taken into account in it as in qisas (retribution). This view is weak, because the killing here is not merely a killing, but a general corruption through terror and the seizure of property. God said: ﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption is that they be killed﴾. So He commanded the implementation of the hudud (fixed penalties) upon the muharib when he combines two things: waging war and striving to cause corruption on earth. He did not single out a noble from a lowly person, nor an exalted person from a base one.

The eighth point: If muharibun go out and fight a caravan, and some of them kill while others do not, then all of them are killed. al-Shafi'i said that only the one who killed is killed. This too is weak, for whoever attends the attack is a partner in the spoils, even if not all of them killed. It is agreed among us that the ridf (the one who stands behind to support), namely the lookout (talai'ah), is to be killed, so the muharib is more deserving of this.

The ninth point: When muharibun terrorize the road and cut off the way, it is obligatory upon the imam to fight them without first calling on them to submit, and it is obligatory upon the Muslims to cooperate in fighting them and in restraining them from harming Muslims. If they flee, none of the fleeing ones is pursued unless he has killed and taken property. If that is the case, he is pursued so that he may be seized and the penalty due for his crime may be carried out against him. None of them may finish off a wounded person (yudaffif, to put an end to one who is wounded) unless he himself has killed. If they are captured and property belonging to a specific person is found in their possession, it is returned to him or to his heirs. If no owner can be found, it is placed in the bayt al-mal (public treasury). Whatever property they destroyed belonging to anyone, they must compensate for it. There is no blood money (diyah) for those they killed if they are overpowered before repentance.

If they repent and come forward as penitents, which is the tenth point: the imam has no authority over them, and what was a hadd (fixed penalty) owed to God falls from them. They are held accountable for the rights of human beings, so retaliation is taken from them for killing and for wounds, and they must pay for the property and blood they destroyed to the heirs of the victims. It is permissible for the victims' heirs to pardon them or to waive the claim, as with other offenders apart from the muharibun. This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and the Ashab al-Ra'y. Whatever property was in their possession is taken, and they pay the value of what they consumed, because that is ghasb (usurpation), so their possession of it is not permitted. It is returned to its owners, or the imam keeps it until its owner is known.

Some of the Companions and the Successors said: Property is demanded only from what was found in his possession, and nothing is demanded for what he consumed. al-Tabari mentioned this from Malik through the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from him. This is also the apparent practice of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) regarding Harithah ibn Badr al-Ghudani, for he was a muharib who repented before he was overpowered, so 'Ali wrote him a public written decree releasing him from the claims of property and blood.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: The reports from Malik differ concerning a muharib upon whom the hadd has been carried out but from whom no property was found. Is he pursued for a debt equal to what he took, or is it dropped from him just as it is dropped from the thief? The Muslim and the dhimmi are equal in this matter.

**Eleventh:** The scholars have agreed that the ruler (al-sultan) is the guardian (wali) over whoever wages war (yuharib). If a muharib (one who wages armed banditry, see below) kills the brother or father of a man while engaged in this hirabah, then the one seeking blood-retaliation has no say in the matter of the muharib, and the pardon of the blood-guardian is not permitted. The one who carries out the punishment is the imam (head of state). They treated this as being in the same category as one of the hudud (prescribed punishments) of God, exalted is He.

I say: This is a collection of rulings concerning the muharibin, whose gems we have gathered and whose pearls we have brought together. Among the strangest things said in explaining it is:

**Twelfth:** The interpretation of Mujahid of it. Mujahid said: "What is meant by hirabah in this verse is adultery (al-zina) and theft (al-sariqa)." This is not correct, for God, glorified is He, has made clear in His Book and through the tongue of His Prophet that the thief's hand is cut off, and that the adulterer is flogged and exiled if he is unmarried (bikr), and stoned if he is married (thayyib muhsan). The ruling on the muharib in this verse differs from that, unless he intends to terrify the road by displaying weapons, aiming to overpower people's chastity (furuj). This is the most vile form of hirabah and worse than taking property, and it falls within the meaning of His saying: ﴿And they strive upon the earth to cause corruption﴾.

**Thirteenth:** Our scholars said: The robber (al-liss) is adjured by God, exalted is He. If he desists, he is left alone; if he refuses, he is fought. If you kill him, it is a worst kind of killing, and his blood is unpunished (hadar). Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayra that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, what do you think if someone attacks my property?" He said: "Then adjure him by God." He said: "If they refuse me?" He said: "Then adjure him by God." He said: "If they refuse me?" He said: "Then adjure him by God." He said: "If they refuse me?" He said: "Then fight, and if you are killed, you are in Paradise, and if you kill, you are in the Fire."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also reported it, though without mention of the adjuration, from Abu Hurayra, who said: A man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, what do you think if a man comes wanting to take my property?" He said: "Then do not give him your property." He said: "What do you think if he fights me?" He said: "Then fight him." He said: "What do you think if he kills me?" He said: "Then you are a martyr." He said: "What if I kill him?" He said: "He is in the Fire."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It has been related from a group of the people of knowledge that they held that fighting robbers and repelling them from their lives and property is permissible. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Qatada, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and al-Nu'man, and the common body of the people of knowledge say this: a man may fight in defence of himself, his family and his property when wrongful aggression is intended, based on the reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) which did not restrict it to one time over another or one situation over another, except for the ruler. The people of hadith are almost unanimous that whoever cannot protect his self and property except by rising against the ruler and fighting him, he should not fight him or rebel against him, based on the reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that enjoin patience with what comes from them of oppression and injustice, and that they should not be fought or rebelled against as long as they establish the prayer.

I say: Our school (madhhab) has differed on whether, when a robber seeks something light such as a garment or food, they should be given it or fought. This disagreement is built on a principle: is the command to fight them because it is changing a wrong (taghyir munkar), or is it from the category of repelling harm (daf' al-darar)? On this basis also the disagreement about calling them to desist before fighting is built. And God knows best.

**Fourteenth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾. This is due to the heinousness of hirabah and the magnitude of its harm. Hirabah is grave in harm because it cuts off the path of earning among people, since most and the greatest of livelihoods is trade, whose pillar and foundation is travel through the land, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of God's bounty﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 20) [See vol. 19, p. 50]. When the road is made fearful, people stop travelling and are obliged to stay in their houses, so the door of trade is closed to them and their earnings are cut off. Therefore God prescribed severe hudud for highwaymen (qutta' al-tariq), and that disgrace in this world is a deterrent to them from their evil deeds and an opening of the door of trade, which He permitted to His servants for those of them who want it, and He promised for it a great punishment in the Hereafter.

This sin may be considered as standing outside the general category of sins and excepted from the hadith of 'Ubada, in the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "Whoever commits any of these and is punished for it in this world, that is his expiation (kaffara)." [The addition [lahu] is from Ibn 'Atiyya.] And God knows best. It is also possible that the disgrace applies to the one who is punished, and the punishment of the Hereafter to the one who escapes punishment in this world, and this sin is treated like other sins. There is no eternity in the Fire for a believer, as has been stated before, but its punishment is magnified because of the magnitude of the sin, and then he is brought out either by intercession or by a handful (of God's mercy). Moreover, this threat is conditional in its execution upon God's will, as in His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ (al-Nisa': 116) [See vol. 5, p. 385]. Yet fear prevails over them in proportion to the threat and the greatness of the disobedience. [This is as it stands in the original and in Ibn 'Atiyya's tafsir. What is in al-Bahr is: "This threat, like others, is restricted by God's will; He may forgive this sin, but in the threat there is fear for the one threatened, that the threat will be executed." This is clearer.]

**Fifteenth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who repent before you have power over them﴾. He, mighty and majestic, excepted those who repent before they are overpowered, and informed that their right (of punishment) is dropped from them by His saying: ﴿Then know that God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. As for retaliation (qisas) and the rights of human beings, these are not dropped. As for one who repents after being overpowered, the apparent meaning of the verse is that repentance does not benefit him, and the hudud are established upon him as previously explained. There is a view of al-Shafi'i that every hadd is dropped by repentance, but the sound position in his school is that whatever involves a human right, whether retaliation or other, is not dropped by repentance made before one has power over him. It was also said: the exception intended is the polytheist who repents and believes before he is overpowered, so the hudud are dropped from him. This is weak, because if he believes after being overpowered he is also not killed, by consensus. It was also said: the hadd is not dropped from the muharibin after they have been overpowered, and God knows best, because they are suspected of lying in their repentance and of feigning it when the hand of the imam reaches them; or because once they are overpowered they are in a position to be made an example of, so their repentance is not accepted, like one who is caught up in punishment among the nations before us, or one who has reached the death-rattle (al-gharghara) and then repents. As for when their repentance precedes their being overpowered, there is no suspicion, and it benefits them, as will be explained in Surat Yunus [See vol. 8, p. 383]. As for drinkers, fornicators and thieves who repent, reform, and whose condition is known, and who are then brought before the imam, it is not proper for him to apply the hadd to them; but if they are brought to him and say "we have repented," they are not left alone, and in this state they are like muharibin who have been overpowered. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 35–36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him﴾. Al-Wasilah is al-qurbah (nearness/closeness), related on the authority of Abu Wa'il, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ata', al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir. It is on the pattern of fa'ilah, from tawassaltu ilayhi, meaning taqarrabtu (I drew near). 'Antarah said:

Indeed the men have a means (wasilah) to you,
If they take you, then adorn yourself with kohl and dye.

The plural is al-wasa'il. He said:

When the slanderers are heedless, we return to our union,
And the purity between us returns, and the means (al-wasa'il).

It is also said: from it, saltu, as'alu, meaning talabtu (I sought). The two of them tasawalan, meaning each one seeks from his companion. So the root is seeking (al-talab), and al-wasilah is the nearness by which one should seek. Al-Wasilah is a degree in Paradise, and it is the one about which the sound hadith came in his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: (Whoever asks Allah for al-wasilah for me, intercession becomes lawful for him).

Yazid al-Faqir said: It was said to Jabir ibn Abdullah, "You, O companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), say that a people will come out of the Fire, and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they will not come out of it﴾." Jabir said: "You make the general (al-'amm) specific and the specific general. This applies only to the disbelievers specifically. I recited the whole verse from its beginning to its end, and it is indeed about the disbelievers specifically."

And "muqim" means lasting, enduring, unchanging, neither ceasing nor shifting. The poet said:

"Indeed, for you, on the Day of al-Sha'b, from me, there is a punishment, lasting and enduring for you."

In it are twenty-seven [sic: the editions all say this, though the count is twenty-six; the thirteenth issue is missing in all copies except L, and the twenty-sixth is missing from it] issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ [Q 5:38]. When Allah mentioned the taking of wealth by way of roaming the earth in corruption, He mentioned the ruling on the thief who does not use armed robbery (*hirabah*), as will be explained during the chapter. He, glorified is He, began with the male thief before the female thief, the reverse of the order for fornication (*zina*), as we will explain at the end of the chapter.

The thief was cut off in the pre-Islamic era (*Jahiliyyah*). The first person sentenced to amputation in the pre-Islamic era was al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Then Allah commanded amputation in Islam. The first thief whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ amputated in Islam, among men, was al-Khiyar ibn Adi ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf, and among women, Murrah bint Sufyan ibn Abd al-Asad of the Banu Makhzum. Abu Bakr cut off the right hand of al-Yamani [a man from Yemen who was missing a hand and a foot, who stole a necklace belonging to Asma bint Umays, the wife of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, so he cut off his left hand], who stole the necklace. Umar cut off the hand of Ibn Samurah, the brother of Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah. There is no disagreement on this.

The apparent meaning of the verse is general, covering every thief, but this is not the case, due to his saying, upon him be peace: "The hand of the thief is not cut off except for a quarter of a dinar or more." Thus it clarifies that by his saying "the thief, male and female," He intended some thieves and not others. So the hand of the thief is not cut off except for a quarter of a dinar, or for something whose value is a quarter of a dinar. This is the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab, Uthman ibn Affan and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr also held this view.

Malik said: the hand is cut off for a quarter of a dinar or for three dirhams. If someone steals two dirhams, which is a quarter of a dinar due to the fall in the exchange rate, his hand is not cut off for them. Goods (*'urud*) are not cut for unless they reach three dirhams, whether the exchange rate is low or high. Malik treated gold and silver (*al-wariq*) each as a basis in itself, and made the valuation of goods in dirhams the well-known position.

Ahmad and Ishaq said: if he steals gold, then the threshold is a quarter of a dinar; if he steals something other than gold and silver, its value must be a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams of silver. This is close to what Malik adopted in his other view.

The proof for the first view is the hadith of Ibn Umar that a man stole a shield (*hajfah*) [the *hajfah* with a vowelled *ha* is a shield; it is said to be specifically made of hide, like a *darqah*], and was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, who ordered that it be valued, and it was valued at three dirhams.

Al-Shafi'i made the hadith of A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, concerning a quarter of a dinar the basis, to which he referred the valuation of goods, not by three dirhams, adjusting for the rise and fall of gold's price. He set aside the hadith of Ibn Umar because, as he saw it, and Allah knows best, there was disagreement among the Companions about the shield with which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cut off a hand. Ibn Umar says three dirhams, Ibn Abbas says ten dirhams, and Anas says five dirhams. The hadith of A'ishah about a quarter of a dinar is a sound, established hadith, on which there is no disagreement from A'ishah, except that some narrators stopped it at her (as a statement of hers) while others traced it to the Prophet. [The hadith of A'ishah is sound according to the Ibadiyyah, traced to the Prophet as in the *Musnad* of al-Rabi'; the hadith of the shield also has a version from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, to be mentioned below, with four dirhams, but the practice follows the hadith of A'ishah.] It is obligatory to act on the statement of the one who is preserved in memory and reliable, as Abu Umar and others said.

On this basis, if the stolen item reaches a quarter of a dinar in valuation, its thief's hand is cut off. This is the view of Ishaq. So understand these two principles, for they are the foundation of the chapter, and [consider] which of what has been said about it is most sound.

Abu Hanifah, his two companions, and al-Thawri said: the hand of the thief is not cut off except for ten dirhams by weight, or a dinar of gold in coin or by weight. It is not cut off until the goods have left the owner's possession. Their proof is the hadith of Ibn Abbas, who said: the shield with which the Prophet ﷺ cut off a hand was valued at ten dirhams. Amr ibn Shu'ayb related it from his father from his grandfather: "The price of the shield on that day was ten dirhams." Al-Daraqutni and others recorded both.

There is a fourth view in this issue, which is what al-Daraqutni related from Umar: "The five is not cut off except for five," and Sulayman ibn Yasar, Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubrumah held this view. Anas ibn Malik said: Abu Bakr, may Allah have mercy on him, cut off a hand for a shield valued at five dirhams.

A fifth view: the hand is cut off for four dirhams or more. This was related from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

A sixth view: the hand is cut off for one dirham or more. Uthman al-Batti said this. Al-Tabari mentioned that Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr cut off a hand for one dirham.

A seventh view: the hand is cut off for anything that has a value, on the apparent meaning of the verse. This is the view of the Kharijites, and it was related from al-Hasan al-Basri, who has three reported positions: the first is this one; the second is as related from Umar; and the third is that Qatadah related from him that he said: "We discussed the amount for which amputation applies in the time of Ziyad, and our opinion agreed on two dirhams."

These are views of comparable standing, and the sound one among them is what we have presented to you before.

If it is said: al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Hurayrah, who said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah curses the thief who steals an egg and has his hand cut off, and who steals a rope and has his hand cut off." This agrees with the apparent meaning of the verse regarding amputation for little and much [from ʿ].

The answer is that this came in the form of a warning about small things leading to large ones, just as it came in the form of encouragement for little things treated as though they were great, in his saying, upon him be peace: "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah, even as small as the nest of a sand grouse (*qata*), Allah will build for him a house in Paradise."

It has also been said that this is metaphorical in another way: if someone grows used to stealing little, he will steal much and then his hand is cut off. Better than this is what al-Amash said, which al-Bukhari recorded at the end of the hadith as an explanation: "They used to think that [the egg] was an iron helmet (*bayd al-hadid*), and as for the rope, they used to think that it was one of those whose value equals dirhams." I say: such as ship ropes and the like. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Most people agree that amputation applies only to one who takes out of a secured place (*hirz*) an item for which amputation is due. Al--Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: if someone gathers the garments in a house, he is cut off. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan also said, in another statement, the same as the statement of the rest of the scholars, and so it became a sound consensus. Praise be to Allah.

**The third issue:** The *hirz* is what is set up as usual for guarding people's wealth, and it varies for each thing according to its condition, as will be explained. Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is no established report on this subject that the scholars do not dispute; rather, it is like a consensus among the scholars. It is related from al-Hasan and the Zahiris that they did not require a secured place. In the *Muwatta'* of Malik, from Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Husayn al-Makki, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no amputation for hanging fruit [the hanging fruit is fruit on the trees; *hariysat al-jabal* is what is guarded on the mountain; *al-jarin* is the threshing floor, a place where wheat is trodden and which may also be for dates and grapes] and no amputation for what is guarded on a mountain. When the stable (*al-mura*) or the threshing floor shelters it, then amputation applies to what reaches the value of a shield." Abu Umar said: this is a hadith whose meaning is connected to the hadith of Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As and others. This Abd Allah is trustworthy according to all, and Ahmad used to praise him.

From Abd Allah ibn Amr, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he was asked about hanging fruit and said: "Whoever takes some of it out of need, without making a pouch (*khubnah*) [the *khubnah* is the waistband of trousers, and also a bag in which something is carried, and what is carried under the armpit], there is nothing upon him. Whoever leaves with something from it, upon him is amputation. Whoever steals less than that, upon him is a fine of twice its value, and punishment." In another narration, "lashes as a deterrent" replaces "punishment." The scholars said: the lashing was later abrogated and amputation was put in its place. Abu Umar said: his saying "a fine of twice its value" is abrogated; I know of no jurist who held it except what came from Umar concerning the flour of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, which Malik narrated, and which is a report from Ahmad ibn Hanbal. What the people hold concerning compensation is by the equivalent, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So whoever has assaulted you, assault him in the same way as he has assaulted you﴾ [Q 2:194]. [See vol. 2 p. 354.]

Abu Dawud related from Safwan ibn Umayyah who said: I was sleeping in the mosque with a cloak (*khamisah*) of mine, worth thirty dirhams, and a man came and snatched it from me. The man was caught and brought to the Prophet ﷺ, who ordered that he be cut off. I came to him and said: "Will you cut off his hand over thirty dirhams? I will sell it to him and give him its price on credit." He said: "Why was this not before you brought it to me?" [The *khamisah* is a garment of silk and wool with patterns; it is said it is not called *khamisah* unless it is black and patterned.]

From the viewpoint of reasoning: wealth was created ready to be benefited from by all creatures. Then the primary wisdom ruled that it be specially assigned to individuals, which is ownership under the law, and desires remained attached to it, and hopes hovered over it. Chivalry and religious commitment restrain these desires in the fewest of people, and protection and securing restrain them among most people. When its owner secures it, then protection and securing come together, which is the utmost possible for a human being. When both are violated, the offence becomes grave and the punishment is severe. When one of the two protections is violated, which is ownership, then compensation and discipline become obligatory.

**The fourth issue:** When a group gather and together take a quorum (*nisab*) out of its secured place, then either some of them are able to remove it alone, or none can remove it except by their cooperation. If it is the first case, our scholars disagreed on it in two views: one holds that amputation applies, and the other holds that it does not. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i also held this, and they said: those who jointly steal are not cut off unless each one's share must reach a quorum, based on his saying, upon him be peace [from ʿ and j]: "The hand of the thief is not cut off except for a quarter of a dinar or more." Each one of these did not steal a quorum, so there is no amputation for them.

The reasoning for amputation in one of the two reports is that joint participation in a crime does not remove its punishment, just as joint participation in killing does not. Ibn al-Arabi said: how close these two are! For we only kill the group for one person in order to protect blood, so that enemies do not cooperate to shed it. Likewise with wealth, the same applies, especially since al-Shafi'i agreed with us that if a group jointly cut off a man's hand, they are cut off, and there is no difference between the two.

If it is the second case, which cannot be removed except by cooperation, then all of them are cut off by the agreement of the scholars, as Ibn al-Arabi mentioned.

**The fifth issue:** If they jointly steal in such a way that one breaches the secured place and another removes the goods, then if the two cooperated, both are cut off. If each acted alone without agreement between them, such as when one comes and another takes out, then neither of them is cut off.

If the two cooperated in the breaching but one alone took out, then the amputation applies to him alone. Al-Shafi'i said: there is no amputation, because this one breached but did not steal, and the other stole from a secured place whose sanctity had been violated. Abu Hanifah said: if he took part in the breaching and entered and took, he is cut off.

Participating in the breaching does not require pressing on one tool together; rather, taking turns in striking is enough to constitute a partnership.

**The Sixth Issue:** If one of them enters and carries the goods out to the entrance of the protected place (*hirz*), and then the other reaches in and takes them, the second is liable to the hand's amputation, and the first is to be punished. Ashhab said: both are to have their hands cut off.

If he places the goods outside the protected place, the amputation is due from him alone, not from the one who takes them. If he places them in the middle of the breach (*naqb*), and the other takes them and their hands meet in the breach, both are to have their hands cut off.

**The Seventh Issue:** A grave and a mosque are protected places (*hirz*). According to the majority, the grave-robber (*nabbash*) has his hand cut off. Abu Hanifa said: there is no amputation for him, because he stole from a place that was not protected, property exposed to destruction, which has no owner, since the dead do not own.

Some of them deny that this is theft at all, because there is no one residing there, and theft is only where eyes are avoided and people are guarded against. The people of Transoxiana (*ma wara' al-nahr*) relied on the denial of theft.

The majority said: he is a thief, because he has wrapped himself in the cloak of the night and avoided eyes, and he has chosen a time when no one is watching or prying. He is in the position of one who steals at a time when people have gone out for the festival and the town is empty of all of them.

As for their claim that the grave is not a protected place, it is invalid, because the protected place of anything is according to its possible condition.

As for their claim that the dead do not own, it is also invalid, because it is not permitted to leave the dead naked. This need requires that the grave be a protected place.

Allah, exalted is He, has drawn attention to this by His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ (al-Mursalat 77:25–26), so that the living may dwell upon it and the dead be buried in it.

As for their claim that it is "exposed to destruction": everything the living wear is also exposed to destruction and wear through use, except that one of the two matters is quicker than the other. Abu Dawud related from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called me and said:

(How will you be when death strikes the people, such that the house [the grave here] will be bought with a servant?) He meant the grave. I said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: (Then you must be patient.)

Hammad said: On this basis, those who said that the hand of the thief is cut off said so, because he has entered the house of the dead.

As for the mosque: whoever steals its mats (*husur*) has his hand cut off. This was related by Isa from Ibn al-Qasim, even if the mosque has no door, and he considered them protected.

If he steals the doors, he is also to have his hand cut off. It is also related from Ibn al-Qasim that if his theft of the mats was by day, he is not amputated; but if he climbed over the wall by night, he is amputated. It is mentioned from Sahnun that if his mats were sewn together, one part to another, he is amputated; otherwise he is not.

Asbagh said: the thief of the mosque's mats, its lamps, and its paving is to be amputated, just as if he stole its door secretly, or a beam from its roof, or from its supports (*jawa'iz*).

[Editorial note: the *jaʾiz* is the wooden beam that carries the house's timber; its plural is *ajwiza*, *jawazan*, and *jawa'iz*.]

Ashhab said in the Book of Muhammad: there is no amputation for anything from the mosque's mats, its lamps, or its paving.

**The Eighth Issue:** The scholars differed as to whether there is a fine (*gharm*) together with the amputation or not.

Abu Hanifa said: the fine never combines with the amputation in any circumstance, because Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And as for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, a punishment from Allah﴾ and He did not mention a fine.

Al-Shafi'i said: he pays the value of what he stole, whether he is wealthy or poor, and it becomes a debt upon him; when he becomes wealthy, he pays it. This is also the view of Ahmad and Ishaq.

As for our scholars, Malik and his companions, they said: if the item itself is still present, he returns it; if it has been destroyed, then if he is wealthy he pays, and if he is poor, he is not pursued for it as a debt and nothing is owed by him. Malik related the same from al-Zuhri.

Shaykh Abu Ishaq said: It has also been said that he is pursued for it as a debt together with the amputation, whether wealthy or poor. He said: This is the view of more than one of our scholars from the people of Medina. Its soundness is argued from the fact that these are two rights of two claimants, so neither cancels the other, like blood-money (*diya*) and expiation (*kaffara*). Then he said: "And this is what I say."

The qadi Abu al-Hasan argued for the well-known position with his (ﷺ) saying: (When the prescribed punishment is carried out on the thief, there is no liability upon him.) He traced it in his book.

Some of them said: pursuing him for the fine is a punishment, and amputation is a punishment, and two punishments are not combined. On this the qadi Abd al-Wahhab relied.

The correct view is the view of al-Shafi'i and whoever agrees with him. Al-Shafi'i said: the thief pays what he stole, whether wealthy or poor, whether he is amputated or not. Likewise when highway robbers commit banditry. He said: The prescribed punishment does not cancel what he destroyed of the servants' rights.

As for what our scholars argued from the hadith, (If he is poor), the Kufans argued with it, and it is the view of al-Tabari. There is no proof in it. It was related by al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf.

Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) said: This hadith is not strong, and no proof is established by it. Ibn al-Arabi said: This hadith is false.

Al-Tabari said: The analogy is that he owes the value of what he consumed. But we have set that aside, following the report on this matter.

Abu Umar said: Abandoning analogy for a weak report is not permissible, because a weak report does not establish a ruling.

**The Ninth Issue:** It has been disputed concerning the amputation of the hand of one who steals property from the one who stole it. Our scholars said: he is amputated.

Al-Shafi'i said: he is not amputated, because he stole from one who is not the owner and from a place that is not protected.

Our scholars said: the owner's sanctity over it remains; it has not been severed from him. The thief is like the usurper: if the usurped property is stolen from him, he is amputated. If it is said: "Treat its protection as no protection," we say: The protection remains, and the ownership remains, and ownership has not been nullified in it, so they could not say to us: "Nullify the protection."

**The Tenth Issue:** They differed if he repeats the theft after the amputation, concerning the same stolen item. The majority said: he is amputated.

Abu Hanifa said: there is no amputation for him.

The generality of the Qur'an requires amputation for him, and it refutes his view.

Abu Hanifa also said, concerning a thief who comes to own the stolen item by purchase or gift before the amputation: he is not amputated. But Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And as for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾. So when amputation has become due as a right of Allah, exalted is He, nothing removes it.

**The Eleventh Issue:** The majority read ﴿wa-l-sariqu﴾ ("and the thief") with the nominative (*raf'*).

Sibawayh said: the meaning is, "And among what has been prescribed for you is the thief, male and female."

It was also said: the nominative in both is by way of the inceptive (*ibtida'*), and the predicate is ﴿faqtaʿu aydiyahuma﴾ ("cut off their hands").

The intention is not toward a specific individual, for if the intention were a specific individual, the accusative would be required. You say: "Zaydan, strike him." Rather, it is like your saying: "Whoever steals, cut off his hand."

Al-Zajjaj said: This is the view that is preferred.

It was also read as ﴿wa-l-sariqa﴾ with the accusative in both, by way of the implied verb "cut off the thief, male and female." This is the choice of Sibawayh, because the verb with an imperative is more fitting. Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The usual form in the speech of the Arabs is the accusative, as you say, 'Zaydan, strike him.' But the common readers (*'amma*), most of them, refused anything but the nominative." So Sibawayh placed the general category of the thief in the position of a specific individual.

Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿wa-l-sarikuna wa-l-sarikatu fa-qtaʿu aymanahum﴾ ("and the thieves, male and female, cut off their right hands"), and this strengthens the reading of the community.

*Al-saraq* and *al-sarqa* with a kasra on the *ra'* in both are the name of the stolen thing. The verbal noun of *saraqa* (yasriqu) is *saraq*, with a fatha on the *ra'*. This was said by al-Jawhari.

The origin of this word is taking something in secret from eyes. From it comes *istaraqa al-sam'* (he eavesdropped), and *sarraqahu al-nazar* (the glance stole from him).

Ibn Arafa said: In the view of the Arabs, the thief is one who comes stealthily to a protected place and takes from it what is not his. If he takes from the open, he is a plunderer (*mukhtalis*), a snatcher (*mustalib*), a looter (*muntahib*), or a hunter-thief (*muhtaris*). [Editorial note: the *muhtaris* is one who steals the game of the mountain.] If he resists with what is in his hand, he is a usurper (*ghasib*).

I say: In a report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): (The worst theft is the one who steals from his prayer.) They said: "How does one steal from his prayer?" He said: (He does not complete its bowing or its prostration.) Al-Muwatta' and others recorded it. So he called him a thief, though he is not a thief in the sense of the root of the derivation, for there is not in it, generally, the stealth of eyes.

**The Twelfth Issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿faqtaʿu﴾ ("cut off"). *Al-qat'* means separating and removing. It is not made obligatory except by the gathering of attributes which are considered in the thief, in the stolen item, in the place from which it was stolen, and in its description.

As for what is considered in the thief: there are five attributes: puberty (*bulugh*), sound mind (*'aql*), that he is not the owner of the stolen property from its possessor, and that he has no authority over it. So a slave is not amputated if he steals from his master's property, and likewise a master, if he takes the property of his slave, is never amputated, because the slave and his property belong to his master.

No one has been amputated for taking the property of his own slave, because he is taking his own property. The amputation of a slave is dropped by the consensus of the Companions and by the saying of the caliph [the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him; the thief was a slave of Abd Allah ibn Amr al-Hadrami, who stole a mirror belonging to his wife, worth sixty dirhams]: "Your slave has stolen your goods."

Al-Daraqutni related from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (There is no amputation upon a runaway slave if he steals, nor upon a dhimmi.) He said: Only Fahd ibn Sulayman raised it [to the Prophet], and the correct form is that it is a *mawquf* report [stopping at Ibn Abbas].

Ibn Majah related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (If a slave steals, sell him, even for a *nashsh*.) [The *nashsh* (with a fatha on the *n* and a shadda on the *sh*) is twenty dirhams; it is also used for half of anything, so the meaning is selling even for half the value.] (He transmitted it from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba, who related from Abu Usama, from Abu Awana, from Umar ibn Abi Salama, from Abu Hurayra.) Ibn Majah said: And Jubara ibn al-Mughallis related to us, from Hajjaj ibn Tamim, from Maymun ibn Mihran, from Ibn Abbas, that a slave of the one-fifth (*raqiq al-khums*) stole from the one-fifth, and he was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not amputate him, and he said: (The property of Allah, some of it stole from some of it.) Jubara ibn al-Mughallis is abandoned (*matruk*), as said by Abu Zur'a al-Razi.

There is no amputation upon a child or a madman.

It is obligatory upon a dhimmi, a treaty-holder (*mu'ahad*), and an enemy alien (*harbi*) who entered under safe conduct.

As for what is considered in the stolen item: there are four attributes. They are the minimum value (*nisab*), which has already been discussed; that it be something that is valued and owned, and whose sale is lawful. If it is something that is not valued and whose sale is not lawful, such as wine and swine, there is no amputation for it by agreement, except for a free young child according to Malik and Ibn al-Qasim. It was said: there is no amputation for him, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa, because he is not property.

Our scholars said: he is among the greatest of property, and the thief is not amputated for property in itself. Amputation is only for the attachment of souls to it, and the attachment of souls to a free person is greater than their attachment to a slave.

If it is something whose possession is permitted but whose sale is not permitted, such as a dog whose keeping is authorized and the flesh of sacrificial animals, there is a disagreement between Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab.

Ibn al-Qasim said: The thief of a dog is not amputated. Ashhab said: That applies to a dog whose keeping is forbidden. But as for one whose keeping is authorized, its thief is amputated.

He said: Whoever steals the meat or the hide of a sacrifice is amputated if its value is three dirhams.

Ibn Habib said, Asbagh said: If he steals the sacrificial animal before it is slaughtered, he is amputated; but if he steals it after slaughter, he is not amputated.

The thief takes such an item if its base material may be lawfully owned and sold, but he fashions from it something whose use is forbidden, such as a *tunbur* (a long-necked lute) or other instruments of amusement, like the flute, the *'ud* (lute), and similar instruments of entertainment. In that case it is examined: if what remains of it after its forms are destroyed and its intended benefit is removed amounts to a quarter of a dinar or more, the hand is cut off.

The same ruling applies to vessels of gold and silver whose use is forbidden, which are ordered to be broken. Only the gold or silver in them is valued, without their craftsmanship.

Likewise, a cross of gold or silver, and impure oil, are subject to the same rule: if their value, despite their impurity, reaches a *nisab* (the minimum value for amputation), the hand is cut off for it.

The third condition: the thief must have no ownership (*milk*) in the stolen property, such as one who steals what he has pledged or what he has rented. There must also be no shubha milk (a semblance of ownership). Our scholars and others differ over whether a semblance of ownership is to be taken into account, as in the case of one who steals from the spoils of war (*maghnam*) or from the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*), because he has a share in it.

It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man who had stolen a *mighfar* [[*al-mighfar* (with a kasra on the *mim*): a chainmail covering woven to fit the head, worn beneath the cap.]] from the fifth (*khums*) was brought to him. He did not see a cutting (of the hand) upon him, and he said: "He has a share in it."

On this basis is the position of the majority regarding the public treasury.

It has been said: he must have the hand cut off, adhering to the general wording of the verse about theft.

The property must also be something that can validly be stolen, such as a young slave or a non-Arabic-speaking adult slave, because what cannot validly be stolen, such as an eloquent (Arabic-speaking adult) slave, does not incur amputation.

As for what is required regarding the place from which the item is stolen, there is one condition: the protected place (*hirz*) appropriate to that kind of item.

The summary on this: every thing has a known place, and its place is its *hirz*; and every thing that has a guardian with it, its guardian is its *hirz*. Houses, dwellings and shops are a *hirz* for what is in them, whether their owners are absent or present. Likewise the public treasury is a *hirz* for the community of Muslims, and the thief has no right in it, even if before the theft he was among those whom the imam may give to. The right of each Muslim becomes determined only by the actual giving. Do you not see that the imam may direct the entire wealth to one of the public interests and not distribute it among the people, or he may distribute it in one city and not another, and withhold it from some people and not others? So, by presumption, this thief is one who has no right in it.

Likewise, the spoils of war are of two kinds:
either they become determined by division, in which case the ruling is what we mentioned regarding the public treasury; or they become determined by the mere taking of them by those who witnessed the battle. In that case the thief's taking must be measured against the amount he stole: if it exceeds his right, his hand is cut off; otherwise it is not cut off. [[All the original manuscripts omit the thirteenth point except *k*, and then the nineteenth point is dropped from them.]]

**The fourteenth point:** The backs of animals are a *hirz* for what they carry. The forecourts of shops are a *hirz* for what is placed in them at the place of sale, even if there is no shop there, whether its people are present or not, whether it was stolen by night or by day.

Likewise the place where a sheep stands in the market, whether tied or untied, and animals at their tethering places are protected, whether their owners are with them or not. But if the animal is at the door of a mosque or in the market, it is not protected unless there is a guardian with it. Whoever ties it at his forecourt or makes a place for his animals to be tethered, that is a *hirz* for them.

A ship is a *hirz* for what is in it, whether it is adrift or moored. If the ship itself is stolen, it is like an animal: if it is adrift, it is not protected; but if its owner has moored it at a place and anchored it there, then its mooring is a *hirz*. Likewise, if someone is with it wherever it is, then it is protected, like an animal at the door of a mosque with a guardian. Except that if the travellers halt with the ship at a stopping-place during their journey and tie it up, then that is a *hirz* for it, whether its owner is with it or not.

**The fifteenth point:** There is no disagreement that residents of one building, like the hostels in which each man has his own room, are such that whoever among them steals from his fellow's room is cut off, if he is caught after he has come out with his theft into the courtyard of the building, even if he has not taken it into his own room nor carried it out of the building.

There is no disagreement that whoever among them steals from the courtyard of the building is not cut off for anything, even if he takes it into his room or carries it out of the building. This is because its courtyard is open to everyone for buying and selling, except if it is an animal in its tethering place or something similar to it of goods.

**The sixteenth point:** Parents are not cut off for stealing their son's property, because of his (ﷺ) saying: "You and your property belong to your father." But they are cut off for stealing their property, because the son has no semblance of right in it.

It has been said: they are not cut off. This is the view of Ibn Wahb and Ashhab, because a son is generally at ease with his father's property. Do you not see that a slave is not cut off for stealing his master's property? So it is all the more fitting that a son should not be cut off for stealing his father's property.

They differed about the grandfather. Malik and Ibn al-Qasim said: he is not cut off. Ashhab said: he is cut off.

Malik's view is the more correct, because he is a father. Malik said: "It is more beloved to me that grandparents, on the paternal or maternal side, not be cut off, even if they are not entitled to maintenance." Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab said: "Anyone other than them among the relatives is cut off."

Ibn al-Qasim said: "Whoever steals out of hunger that befell him is not cut off."

Abu Hanifa said: "No one among those within the prohibited degrees is cut off, such as the paternal aunt, maternal aunt, sister, and others." This is also the view of al-Thawri.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: whoever steals from these is cut off.

Abu Thawr said: every thief who steals what is subject to the cutting of the hand is cut off, unless they agree upon something, in which case it is submitted to the consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement). And Allah knows best.

**The seventeenth point:** They differed concerning the thief of a *mushaf* (a copy of the Qur'an). Al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf and Abu Thawr said: he is cut off if its value is that for which the hand is cut off. Ibn al-Qasim also said this.

Al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifa) said: "The thief of a *mushaf* is not cut off."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The thief of a *mushaf* is cut off."

They differed about the *tarrar* (pickpocket) [[*al-tarrar*: one who slits a man's sleeve and extracts what is in it, from *tarr*, meaning cutting and slitting.]] who slits the purse from the sleeve. One group said: whoever slits from inside the sleeve or from outside is cut off. This is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr and Ya'qub.

Abu Hanifa, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and Ishaq said: if the dirhams were tied in the outer part of his sleeve and he slit them and stole them, he is not cut off; but if they were tied towards the inside of the sleeve and he put his hand in and stole them, he is cut off.

Al-Hasan said: he is cut off.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: he is cut off from whichever direction he slit.

**The eighteenth point:** They differed concerning cutting off the hand while on a journey, and the establishing of the *hudud* (prescribed punishments) in enemy territory. Malik and al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: the *hudud* are established in enemy territory, and there is no difference between the abode of war and the abode of Islam.

Al-Awza'i said: whoever goes out to war with an army, even if he is not the governor of one of the cities, establishes the *hudud* among his troops, except the cutting (of the hand).

Abu Hanifa said: when the troops invade enemy territory and have a commander over them, he does not establish the *hudud* among his troops, unless he is the imam of Egypt, Syria, Iraq or something similar, in which case he establishes the *hudud* among his troops.

Al-Awza'i and those who follow his view relied on the hadith of Junada ibn Abi Umayya, who said: "We were with Busr ibn Arta'a at sea, and a thief called Misdar, who had stolen a *bukhtiyya* [[*al-bukhtiyya*: the female of the *bukht* camels, which are camels with long necks; the word is Arabicized.]] was brought to him. He said: 'I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Hands are not cut off in battle" [[In *al-Tahdhib* and *Usd al-Ghaba*: "on a journey."]]. Were it not for that, I would have cut him off.'"

It is said that this man was born in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he had a bad reputation regarding 'Ali and his companions. He is the one who slaughtered two children of 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas, so their mother lost her reason and wandered aimlessly. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, invoked against him that Allah prolong his life and take away his reason, and so it happened. [[So it is in the original manuscripts. In *al-Tahdhib* and *Usd al-Ghaba*: he killed 'Abd al-Rahman and Qutham, the two sons of 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-'Abbas.]]

Yahya ibn Ma'in said: Busr ibn Arta'a was a bad man.

Those who hold the view of amputation relied on the general wording of the Qur'an, and this is the sound view, Allah willing.

The strongest argument for those who prohibit amputation in enemy territory and the *hudud* is the fear that this may lead to association (*shirk*).

And Allah knows best.

**The nineteenth point:** When the hand or foot is cut off, where is it to be cut?

The majority said: the hand is cut from the wrist, and the foot from the ankle joint, and the leg is cauterized when it is cut.

Some said: it is cut to the elbow.

It has been said: to the shoulder, because the term "hand" includes that.

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the foot is cut from the middle of the foot, and the heel is left for him [[*al-'aqib*: the back part of the front of the foot.]]. Ahmad and Abu Thawr said likewise.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he ordered the hand of a man to be cut off, and he said: "Cauterize it" (*uhsimuha*). Its chain of transmission has been questioned. A group, including al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and others, recommended this, and this is the better view, since it is closer to healing and further from destruction.

**The twentieth point:** There is no disagreement that the right hand is the one cut off first. Then they differed if he steals a second time. Malik, the people of Medina, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and others said: his left foot is cut off; then for a third theft his left hand; then for a fourth theft his right foot. Then if he steals a fifth time, he is disciplined (*yu'azzar*) and imprisoned.

Abu Mus'ab, one of our scholars, said: he is killed after the fourth theft, and he cited a hadith recorded by al-Nasa'i from al-Harith ibn Hatib: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought a thief, and he said: "Kill him." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, he only stole." He said: "Cut off his hand." Then he stole, and his foot was cut off. Then he stole during the time of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, until all his limbs were cut off. Then he stole again, the fifth time. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew better about this when he said, 'Kill him.'" Then he handed him over to a group of young men from Quraysh to kill him, among them 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who loved leadership. He said: "Appoint me over you." They appointed him over them, and whenever he struck, they struck, until they killed him.

And with the hadith of Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered a thief in the fifth theft to be killed, and he said: "Kill him." Jabir said: "We took him and killed him, then we dragged him and threw him in a well, and we threw stones upon him."

Abu Dawud narrated it, and al-Nasa'i recorded it and said: "This is a *munkar* (rejected) hadith, and one of its narrators, Mus'ab ibn Thabit [[Al-Nasa'i's words.]], is not strong. I know of no sound hadith on this subject." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "It is established from Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they cut off the hand after the hand and the foot after the foot." It is also said: in the second theft his left foot is cut off, and no amputation is made for anything other than that; then if he returns, he is disciplined and imprisoned. This is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and it is the view of al-Zuhri, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.
