**Two issues arise here.** The first is his repetition of the words ﴿listeners to falsehood﴾ for emphasis and magnification, which has already been discussed [cf. vol. 11, p. 211]. The second is his words ﴿devourers of unlawful gain (suht)﴾, which indicate abundance.

In the language, *suht* originally means ruin and severity. God says: ﴿so that He destroy you with a punishment﴾ [20:61]. [In the other manuscripts: "and this has been discussed in al-Baqarah."] Al-Farazdaq said:

*"The bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left nothing of wealth*
*except what is stripped bare (mashtan), or scraped clean (mujallaf)."*

[The verse is also transmitted as "except *mashtat*," and whoever transmits it this way takes "has left nothing" to mean "has not left remnant." The verse is as transmitted. *Mujallaf* means that of which some remnant remains. It may also be read as *mujallafun* in the nominative, as a conjunction with the meaning, because "has left nothing" means "has not left remaining."] [Source: Lisan al-'Arab, entry *sahata*.]

It is said of one who shaves [the head]: *asaḥta*, meaning he uprooted completely. Unlawful wealth is called *suht* because it destroys (*yasḥatu*) acts of obedience, meaning it removes them and uproots them.

Al-Farra' said: its origin is the ravenousness of hunger. It is said of a man: *masḥūt al-ma'ida*, meaning a great eater. So the one who takes bribes and eats unlawful wealth, out of greed for what he is given, resembles one whose stomach is ravenous through gluttony.

It has also been said: unlawful wealth is called *suht* because it destroys a person's manliness (*muruwwa*).

I say: the first view is better, because with the loss of religion manliness is lost, and there is no manliness for one who has no religion.

Ibn Mas'ud and others said: *suht* is bribery (*rushā*).

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the bribe of a judge is *suht*.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Every flesh that grew from *suht*, the Fire is more deserving of it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is *suht*?" He said: "Bribery in judgment."

It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: *suht* is that a man settles a need for his brother and then he gives him a gift, and he accepts it.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: among *suht* is that a man eats by means of his influence. That is, he has standing with the ruler, and a person asks him for a need, and he does not grant it except in return for a bribe he takes.

There is no disagreement among the early scholars (*salaf*) that taking a bribe to nullify a right, or for what is not permissible, is unlawful *suht*.

Abu Hanifa said: if the judge takes a bribe, he is dismissed from office at that moment even if he is not formally removed, and every ruling he issued after that is void.

I say: this is not something that should be disputed, God willing, because taking a bribe is wickedness (*fisq*) on his part, and the ruling of a wicked person is not valid.

And Allah knows best.

The Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allah has cursed the one who gives a bribe and the one who takes it."

It is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: *suht* is bribery, the *ḥulwān* of the soothsayer [*ḥulwān* is what is given for soothsaying], and seeking a fee in a legal case. [In manuscripts J, K, 'Ayn and Z: "seeking a fee for an act of disobedience."]

It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that he was asked: "Is bribery unlawful in every case?" He said: "No. What is disliked of bribery is that you pay a bribe in order to be given what is not yours, or to avoid a right that has become binding upon you. As for paying a bribe to protect your religion, your blood, or your wealth, that is not unlawful."

Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi, the jurist, said: "We take according to this. There is no harm in a man defending himself and his wealth with a bribe."

This is like what is related from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, that he was in Abyssinia and paid two dinars as a bribe, and said: "The sin is only upon the one who receives, not upon the one who gives."

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever considers the earnings of the cupper (*hajjām*) and those mentioned with him to be *suht* means that it destroys the manliness of the one who takes it.

I say: the correct view regarding the earnings of the cupper is that it is good (*ṭayyib*), and whoever takes what is good does not lose his manliness nor is his rank lowered.

Mālik related from Humayd al-Ṭawīl, from Anas, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was cupped; Abu Ṭayba cupped him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that he be given a *ṣā'* of dates, and he ordered his family to lighten his *kharāj* (tax) for him."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: this indicates that the earnings of the cupper are good, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not make a price, a fee, or a return for anything that is falsehood.

The hadith of Anas abrogates (*nāsikh*) what the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibited concerning the price of blood, and it abrogates what he disliked concerning the hiring of the cupper.

Al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was cupped, and he gave the cupper his wage. Had it been *suht*, he would not have given it."

*Suht* and *suḥt* are two dialect forms, and both have been read. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read it with two *ḍammas*, and the rest read it with *ḍamma* on the *sīn* alone.

Al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl related from Khārija ibn Muṣ'ab, from Nafi', the reading ﴿devourers of *al-suḥt*﴾ with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn* and a sukun on the *ḥā'*. This is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) from *saḥatahu*. It is said: *asḥata* and *saḥata* have the same meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: *saḥatahu* means he took it away little by little.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿So if they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [5:42]. This is an option (*takhyīr*) from God, the Exalted. Al-Qushayrī mentioned this. Its meaning has already been explained: they were people of a truce (*muwāda'a*), not people of protection (*dhimma*), since when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina he made a truce with the Jews.

It is not obligatory upon us to judge between non-believers when they are not *ahl al-dhimma* (protected non-Muslims). Rather, it is permissible to judge if we wish.

As for the *ahl al-dhimma*, is it obligatory upon us to judge between them when they bring their dispute to us?

There are two opinions of al-Shafi'i. If the dispute involves a Muslim, judgment is obligatory.

Al-Mahdawi said: The scholars agreed that the ruler must judge between a Muslim and a *dhimmī*.

They differed concerning disputes among *dhimmīs*. Some of them held that the verse is *muḥkam* (not abrogated) and that the judge has a choice. This was related from al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi and others, and it is the position of Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī and others, except what is related from Mālik concerning not carrying out the *ḥadd* (prescribed punishment) on the People of the Book for adultery. He said: if a Muslim commits adultery with a Christian woman, he is punished and she is not. If both adulterers are *dhimmīs*, neither is punished. This is the position of Abu Hanifa, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and others.

It has also been related from Abu Hanifa that he said: they are to be flogged and not stoned.

Al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, Abu Thawr and others said: both are subject to the *ḥadd* if they come willingly to our judgment.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: The ruler does not send for them when one of them seeks the help of authorities against another, nor does he bring the opponent to his assembly, unless it concerns injustices (*maẓālim*) from which corruption spreads, such as murder, plundering of houses, and similar matters. As for debts, divorce, and all other transactions, he does not judge between them except after mutual consent. The preferred course for him is not to judge and to refer them back to their own judges.

If he does judge between them, he judges by the rule of Islam.

As for compelling them to submit to Muslim judgment in matters where corruption spreads, this is because we did not make a treaty with them for corruption. It is obligatory to cut off corruption from them and from others, because this preserves their wealth and their blood. Perhaps their religion permits such things, and corruption would spread among us. For this reason we prevented them from openly selling wine and from openly displaying adultery and other filth, so that the foolish among the Muslims would not be corrupted by them.

As for the judgment in matters specific to their religion, such as divorce, adultery and the like, they are not obliged to follow our religion. To judge between them by our law in these matters would harm their judges and change their religious community. This does not apply to debts and transactions, because in these there is a kind of injustice and the cutting off of corruption.

And Allah knows best.

There is a second opinion regarding the verse. It is what has been related from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and also from al-Nakha'i, that the option mentioned in the verse is abrogated by God's words: ﴿and judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [5:49]. And that the judge is obliged to judge between them. This is the position of 'Ata' al-Khurasani, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and others.

It is related from 'Ikrima that he said: ﴿So if they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them﴾ was abrogated by another verse: ﴿and judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [5:49].

Mujahid said: Only two verses of *al-Mā'ida* have been abrogated: His words ﴿either judge between them or turn away from them﴾, which were abrogated by ﴿and judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾, and His words ﴿Do not violate the sacred rites of Allah﴾ [5:2], which were abrogated by ﴿then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [9:5].

Al-Zuhri said: The established practice (*sunna*) has been that the People of the Book are referred in their rights and inheritances to the people of their own religion, unless they come desiring the judgment of Allah, and then he judges between them by the Book of Allah.

Al-Samarqandi said: This view agrees with the view of Abu Hanifa that they are not judged between unless they consent to our judgment.

Al-Nahhas said in his book *al-Nāsikh wa'l-Mansūkh*: God's words ﴿So if they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them﴾ are abrogated, because it was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) first came to Medina, and at that time there were many Jews in it. It was more beneficial and more appropriate for them to be referred to their own laws. When Islam became strong, God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed ﴿and judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾.

This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Zuhri, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Suddi, and it is the sound view of al-Shafi'i. He said in the *Book of Jizya*: "He has no option when they come to him for judgment, because of God, Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled﴾ [9:29]."

Al-Nahhas said: This is among the soundest arguments, because if the meaning of His words ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is that the rulings of the Muslims are applied to them, then it is obligatory that they not be referred back to their own rulings. Once this is established, the verse is abrogated.

This is also the view of the Kufan scholars: Abu Hanifa, Zufar, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, with no disagreement among them that when the People of the Book bring their case to the Imam, he may not turn away from them. Except that Abu Hanifa said: if a woman and her husband come, he must judge between them with justice; but if the woman comes alone and the husband does not consent, he does not judge.

The rest said: he judges.

Thus it is established that the view of most scholars is that the verse is abrogated, together with what is established in it through the authoritative report (*tawqīf*) of Ibn 'Abbas. Even if the hadith from Ibn 'Abbas had not come, reasoning would require that it be abrogated, because they have agreed that when the People of the Book bring their case to the Imam, he may judge between them, and that if he judges between them he is correct according to the majority, and that to turn away from them would, according to some scholars, mean leaving an obligation and doing what is not lawful and not permissible for him.

Al-Nahhas said: Among the Kufans who hold that it is abrogated, there is another view. Some of them say: the Imam must, if he knows of a *ḥadd* of the *ḥudūd* of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, among the People of the Book, enforce it even if they do not come to him for judgment. They argue that God's words ﴿and that you judge between them﴾ admit of two meanings:

One: judge between them if they come to you for judgment.

The other: judge between them even if they do not come to you, if you know this about them.

They said: We found in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and in the Sunna of His Messenger (ﷺ), what makes it obligatory to establish the right against them even if they do not come to us for judgment. As for what is in the Book of Allah, it is His words: ﴿O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah﴾ [4:135].

As for what is in the Sunna, it is the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: "A Jew who had been flogged and blackened was passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Is this how the *ḥadd* for adultery is with you?' They said: 'Yes.' He called a man of their scholars and said:

("Do you swear by God, is this the punishment of the adulterer among you?") He said: "No."

[The hadith continues], and it has already been mentioned.

Al-Nahhas said: They argued that the Prophet ﷺ judged between them, though they had not brought the matter to him for this ruling, in this hadith.

If someone says: In the hadith of Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that the Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ... it is said to him: Neither does the hadith of Malik state that the two who committed adultery consented to the judgment, and yet the Prophet ﷺ stoned them.

Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr said: Had those who argued from the hadith of al-Bara' reflected upon it, they would not have argued thus, because in the course of the hadith there is an explanation of the words of the Mighty and Majestic One: "If you are given this, then take it, and if you are not given it, then beware" [al-Ma'idah 5:41]. He says: If they give you the flogging and blackening (al-tahmim), then take it; and if they give you stoning, then beware. This is evidence that they had made him judge.

This is clear in the hadith of Ibn Umar and others.

If someone says: In the hadith of Ibn Umar there is nothing stating that the two adulterers appointed the Messenger of God ﷺ as judge, nor that they consented to his ruling.

It is said to him: The punishment for adultery is a right of God Most High which the ruler is bound to enforce. It is known that the Jews had a ruler who judged among them and enforced their punishments upon them, and he is the one to whom the Messenger of God ﷺ referred.

And God knows best.

God Most High said: "And if you judge, then judge between them with justice" [al-Ma'idah 5:42]. Al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Qurayzah and al-Nadir were two tribes, and al-Nadir was more honoured than Qurayzah. Whenever a man from Qurayzah killed a man from al-Nadir, he was killed in retaliation; and whenever a man from al-Nadir killed a man from Qurayzah, he paid a diyah of one hundred wasq [[al-wasq: sixty sa']] of dates. When the Messenger of God ﷺ was sent, a man from al-Nadir killed a man from Qurayzah. They said: Hand him over to us so that we may kill him. They said: Between us and you is the Prophet ﷺ. So there was revealed: "And if you judge, then judge between them with justice," and "a life for a life," and there was revealed: "Do they seek the judgment of the age of ignorance?" [al-Ma'idah 5:50].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And how would they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?﴾ Al-Hasan said: it is stoning (al-rajm). Qatadah said: it is retaliation (al-qawad). It is said: does His saying, ﴿in which is the judgment of Allah﴾, indicate that it has not been abrogated (lam yunsakh)? The answer: Abu 'Ali said: Yes, because if it had been abrogated, it would not be said of it after the abrogation that it is the judgment of Allah, just as it is not said that the judgment of Allah is the permissibility of wine or the prohibition of the Sabbath. And His saying: ﴿and those are not believers﴾ means: not by your judgment that it is from Allah. Abu 'Ali also said: whoever seeks other than the judgment of Allah, out of not being content with it, is a disbeliever, and this was the state of the Jews.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾. That is, [it contains] clarification, illumination, and an explanation that Muhammad (ﷺ) is true. "Guidance" (hudan) is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and "light" (nur) is in conjunction with it. ﴿By it the prophets who submitted [aslamu] judged for those who were Jews﴾.

It has been said: the intended "prophets" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and he was referred to with the plural form. It has also been said: it refers to everyone sent after Moses to uphold the Torah. The Jews said that the prophets were Jews, and the Christians said they were Christians, so God, mighty and majestic, exposed their lie.

The meaning of "submitted" (aslamu) is that they affirmed the Torah from the time of Moses until the time of Jesus, peace be upon them both. Between them there were a thousand prophets, and it is said four thousand. It is also said there were more than that, and they used to judge by what is in the Torah.

It has been said: the meaning of "submitted" is that they humbled themselves and yielded to God's command in what they were sent with. It has also been said: the meaning is "by it the prophets who are upon the religion of Abraham (ﷺ) judge," and the meaning is one.

The meaning of ﴿for those who were Jews﴾ is "over those who were Jews," so the lam carries the sense of "over" ('ala). It has been said: the meaning is "by it the prophets who submitted judge for those who were Jews and over them," and "over them" has been omitted. The phrase "who submitted" here is a qualifier carrying the sense of praise, like ﴿In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾.

"Were Jews" (hadu) means "repented from disbelief." It has been said there is inversion in the verse, meaning: "Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light for those who were Jews. The prophets, the rabbaniyyun (masters of divine knowledge, those who govern people by knowledge and raise them on its minor matters before its major ones) and the ahbar (rabbis) judge by it." That is, the rabbaniyyun judge by it. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others. This was already discussed in Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 122].

Abu Razin said: the rabbaniyyun are the learned, wise scholars and the ahbar. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the jurists. The hibr and habr mean a learned man, and it is derived from al-hibar, which means embellishment. So they "embellish" (yuhabbirun) knowledge, that is, they clarify it and adorn it, and it is "embellished" in their chests. Mujahid said: the rabbaniyyun are above the scholars, and the alif and lam are for emphasis.

Al-Jawhari said: hibr and habr are both the singular of the ahbar of the Jews, and the kasra form is more eloquent, because it is pluralized in the pattern af'al rather than fu'ul. Al-Farra' said: it is hibr with a kasra, and this is said of a learned person. Al-Thawri said: I asked al-Farra' why the hibr was called hibr? He said: a learned person is called hibr and habr, so the meaning is "ink of a hibr," then it was omitted, as He said: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], meaning "ask the people of the town." He said: I asked al-Asma'i, and he said: this is nothing; it was named hibr for its effect. It is said: "on his teeth is a hibr," meaning a yellowness or blackness. Abu al-'Abbas said: the ink with which one writes is called hibr because it is "made beautiful" (yuhbar) with it, that is, it is verified with it. Abu 'Ubayd said: what I hold concerning the singular of the ahbar is al-habr with a fatha, and its meaning is the one who knows how to beautify speech and knowledge and adorn it. He said: thus all the transmitters narrate it with a fatha. The hibr with which one writes, and its place, is the mihbarah with a kasra. Al-Hibr also means a trace, and its plural is hubur, narrated from Ya'qub.

﴿By what they were entrusted to preserve from the Book of God﴾, that is, what was deposited with them of its knowledge. The ba' is connected to "the rabbaniyyun and the ahbar," as if He said: "and the scholars by what they were entrusted to preserve." Or it may be connected to "judge," meaning they judge by what they were entrusted to preserve.

﴿And they were witnesses over it﴾, that is, over the Book, that it is from God. Ibn 'Abbas said: witnesses over the judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ), that it is in the Torah. ﴿So do not fear the people﴾, that is, regarding the manifestation of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the manifestation of stoning. ﴿And fear Me﴾, that is, regarding concealing that. So the address is to the scholars of the Jews. It may also include, in meaning, everyone who concealed a truth that was obligatory upon him and did not make it manifest. The meaning of ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ has already been explained fully [see vol. 1, p. 334].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has sent down, those are the disbelievers﴾. "The wrongdoers" and "the defiantly disobedient" were all revealed concerning the disbelievers. This is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of al-Bara', and it has already been mentioned. This is the view of the majority. As for the Muslim, he does not become a disbeliever even if he commits a major sin.

It has been said: there is an implied element in it, meaning: "and whoever does not judge by what God has sent down, rejecting the Qur'an and denying the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is a disbeliever." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, and according to this, the verse is general. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan said: it is general to everyone who does not judge by what God has sent down, among the Muslims, the Jews, and the disbelievers, meaning one who holds that and considers it lawful. As for one who does that while believing he is committing a prohibited act, he is among the defiantly disobedient Muslims, and his affair is with God, the Exalted: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him.

Ibn 'Abbas said in one narration: whoever does not judge by what God has sent down has done an act resembling the acts of the disbelievers. It has been said: meaning, whoever does not judge by all that God has sent down is a disbeliever. As for one who judges by monotheism but does not judge by some of the laws, he does not enter this verse. The correct view is the first, except that al-Sha'bi said: it refers specifically to the Jews. Al-Nahhas preferred this and said: three things indicate this. Among them, the Jews were mentioned before this in His saying "for those who were Jews," so the pronoun returns to them. Among them, the context of the speech indicates this, do you not see that after it is "And We prescribed for them," and this pronoun refers to the Jews by consensus. Also, the Jews are those who denied stoning and retaliation.

If someone says: "whoever" (man), when used as a conditional, is general unless evidence specifies it? It is said to him: "whoever" here means "the one who," together with the evidences we have mentioned, and the implied meaning is: "and the Jews who did not judge by what God has sent down, those are the disbelievers." This is among the best of what has been said on this. It is narrated that Hudhayfah was asked about these verses: are they about the Children of Israel? He said: yes, they are about them, and you will surely follow their path step by step, like the sandal to the sandal.

It has been said: "the disbelievers" refers to the Muslims, "the wrongdoers" to the Jews, and "the defiantly disobedient" to the Christians. This is the choice of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, who said: because it is the apparent meaning of the verses. It is also the choice of Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ibn Abi Za'idah, Ibn Shubrumah, and al-Sha'bi too. Tawus and others said: it is not a disbelief that removes one from the religion, but a disbelief short of disbelief. [Al-Bahr says: meaning the disbelief of a Muslim is not like the disbelief of a disbeliever. I say: it is the disbelief of ingratitude according to the Ibadiyyah.] This differs: if one judges by what he has, claiming it is from God, then it is an alteration of it that necessitates disbelief; but if he judges by it out of desire and disobedience, then it is a sin that forgiveness may reach, according to the principle of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding the forgiveness of sinners.

Al-Qushayri said: the doctrine of the Kharijites is that whoever takes a bribe and judges by other than God's judgment is a disbeliever, and this is attributed to al-Hasan and al-Suddi. Al-Hasan also said: God, mighty and majestic, took three things from the judges: that they not follow desire, that they not fear the people and fear Him instead, and that they not exchange His signs for a small price.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 45 (part 1 of 5):

There are thirty issues in it.

**First issue:** God's saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾. God explained that He had made life equal to life in the Torah, but they opposed that and went astray. So the blood-money (diyya) of the Nadiri was greater, and the Nadiri would not be killed for a Qurazi, but the Qurazi would be killed for a Nadiri. When Islam came, the Banu Qurayza appealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning this, and he ruled for equality. The Banu al-Nadir said: "You have lowered us," and this verse was revealed.

"Kataba" here means "faradna" (We enjoined), and this has already been mentioned.

Their law was retaliation (qisas) or pardon, and there was no blood-money among them, as its explanation was given earlier in al-Baqara.

Abu Hanifa and others relied on this verse and said: a Muslim is killed for a dhimmi, because it is "life for life." The explanation of this was given earlier in al-Baqara.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he was asked: "Did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) single you out with anything?" He said: "No, except what is in this," and he brought out a document from the scabbard of his sword, and in it was: "The believers' blood is equal, and they are a single hand against others, and no Muslim is to be killed for a disbeliever, nor a person under a covenant during his covenant."

Also, the verse came only to refute the Jews regarding the preference among tribes, and their taking one man from one tribe in exchange for one man, and from another tribe two men.

The Shafi'is said: "This is a report about the law of those before us, and the law of those before us is not a law for us." What suffices in refuting them has already passed in al-Baqara, so reflect on it there.

**Fourth point:** God said: "And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life," and this was written for the People of the Torah, who were one religion, and they did not have dhimmis as the Muslims have dhimmis, because the jizya and the spoils (fay') which God granted to the believers were not given to anyone before this nation, and no prophet in the past was sent except to his own people. So the verse obligated the ruling upon the Children of Israel, since their blood was equal. It is like the saying of one of us regarding the blood of others than Muslims, "the life is for the life," when he points to specific people and says: "The ruling concerning these people is that the life among them is for the life." Thus, what is obligatory by the ruling of this verse upon the people of the Qur'an is that it be said to them among themselves in this manner: "The life is for the life." There is nothing in the Book of God that indicates that a life is for a life when the religion differs.

**Second issue:** The companions of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: if someone wounds or cuts off an ear or a hand and then kills, that is done to him, because God, the Exalted, said: "And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye." So he takes what he took, and it is done to him as he did.

Our scholars (the Malikis) said: if he intended mutilation (muthla), then the same is done to him. If it happened in the course of their fighting and struggle, he is killed by the sword. They only said that the same is obligatory in the case of mutilation because the Prophet (ﷺ) had the eyes of the 'Uranis branded (samala), as was mentioned earlier in this surah.

**Third issue:** God's saying: "And the eye for the eye." Nafi', 'Asim, al-A'mash and Hamza read all of them in the accusative (naṣb) by way of coordination (ʿaṭf). It is permissible to lighten "anna" (an-na) and to read all of them in the nominative (raf') by beginning a sentence and coordinating.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read all of them in the accusative except the wounds (al-juruh).

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayd used to read "wal-'ayna bil-'ayni wal-anfa bil-anfi wal-udhna bil-udhni wal-sinna bis-sinni wal-juruha" in the nominative in all of them.

Abu 'Ubayd said: Hajjaj related to us from Harun, from 'Abbad ibn Kathir, from 'Uqayl, from al-Zuhri, from Anas: the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: "And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and the wounds are retaliation (qisas)." [In al-Bahr: "bi-takhfif anna" (with the lightening of anna). Then he said: "It is possible that there are two aspects, one of which is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya)," etc.]

The nominative has three aspects: by beginning and predicate, and by the meaning, on the position of "anna al-nafs," because the meaning is "We said to them: the life is for the life."

The third aspect, which Al-Zajjaj stated, is that it is a coordination with the pronoun in "al-nafs," because the pronoun in "al-nafs" is in the nominative position, since the implied sense is "that the life is taken for the life," so the nouns are coordinated with "hiya" (it).

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Whoever reads in the nominative makes that the beginning of a speech, a ruling concerning the Muslims [i.e., and a statement of a new ruling for the Muslims, as in Ruh al-Ma'ani]. This is the more correct of the two views, because it is the recitation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), "wal-'ayna bil-'ayni," and likewise what follows it.

The address is to the Muslims, who were commanded with this.

As for whoever singles out the wounds for the nominative, it is by way of a break from what precedes it and beginning a new statement with it, as if the Muslims were commanded with this specifically, and what came before it was not addressed to them with it.

**Fourth issue:** This verse indicates the applicability of retaliation (qisas) in what has been mentioned. Ibn Shubruma relied on the generality of His saying "and the eye for the eye," that the right eye is put out by the left, and likewise in reverse, and he applied this to the right hand and the left hand. He said: "The incisor is taken for the molar, and the molar for the incisor," based on the generality of His saying, the Exalted: "and the tooth for the tooth."

Those who disagreed with him, and they are the scholars of the Ummah, said: the right eye is the one taken for the right when it exists, and it does not go beyond that to the left unless with consent [in the originals: "illa ma' al-rida" (except with consent), the correct reading as in al-Bahr]. This makes clear to us that what is meant by His saying "and the eye for the eye" is the taking of what is similar to it from the offender, so it is not permissible for him to exceed to another, just as one does not exceed from the leg to the hand in all circumstances, and this is beyond doubt.

**Fifth issue:** The scholars agreed that if both eyes are struck by mistake, the blood-money is due for both, and for one eye, half the blood-money.

For the eye of a one-eyed man (al-a'war) if it is put out, the full blood-money is due. This was related from 'Umar and 'Uthman, and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, al-Zuhri, Qatada, Malik, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, Ahmad and Ishaq said the same.

It was also said: half the blood-money. This was related from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughaffal, Masruq and al-Nakha'i, and al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i and al-Nu'man also said so.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "We say the same, because in the hadith there is: 'In both eyes is the blood-money,' and by reason, when it is so, one of them has half the blood-money."

Ibn al-Arabi said: "This is the apparent analogy, but our scholars said: the benefit of the one-eyed man with his sight is like the benefit of the sound person, or close to it, so the same blood-money is obligatory for him."

**Sixth issue:** They differed about a one-eyed man who puts out the eye of a sound person. It was related from 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali that there is no retaliation (qawad) against him, and the full blood-money is due. 'Ata', Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said the same.

Malik said: "If he wishes, he may take retaliation and leave him blind, and if he wishes, he may take the full blood-money (the blood-money of the eye of the one-eyed man)." [In the originals, "diyat 'ayn al-a'war" (the blood-money of the eye of the one-eyed man), except in 'Ayn, where it is "diyat ghayr al-a'war" (the blood-money of other than the one-eyed man), which is the correct reading.]

Al-Nakha'i said: "If he wishes, he may take retaliation, and if he wishes, he may take half the blood-money."

Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said: "Retaliation is due against him." This was related from 'Ali also, and it is the view of Masruq, Ibn Sirin and Ibn Ma'qil. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Arabi chose it, because God, the Exalted, said: "and the eye for the eye," and the Prophet (ﷺ) made the blood-money for both eyes, so for one eye there is half the blood-money, and retaliation between a sound eye and a one-eyed man is the same as between all other people.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal's argument is that in retaliation from it there is taking all the sight for part of it, and that is not equality. He also relied on what was related from 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali concerning this. Malik's basis is that when the evidences conflicted, the injured party was given the choice.

Ibn al-Arabi said: "Acting on the generality of the Qur'an is preferable, for it is safer before God, the Exalted."

**Seventh issue:** They differed about the eye of a one-eyed man that does not see with it. It was related from Zayd ibn Thabit that he said: "In it there are one hundred dinars." From 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "In it there is a third of its blood-money," and Ishaq said the same. Mujahid said: "In it there is half its blood-money." Masruq, al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and al-Nu'man said: "In it there is a hukuma" (an assessment by arbitration, i.e., a discretionary compensation). Ibn al-Mundhir said: "We say the same, because it is the least of what has been said."

**Eighth issue:** In the destruction of sight in both eyes, while the pupils remain, the full blood-money is due, and this applies equally to the one with weak sight (al-a'mash) [al-a'mash: weakness of sight with tearing most of the time] and the one with night blindness (al-akhfash) [al-khafash: weakness of sight from birth, narrowness of the eye, or defect of the eyelids without pain, or seeing at night but not during the day, or on a cloudy day but not a clear one].

In destroying the sight of one of the two eyes while the other remains, half the blood-money is due.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The best thing said about this is what 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: that he [a man] was ordered to have his sound eye covered, and a man was given an egg and went with it looking until his sight reached its limit, then a mark was made at that point. Then he was ordered to have his other eye covered, and the sound one was opened, and a man was given an egg and went with it looking until his sight reached its limit, then a mark was made at that point. Then he was ordered to be moved to another place, and the same was done to him, and it was found to be the same, so he was given from the other man's property what his sight had lost." This is according to the school of al-Shafi'i, and it is the view of our scholars, and it is:

**Ninth issue:** There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that there is no retaliation for part of the sight, since it is impossible to reach it.

The way retaliation is carried out for the eye is that a mirror is heated and then placed on the other eye with a piece of cotton, then the mirror is brought close to his eye until its pupil flows. This was related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him; al-Mahdawi and Ibn al-Arabi mentioned it.

They differed about the eyelid of the eye. Zayd ibn Thabit said: "In it there is a quarter of the blood-money." This is the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu Hashim [Abu Hashim dropped out of Ka and A, and he is al-Rummani, a contemporary of al-Thawri; in J it reads "Ibn Hashim"], al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).

It was related from al-Sha'bi that he said: "For the upper eyelid there is a third of the blood-money, and for the lower eyelid two-thirds of the blood-money," and Malik said the same.

**Tenth issue:** God's saying: ﴿And the nose for the nose﴾. A hadith came from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "For the nose, when it is entirely cut off (uʿibba jadʿan), there is the blood-money." [uʿibba: i.e., its cutting was completely eradicated.]

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Every person of knowledge who is preserved from them agreed on this statement, and retaliation for the nose, when the offence is deliberate, is like retaliation for all other limbs according to the Book of God, the Exalted."

They differed about breaking the nose. Malik held that in a deliberate case there is retaliation (qawad), and in an accidental case, ijtihad (independent judgment assessed by a jurist).

Ibn Nafi' related that there is no blood-money for the nose until it is entirely removed from its root.

Abu Ishaq al-Tunisi said: "This is an anomalous view (shadhdh), and the well-known one is the first."

When we base ourselves on the well-known view, then for part of the cartilage (al-marin) of the nose there is a proportional part of the blood-money according to the calculation of the cartilage.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "What is cut off from the nose is according to its proportion. This was related from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz and al-Sha'bi, and al-Shafi'i said the same."

Abu 'Umar said:

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 45 (part 2 of 5):

They differed concerning the nose's cartilage (al-marin) when it is cut off without the whole nose being uprooted. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and their companions held that in this case the full blood-money (diyya) is due, and if some of it is cut off after that, then there is a discretionary assessment (hukumah) for it.

Malik said:
The nose's portion for which the full blood-money is due is that the cartilage (al-marin) be cut off, and it lies below the bone.

Ibn al-Qasim said:
Whether the cartilage is cut from the bone, or the nose is uprooted from the bone beneath the two eyes, the full blood-money is due in either case, just as the full blood-money is due for the glans (al-hashafa).
And for the uprooting of the male organ the full blood-money is due.

The eleventh issue: Ibn al-Qasim said:
If the nose is slit or broken and heals crookedly (ala 'athm) [the 'athm is setting that is not straight], then the matter is left to judgment (ijtihad), and there is no fixed blood-money for it.
And if it heals without crookedness, there is nothing due for it.
He said:
A slit nose that heals without crookedness is not like a mudihah (a wound that exposes the bone) which heals without crookedness, for which its blood-money is due, because that was established by the Sunnah, and there is no report concerning a slit nose.
He said:
The nose is a single bone that has no mudihah.
Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions agreed that there is no ja'ifah (a wound reaching the interior of the body) in it, and in their view there is no ja'ifah except in what is within the cavity.
The marin is the soft part of the nose. Al-Khalil and others said the same.
Abu 'Umar said:
I think its rawthah is its marin and its arnabah is its tip.
It has also been said: the arnabah, the rawthah and the 'artamah are the tip of the nose.
And what the jurists, Malik, al-Shafi'i and the Kufans and those who followed them, hold regarding the sense of smell, if it is diminished or lost, is a discretionary assessment (hukumah).

The twelfth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the ear for the ear﴾. Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said concerning one who cuts off a man's two ears: there is a discretionary assessment for it. The full blood-money is due only for hearing, and its diminution is measured just as it is measured for sight.
In the case of destroying the hearing of one of the two ears, half the blood-money is due, even if he could hear only with it, unlike the one-eyed (al-'ayn al-'awra) for whom the full blood-money is due, as previously stated.
Ashhab said:
If, when asked about the hearing, it is said that one of the two ears hears what both ears hear, then in my view it is like sight. When hearing is doubted, it is tested by calling to him from several places, and this is measured. If the results are equal or close, he is given an amount corresponding to what he has lost of his hearing, and he is made to swear an oath concerning that.
Ashhab said:
It is reckoned for him by comparison with the average hearing of a man like him. If he is tested and his responses are inconsistent, he is owed nothing.
Isa ibn Dinar said:
If his responses are inconsistent, he is awarded the lesser amount together with his oath.

The thirteenth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the tooth for the tooth﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he exacted retaliation for a tooth and said: "The Book of God is retaliation." And a hadith came from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "For a tooth, five camels." Ibn al-Mundhir said: We hold to the apparent meaning of this hadith, that there is no preference of the incisors (al-thaniyah) over the canines (al-anyab), the molars (al-adras) and the premolars (al-ruba'iyat) [the rubā'iyah is the tooth between the incisor and the canine], since all of them enter into the apparent meaning of the hadith. The majority of the people of knowledge also say this. Among those who held to the apparent meaning of the hadith and did not prefer any of them over another were 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Tawus, al-Zuhri, Qatadah, Malik, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Nu'man and Ibn al-Hasan. This was also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas and Mu'awiyah.
There is a second opinion, which we have related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: that he decided for what is in the front of the mouth five fara'id, five fara'id, which is fifty dinars, the value of each fara'id being ten dinars. And for the molars, a camel for each. 'Ata' used to say: for the tooth, the two premolars and the two canines, five each; and for the rest, two camels each. The upper and lower parts of the mouth are equal, and the molars are equal.
Abu 'Umar said: As for what Malik related in his Muwatta' from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, that 'Umar decided for the molars a camel for each, the meaning is that there are twenty molars and twelve teeth: four incisors, four premolars and four canines. So according to 'Umar's view the blood-money becomes eighty camels: for the teeth, five each, and for the molars, one camel each. According to Mu'awiyah's view, for the molars and teeth, five camels each, making the blood-money one hundred and sixty camels. According to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib's view, two camels each for the molars, which are twenty, so forty are due; and for the teeth, five camels each, which is sixty. These make up the hundred camels, which is the full blood-money in camels. The disagreement among them concerns only the molars, not the teeth.
Abu 'Umar said: The disagreement of the scholars among the Companions and the Successors concerning the blood-money for teeth, and preferring some over others, is very great. The proof stands for what the jurists Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri adopted, based on the apparent words of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "And for a tooth, five camels," and the molar is a tooth among the teeth. Ibn 'Abbas related that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The fingers are equal, and the teeth are equal: the incisor and the molar are equal, this and that are equal." This is an explicit text, related by Abu Dawud. Abu Dawud also related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ made the fingers of the two hands and the two feet equal.
Abu 'Umar said: On these reports, the body of jurists of the regions and the majority of the people of knowledge hold that all fingers are equal in blood-money, and that all teeth are equal in blood-money, the incisors, the molars and the canines, none of them being preferred over another, according to what is in the book of 'Amr ibn Hazm. al-Thawri reported from Azhar ibn Muharib, who said: Two men brought a dispute before Shurayh. One had struck the incisor of the other, and the other had struck his molar. Shurayh said: The incisor and its beauty, and the molar and its usefulness, are a tooth for a tooth; let them be valued. Abu 'Umar said: On this, the practice today is in all the regions. And God knows best.

The fourteenth issue: If someone strikes a man's tooth and it turns black, then the full blood-money is due for it according to Malik and al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and Abu Hanifa said the same. It was also related from Zayd ibn Thabit, and it is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin and Shurayh. It was related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that a third of its blood-money is due, and Ahmad and Ishaq said the same. al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: a discretionary assessment (hukumah) is due for it.
Ibn al-'Arabi said: This disagreement, in my view, returns to agreement. If its blackness has removed its usefulness and only its form remains, like a paralysed hand or a blind eye, then there is no disagreement that the blood-money is due. If some of its usefulness or all of it remains, then only a discretionary assessment (hukumah) is due for the amount by which its usefulness has decreased. And what was related from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, that a third of its blood-money is due, has not been soundly transmitted from him either in chain or in jurisprudence.

The fifteenth issue: They differed concerning the tooth of a child that is pulled out before he has shed his milk teeth (yuthghir) [yuthghir means that the milk teeth have fallen out]. Malik, al-Shafi'i and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: If the child's tooth is pulled out and then grows back, nothing is due from the one who pulled it. However, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: If it grows back shorter than the one next to it, then a part of its compensation (arsh) is taken corresponding to the amount of its shortfall. A group said: a discretionary assessment (hukumah) is due for it. This was related from al-Sha'bi, and al-Nu'man also said so. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It should be deferred until the time when people of experience say it will not grow back. When that is the case, the full amount is due for it, according to the apparent meaning of the hadith; and if it grows back, the compensation is returned. Most of the people of knowledge who are transmitted from say: it should be deferred for a year. This was related from 'Ali, Zayd, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Shurayh, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Malik and the people of opinion. al-Shafi'i did not set a fixed period for this.

The sixteenth issue: If the tooth of an adult is pulled out, and he takes its blood-money and then it grows back, Malik said he does not return what he took. The Kufans said: he returns it if it grows back. al-Shafi'i had two opinions: he returns it, and he does not return it, because this is a growth not customary, and a ruling is not established by the rare. This is the view of our scholars. The Kufans relied on the argument that its replacement has grown, so it is returned, its origin being the tooth of a child. al-Shafi'i said: If another person then injures it after it has grown back sound, its full compensation is due from him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the more correct of the two opinions, because each of them is a puller of a tooth, and the Prophet ﷺ made five camels due for a tooth.

The seventeenth issue: If a man pulls out another man's tooth and its owner reinserts it and it knits, then nothing is due for it according to us. al-Shafi'i said: he may not reinsert it, because it is impure; this was also said by Ibn al-Musayyib and 'Ata'. If he does reinsert it, he must repeat every prayer he prayed, because it is carrion. The same applies if his ear is cut off and he reattaches it while the blood is still warm, and it sticks. 'Ata' said: the ruler compels him to remove it, because it is carrion that he attached. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is an error, and whoever is unaware that returning the tooth and its reattachment in its form does not make it return to its ruling, has erred, because its impurity was due to its separation, and it has now returned connected; the rulings of the Sharia are not attributes of physical objects, but are rulings which return to God's word concerning them and His report about them.
I say: What Ibn al-'Arabi reported from 'Ata' is the opposite of what Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: They differed concerning a tooth pulled out as retaliation and then reinserted in its place and it grows. 'Ata' al-Khurasani and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: there is no harm in that. al-Thawri, Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is pulled out, because retaliation is for disfigurement. al-Shafi'i said: he may not reinsert it, because it is impure, and the ruler compels him to pull it out.

**Eighteenth:** If a person has an extra tooth that is extracted, then there is a *hukumah* (an assessed compensation, determined by a judge rather than a fixed amount). This is the view of the jurists of the major cities. Zayd ibn Thabit said: "For it is one-third of the *diyah* (blood-money)." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "There is no evidence for a fixed figure, so the *hukumah* is more just." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "What is narrated from Zayd is not authentic. It has been narrated from 'Ali that he said: 'For a tooth that has been partly broken, its owner is given compensation in proportion to what was lost from it.' This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and others." I say: Here ends what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, specified of the limbs, and He did not mention the two lips and the tongue. They are:

**Nineteenth:** The majority said: "For the two lips there is the full *diyah*, and for each one of them there is half of the *diyah*. The upper lip has no precedence over the lower." It was narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Zuhri: "For the upper lip there is one-third of the *diyah*, and for the lower lip there are two-thirds of the *diyah*." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I hold the first view, because of the marfu' (traced to the Prophet) hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: '(For the two lips there is the *diyah*).' Also, the two hands carry the full *diyah*, and their benefits differ. What is cut from the two lips is assessed accordingly." As for the tongue, a hadith came from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "(For the tongue there is the *diyah*)." The scholars of Madinah, the scholars of Kufa, the people of hadith and the people of opinion (*ahl al-ra'y*) unanimously agreed upon this, as Ibn al-Mundhir stated.

**Twentieth:** The scholars differed regarding a man who injures another man's tongue, cutting off part of it, so that some of his speech is lost. Most scholars said: "One looks at the amount of speech that has been lost out of twenty-eight letters, and he owes from the *diyah* an amount equal to what of his speech has been lost. If all speech is lost, then the full *diyah* is due." This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and the people of opinion. Malik said: "There is no *qawad* (retaliation) for the tongue, because it is not possible to exact retaliation precisely. If it were possible, then retaliation would be the original ruling."

**Twenty-first:** The scholars differed regarding cutting the tongue of a mute person. Al-Sha'bi, Malik, the people of Madinah, al-Thawri, the people of Iraq, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifah) and his two companions said: "For it there is a *hukumah*." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "There are two anomalous views concerning it. The first is the view of al-Nakha'i, that the full *diyah* is due. The second is the view of Qatadah, that one-third of the *diyah* is due." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The first view is the most sound, because it is the least of what has been said."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Allah, glorified is He, specified the principal limbs and left the rest to be judged by analogy to them. Thus every limb in which retaliation is possible, when it can be done and there is no fear of death from it, carries retaliation. Likewise, every limb whose function has been lost while its form remains has no retaliation, and for it there is the *diyah*, because retaliation cannot be carried out on it."

**Twenty-second:** His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And for wounds there is retribution﴾, meaning *muqasassah* (mutual retaliation). It has already been discussed in *al-Baqarah* (see vol. 2, p. 244 onward). There is no retaliation for every wound that is dangerous, nor for a wound where retaliation cannot be reached unless the striker errs, exceeds or falls short. Retaliation is exacted for deliberate wounds when retaliation is possible for them. All of this concerns deliberate acts. As for accidental injury, the *diyah* is due, and if the *diyah* applies to accidental killing, then likewise it applies to wounds.

In the Sahih of Muslim, from Anas, that the sister of al-Rubayyi' (Umm Harithah) wounded a person, and they brought the matter before the Prophet ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "(Retaliation, retaliation)." Umm al-Rubayyi' said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall retaliation be taken against so-and-so? By Allah, retaliation shall not be taken against her!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Subhan Allah! O Umm al-Rubayyi', retaliation is the Book of Allah." She said: "[No,] by Allah, retaliation shall never be taken against her." [He said:] "She kept on until they accepted the *diyah*, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: '(Indeed among the servants of Allah are those who, if they swear by Allah, He fulfills their oath).'"

I say: The one wounded in this hadith was a young girl, and the wound was the breaking of her front tooth. Al-Nasa'i also narrated from Anas that his paternal aunt broke the front tooth of a girl, and the Prophet of Allah ﷺ ruled for retaliation. Her brother Anas ibn al-Nadr said: "Shall the front tooth of so-and-so be broken? No, by Him who sent you with the truth, her tooth shall not be broken!" He said: "Before that, they had asked her family for pardon and compensation. When her brother swore, and he was the paternal uncle of Anas, who was martyred at Uhud, the people agreed to pardon. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: '(Indeed among the servants of Allah are those who, if they swear by Allah, He fulfills their oath).'" Abu Dawud also narrated it. He said: "I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal. He was asked: 'How is retaliation taken for a tooth?' He said: 'It is filed down.'"

I say: There is no contradiction between the two hadiths, for it is possible that each of them swore, and Allah fulfilled both of their oaths. This indicates the *karamat* (miraculous gifts) of the saints, as will be explained, God willing, in the story of al-Khidr [this is his well-known story with Prophet Musa, peace be upon them both, and it will come in *al-Kahf*, God willing, vol. 11, p. 16 onward]. So we ask Allah for steadfastness in faith in their miracles, and that He include us in their company without trial or tribulation.

**Twenty-third:** The scholars unanimously agreed that His saying, "And the tooth for the tooth" refers to deliberate injury. Whoever deliberately strikes someone's tooth, retaliation applies to him, based on the hadith of Anas. They differed regarding all the other bones of the body when they are deliberately broken. Malik said: "All bones of the body carry retaliation, except those whose injury is dangerous, such as the thigh, the spine, the *ma'mumah* (a head wound reaching the brain), the *munaqqilah* (a head wound that dislodges bone fragments) and the *hashimah* (a head wound that fractures the skull). For these there is the *diyah*." The Kufans said: "There is no retaliation for a bone that is broken, except the tooth, because of His saying, 'And the tooth for the tooth.'" This is also the view of al-Layth and al-Shafi'i. Al-Shafi'i said: "A break cannot be exactly matched by another break, so it is prohibited." Al-Tahawi said: "They agreed that there is no retaliation for the bone of the skull, and likewise for all bones." The proof for Malik is the hadith of Anas concerning the tooth, which is a bone, so all other bones are likewise, except for a bone for which they unanimously agreed there is no retaliation, because of the fear of losing the soul from it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Whoever says there is no retaliation for a bone contradicts the hadith, and it is not permissible to turn to reasoning when the report exists."

I say: This is also indicated by His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194], and His saying: "And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished" [al-Nahl: 126]. What the scholars unanimously agreed upon is not included in these verses. [And Allah knows best], and success is from Allah.

**Twenty-fourth:** Abu 'Ubayd said, regarding the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the *mudihah* (a wound that exposes the bone), and what came from others concerning the *shijaj* (head wounds): Al-Asma'i and others said: "The speech of some of them has entered into that of others. The first of the *shijaj* is the *harisah*, which is the one that splits the skin, meaning the one that splits it slightly. From this it is said: 'The launderer *harasa* the cloth' when he tore it. It is also called *al-harsah*. Then the *ba'idah*, which is the one that splits the flesh after the skin. Then the *mutalahimah*, which is the one that has taken hold in the skin and has not reached the *simhaq* (the membrane over the bone)."

Al-Simhaq (ﻭﺍﻟﺴِّﻤْﺤَﺎﻕ): a thin skin or membrane between the flesh and the bone. Al-Waqidi said: "Among us it is al-Milta (ﺍﻟﻤِﻠْﻄَﻰ)." Others said: "It is al-Miltah (ﺍﻟﻤِﻠْﻄَﺎﺓ)," and he said: "It is the one about which the hadith came: (It is judged in al-Miltah by its blood)."

Then al-Muwadihah (ﺍﻟﻤُﻮﺿِﺤَﺔ), which is the wound that scrapes off that skin or cuts until the whiteness of the bone (wadah al-'azm [[Wadah al-'azm: its whiteness appears.]]) becomes visible. That is the muwadihah. Abu 'Ubayd said: "There is no retaliation (qisas) for any of the head wounds except the muwadihah alone, because none of the others has a fixed limit that is reached other than it. As for the other head wounds, their blood money (diyah) is due."

Then al-Hashimah (ﺍﻟﻬَﺎﺷِﻤَﺔ), which is the wound that breaks the bone.

Then al-Munaqqilah (ﺍﻟﻤُﻨَﻘِّﻠَﺔ), with the qaf vocalized with a kasra (as related by al-Jawhari), which is the wound that dislodges the bone, meaning breaks it, until the splinters of the bones come out of it along with the medicine.

Then al-Ma'mumah (ﺍﻟﺂﻣَّﺔ), also called al-Ma'mumah (ﺍﻟﻤَﺄْﻣُﻮﻣَﺔ), which is the wound that reaches the umm al-ra's (the skull's inner membrane), meaning the brain.

Abu 'Ubayd said: What is said regarding his words (It is judged in al-Miltah by its blood) is that when the one who wounds someone inflicts a head wound, judgment is made against him in favour of the wounded person according to the amount of the wound at the moment it was inflicted, and one does not wait for it to develop. He said: "As for all the other head wounds, among us they are held in abeyance until one sees how their condition develops, and only then is a judgment made concerning them." Abu 'Ubayd said: "Among us the rule for all head wounds and all injuries is that they are held in abeyance. Hushaym related to us from Husayn, who said: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: Whatever is less than the muwadihah is mere scratches, and in it there is a settlement (sulh).'" Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "There is no qisas for what is less than the muwadihah." Malik said: "Qisas applies to what is less than the muwadihah: al-Milta, al-Damiyah, al-Ba'idah, and what resembles these." The Kufans said likewise, and they added al-Simhaq. Ibn al-Mundhir related it.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "Al-Damiyah is the wound that bleeds without blood flowing from it. Al-Dami'ah is the wound from which blood flows." There is no qisas for what is less than the muwadihah.

Al-Jawhari said: "Al-Damiyah is the head wound that bleeds but does not flow." Our scholars said: "Al-Damiyah is the one that makes blood flow."

There is no qisas for what comes after the muwadihah: the hashimah, which breaks the bone, and the munaqqilah, with a difference of opinion about it specifically. Al-Ma'mumah is the one that reaches the umm al-ra's, and al-Damighah is the one that pierces the membrane of the brain. In the hashimah of the body there is qisas, except where it is dangerous, such as the thigh and what resembles it. As for the hashimah of the head, Ibn al-Qasim said: "There is no qawad (retaliation) for it, because it will inevitably turn into a munaqqilah." Ashhab said: "There is qisas for it, unless it dislodges the bone and becomes a munaqqilah, in which case there is no qawad for it."

As for the limbs, qisas is obligatory in all the joints (mafasil), except those that are dangerous. The parts that are in the sense of joints include the parts of the nose (marin), the two ears, the penis, the eyelids and the two lips, because they are capable of measurement (taqdir). There are two reports concerning the tongue. Qisas applies to the breaking of bones, except where it causes destruction, such as the bones of the chest, the neck, the spine and the thigh, and what resembles them. For the breaking of the upper arm bone (adud), there is qisas.

Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn Hazm judged that a man who broke the thigh of another man should have his own thigh broken. 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Khalid ibn Usayd did the same in Makkah. It is also related that 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz did this. This is the position of Malik, as we have mentioned. He said: "It is the matter agreed upon among them (the scholars), and the practice followed in our lands: a man who strikes another, who protects himself with his hand, and breaks it, is subjected to retaliation."

The twenty-fifth issue: The scholars said: "Head wounds (shijaj) are on the head, and injuries (jirah) are on the body." The people of knowledge agreed that for what is less than the muwadihah there is an arsh (fixed compensation), as Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned, but they differed about the amount of that arsh.

What is less than the muwadihah consists of five head wounds: al-Damiyah, al-Dami'ah, al-Ba'idah, al-Mutalahimah and al-Simhaq. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq [[From j, k, h, and a, z.]] and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: for al-Damiyah there is a hukumah (judicial assessment), for al-Ba'idah there is a hukumah, and for al-Mutalahimah there is a hukumah. 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Zayd ibn Thabit that he said: "For al-Damiyah there is one camel, for al-Ba'idah two camels, for al-Mutalahimah three camels of the camels, for al-Simhaq four, for al-Muwadihah five, for al-Hashimah ten, for al-Munaqqilah fifteen, for al-Ma'mumah one third of the diyah, and for a man who is struck until his intellect is lost, the full diyah. Or he is struck until he speaks through his nose [[Yughunn means his voice comes out through his nostrils. In k and a: yajunn. It is missing in j. Or he is struck etc.]] and cannot make himself understood, the full diyah; or until he becomes hoarse and cannot make himself understood, the full diyah. For the eyelid of the eye there is one quarter of the diyah, and for the nipple of the breast there is one quarter of the diyah." [[In a: the full diyah.]]

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is related from 'Ali concerning al-Simhaq the same as Zayd's view. It is related from 'Umar and 'Uthman that they both said: "In it there is half the muwadihah." Al-Hasan al-Basri, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Nakha'i said: "In it there is a hukumah," and likewise Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said.

The scholars do not differ that the muwadihah carries five camels, according to the hadith of 'Amr ibn Hazm, in which it says: "And for the muwadihah, five." The people of knowledge agreed that the muwadihah occurs on the head and the face. They differed about whether the muwadihah of the face is preferred over the muwadihah of the head. It is related from Abu Bakr and 'Umar that they were equal, and a group of the Followers (tabi'un) held their view, and al-Shafi'i and Ishaq say so. It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that the muwadihah of the face is valued at double that of the head. Ahmad said: "The muwadihah of the face is more deserving of an increase."

Malik said: "The ma'mumah, the munaqqilah and the muwadihah occur only on the head and the face, and the ma'mumah occurs only on the head, specifically when it reaches the brain." He said: "The muwadihah is what occurs on the skull of the head, and what is below it is from the neck, where there is no muwadihah." Malik said: "The nose is not part of the head, and there is no muwadihah in it; likewise the lower jaw has no muwadihah."

They differed about the muwadihah in parts other than the head and face. Ashhab and Ibn al-Qasim said: "For the muwadihah of the body, its munaqqilah and its ma'mumah, there is nothing but ijtihad (independent judgment), and there is no fixed arsh for them." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "This is the position of Malik, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq, and we say the same."

It is related from 'Ata al-Khurasani that if the muwadihah is on a person's body, there are twenty-five dinars for it. Abu 'Umar said: Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions agreed that whoever wounds a man with two ma'mumahs, or two muwadihahs, or three ma'mumahs, or muwadihahs, or more, in a single blow, then for all of them, even if they joined and became one, there is a full diyah. As for the hashimah, there is no diyah for it according to us, but only a hukumah.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "I did not find in the books of the Madinans any mention of the hashimah. Malik said of one who broke a man's nose, if it was by mistake, there is ijtihad in it." Al-Hasan al-Basri did not fix anything for the hashimah. Abu Thawr said: "If they differed about it, then in it there is a hukumah." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Reasoning points to this, since there is no sunnah concerning it and no consensus." Al-Qadi Abu al-Walid al-Baji said: "In it is what is in the muwadihah. If it becomes a munaqqilah, then fifteen, and if it becomes a ma'mumah, then one third of the diyah."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "We found that most of those we met and of whom we heard among the people of knowledge make ten camels for the hashimah. We have related this view from Zayd ibn Thabit, and Qatadah, 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan and al-Shafi'i said it." Al-Thawri and the people of opinion said: "For it there are a thousand dirhams," and by this they mean one tenth of the diyah.

As for the munaqqilah, Ibn al-Mundhir said: "A hadith came from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: (For the munaqqilah, fifteen camels)." The people of knowledge agreed on this view. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Every scholar from whom knowledge is preserved said that the munaqqilah is that from which the bones are dislodged." Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and the people of opinion (this is also the view of Qatadah and Ibn Shubrumah) said: "For the munaqqilah there is no qawad." It is related from Ibn al-Zubayr, though it is not authentic from him, that he exacted retaliation for a munaqqilah. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The first view is more correct, because I know of no one who disagreed on this."

As for the ma'mumah, Ibn al-Mundhir said: "A hadith came from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: (For the ma'mumah, one third of the diyah)." The majority of the people of knowledge agreed on this view, and we know of no one who disagreed except Makhul, who said: "If the ma'mumah is intentional, then in it there are two thirds of the diyah, and if it is by mistake, then in it there is one third of the diyah." This is an anomalous view (shadhdh), and I say with the first view. They differed about qawad for the ma'mumah. Most people of knowledge said: "There is no qawad for it." It is related that Ibn al-Zubayr exacted retaliation for a ma'mumah, and the people denied this. 'Ata said: "We know of no one who exacted retaliation from us before Ibn al-Zubayr."

As for the jaifah (penetrating wound to the body cavity), there is one third of the diyah for it, according to the hadith of 'Amr ibn Hazm, and there is no disagreement about this except what is related from Makhul that he said: "If it is intentional, then in it there are two thirds of the diyah, and if it is by mistake, then in it there is one third of the diyah." The jaifah is every wound that pierces into the cavity, even if it is the size of the entrance of a needle. If it passes through from two sides, then according to them it is two jaifahs, and for it there are two thirds of the diyah. Ashhab said: "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, judged in a penetrating jaifah that exits from the other side with the diyah for two jaifahs." 'Ata, Malik, al-Shafi'i and the people of opinion all said: "There is no qisas for the jaifah." Ibn al-Mundhir said: "And we say the same."

The twenty-sixth issue: They differed about qawad for slapping and the like. Al-Bukhari related from Abu Bakr, 'Ali, Ibn al-Zubayr and Suwayd ibn Muqarrin, may God be pleased with them, that they exacted retaliation for slapping and the like. It is related that 'Uthman and Khalid ibn al-Walid did the same, and this is the view of al-Sha'bi and a group of the people of hadith. Al-Layth said: "If the slap is on the eye, there is no qawad for it, because of the danger to the eye, and the ruler (sultan) punishes him. If it is on the cheek, then there is qawad for it."

Another group said: "There is no qisas for slapping." This was related from al-Hasan and Qatadah, and it is the view of Malik, the Kufans and al-Shafi'i. Malik argued for this, saying: "The slap of a weak sick man is not like the slap of a strong man, and a black slave who is slapped is not like a man of rank and standing. In all of this there is only ijtihad, because we do not know the measure of the slap."

**Twenty-seventh issue:** Scholars differed over retaliation (qawad) for an injury caused by a whip. Al-Layth and al-Hasan[[[From manuscripts ʿ and K.]]] said: retaliation is taken for it, and additional punishment is imposed for the transgression[[In ʿ: "for the sake of the transgression."]]. Ibn al-Qasim said: retaliation is taken for it. According to the Kufans and al-Shafi'i, retaliation is not taken for it unless it wounds, and al-Shafi'i said: if the whip wounds, then there is compensation for the wound (hukumah). Ibn al-Mundhir said: whatever a person is struck with, whether a whip, a stick, or a stone, if it falls short of killing, it is a deliberate injury, and retaliation is due for it. This is the view of a group of the people of hadith. In al-Bukhari, it is reported that ʿUmar took retaliation for a blow with a *durrah*[[*Al-durrah* (with a kasrah): the instrument with which one strikes.]], and ʿAli ibn Abi Talib took retaliation for three lashes. Shurayh exacted retaliation for a whip-lash and for scratches (khumush). Ibn Battal said: the hadith about the *lad*[[*Al-lad*: the medicine is poured into one side of the child's mouth, between the tongue and the cheek, and the child is made to swallow it. The hadith of the *lad* is that the Prophet ﷺ was given medicine during his illness; when he recovered, he said: "Let no one remain in the house without being given medicine (lud)." He did this as a punishment for them, because they had given it to him without his permission.]] of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the members of his household is evidence for those who hold that retaliation applies to every pain, even where there is no wound.

**Twenty-eighth issue:** Scholars differed over the blood money (ʿaql) for injuries to women. In the *Muwatta'*, from Malik, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, it is reported that he used to say: a woman is equal to a man in blood money up to a third of the man's diyah[[It means that for what is less than a third of the diyah, her compensation is the same as a man's, until, when the compensation for what has been inflicted on her reaches a third of the diyah, her compensation becomes half the man's. His saying "her finger is like his finger... etc." means that the compensation for all of these is less than a third, and so she is equal to the man in it (al-Muwatta').]]: her finger is like his finger, her tooth is like his tooth, her *muwadihah*[[A wound that exposes the bone.]] is like his *muwadihah*, and her *munaqqilah*[[A wound that causes the bone to be displaced.]] is like his *munaqqilah*. Ibn Bukayr said: Malik said: when her compensation reaches a third of a man's diyah, it is half of a man's diyah. Ibn al-Mundhir said: this view has been transmitted from ʿUmar and Zayd ibn Thabit, and it was held by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, [al-Zuhri][[From manuscripts J, K, H and ʿ.]], Qatadah, Ibn Hurmuz, Malik, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun. Another group said: the diyah of a woman is half the diyah of a man, whether the injury is small or large. This view has been transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, and it was held by al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifah) and his two companions. They argued that since they agreed on the larger amount, which is the full diyah, the smaller amount is similar to it, and we follow this view.

**Twenty-ninth issue:** Qadi ʿAbd al-Wahhab said: every part that has a beauty separate from any benefit at all carries a hukumah, such as the eyebrows, the loss of beard hair, the loss of head hair, the breasts of a man, and his buttocks[[In ʿ and K: "his buttocks (two)."]]. The method of the hukumah is that the injured person is valued as if he were a healthy slave, then he is valued with the injury, and what the price lost is made a portion of his diyah, whatever amount that reaches. Ibn al-Mundhir related this from every scholar whose views are preserved, and he said: the testimony of two trustworthy people with knowledge in this matter is accepted. It was also said: the testimony of one just person is accepted. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best.

These are some of the rulings on wounds and limbs contained within the meaning of this verse. For one who limits himself to them, they are sufficient. And Allah is the One who grants success in guidance, by His favour and generosity[[[From manuscripts ʿ and K.]]].

**Thirtieth issue:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿Whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him﴾ are a conditional clause with its response. That is: whoever gives up retaliation and pardons, it is an expiation for him, that is, for that person who forgives. It was also said: it is an expiation for the one who inflicted the injury, so he will not be held to account for his offence in the Hereafter, because forgiveness takes the place of exacting his right from him, and the reward belongs to the one who forgives. Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned both views. Most of the Companions and those after them held the first view. The second was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi, with differing reports from them. The first view is more apparent, because the pronoun referring back in it points to something already mentioned, namely "whoever" (man). It is reported from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet ﷺ: "No Muslim is afflicted with any harm to his body and then forgives it, except that Allah raises him one degree thereby and removes from him one sin thereby." Ibn al-ʿArabi said: the claim that if the injured person pardons, Allah pardons him, has no evidence to support it, so it has no meaning.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 46–47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, son of Mary﴾, meaning: We made Jesus follow their traces, that is, the traces of the prophets who submitted (aslamu).

(confirming what was before him) means the Torah. He saw the Torah as true, and he saw the obligation of acting by it until a abrogating (nasikh) text comes. "Confirming" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of Jesus.

(In it was guidance) is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). "And light" is conjoined to it. "And confirming" has two possibilities: it may refer to Jesus, conjoined to the first "confirming"; or it may be a circumstantial state of the Gospel (Injil), the sense being: "And We gave him the Gospel, settled in it being guidance, and light, and confirming."

(And guidance and admonition)

is conjoined to "confirming," meaning guiding and admonishing. "For the God-fearing (muttaqin)": He specified them because they are the ones who benefit from these two. It is also permissible to read them in the nominative, conjoined to his saying "in it is guidance and light."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein﴾. Al-A'mash and Hamzah read the verb in the accusative, with the lam being the lam of purpose (lam kay). The rest read it in the jussive, as a command.
