According to the first reading, the lam is connected to his saying "and We gave him," so one may not pause, meaning: "And We gave him the Gospel so that its people might judge by what Allah revealed therein." Whoever reads it as a command is like His saying: "And judge between them by what Allah has revealed" [al-Ma'idah: 49]. It is then a new, independent obligation that begins anew, meaning: let the People of the Gospel judge at that time; but now it has been abrogated. It was also said: this is a command to the Christians now to believe in Muhammad ﷺ, for the Gospel contains the obligation of believing in him, and abrogation is only conceivable in the derivative rulings (furu') and not in the fundamentals (usul). Makki said: the preferred reading is the jussive, because the community is upon it, and because what follows of threat and warning indicates that it is an obligation from Allah, may He be exalted, upon the People of the Gospel. An-Nahhas said: the correct view in my opinion is that they are two good readings, because Allah, mighty and majestic, sent no Book except that it be acted upon, and He commanded acting by what is in it; so both are sound.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ). And "the Book" is the Qur'an, (with the truth), i.e., it is [[[from j.]]] with the true command, (confirming) is a circumstantial clause (of what was before it of the Book), i.e., of the same kind as the (previous) books.

(And a guardian over it), i.e., exalted over them and elevated. This indicates the interpretation of those who say it refers to excellence, i.e., in the abundance of reward, as was previously alluded to in "al-Fatihah" [[See vol. 1, p. 109.]], and it is the view chosen by Ibn al-Hassar in his book Sharh al-Sunnah. We have mentioned what he mentioned in our book on the explanation of the [[[from p.]]] Beautiful Names of Allah, and praise be to Allah. Qatadah said: al-muhaymin means the witness (al-mushahid). It was also said: the guardian (al-hafiz). Al-Hasan said: the confirmer (al-musaddiq), and from this is the saying of the poet:

Indeed the Book is a guardian for our Prophet... and the truth is known by those of sound minds.

Ibn Abbas said: "and a guardian over it" means one entrusted over it (mu'taman). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the Qur'an is entrusted over what came before it of the books. And from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan also: al-Muhaymin is al-Amin (the trustworthy). Al-Mubarrad said: its origin is mu'aymin, the hamza being replaced by a ha', as is said regarding araqtu al-ma' (I poured out the water) becoming haraqtu. Al-Zajjaj also said this, and Abu Ali. It has been inflected: it is said hayman, yuhayminu, haymanatan, and muhaymin means "was trustworthy." Al-Jawhari said: it is the one who grants others security from fear; its origin is ta'mana, so it is mu'a'man with two hamzas; the second hamza was changed to ya' out of dislike of their juxtaposition, so it became mu'ayman; then the first was changed to ha', as they say haraqa al-ma' and araqahu. It is said of it: hayman 'ala al-shay' yuhayminu, when one is a guardian of a thing, so he is muhaymin, from Abu Ubayd.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin recited: "wa-muhaymanan 'alayh" with a fatha on the mim. Mujahid said: i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ) is entrusted over the Qur'an.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has sent down﴾ requires judgment. It was said: this is an abrogation of the option in His saying: "so judge between them or turn away from them." It was also said: this is not an obligation, and the meaning is: judge between them if you wish, since it is not obligatory upon us to judge between them when they are not among the people of the dhimmah. Regarding the people of the dhimmah there is hesitation, and the discussion of it has passed. It was also said: He meant judge among the creation, and this was obligatory upon him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow their desires﴾. In it are two issues [[So in the originals; the author did not mention the second, and perhaps it is His saying: (For each of you We have made a law) the verse.]]: The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow their desires﴾ means: do not act according to their desires and wishes, away from what has come to you of the truth; i.e., do not abandon judging by what Allah has made clear in the Qur'an regarding the explanation of the truth and the explanation of the rulings. The plural of hawa is ahwa', and it is not pluralized as ahwiyah; this has been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 24.]]. So He forbade him from following them in what they desire. This indicates the invalidity of the view of one who says: wine is valued against the one who destroyed it for them, since it is not property belonging to them, so it is not guaranteed against the one who destroys it; because requiring its compensation from the one who destroys it is a ruling according to the desires of the Jews, and we have been commanded to act contrary to that. The meaning of (away from what has come to you) is: over what has come to you.

(For each of you We have made a law and a way) indicates the lack of attachment to the laws of the earlier peoples. The shir'ah and the shari'ah are the apparent path by which salvation is reached. The shari'ah in the language is the path by which one reaches water. The shari'ah is what Allah has prescribed for His servants of the religion; he prescribed for them, yashra'u, shar'an, i.e., he laid down. The sharr' is the greatest path. The shir'ah is also the watercourse (al-watr), its plural being shir' and shuru', and shira' is the plural of the plural, from Abu Ubayd, so it is a homonym. The minhaj is the continuous path, and it is the nahj and the manhaj, i.e., the clear one. The rajiz said:

Whoever is in doubt, here is a clear stream... sweet water and a straight path

Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Yazid said: the shari'ah is the beginning of the path, and the minhaj is the continuous path. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and others: "shir'atan wa-minhajan" means sunnah and way. The meaning of the verse is that He gave the Torah to its people, the Gospel to its people, and the Qur'an to its people; and this is in the laws and acts of worship, while the foundation is monotheism, about which there is no disagreement. This meaning was narrated from Qatadah. Mujahid said: the shir'ah and the minhaj are the religion of Muhammad, upon him be peace, and by it everything else has been abrogated.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, i.e., He would have made your law one, and you would have been upon the truth. So He made clear that by the difference He intended the faith of one people and the disbelief of another.

(But to test you in what He has given you) there is an omission in the speech to which the lam of purpose is attached, i.e., but He made your laws differing in order to test you. The ibtila' is the testing.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾, i.e., hasten to the acts of obedience. This indicates that advancing the obligatory acts is better than delaying them, and there is no disagreement about this in all acts of worship except for prayer at the beginning of its time, for Abu Hanifah holds that it is preferable to delay it; the generality of the verse is evidence for it, as al-Kiya said [[In one manuscript: al-Tabari; it is al-Kiya al-Tabari.]]. It also indicates that fasting while traveling is better than breaking the fast; and all of this has been discussed previously in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 280.]].

(To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to differ about), i.e., about what you differed in, and doubts will be removed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. The discussion of it has already been given, and that it abrogates the option (*takhyir*, the option of judging or declining). Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is a sweeping claim, for the conditions of abrogation (*naskh*) are four. One of them is knowledge of the chronology (*tarikh*), by establishing which is earlier and which is later. This is unknown from these two verses, so it is impossible to claim that either of them abrogates the other, and the matter remains as it was."

I say: We have already related from Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas that this verse was revealed later, and so it would be abrogating, unless one supposes in the sentence "And judge between them by what Allah has revealed" the phrase "if you wish." For the option was already mentioned to him, so the latter part of the sentence omits the option, since it is indicated by the first part, because it is conjoined to it (*ma'tuf 'alayhi*). The ruling on the option is thus the ruling on the thing it is conjoined to. The two are partners, and the latter is not disconnected from what precedes it, for that would have no meaning and would not be valid. Therefore his saying, "And judge between them by what Allah has revealed," must be conjoined to what precedes it from His saying, "And if you judge, then judge between them with justice," and from His saying, "So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them." The meaning of "And judge between them by what Allah has revealed" is: judge by it if you judge and choose to judge. So all of it is *muhkam* (not abrogated), not abrogated, because the abrogating text is not linked to the abrogated text as something conjoined to it. Therefore the option given to the Prophet ﷺ in this matter is *muhkam*, not abrogated. Makki, may Allah have mercy on him, said this.

"And judge between them" is in a position of accusative (*nasb*) by conjunction to "the Book," meaning: "And We have sent down to you that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed," that is, by the judgment of Allah which He has revealed to you in His Book.

(﴿And beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾). The word "an" (lest) is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun of "beware of them," and it is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion). Or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), meaning: for fear that they tempt you. It is related from Ibn Ishaq, who said that Ibn 'Abbas said: A group of the rabbis gathered, among them Ibn Suriya, Ka'b ibn Asad, Ibn Sulba, and Shas ibn 'Adi, and they said: "Let us go to Muhammad, perhaps we can tempt him away from his religion, for he is only a human being." So they came to him and said: "You know, O Muhammad, that we are the rabbis of the Jews, and if we follow you, no one among the Jews will oppose us. Between us and a people there is a dispute, and they will bring it before you. So rule for us against them, and we will believe in you." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused, and this verse was revealed.

The origin of *fitnah* is testing, as has been mentioned before, but its meaning varies. His saying here, "yaftinuka" (tempt you), means: to turn you away and repel you. *Fitnah* may mean polytheism (*shirk*), as in His saying, "And *fitnah* is greater than killing" [2:217], and His saying, "And fight them until there is no *fitnah*" [2:193]. It may mean a lesson (*'ibrah*), as in His saying, "Do not make us a trial for those who disbelieve" [60:5], and His saying, "Do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people" [10:85]. And *fitnah* may mean turning away from the path, as in this verse.

The repetition of "And judge between them by what Allah has revealed" is for emphasis; or they are different conditions and rulings, in each of which He commanded him to judge by what Allah has revealed.

In the verse is evidence for the permissibility of forgetfulness (*nisyan*) on the part of the Prophet ﷺ, for He said, "lest they tempt you," and that only occurs through forgetfulness, not deliberate intent. It has also been said that the address is to him while the intended meaning is others. The explanation of this will come in *Surat al-An'am*, Allah willing.

The meaning of (﴿from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾) is: from all of what Allah has revealed to you. "Some" (*ba'd*) is used in the sense of "all." The poet said [Labid; the first half is: "You see the places, when I do not dwell in them"; in Lisan al-'Arab the reading is "or it is tied"; Ibn Sida said: "This is not, in my view, what the lexicographers claim, that *ba'd* means *kull*; this is a refutation, and there is no proof in this line, for he only meant by 'some of the souls' himself"]:

*"Or the fate of death seizes some of the souls"*

It is also narrated as "or it binds" (*yartabit*). He meant all souls. On this reading they interpreted His saying, "And so that I may make clear to you some of that about which you differ" [43:63].

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The correct view is that 'some' (*ba'd*) keeps its meaning in this verse, and that what is meant is the stoning or the ruling that they wanted, and they did not intend to tempt him away from the whole." And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, meaning: if they refuse your ruling and turn away from it. (﴿then know that Allah intends only to afflict them for some of their sins﴾), meaning: He will punish them by exile, the poll-tax (*jizyah*), and killing. And so it was. He said "for some" because punishment for some of their sins was sufficient to destroy them.

(﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾), meaning the Jews.

There are three issues here.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿Do they seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance)?﴾ "Afahukma" is in the accusative, governed by "yabghun" (they seek). The meaning is that the people of Jahiliyyah used to make the judgment for the noble different from the judgment for the lowly, as has been mentioned in more than one place. The Jews used to enforce the prescribed punishments (hudud) on the weak and the poor, but would not enforce them on the powerful and the rich. Thus they resembled the people of Jahiliyyah in this act.

The second issue: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah related from Ibn Abi Najih, from Tawus, who said: When they asked him about a man who favours some of his children over others, he would recite this verse, ﴿Do they seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah?﴾ Tawus would say: It is not permitted for anyone to favour some of his children over others. If he does so, it is not enforced and is annulled. This is also the view of the Zahiris (literalist school). The same was related from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he disliked it. Al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak and Ishaq disliked it as well, but if someone does it, it is enforced and not reversed. Malik, al-Thawri, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i and the People of Opinion (ashab al-ra'y, i.e. the Hanafis) permitted it. They cited the act of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him) in gifting 'A'ishah more than his other children, and the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): (Take it back). [[Al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that his father, Bashir ibn Sa'd, came with his son al-Nu'man and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have gifted this son of mine a slave that I owned." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Have you gifted all your sons like this?" He said: "No." He said: "Then take it back." I say: This is in all the versions, and as one can see, it is evidence for the first group, as will come.]] And his saying: (Then call someone else to witness this). The first group cited the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) to Bashir: (Do you have another child besides this one?) He said: "Yes." He said: (Have you given all of them the like of this?) He said: "No." He said: (Then do not make me a witness, for I do not bear witness to injustice). In another narration: (For I bear witness only to what is right). They said: Whatever is unjust and not right is void and not permissible. The saying (Call someone else to witness this) is not a permission to bear witness; rather it is a deterrent from it, because he (peace be upon him) called it injustice and refused to bear witness to it. Therefore it is not possible for any Muslim to bear witness to it in any way. As for the act of Abu Bakr, the saying of the Prophet ﷺ cannot be opposed by it, and perhaps he had given his children gifts equivalent to that. If it is said: The principle is that a person has unrestricted disposal over his property, it is replied: The universal principle and a specific case that contradicts that principle do not conflict, just as with general and specific (al-'umum wa al-khusus, a principle in legal theory). In the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh, the science of legal theory), the sound view is to build the general upon the specific. Furthermore, this leads to disobedience to parents (al-'uquq), which is the greatest of the major sins, and that is forbidden. Whatever leads to what is forbidden is also prohibited. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: (Fear Allah and be just among your children). Al-Nu'man said: So my father returned and took back that charity. A charity cannot be reclaimed by a father after it has been spent. His saying (Take it back) is to be understood as meaning (Return it), and "returning" is clearly a reference to annulment, as he (peace be upon him) said: (Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected), meaning it is returned and annulled. All of this is clear and strong, and a clear preference for the prohibition.

The third issue: Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read "Afahukmu" with a damma on the mim (nominative), meaning "yabghunahu" (they seek it), and they omitted the pronoun (ha') as Abu al-Najm omitted it in his saying:

"Umm al-Khiyar has begun to claim against me a sin, all of which I did not commit."

Here "kulluhu" is read in the nominative by those who narrate it so. It is also possible that the sense is: "Afahukmu al-Jahiliyyah hukmun yabghunahu," where the described noun has been omitted. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-A'raj and al-A'mash read "Afahakama" with a fatha on the ha' and the kaf and a fatha on the mim, and this reverts to the meaning of the reading of the majority, since the intended meaning is not the arbiter himself but the judgment. So it is as if he said: "Do they seek the judgment of the judgment of the Jahiliyyah?" The arbiter (hakam) and the judge (hakim) may be the same in language, and they may mean the soothsayer and those similar to him among the judges of the Jahiliyyah. Thus the intended meaning of "hukm" is generality and genus, since no specific judge is meant. It is permissible for the annexed noun to be generic, just as in their saying: "Misr (Egypt) has withheld its irdabb (a dry measure known to the people of Egypt)," and similar. Ibn 'Amir read "tabghun" with a ta', and the rest read it with a ya'.

As for His saying, ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ This is an interrogative in the form of rejection, meaning: no one is better. So this is an inchoate subject and predicate. "Hukman" is in the accusative as an explanatory specification (tamyiz/bayan). "Liqawmin yuqinun" means: for a people who are certain, i.e., among a people who are certain.

There are two issues here.

The first: "al-yahūda wa-l-naṣārā awliyāʾ" (the Jews and the Christians as allies) is the two objects of *tattakhidhū* (take) [from K and ʿAyn]. This shows that *muwālāt* (loyalty and alliance, *mawālāh*) with them is severed by the Sharia. Its explanation has already passed in Āl ʿImrān [see vol. 4, p. 188]. Then it was said: the intended group is the hypocrites, meaning, O you who believe, by their outward profession. They used to ally with the polytheists and inform them of the secrets of the Muslims. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abū Lubāba, related from ʿIkrima. Al-Suddī said: it was revealed concerning the incident of the Day of Uhud, when the Muslims were afraid, to the point that a group of them intended to ally with the Jews and the Christians. It was also said: it was revealed concerning ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit and ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl. ʿUbāda [may Allah be pleased with him] [from ʿAyn] disassociated himself from alliance with the Jews, while Ibn Ubayy held onto it and said: "I fear that the cycles of fortune will turn against us."

"Some of them are allies of others" (*baʿḍuhum awliyāʾu baʿḍin*) is a subject and predicate. It indicates that the Sharia establishes alliance among them, to the extent that Jews and Christians inherit from one another.

The second issue is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them﴾. That is, whoever supports them against the Muslims. Allah the Exalted has made clear that his ruling is the same as theirs. This prevents a Muslim from inheriting from an apostate (*murtadd*). The one who took them as allies was Ibn Ubayy. This ruling remains until the Day of Resurrection concerning the severing of alliance. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you﴾ [Hud 11:113]. He also said in Āl ʿImrān: ﴿Let not the believers take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:28]. He said: ﴿Do not take as intimates others than your own﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:118]. The discussion of this has already passed.

It was also said: the meaning of "some of them are allies of others" is in support. The conditional clause ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them﴾ has its answer in what follows: because he has opposed Allah the Exalted and His Messenger just as they opposed them, opposing him becomes obligatory just as opposing them is obligatory, and the Fire becomes due to him just as it is due to them. Thus he becomes one of them, that is, one of their companions.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 52–53:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ means doubt and hypocrisy. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 197.]]. The intended ones are Ibn Ubayy and his companions. (﴿They hasten toward them﴾) means they hasten toward their alliance and their support.

(﴿They say, "We fear that a calamity may befall us."﴾) means that the turns of fortune may turn against us, either through drought, so that they will not supply us with food or grant us favour, or through the Jews gaining victory over the Muslims, so that the affair will not remain with Muhammad ﷺ. This view is closer to the meaning. It is as if it derives from *dārat tadūru* (it turns), meaning "we fear that the affair may turn." This is supported by His saying, exalted and majestic: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring a conquest﴾. The poet said:

*It turns away from you the decree that has been decreed,*
*and the revolving turns of time, lest they turn.*

He means the alternations of time that turn from one people to another.

There is disagreement about the meaning of *al-fath* (the conquest). It was said: *al-fath* is the decisive judgment and ruling, related by Qatadah and others. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah brought the conquest, so the fighting men of Banu Qurayzah were killed, their offspring were taken captive, and Banu al-Nadir were expelled. Abu ʿAli said: it is the conquest of the lands of the polytheists by the Muslims. al-Suddi said: by *al-fath* is meant the conquest of Makkah.

(﴿Or a command from Him﴾). al-Suddi said: it is the jizyah (poll tax). al-Hasan said: it is the exposure of the affair of the hypocrites, the disclosure of their names, and the command to kill them. It was also said: it is abundance and prosperity for the Muslims. (﴿Then they will become, over what they concealed within themselves, regretful﴾) means they will become regretful for their allegiance to the disbelievers when they see Allah's help for the believers, and when they witness death and are given the tidings of punishment.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe will say﴾. The people of Madinah and the people of Syria read *yaqūlu* without the *waw*. Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *wa-yaqūla* with the *waw* and in the accusative, as a conjunction with *an yaʾtiya* (that He bring), according to most grammarians. The sense is: *fa-ʿasā Allāhu an yaʾtiya bil-fath wa-an yaqūla* (Allah may bring the conquest and that they say). It was also said that it is a conjunction on the meaning, because the meaning of *fa-ʿasā Allāhu an yaʾtiya bil-fath* is *wa-ʿasā an yaʾtiya Allāhu bil-fath* (and perhaps Allah will bring the conquest). It is not permissible to say *ʿasā Zaydun an yaʾtiya wa-yaqūma ʿAmrun* (Zayd may come and ʿAmr may stand), because the meaning does not hold when you say *wa-ʿasā Zaydun an yaqūma ʿAmrun*. But if you say *ʿasā an yaqūma Zaydun wa-yaʾtiya ʿAmrun*, it is good. When you assume the fronting of *an yaʾtiya* next to *ʿasā*, it becomes good, because the construction becomes *ʿasā an yaʾtiya wa-ʿasā an yaqūma*, and it falls under the pattern of the saying:

*And I saw your husband in the battle,*
*girded with a sword and a spear.*

[[It is transmitted thus in the originals. In al-Lisan and in the commentary on the shawahid of Sibawayh, it reads: "Would that your husband had set out."]]

There is a third view: that it is a conjunction on *al-fath*, as the poet said:

*The wearing of a cloak, and the cooling of my eye,*
*are dearer to me than the wearing of sheer garments.*

[[The complete line is: "are dearer to me than the wearing of sheer garments."]]

It is also permissible to make *an yaʾtiya* a substitute (*badal*) for the name of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, so that the construction becomes: *ʿasā an yaʾtiya Allāhu wa-yaqūla alladhīna āmanū* (that Allah may bring it, and that those who believe may say). The Kufans read *wa-yaqūlu alladhīna āmanū* with *ḍamm* (the nominative), as a new sentence (*qaṭʿ*) from the first.

(﴿Are these the ones﴾) refers to the hypocrites.

(﴿Who swore by Allah﴾) means they swore and exerted themselves in their oaths.

(﴿That they were indeed with you﴾) means they said that they were indeed with you. It is also permissible to read *annahum* in the accusative, governed by *aqsamū* (they swore). The meaning is that the believers said to the Jews, by way of rebuke: "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with the utmost of their oaths that they would support you against Muhammad?" It may also be that the believers spoke to one another, meaning: "These are the ones who used to swear that they were believers, but Allah has today exposed their concealment."

(﴿Their deeds have become void﴾) means they became void because of their hypocrisy.

(﴿So they became losers﴾) means losers of the reward. It was also said: they lost through their allegiance to the Jews, so no fruit came to them after the Jews were killed and expelled.

There are four issues in this verse.

**First:** God's words ﴿Whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾ form a conditional clause (shart), and its response (jawab) is "then God will bring forth." The recitation of the people of Madina and Syria is "مَنْ يَرْتَدِدْ" with two dals, while the rest read "مَنْ يَرْتَدَّ" (with a doubled dal). This is one of the signs of the Qur'an's inimitability (i'jaz) and of the Prophet ﷺ's prophethood: he foretold their apostasy when it had not yet happened, and it was an unseen matter (ghayb). It came to pass after a period of time, and the people of apostasy (ahl al-ridda, the apostasy movement) appeared after his death (ﷺ). Ibn Ishaq said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken, the Arabs apostatized except for three mosques: the Mosque of Madina, the Mosque of Makka, and the Mosque of Juwathā [[Juwathā, with a hamza: the name of a fortress in Bahrain. A hadith says: "The first Friday prayer (jumu'a) held after Madina was held at Juwathā." (al-Nihaya).]]. In their apostasy they were of two kinds. One kind rejected the Sharia entirely and left it. The other kind rejected the obligation of zakat while acknowledging the obligation of the rest, saying: "We fast and we pray, but we will not pay zakat." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq fought all of them, and sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to them with armies, and he fought them [[In the manuscripts j, k, z and ʿ: "and he killed them."]] and took them captive, as is well known from their reports.

**Second:** God's words ﴿then God will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him﴾ are in the position of a descriptive clause (na't). Al-Hasan, Qatada and others said: It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and his companions. Al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning the Ansar. It has also been said: It refers to a people who were not present at that time, and that Abu Bakr fought the people of apostasy with a people who were not present when the verse was revealed, but who were alive, from Yemen, from Kinda, Bajila and Ash'a. It has also been said: It was revealed concerning the Ash'aris. According to a report, when it was revealed, shortly afterward the ships of the Ash'aris and the tribes of Yemen arrived by sea, and they had a notable role in Islam during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Most of the conquests of Iraq in the time of Umar (may God be pleased with him) were carried out by the tribes of Yemen. This is the most sound of what has been said about its revelation, and God knows best. Al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah related in al-Mustadrak, with his chain of transmission, that the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari when this verse was revealed and said: "They are the people of this man." Al-Qushayri said: The followers of Abu al-Hasan are from his people, because every place where a people is attributed to a prophet, what is meant is his followers.

**Third:** God's words ﴿humble toward the believers﴾: "humble" (adhilla) is a descriptive modifier of "a people," and so is "mighty" (a'izza) in the same way. That is, they are gentle with the believers, show them mercy and compassion, and are lenient toward them, from the expression "a tame animal (dabba dhalul)," meaning one that is docile and easily led, and it has nothing to do with humiliation (dhull). And they are stern toward the disbelievers and oppose them. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are to the believers like a parent to a child and a master to a slave, and they are toward the disbelievers in sternness like a beast of prey toward its prey. God the Exalted said: ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. It is also permissible to read "adhillatan" in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: He loves them and they love Him in this state. The meaning of God's love for His servants and their love for Him has been discussed earlier [[See vol. 4, p. 59 and what follows.]].

**Fourth:** God's words ﴿who strive in the way of God﴾ are also in the position of a descriptive clause.

﴿and do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾: unlike the hypocrites, who fear misfortunes. This indicates the affirmation of the leadership (imama) of Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali (may God be pleased with them), because they struggled for the sake of God, the Mighty and Majestic, during the lifetime of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and fought the apostates after him. It is known that whoever possesses these qualities is a friend (wali) of God, the Exalted. It has also been said: The verse is general, applying to everyone who fights the disbelievers until the Hour arrives. And God knows best.

﴿That is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills﴾: "That" is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows is the predicate (khabar).

﴿And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: that is, abundant in bounty, and knowing of the interests of His creation.

**The first issue: the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe﴾.** Jabir ibn Abdullah said: Abdullah ibn Salam said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Our people from Qurayza and al-Nadir have abandoned us and sworn that they would not sit with us, and we cannot sit with your Companions because of the distance between our homes." So this verse was revealed, and he said: "We are pleased with Allah, His Messenger, and the believers as guardians." The phrase "those who believe" is general, covering all believers. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them all, was asked about the meaning of ﴿Your guardian is only Allah and His Messenger and those who believe﴾: "Is it Ali ibn Abi Talib?" He said: "Ali is one of the believers," meaning that this applies to all believers. Al-Nahhas said: "This is a clear statement, because ﴿those who﴾ is in the plural." Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. In another narration he said: it was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. Mujahid and al-Suddi also said this, and what led them to it is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿who establish prayer and give zakat (obligatory almsgiving) while bowing﴾.

**The second issue:** A beggar asked in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one gave him anything. Ali was in prayer, in the bowing position, and there was a ring on his right hand. He gestured to the beggar with his hand until he took it. Ilkiya al-Tabari said: This shows that a small action does not invalidate the prayer, since giving away a ring while bowing is an action performed during prayer, and the prayer was not invalidated by it. The words ﴿and give zakat while bowing﴾ show that voluntary charity is also called zakat, since Ali gave away his ring while bowing. This is similar to the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And whatever you give in zakat, seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ [al-Rum: 39]. The obligatory and the voluntary are both included, so the term zakat covers both obligatory and voluntary giving, just as the term sadaqa (charity) and the term salat (prayer) each comprise both.

I say: According to this view, what is meant by zakat is giving away the ring. Interpreting the word zakat as giving away a ring is far-fetched, because zakat is only used with its specific term, which is obligatory zakat, as explained earlier at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara. Moreover, the verse is preceded by ﴿who establish prayer﴾, and establishing prayer means performing it at its times with all its requirements, and what is meant is the obligatory prayer. Then He said ﴿while bowing﴾, that is, the voluntary. It is also said: He singled out bowing for mention as an honour. It is also said: at the time the verse was revealed, the believers were either completing the prayer or bowing in it. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿and give zakat while bowing﴾ include the permissibility of a small action during prayer, because this was stated in the manner of praise, and the least that can be said in the context of praise is that it is permissible. It is narrated that Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, gave the beggar something while he was in prayer. It may also be that this was a voluntary prayer, since such an action is disliked during an obligatory prayer. It is possible that the praise is directed at the combination of two states, as if it describes one who believes in the obligation of prayer and zakat, so prayer is expressed by bowing and the belief in its obligation by the action. This is like saying: "The Muslims are the ones who pray," and you do not mean that they are praying at that very moment, and praise is not directed at the state of prayer itself; rather, it refers to one who does this action and believes in it.

He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever takes as allies Allah and His Messenger and those who believe﴾. That is, whoever entrusts his affair to Allah, obeys the command of His Messenger, and takes the Muslims as allies, then he is of the party of Allah. It is also said: that is, whoever undertakes the task of obeying Allah, supporting His Messenger and the believers.

﴿Indeed, the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾. Al-Hasan said: The party (hizb) of Allah is the army (jund) of Allah. Others said: the supporters (ansar) of Allah. The poet said:

"And how could I be humiliated [[adwa: that is, to be made weak and oppressed, from the thing that is weak (al-dawi). (al-Tabari). In manuscript ʿ: "And how could I be disgraced."]] while Bilal is my party (hizbi)?"

That is, my supporters (nasiri). The believers are the party of Allah, so they indeed overcame the Jews by taking captives, killing, expulsion, and imposing the jizya. The hizb is a category of people. Its root comes from the calamity (al-nā'ibah), from their saying: "hazabahu kadhā," meaning it befell him, as if those who gather together into a party are assembled as people gathered around a calamity. The hizb of a man is his companions. The hizb is also the portion (wird), and from it the hadith: "Whoever misses his hizb of the night..." And "I have divided the Qur'an into hizbs (hazzabtu al-Qur'an)." The hizb is also a group. "Tahazzabu" means they gathered together. "Al-Ahzab" are the groups that gather to fight the prophets [[In manuscripts H and ʿ: "the enemies."]]. And "hazabahu amr" means a matter befell him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 57:

In this there are two issues.

The first: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that a group of the Jews and the polytheists mocked the Muslims at the time of their prostration, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take those who have taken your religion as mockery and play, [neither] from among those who were given the Scripture before you nor the disbelievers as allies﴾, up to the end of the verses. The meaning of mockery (al-huzu') has already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 446].

As for ﴿and the disbelievers as allies﴾, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (al-khafd), with the meaning "and of the disbelievers." Al-Kisa'i said: "In the codex of Ubayy, may Allah have mercy on him, it reads 'and of the disbelievers,' and 'min' here is for specifying the category (li-bayan al-jins), though the accusative is clearer and more evident." This is what al-Nahhas said.

It is also said that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the nearer of the two governing words to it, which is His saying: ﴿from among those who were given the Scripture﴾. Thus Allah forbade them to take the Jews and the polytheists as allies, and informed them that both groups had taken the religion of the believers as mockery and play.

Whoever reads it in the accusative coordinates it with the first "those" in His saying: ﴿Do not take those who have taken your religion as mockery and play, and the disbelievers as allies﴾, meaning: do not take these and those as allies. In this reading, the one described as mocking and playing is the Jews alone and no others. The ones forbidden to be taken as allies are the Jews and the polytheists, and both, in the reading with the genitive, are described as mocking and playing.

Makki said: "Had there not been consensus of the community on the accusative, I would have chosen the genitive, for its strength in grammatical construction, in meaning and interpretation, and in its proximity to the word it is coordinated with."

It is also said that the meaning is: do not take the polytheists and the hypocrites as allies, based on their saying: ﴿We are only mockers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:14] [see vol. 1, p. 206]. All polytheists are disbelievers, but the term "disbelievers" is generally applied to the polytheists, and for this reason the mention of the People of the Book was separated from the disbelievers.

The second issue: Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: This verse is like His saying: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:51], and ﴿Do not take as intimates outside your own [folk]﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:118]. They include the prohibition of seeking support and victory through the polytheists and the like.

And Jabir related that when the Prophet ﷺ intended to go out to Uhud, a group of Jews came to him and said: "We will march with you." So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We do not seek help in our affair from the polytheists." This is the sound position in the school of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah permitted seeking victory through them over the polytheists for the Muslims, but the Book of Allah the Exalted indicates the opposite of what they said, along with what has come in the Sunnah to that effect. And Allah knows best.

**Twelve issues arise from this verse.**

**First issue:** Al-Kalbi said: When the caller (muadhdhin) called the adhan (call to prayer) and the Muslims stood up for prayer, the Jews said, "They have stood up; may they never stand up!" They would laugh when the Muslims bowed and prostrated, and they said about the adhan, "You have invented something we never heard of among the nations before. Where did you get a shout like the braying of a donkey? How ugly a sound, and how vulgar a matter!"

It is also said that when the muadhdhin called to prayer, they would laugh among themselves and wink at one another in a manner of mockery and buffoonery, in order to belittle its people and to repel people from it and from the one who called to it.

It is also said that they regarded the one who called to prayer as a player and a mocker of its practice, out of ignorance of its status. So this verse was revealed, and Allah, glorified is He, also revealed His saying: "And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah and does righteous deeds" (Fussilat 33) [See vol. 15, p. 359.]

*Al-nida'* means calling with a raised voice. It may be pronounced *nudā'*, like *du'a'* and *ru'a'*. One says *nadahu munadah* and *nidā'*, meaning he shouted at him. *Tanadaw* means they called to one another. *Tanadaw* also means they sat in the *nadi* (assembly), and *nadāhu* means he sat with him in the assembly.

There is no mention of the adhan in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, except in this verse. Indeed, it is mentioned regarding Friday prayer by specific reference.

**Second issue:** The scholars said: The adhan was not called in Makkah before the Hijrah. Instead, they would call out, "Prayer is gathered" (*al-salat jami'ah*). When the Prophet (ﷺ) emigrated and the qiblah was turned toward the Ka'bah, he was commanded to call the adhan, and the call "Prayer is gathered" remained for a matter that arose. [In manuscript Z: "bāqiyat" (feminine form).]

The Prophet (ﷺ) was greatly concerned about the matter of the adhan until Abdullah ibn Zayd, Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with them) were shown it in a dream. The Prophet (ﷺ) had heard the adhan on the night of the Isra' in the heavens. As for the dream of Abdullah ibn Zayd al-Khazraji al-Ansari and of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with them both), it is well known. Abdullah ibn Zayd informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of it at night when he visited him with it, and Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When I awoke, I informed the Prophet (ﷺ)." So the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Bilal, and he called the adhan for prayer in the manner in which people call it today.

Bilal added in the dawn prayer, "Prayer is better than sleep," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved it. It is not in the dream of the Ansari. Ibn Sa'd reported this from Ibn Umar.

Al-Daraqutni, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was shown the adhan, and that he informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of it, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded Bilal to call the adhan before the Ansari informed him. He mentioned this in his book *al-Mudabbaj*, in the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and the hadith of Abu Bakr from him.

**Third issue:** The scholars differed regarding the obligation of the adhan and the iqamah (the second call before the prayer). As for Malik and his companions, the adhan is obligatory only in mosques for congregational prayers where people gather. Malik explicitly stated this in his *Muwatta'*.

The later scholars among his companions differed on two views:

The first: It is a confirmed sunnah (*sunnah mu'akkadah*) and an obligation of sufficiency (*fard kifayah*) in a city (*misr*) and in places that follow the rule of a city among the villages.

Some of them said: It is an obligation of sufficiency.

The companions of al-Shafi'i likewise differed. Al-Tabari reported from Malik that he said: "If the people of a city deliberately abandon the adhan, they must repeat the prayer." Abu Umar said: "I know of no disagreement that the adhan is obligatory in general upon the people of a city, because the adhan is the distinguishing sign between the abode of Islam and the abode of disbelief. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out a detachment, he would say to them: 'If you hear the adhan, then hold back and refrain; and if you do not hear the adhan, then raid,' or he said, 'then launch the raid.'"

In Sahih Muslim, it is reported: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to raid when dawn broke. If he heard an adhan, he refrained; otherwise he raided..." the hadith.

Ata', Mujahid, al-Awza'i, and Dawud said: The adhan is an obligation (*fard*) and they did not say "of sufficiency."

Al-Tabari said: The adhan is a sunnah and not an obligation.

It is reported from Ashhab, from Malik: "If a traveler deliberately abandons the adhan, he must repeat the prayer."

The Kufans disliked that a traveler should pray without an adhan or iqamah. They said: As for a resident of a city, it is recommended for him to call the adhan and the iqamah. If he is satisfied with the adhan and iqamah of the people, it suffices him.

Al-Thawri said: The iqamah suffices in place of the adhan during travel; if you wish, you may call the adhan and the iqamah.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: The traveler calls the adhan according to the hadith of Malik ibn al-Huwayrith.

Dawud said: The adhan is obligatory upon every traveler for himself, and the iqamah as well, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Malik ibn al-Huwayrith and his companion: "When you are on a journey, call the adhan and the iqamah, and let the older of you lead the prayer." Al-Bukhari transmitted it, and this is the view of the Zahiris.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Malik ibn al-Huwayrith and to a cousin of his: "When you travel, call the adhan and the iqamah, and let the older of you lead the prayer."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Therefore the adhan and the iqamah are obligatory upon every congregation, whether resident or traveling, because the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the adhan, and his command implies obligation. [In manuscripts J, K, A, Z: "on the obligation" (instead of "on obligation").]

Abu Umar said: Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and al-Tabari agreed that if a traveler abandons the adhan, deliberately or forgetfully, his prayer is valid. The same applies, in their view, if he abandons the iqamah, although they are more strongly opposed to abandoning the iqamah. [From manuscripts J and A.]

Al-Shafi'i argued that the adhan is not obligatory and is not one of the obligatory elements of the prayer, because the adhan is waived for one who combines prayers at 'Arafah and Muzdalifah. The position of Malik regarding the adhan in travel is, in essence, the same as that of al-Shafi'i.

**Fourth issue:** Malik, al-Shafi'i, and their companions agreed that the adhan is repeated in pairs (*mathna*) and the iqamah is said once each, except that al-Shafi'i makes the first takbir four times. This is preserved in the reliable narrations in the hadith of Abu Mahdhurah [Abu Mahdhurah Samurah ibn Mi'ayr, the muadhdhin of the Prophet (ﷺ), who had the most beautiful adhan and the most resonant voice], and in the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd, who said: "...". This is an addition that must be accepted.

Al-Shafi'i claimed that the adhan of the people of Makkah remained in this form among the family of Abu Mahdhurah until his time and era. His companions said: It is the same among them now. What Malik adopted also appears in authentic hadiths about the adhan of Abu Mahdhurah and the adhan of Abdullah ibn Zayd. The practice in Madinah among the family of Sa'd al-Qurazi was also in accordance with this up to their time.

Malik and al-Shafi'i agreed on the *tarji'* in the adhan. This is the muadhdhin's returning, when he says: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah" twice, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah" twice; he repeats them, and extends his voice as much as he can.

There is no disagreement between Malik and al-Shafi'i regarding the iqamah except in his saying "Qad qamati al-salah" (the prayer has begun). Malik says it once, and al-Shafi'i says it twice. Most scholars follow what al-Shafi'i said, and the reports support it.

Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Hayy said: The adhan and the iqamah are both in pairs (*mathna mathna*). The takbir according to them at the beginning of the adhan and the beginning of the iqamah is "Allahu akbar" four times. According to them there is no *tarji'* in the adhan. Their argument for this is the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) told us that Abdullah ibn Zayd came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I saw in a dream a man standing with two green garments on the remains of a wall. He called the adhan in pairs and the iqamah in pairs, and he sat between them for a sitting.' Bilal heard of this, so he stood and called the adhan in pairs, sat for a sitting, and then recited the iqamah in pairs." Al-A'mash and others narrated it from Amr ibn Murrah from Ibn Abi Layla. This is the view of a group of the Successors (*tabi'un*) and the jurists of Iraq.

Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i said: The companions of Ali and Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) used to repeat the adhan and iqamah in pairs. This is the adhan of the people of Kufa, handed down among them and practiced generation after generation, just as the people of the Hijaz hand down theirs. Their adhan includes four takbirs, like the people of Makkah.

Then comes the testimony that there is no god but Allah once, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah once; then "Come to the prayer" once, then "Come to success" once; then the muadhdhin returns, extends his voice, and says: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah," the whole adhan, twice each, to the end.

Abu Umar said: Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Dawud ibn Ali, and Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari held that any wording reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is permissible, and they understood this as permissibility and choice. They said: All of that is permitted, because all of it has been established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his companions practiced it. Whoever wishes may say "Allahu akbar" twice at the beginning of the adhan, and whoever wishes may say it four times; whoever wishes may return in his adhan, and whoever wishes may not return; whoever wishes may repeat the iqamah in pairs, and whoever wishes may say it singly, except for his saying "Qad qamati al-salah," which is always said twice, in every case!

**Fifth issue:** They differed regarding *al-tathwib* for the dawn prayer, which is the muadhdhin's saying: "Prayer is better than sleep." Malik, al-Thawri, and al-Layth said: The muadhdhin in the dawn prayer, after his saying "Come to success" twice, says "Prayer is better than sleep" twice. This is also the view of al-Shafi'i in Iraq, while in Egypt he said: He does not say it.

Abu Hanifa and his companions said: He says it after finishing the adhan, if he wishes. It is also reported from them that it is said within the adhan itself, and this is the practice of people at the dawn prayer.

Abu Umar said: It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), in the hadith of Abu Mahdhurah, that he commanded him to say in the dawn adhan: "Prayer is better than sleep." It is also reported from him from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd. It is reported from Anas that he said: "It is from the sunnah that 'Prayer is better than sleep' be said at dawn." It is reported from Ibn Umar that he used to say it.

As for Malik's statement in the *Muwatta'* that it reached him that the muadhdhin came to Umar ibn al-Khattab to inform him of the dawn prayer, found him sleeping, and said: "Prayer is better than sleep." Umar commanded him to put it in the dawn call. [The addition is from the *Muwatta'* of Malik.] I do not know that this was reported from Umar through a channel that can be relied upon and whose soundness is known. There is only the hadith of Hisham ibn Urwah from a man called "Isma'il," so take note of him. Ibn Abi Shaybah reported: Abdah ibn Sulayman narrated to us from Hisham ibn Urwah from a man called "Isma'il," who said: "The muadhdhin came to Umar to inform him of the dawn prayer, and he said, 'Prayer is better than sleep.' Umar was pleased with it and said to the muadhdhin: 'Keep it in your adhan.'"

Abu Umar said: The meaning of it, in my view, is that he said to him: "The call for dawn is the place for saying it, not here," as if he disliked that there should be another call at the gate of the ruler, as the rulers later introduced.

Abu Umar said:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 58 (part 2 of 2):

The only thing that led me to this interpretation, even though the apparent sense of the report is otherwise, is that the tathwib (the call "al-salatu khayrun min al-nawm," "Prayer is better than sleep") during the dawn prayer is more widely known among the scholars and the common people, so it cannot be supposed of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was ignorant of [a sunnah] of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and ordered his muezzins to do it: in Medina Bilal, and in Mecca Abu Mahdhurah. This is preserved and well known regarding the adhan of Bilal, and the adhan of Abu Mahdhurah at the dawn prayer in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ is famous among the scholars.

Waki' narrated from Sufyan, from Imran ibn Muslim, from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, that he sent a message to his muezzin: "When you reach 'Hasten to the success' (hayya 'ala al-falah), say: 'Prayer is better than sleep,' for that is the adhan of Bilal." It is known that Bilal never called the adhan for 'Umar, and he did not hear it after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ except once, in al-Sham, when he entered it.

Sixth: The scholars agreed that it is part of the Sunnah that the adhan for prayer is not called until its time has entered, except for the dawn prayer, for which the adhan is called before the dawn breaks. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. Their evidence is the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Bilal calls the adhan at night, so eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls the adhan."

Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The adhan for the dawn prayer is not called until its time enters, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to Malik ibn al-Huwayrith and his companion: "When the prayer comes, call the adhan, then the iqamah, and let the eldest of you lead you," and by analogy with all the other prayers.

A group of the people of hadith said: If the mosque has two muezzins, one of them calls the adhan before the dawn breaks and the other after the dawn breaks.

Seventh: The scholars differed concerning the case where one muezzin calls the adhan and another gives the iqamah. Malik, Abu Hanifah and their companions held that there is no harm in this, based on the hadith of Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Zayd, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered him, when he saw the call in a dream, to convey it to Bilal, so Bilal called the adhan, then he ordered Abd Allah ibn Zayd and he gave the iqamah.

Al-Thawri, al-Layth and al-Shafi'i said: Whoever calls the adhan should also give the iqamah, based on the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn An'um, from Ziyad ibn Nu'aym, from Ziyad [[In the original: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith al-Sada'i, which is an error; the correction is from the books of terminology and from al-Tirmidhi in the chain of this hadith.]] ibn al-Harith al-Sada'i, who said:
I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and when it was the beginning of dawn he ordered me, so I called the adhan. Then he stood up for the prayer, and Bilal came to give the iqamah.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The brother of Sada' has called the adhan, and whoever calls the adhan should give the iqamah."

Abu 'Umar said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad is al-Ifriqi, and most of them weaken him. No one else narrates this hadith. The first one has the better chain, if Allah wills. If the hadith of al-Ifriqi is sound, then some scholars regard him as trustworthy and praise him, so acting on it is preferable, because it is an explicit text on the point of disagreement. It is also later than the story of Abd Allah ibn Zayd with Bilal, and the later of the commands of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is more deserving of being followed. Despite this, I prefer that when the muezzin is a single, regular appointee, he be the one to give the iqamah. If someone else gives it, the prayer is valid by consensus, and praise be to Allah.

Eighth: It is the duty of the muezzin to call the adhan slowly and deliberately, and not to embellish it with melodic extension (tatrib, meaning prolonging and beautifying the voice), as many ignorant people do today. Rather, many of the rabble and the common people have taken it beyond the limit of moderation, making many trills and many breaks in it, until what he says cannot be understood, nor what he is calling to.

Al-Daraqutni narrated, through the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had a muezzin who embellished his call, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The adhan is easy and smooth. If your adhan is easy and smooth, then call it; otherwise, do not call it."

It is recommended that he face the qiblah while calling the adhan according to a group of [[In 'A and H: the group of the scholars.]] scholars, and that he turn his head right and left at "Hasten to prayer, hasten to success," according to many of the scholars.

Ahmad said: He should not turn fully around, unless he is on a minaret wanting to make the people hear him. Ishaq also said this. The best is that he be in a state of ritual purity.

Ninth: It is recommended for the one who hears the adhan to repeat it until the end of the two testimonies (tashahhud), and if he completes it, that is permissible, based on the hadith of Abu Sa'id [[The apparent reference is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, since it is authentically transmitted from him: "When you hear the muezzin, say the same as he says," in Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Abu Dawud and Ahmad.]]. In Sahih Muslim, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
"When the muezzin says 'Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar,' and one of you says 'Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar,' then he says 'Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah,' and he says 'Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah'; then he says 'Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah,' and he says 'Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah'; then he says 'Hayya 'ala al-salah,' and he says 'La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah'; then he says 'Hayya 'ala al-falah,' and he says 'La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah'; then he says 'Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar,' and he says 'Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar'; then he says 'La ilaha illa Allah,' and he says 'La ilaha illa Allah' from his heart, he will enter Paradise."

And in it, from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever says, when he hears the muezzin, 'Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lahu, wa anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluhu, radītu billahi rabban, wa bi-Muhammadin rasulan, wa bil-Islami dinan,' his past sins will be forgiven."

Tenth: As for the virtue of the adhan and the muezzin, sound reports have also come concerning it. Among them is what Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the call to prayer is made, the Shaytan turns his back and passes wind so that he does not hear the adhan," the hadith in full.

It is enough for you that it is the emblem of Islam and a sign of faith, as has already been mentioned.

As for the muezzin, Muslim narrated from Mu'awiyah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The muezzins will have the longest necks of people on the Day of Resurrection."

This is an indication of security from the terror of that day. And Allah knows best.

The Arabs use long-neckedness as a metaphor for the nobles and chiefs of a people, as one of their poets said:
"Tall ones, of the long necks and the locks of hair" [the verse is attributed to Layla al-Akhyaliyya; it is also attributed to al-Shammardal ibn Shurayk al-Yarbu'i, and it is the second half of a line whose first half is: "They resemble kings in their majesty" (or, according to another version: "They resemble swords in their scabbards").
Al-Nudi is the space between the head and the shoulder-blade of the neck.
Al-Limmah (with a kasrah): hair that extends past the earlobe; when it reaches the shoulders it is called jummah.
In al-Lisan: the correct reading is "wal-umam," the plural of ummah, which means stature, because elderly men are not praised for long locks of hair; it is praised in women and young men.]

In the Muwatta' (of Malik), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "No jinn, no human, and no thing hears the extent of the muezzin's voice without bearing witness for him on the Day of Resurrection."

In Sunan Ibn Majah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever calls the adhan seeking reward for seven years, a document of freedom from the Fire is written for him." And in it, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever calls the adhan for twelve years, Paradise becomes obligatory for him, and for his adhan each day sixty good deeds are written for him, and for each iqamah thirty good deeds." Abu Hatim said: This chain is munkar (rejected), but the hadith is sound.

And from 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, who said: The last thing the Prophet ﷺ instructed me was: "Do not take a muezzin who accepts payment for his adhan." This is an established hadith.

Eleventh: The scholars differed concerning taking payment for the adhan. Al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman [[In 'A and K: al-Qasim ibn Muhammad.]] and the companions of opinion (the Hanafis) disliked this. Malik permitted it and said: There is no harm in it. Al-Awza'i said: That is disliked, but there is no harm in taking provision for it from the public treasury (bayt al-mal). Al-Shafi'i said: The muezzin is only to be provided from the fifth of the fifth, the share of the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Taking payment for the adhan is not permissible.

Our scholars have used the hadith of Abu Mahdhurah as evidence for taking payment, but this is open to question. It was recorded by al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others, who said: I went out with a group of men, and when we were on part of the road the muezzin of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the adhan for prayer in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. We heard the voice of the muezzin while we were turning away from it [mutanakkibun: active participle of tanakkaba 'anhu, meaning deviating from it, i.e., turning away and avoiding it. In J: mutanakkirun] so we began to shout, imitating it and mocking it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard us and sent people to us, who seated us before him. He said: "Which of you is the one whose voice I heard raised?" All the people pointed at me, and they spoke the truth, so he sent them all away and kept me back, and said to me: "Stand and call the adhan." I stood up, and there was nothing more hateful to me than the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, nor anything he ordered me to do. So I stood before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he himself taught me the adhan: "Say: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah, ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah." Then he said to me: "Raise your voice and extend it: Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah, ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah, Hayya 'ala al-salah, hayya 'ala al-salah, hayya 'ala al-falah, hayya 'ala al-falah, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah." Then he called me back when I had finished the adhan, and gave me a purse containing some silver. Then he placed his hand on the forelock of Abu Mahdhurah and drew it over his face, then over his chest [bayn: in J, K and 'A: between], then over his breasts, then over his liver, until the hand of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reached the navel of Abu Mahdhurah. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah bless you and bless upon you." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, command me to call the adhan in Mecca." He said: "I have already commanded you." So all the aversion I had felt toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ vanished, and all of that turned into love for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then I went to 'Attab ibn Asid, the governor of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Mecca, and I called the adhan with him for the prayer, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had commanded. (This is the wording of Ibn Majah.)

Twelfth: The words of the Exalted: ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, meaning that they are in the position of one who has no intellect to restrain him from ugly deeds.

It is reported that a man from the Christians, who lived in Medina, whenever he heard the muezzin say "Ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah," would say: "May the liar be burned." A spark of fire fell into his house while he was asleep, and it caught hold of the house and burned it, and burned that disbeliever along with it. It became a lesson for the creatures: "Calamity is entrusted to speech." They used to be given respite in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ until they asked for an opening (a sign), and then they were not delayed after that. Ibn al-'Arabi mentioned this.

**Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 59–60:**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us for anything except that we believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: A group of Jews, among them Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab and Rafi' ibn Abi Rafi', came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about which of the messengers (peace be upon them) he believed in. He said: "We believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham and Ishmael ... " up to His words: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾ [2:133]. When Jesus (peace be upon him) was mentioned, they denied his prophethood and said: "By Allah, we do not know any people with less share in this world and the Hereafter than you, nor a religion worse than your religion." Then this verse and what follows it was revealed. It is connected to what preceded it, namely their denial of the call to prayer (adhan). It combines testimony to Allah's oneness and to Muhammad's prophethood. The contradictory religion is that of one who distinguishes between the prophets of Allah, not the religion of one who believes in all of them.

It is permissible to assimilate the lam into the ta' (idgham), since they are close to each other. The verb ﴿tanqimun﴾ means "you are displeased," and it has been said: "you dislike," and it has been said: "you disapprove." The meanings are close. It is said: naqama min kadha yanqimu and naqima yanqamu, and the first is more common. 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"They held nothing against the Banu Umayyah
except that they are forbearing when they are angered."

In the revelation: ﴿they held nothing against them﴾ [85:8]. It is also said: naqimtu 'ala al-rajul (with kasrah) fa-ana naqim, when I blame him. It is said: ma naqimtu 'alayhi al-ihsan ("I held no grievance against him for his kindness"). Al-Kisa'i said: naqimtu with kasrah is a dialectal form, and naqamtu al-amr as well, and naqimtuhu when I disliked it. Allah "intaqama minhu," meaning He punished him. The noun derived from it is al-naqimah, its plural is naqamat and naqim, like kalimah, kalimat and kalim. If you wish, you may make the qaf sukun and transfer its vowel to the nun, saying: niqmah, plural niqam, like ni'mah and ni'am.

(﴿Except that we believe in Allah﴾) is in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by ﴿tanqimun﴾. And ﴿tanqimun﴾ here means "you blame." That is: "Do you resent us for anything except our belief in Allah, when you know that we are upon the truth?"

(﴿And that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾) means: in your abandoning of belief and your departure from obedience to Allah's command. It has been said that this is like the saying of one who says: "Do you blame me for anything except that I am chaste and you are immoral?" It has also been said: meaning, "Because most of you are defiantly disobedient, you resent us for that."

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that as recompense from Allah?"﴾ That is, something worse than your resentment toward us. It has been said: something worse than what you wish against us of harm. This is the answer to their saying: "We know no religion worse than yours."

"Mathubah" is in the accusative as an explanatory apposition (tamyiz/bayan). Its original form is mafu'ah. The vowel of the waw was moved onto the tha', so the waw became sakin, and since after it there was another sakin waw, one of them was dropped for that reason. Similar to it are maqulah, majuzah and madufah, in the sense of a verbal noun, as the poet said:

"Whenever my neighbour called me for a calamity (madufah),
I would hitch up my waistwrap until it reached halfway up my shin."

It has also been said: it is of the pattern maf'alah, like makrumah and ma'qulah.

(﴿Whom Allah has cursed﴾): "man" here is in the nominative position, as He said: ﴿something worse than that: the Fire﴾ [22:72]. The implied meaning is: "it is the curse of the one whom Allah has cursed." It may also be in the accusative position, meaning: "Say, shall I inform you of something worse than that, the one whom Allah has cursed." It may also be in the genitive position as a substitution (badal) for "sharr," and the implied meaning is: "Shall I inform you of the one whom Allah has cursed?" The intended referent is the Jews.

The discussion of al-Taghut has already been given. The meaning is: "And He made among them those who worship al-Taghut." The relative pronoun is omitted according to al-Farra'. The Basran grammarians said: it is not permissible to omit the relative pronoun, and the meaning is: "whom Allah has cursed and who worshipped al-Taghut."

Ibn Wathhab al-Nakha'i recited ﴿anabbi'ukum﴾ with light pronunciation (takhfif).

Hamzah recited ﴿'abud al-taghut﴾ with a damma on the ba' and a kasrah on the ta'. He made it a noun of the pattern fa'ul, like 'adud, and thus it is a form of intensification and abundance, like yaqudh, nadus (meaning shrewd, perceptive) and hadhur. Its original form is an adjective. From it is the saying of al-Nabighah (the Dhubyani):

"From the wild cattle of Wajrah, whose legs are speckled,
lean in the belly, like the sword of the polisher, the unique."

With a damma on the ra'. And it is in the accusative governed by "ja'ala," meaning: "He made from them servants of al-Taghut." He made 'abud an annexed noun to al-Taghut and so put it in the genitive. "Ja'ala" here means "created." The meaning is: "And He created from them those who exaggerate in the worship of al-Taghut."

The rest of the readers recited with a fatha on the ba' and the ta', and made it a past verb, coordinating it with the past verbs "ghadiba" and "la'ana." Their meaning is: "those whom Allah has cursed and those who worshipped al-Taghut." Or it is in the accusative governed by "ja'ala," meaning: "He made from them apes and swine and [those who] worshipped al-Taghut." The pronoun in "'abada" is singular, taking into account the wording of "min" rather than its meaning.

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿wa-'abadu al-taghut﴾ according to the meaning. Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿wa-'ubud al-taghut﴾. This may be the plural of 'abd, as one says rahn and ruhun, saqf and suquf. It may be the plural of 'ibad, as one says mithal and mithul. It may be the plural of 'abid, like raghif and raghaf. It may be the plural of 'abid (worshipper), like bazil and buzul. The meaning is: "and served al-Taghut."

Also from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿wa-'ubbad al-taghut﴾. [Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this reading is explained as if he meant "'abadan" with tanwin, then it was dropped due to the meeting of two sakins, as in the saying: "wa-la dhakir Allah."] He made it the plural of 'abid, as one says shahid and shuhud, ghaib and ghayb.

From Abu Waqid: ﴿wa-'abbad al-taghut﴾ for intensification, also the plural of 'abid, like 'amil and 'ummal, and darib and dhurrab.

Mahbub mentioned that the Basrans recited ﴿wa-'uyyad al-taghut﴾ as the plural of 'abid too, like qa'im and qiyyam, and it is also possible that it is the plural of 'abd.

Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi recited ﴿wa-'ubida al-taghut﴾ in the passive, and the implied meaning is: "and al-Taghut was worshipped among them."

'Awn al-'Uqayli and Ibn Buraydah recited ﴿wa-'abida al-taghut﴾ in the singular, which conveys the meaning of a group.

Ibn Mas'ud also recited ﴿wa-'ubida al-taghut﴾. [Ibn 'Atiyyah: "'ubida" with a damma on the ayn, fatha on the ba' and dal, and kasrah on the ta', is a singular noun used to mean the plural, like hutam and labad.] Also from him and from Ubayy: ﴿wa-'ubidat al-taghut﴾ in the feminine for the plural, as Allah said: ﴿the bedouins said﴾ [49:14].

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited ﴿wa-a'bud al-taghut﴾, like kalb and aklub.

These are twelve readings.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Those are worse in position﴾ because their place is the Fire, whereas the believers have no evil in their position. Al-Zajjaj said: "Those are worse in position according to your own claim." Al-Nahhas said: among the best things said about it: "Those whom Allah has cursed are worse in position in the Hereafter than your position in this world, because of the evil that befell you." It has also been said: "Those whom Allah has cursed are worse in position than those who resented you." And it has been said: "Those who resented you are worse in position than those whom Allah has cursed."

When this verse was revealed, the Muslims said to them: "O brothers of apes and swine!" and they lowered their heads in disgrace. Concerning them the poet says:

"The curse of Allah upon the Jews,
indeed the Jews are brothers of the apes."
