Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 61–63:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ [5:61], the verse. This is the description of the hypocrites. The meaning is that they gained nothing from what they heard; rather, they entered disbelievers and they left disbelievers. ﴿And Allah knows best what they were concealing﴾ [5:61], i.e., of their hypocrisy. It was also said: what is meant is the Jews who said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, when you return to your homes." This is indicated by what precedes it of their mention and what comes after.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And you see many of them﴾ [5:62], meaning of the Jews. ﴿Hastening to sin and aggression﴾ [5:62], i.e., competing in disobedience and wrongdoing. ﴿And their consuming of unlawful gain (al-suht)﴾ [5:62], ﴿evil indeed is what they used to do﴾ [5:62]. The Exalted's saying: ﴿Why do the rabbis (al-rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (al-ahbar) not forbid them﴾ [5:63]. ("Lawla" is in the sense of "afala" (why not).)

("Yanhahum") means: restrains them.

("Al-rabbaniyyun") means: the scholars of the Christians.

("Al-ahbar") means: the scholars of the Jews, said by al-Hasan. It was also said that all of them refer to the Jews, because these verses are about them. Then He reproached their scholars for their leaving off forbidding them, so He said: ﴿Evil indeed is what they used to produce﴾ [5:63], just as He reproached those who hasten to sin by His saying: ﴿evil indeed is what they used to do﴾. The verse indicates that the one who abandons forbidding evil is like the one who commits evil, so the verse is a rebuke to the scholars for abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil. The discussion of this meaning has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 365 and following.]] and (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 47.]]. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated, saying: Sufyan ibn Sa'id told me, from Mis'ar, who said: It reached me that an angel was commanded to cause a town to be swallowed up. He said: "O Lord, in it is so-and-so, the worshipper." Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Begin with him, for his face has never changed colour (tam'ara) for a single hour."

[[Tam'ara wajhuhu: changed (in colour).]]

In the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi: "When people see the wrongdoer and do not take him by the hands, Allah is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him." It will come later. Al-sun' means action, except that it implies excellence; it is said: "a sayf sani'" (a well-crafted sword) when its work has been perfected.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 61–63:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ [5:61], the verse. This is the description of the hypocrites. The meaning is that they gained nothing from what they heard; rather, they entered disbelievers and they left disbelievers. ﴿And Allah knows best what they were concealing﴾ [5:61], i.e., of their hypocrisy. It was also said: what is meant is the Jews who said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, when you return to your homes." This is indicated by what precedes it of their mention and what comes after.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And you see many of them﴾ [5:62], meaning of the Jews. ﴿Hastening to sin and aggression﴾ [5:62], i.e., competing in disobedience and wrongdoing. ﴿And their consuming of unlawful gain (al-suht)﴾ [5:62], ﴿evil indeed is what they used to do﴾ [5:62]. The Exalted's saying: ﴿Why do the rabbis (al-rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (al-ahbar) not forbid them﴾ [5:63]. ("Lawla" is in the sense of "afala" (why not).)

("Yanhahum") means: restrains them.

("Al-rabbaniyyun") means: the scholars of the Christians.

("Al-ahbar") means: the scholars of the Jews, said by al-Hasan. It was also said that all of them refer to the Jews, because these verses are about them. Then He reproached their scholars for their leaving off forbidding them, so He said: ﴿Evil indeed is what they used to produce﴾ [5:63], just as He reproached those who hasten to sin by His saying: ﴿evil indeed is what they used to do﴾. The verse indicates that the one who abandons forbidding evil is like the one who commits evil, so the verse is a rebuke to the scholars for abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil. The discussion of this meaning has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 365 and following.]] and (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 47.]]. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated, saying: Sufyan ibn Sa'id told me, from Mis'ar, who said: It reached me that an angel was commanded to cause a town to be swallowed up. He said: "O Lord, in it is so-and-so, the worshipper." Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Begin with him, for his face has never changed colour (tam'ara) for a single hour."

[[Tam'ara wajhuhu: changed (in colour).]]

In the Sahih of al-Tirmidhi: "When people see the wrongdoer and do not take him by the hands, Allah is about to encompass them all with a punishment from Him." It will come later. Al-sun' means action, except that it implies excellence; it is said: "a sayf sani'" (a well-crafted sword) when its work has been perfected.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Jews say: Allah's hand is shackled﴾. ʿIkrimah said: This was said only by Finhas ibn ʿAzura, may Allah curse him, and his companions. They had wealth, but when they disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) their wealth diminished, and they said: Allah is stingy, His hand is withheld from us in giving. So the verse refers specifically to some of them. It is also said: when a group said this and the rest did not deny it, they became as though all of them had said it. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is, His hand is withheld from punishing us. It is also said: when they saw the Prophet (ﷺ) in poverty and lack of wealth, and heard ﴿Who will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [see vol. 3, pp. 237, 204], and saw that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to seek their help with blood-money payments, they said: the god of Muhammad is poor, and at times they said: he is stingy. This is the meaning of their saying, "Allah's hand is shackled." This is figurative, as in His saying: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [17:29]. It is said of a miser: "stiff-knuckled," "closed-palmed," "tight-fingered," and "hand-shackled." The poet said:

Khurasan was a land while Yazid was in it,
and every gate of good things was open.
Then after him it took one stiff-fingered,
as though his face had been sprinkled with vinegar.

In the speech of the Arabs, "yad" (hand) has several meanings. It can mean the bodily limb, as in His saying: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle [of grass]﴾ [38:44]. This is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. It can mean a favor, as the Arabs say: "How many a hand (favor) I have with so-and-so," meaning how many blessings I have bestowed upon him. It can mean power, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the one of strength﴾ [38:17], meaning the one of power. It can mean royal authority and power, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾ [3:73]. It can mean "ownership" (ṣila), as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Of what Our hands have made, cattle﴾ [36:71], meaning what We Ourselves have made. And He said: ﴿Or the one in whose hand is the marriage tie [should pardon]﴾ [2:237], meaning the one who holds the marriage tie. It can mean support and aid, as in his saying, peace be upon him: "The hand of Allah is with the judge until he judges, and with the divider until he divides." It is also used to attribute an act to the one who performs it, to honor and ennoble him, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [38:75]. It is not permissible to take this as a bodily limb, because the Creator, exalted and majestic, is One, and division is not permissible for Him. Nor can it be taken to mean power, sovereignty, favor, or ownership, because then the sharing would occur between His friend Adam and His enemy Iblis, and the distinction mentioned, that He honored Adam over him, would be void, since the meaning of specification would be nullified. So it remains only that it be taken to mean two attributes related to the creation of Adam, honoring him, not the creation of Iblis, in the way that power relates to what is decreed, neither by direct contact nor by touch. Similar to this is what is narrated: that He, may His name be exalted and His majesty be high, wrote the Torah with His hand, and planted the Abode of Honor with His hand for the people of Paradise. Other such attributes relate to what they entail.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their hands were shackled, and they were cursed for what they said﴾. The damma was dropped from the yāʾ for heaviness; the meaning is, they were shackled in the Hereafter. It may also be a supplication against them, and likewise "and they were cursed for what they said." The purpose is to teach us, as He said: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills﴾ [48:27]. He taught us the exception (istithnāʾ), just as He taught us to curse Abu Lahab with His saying: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [111:1]. It is also said that the meaning is that they are the most miserly of creatures, so you will not find a Jew who is not stingy. According to this view, there is an implied "wa" (and) in the speech, meaning: they said, "Allah's hand is shackled," and [their] hands were shackled. Cursing means expulsion, and this has been discussed earlier.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outspread﴾. This is a subject and predicate: meaning, rather His bounty is outspread, so "hand" here means bounty. Some said: this is an error, since His saying "Rather, both His hands are outspread" would imply that Allah's bounties are countless, so how can it be "both His bounties are outspread"? The answer is that this may be a dual of kind, not a dual of a single unit, like his saying, peace be upon him: "The likeness of the hypocrite is like a wandering sheep between two flocks," where one kind is the bounty of this world and the second is the bounty of the Hereafter. It is also said: the two bounties of this world are the apparent bounty and the hidden bounty, as He said: ﴿And He has completed His favors upon you, outward and inward﴾ [31:20]. Ibn ʿAbbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said concerning it: "The apparent bounty is what is good of your character, and the hidden bounty is what is concealed from you of your bad deeds." It is also said: His two bounties are rain and plants, by which and from which blessing comes. It is also said: the dual here is for emphasis, like the Arabs' saying, "Labbayka wa Saʿdayka" (at Your service, again and again), and it does not intend only two times. A speaker may also say: "I have no hand or power in this matter." As-Suddi said: the meaning of His saying "His hands" is His two powers, of reward and punishment, unlike what the Jews said: that His hand is withheld from punishing them. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Allah, exalted is He, said to me: Spend, and I will spend upon you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: "The right hand of Allah is full and never diminished by constant pouring, night and day. Have you considered what He has spent since He created the heavens and the earth? It has not decreased what is in His right hand." He said: "And His Throne is upon the water, and in His other hand is the qabḍ (grasp), He raises and lowers." (The sahḥ is abundant pouring. Yaghīḍ means it diminishes.) A parallel to this hadith is His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿Allah withholds and extends﴾ [2:245]. As for this verse, in the reading of Ibn Masʿud it is "Bal yadāhu basṭān" (both His hands are outspread), reported by al-Akhfash, who said: it is said "yad busṭa," meaning free and outspread. (Yunfiq kayfa yashāʾ) means He provides as He wills. It is also possible that "yad" in this verse means power, that His power is all-encompassing: if He wills He expands, and if He wills He restricts.

﴿And surely many of them will increase﴾: the lām is the lām of oath.

﴿What has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾: that is, with what was sent down to you.

﴿Rebellion and disbelief﴾: that is, whenever a part of the Qur'an is revealed and they disbelieve, their disbelief increases.

﴿And We have cast among them﴾: Mujahid said: among the Jews and the Christians, since He said before this: ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [5:51]. It is also said: among the groups of the Jews, as He said: ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are divided﴾ [59:14]. They are hostile to one another while appearing united, so they are the most hated of Allah's creatures to people.

﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war﴾: this refers to the Jews. "Kullamā" is an adverbial time expression: whenever they gather and prepare, Allah scatters their gathering. It is also said: when the Jews corrupted and opposed the Book of Allah, the Torah, Allah sent Bukhtnasr against them. Then they corrupted again, so He sent against them Butrus the Roman. Then they corrupted again, so He sent against them the Magians. Then they corrupted again, so Allah sent against them the Muslims. Whenever their affairs became orderly, Allah scattered them. So "whenever they kindled a fire," meaning stirred up evil and united their resolve to fight the Prophet (ﷺ), "Allah extinguished it," defeated them and weakened their affair. Thus the mention of fire is metaphorical. Qatadah said: Allah, mighty and majestic, humiliated them; Allah sent the Prophet (ﷺ) when they were under the hands of the Magians. Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾, meaning they strive to nullify Islam, and that is among the greatest corruption, and Allah knows best. It is also said that the fire here means the fire of anger: whenever they kindle the fire of anger in themselves and gather with their bodies and the strength of their souls, blazing with rage, Allah extinguishes it until they become weak. This was by the terror He placed as support before His Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 65–66:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if the People of the Scripture had believed and feared Allah⦆ ("anna" is in the nominative position, and likewise "walaw annahum aqamu al-Tawrah").

(Amanu) means they affirmed as true (saddaqu).

(Wa-ittaqaw) means from polytheism (al-shirk) and sins (al-ma'asi).

(Lakaffarna 'anhum) The lam is the response of (law, "if"). Kaffarna means we covered over, and this has already been mentioned. "Iqamat al-Tawrah wal-Injil" means acting in accordance with their requirements and not distorting them. This meaning has already been discussed comprehensively in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 437 and what follows.]].

(Wa-ma unzila ilayhim min rabbihim) means the Qur'an. It has also been said: the books of their prophets.

(La-akalu min fawqihim wa-min tahti arjulihim) Ibn 'Abbas and others said: this means rain and vegetation, and this indicates that they were in a state of drought. It has also been said: the meaning is "We would have widened their provision and they would have eaten continuously." The mention of "above" and "below" is for emphasis regarding what is opened to them of worldly provision. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out and provide for him from where he does not expect⦆ [[See vol. 18, p. 159.]] [al-Talaq: 2], and ﴿And that if they remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water⦆ [[See vol. 19, p. 16.]] [al-Jinn: 16], and ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth⦆ [[See vol. 7, p. 253.]] [al-A'raf: 96]. Thus Exalted is He made piety among the causes of provision, as in these verses, and He promised increase to whoever gives thanks, saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you⦆ [[See vol. 9, p. 342.]] [Ibrahim: 7].

Then Exalted is He informed that among them is a moderate group (muqtasidah), and they are the believers among them, such as al-Najashi, Salman, and 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, who were moderate, so they did not say about 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, anything except what befits them. It has also been said that by moderation He meant a people who did not believe, but they were not among those who harmed or mocked, and Allah knows best. Al-iqtisad is moderation in action, and it derives from al-qasd, and al-qasd is reaching a thing. You say: qasadtuhu, qasadtu lahu, and qasadtu ilayhi, with the same meaning.

(Sa'a ma ya'malun) meaning: evil is what they did; they denied the messengers, distorted the books, and consumed what is unlawful (al-suht).

(Sa'a ma ya'malun) meaning: evil is what they did; they denied the messengers, distorted the books, and consumed what is unlawful (al-suht).

It was said: its meaning is, "Make the proclamation public," because at the beginning of Islam he used to conceal it out of fear of the polytheists. Then he was commanded to make it public in this verse, and God informed him that He would protect him from the people. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, was the first to openly declare his Islam, and he said: "We will not worship Allah in secret." And concerning that, the verse was revealed: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you, and for those of the believers who follow you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] [[See vol. 8, p. 42.]]. The verse thus refutes the view of those who say that the Prophet ﷺ concealed some matter of the religion out of taqiyya (precautionary dissimulation), and it refutes it as false; these are the Rafidah. It also indicates that he ﷺ did not confide any matter of the religion to anyone privately, because the meaning is: "Convey all that has been revealed to you openly." Were this not so, the words of the Mighty and Majestic, "And if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message" (al-Ma'idah: 67), would have no meaning. It was also said: "Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord concerning the matter of Zaynab bint Jahsh al-Asadiyyah, may Allah be pleased with her" [[From manuscript ʿayn.]]. Other views have been stated besides this, but the sound view is the general one. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is, "Convey all that has been revealed to you from your Lord; if you conceal any part of it, then you have not conveyed His message." This is a discipline for the Prophet ﷺ, and a discipline for the bearers of knowledge among his community, that they should not conceal any part of the matters of His law. Allah, exalted is He, knew about His Prophet that he would not conceal any part of His revelation.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Masruq, from ʿAʾishah, she said: "Whoever tells you that Muhammad ﷺ concealed any part of the revelation has lied, and Allah, exalted is He, says: 'O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord; and if you do not do so, then you have not conveyed His message.'" May Allah curse the Rafidah, for they said that he ﷺ concealed something of what was revealed to him, which people needed.

The second matter: the words of Allah, exalted is He, "And Allah will protect you from the people," are evidence of his prophethood, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that he is protected (maʿsum). Whoever is guaranteed protection by Him, glorified is He, it is not permissible that he would have left any part of what Allah commanded him.

The occasion of revelation of this verse: the Prophet ﷺ was resting under a tree when a Bedouin came, drew his sword (ikhtarata: he unsheathed it), and said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Who will protect you from me?" He said, "Allah." So the Bedouin's hand trembled, the sword fell from his hand, and he struck his head against the tree until his brain was scattered. This was related by al-Mahdawi. Qadi ʿIyad also mentioned it in his book al-Shifa, saying: "This story has been related in the Sahih, and that Ghawrath ibn al-Harith was the man in the story, and that the Prophet ﷺ pardoned him, so he returned to his people and said: 'I have come to you from the best of people.'" The discussion of this meaning has already been treated fully in this surah at His words: ﴿When a people intended to stretch out their hands against you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 11] [[See p. 111 of this part, and vol. 5, p. 372.]], and also in al-Nisa' in the mention of the prayer of fear.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, he said: "We went on a military expedition with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ toward Najd, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ caught up with us in a valley full of ʿidah [[ʿidah: a large thorny tree; it is also said: the largest kind of tree.]]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ dismounted under a tree and hung his sword on one of its branches." He said: "The people scattered in the valley, seeking shade under the trees." He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A man came to me while I was sleeping, took the sword, and I awoke to find him standing over my head, and I did not perceive anything until the sword was drawn in his hand. He said to me, 'Who will protect you from me?' I said, 'Allah.' Then he said a second time, 'Who will protect you from me?' I said, 'Allah.'" He said: "Then he sheathed the sword, and there he is, sitting." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not confront him.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah sent me with His message, I was distressed by it, and I knew that among the people there would be those who denied me, so Allah revealed this verse."

Abu Talib used to send every day with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ men from Banu Hashim to guard him, until the verse was revealed: "And Allah will protect you from the people." Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "O uncle, Allah has protected me from the jinn and mankind, so I have no need of anyone to guard me."

I say: This implies that this occurred in Makkah, and that the verse is Meccan, but this is not so, for it has already been mentioned that this surah is Medinan by consensus. Among the evidence that this verse is Medinan is what Muslim related in his Sahih from ʿAʾishah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed awake one night after his arrival in Madinah, and he said: 'Would that a righteous man from my companions would guard me tonight.'" She said: "While we were thus, we heard the clatter of weapons, and he said: 'Who is this?'" It was Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "What brings you here?" He said: "A fear arose in my heart for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so I came to guard him." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ supplicated for him, then slept. In a narration outside the Sahih, she said: "While we were thus, I heard the sound of weapons, and he said: 'Who is this?' They said: 'Saʿd and Hudhayfah; we have come to guard you.' So the Prophet ﷺ slept until I heard his snoring (ghatit: the loud sound of a sleeper), and this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then put his head out of a leather tent and said: 'Disperse, O people, for Allah has protected me.'"

The people of Madinah recited "risalatahu" in the plural (risalatihi), while Abu ʿAmr and the people of Kufah recited "risalatahu" in the singular. Al-Nahhas said: Both readings are good, but the plural is clearer, because revelation came down to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ little by little, and then he made it clear; the singular denotes multiplicity, so it is like a verbal noun (masdar), and the verbal noun in most speech is neither pluralized nor dualized, since it indicates its category by its own form, as in His words: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you will not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34] [[See vol. 9, p. 367.]].

"Indeed Allah does not guide the disbelieving people" (inna Allaha la yahdi al-qawm al-kafirin): that is, He does not guide them aright, and this has already been discussed. It was also said: "Convey, for guidance is up to Us." Its parallel is: "The duty of the Messenger is only to convey" [[See p. 327 of this part.]] (al-Ma'idah: 99). And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 68:

There are three issues concerning it.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: A group of the Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Do you not acknowledge that the Torah is true, from Allah?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Indeed we believe in it, and we do not believe in anything besides it." So the verse was revealed, meaning: you are not upon anything of the religion until you act upon what is in the two Books (the Torah and the Gospel) concerning belief in Muhammad, peace be upon him, and acting upon what that requires from both of them. Abu 'Ali said: It is also possible that this was before the abrogation (naskh) of both of them.

The second: His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾. That is, they disbelieve in it, so they increase in disbelief upon their disbelief. Tughyan (transgression) is exceeding the limit in wrongdoing and going to excess in it. For wrongdoing is of two kinds: minor and major. Whoever exceeds the rank of the minor has committed tughyan. Among its uses is the Exalted's statement: ﴿Indeed, man does transgress [Al-'Alaq: 6]﴾, meaning he exceeds the limit in departing from the truth.

The third: His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾, meaning: do not be sad over them. Asa, ya'sa, asan means he grieved. The poet said:

"And his eyes flowed with tears from excess of grief."

This is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is not a prohibition of grief, because he cannot control it; rather it is a consolation and a prohibition against exposing oneself to grief. This meaning has already passed at the end of (Al 'Imran) in full detail.

The matter has already been discussed, so there is no point in repeating it. "Wal-ladhina hadu" (and those who are Jews) is conjoined (ma'tuf). Likewise, "wal-Sabi'un" (and the Sabians) is conjoined to the pronoun in "hadu" according to the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard al-Zajjaj say, when the view of al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i was mentioned to him: "This is an error from two angles. The first is that conjoining to a independent pronoun in the nominative is ugly unless it is emphasised. The second is that the conjoined element shares the status of what it is conjoined to, so the meaning becomes that the Sabians have entered Judaism, and this is impossible."

Al-Farra' said: The nominative in "wal-Sabi'un" is permitted because "inna" (indeed) is weak, so it affects only the subject and not the predicate. And "alladhina" here does not show its i'rab (case inflection) clearly, so both cases operate in one manner. Hence the nominative of "al-Sabi'in" is permitted, returning to the original structure of the sentence. Al-Zajjaj said: The case of what shows its i'rab and what does not show its i'rab is the same.

Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: The nominative is understood as inversion (taqdim and ta'khir). The implied sense is: "Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteous deeds, there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve, and the Sabians and the Christians likewise." Sibawayh recited, as a parallel to this, the line:

"Otherwise know that we and you
are, as long as we remain, rebels in dissension."

Dhabi' al-Burjumi also said:

"Whoever has his baggage in Medina,
then I and Qayyar, in it, are strangers."

It was also said that "inna" carries the meaning of "na'am" (yes). In that case "al-Sabi'un" is nominative as a beginning (mubtada'), and the predicate is omitted because the second element indicates it. The conjunction, on this reading, comes after the completion of the sentence and the end of the subject and predicate. Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"The blamers rose early in the morning, they reproach me, and I reproach them,
and they say: 'Grey hair has come upon you, and you have grown old.' I say: 'Indeed.'"

Al-Akhfash said: "Innah" (indeed) here means "na'am" (yes), and this "ha'" was added for pausing.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers﴾. The meaning of the covenant (mithaq) and that it is that they should worship none but Allah, and what is connected with it, has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 1, p. 246 and what follows.]]. The meaning of this verse is: do not grieve over the disbelieving people, for We have given them a valid excuse, and We sent the messengers, but they broke the covenants. All of this returns to what the surah opened with, namely His saying: "Fulfil the contracts" [al-Ma'idah: 1].

﴿Whenever there came to them a messenger with what their souls did not desire﴾, i.e. the Jews, ﴿did not agree with their whims﴾, ﴿a party they denied and a party they killed﴾. That is, they denied a party and killed a party. Those they denied were Jesus and those like him among the prophets, and they killed Zechariah, John and others among the prophets. He said "they kill" only to match the verse's ending (ra's al-ayah). It was also said: He meant a party they denied, and a party they killed, and a party they [were going to] deny and a party they [were going to] kill, for this was their habit and custom, so He abbreviated. It was also said: a party they denied without killing them, and a party they killed, and then denied them. "They kill" is a qualifier (na't) of "a party." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 71:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾. The meaning: those to whom the covenant was taken thought that Allah, mighty and majestic, would not send down any test or trial through hardships, deceived by their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." They were deceived only by the long delay (al-imhal).

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "takūna" (takuna, "there would be") with the nominative (raf'), while the rest read it in the accusative (nasb). The nominative reading is based on taking ḥasiba (to reckon, consider) in the sense of 'alima (to know) and tayaqqana (to be certain). Here "an" is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna", and the entry of "la" is a substitute for the lightening; the pronoun is omitted because they disliked the verb coming directly after it, and it is not in its nature to be preceded by it, so they separated between them with (bi-la, "not"). Whoever reads it in the accusative makes "an" a particle governing the verb in the subjunctive, and ḥasiba remains in its own sense of doubt and other senses. Sibawayh said: "ḥasibtu alla yaqūla dhālika", meaning "I thought that he did not say that." And if you wish, you may read it in the accusative. Al-Nahhas said: In the view of the grammarians, the nominative after ḥasiba and its sister verbs is better, as the poet said [[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays, and is transmitted in his Diwan as (alā yuḥsina al-lahwa). Basbasa was a woman of the Banu Asad.]]:

Has not Basbasa claimed today that I have grown old, and that such as I do not attend amusement?

The nominative became the better reading because ḥasiba and its sister verbs are in the position of certainty, since it is a fixed matter.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿fa-ʿamū﴾ (so they became blind), that is, to guidance.

(wa-ṣammū) that is, deaf to hearing the truth, because they did not benefit from what they saw or heard.

(Then Allah turned to them in forgiveness) There is an implied element in the speech: that is, the trial befell them, so they repented, and Allah turned to them by removing the drought, or by sending Muhammad ﷺ to inform them that Allah would accept their repentance if they believed. This is the explanation of "Allah turned to them": that is, He would turn to them if they believed and affirmed, not that they had truly repented.

(Then many of them became blind and deaf again) That is, many of them became blind and deaf after the truth had been made clear to them through Muhammad, peace be upon him. "Kathīr" is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the waw (of the verb). Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: as you say, "I saw your people, two-thirds of them." If you wish, it may be in the nominative by an implied subject, meaning: the blind and the deaf among them are many. If you wish, the meaning may be: the blind and the deaf among them are many. A fourth answer is that it is according to the dialect of those who say "akalūnī al-barāghīth" (the fleas ate me), and on this is the poet's verse [[The verse is by al-Farazdaq, satirising ʿAmr ibn ʿAfra'. Diyaf is a village in Syria, and it is said in al-Jazira; its people are Syrian Nabateans. Al-Salit means oil.]]:

But he is a Diyafi, whose father and mother, and whose kin, in Hawran, press oil.

In this sense is also His statement: ﴿And they secretly conspired, those who did wrong﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3]. Outside the Qur'an it is permissible to read "kathīran" in the accusative, being an adjective of an implied verbal noun.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary."﴾ This is the saying of the Ya'qubiyyah (a Christian sect). Allah refuted them with a decisive proof drawn from what they themselves acknowledge, so He said: (And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.") That is, if the Messiah was saying, "O Lord" and "O Allah," then how could he be calling upon himself, or how could he be asking himself? This is impossible.

(Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah) It was said: this is part of the speech of Jesus. And it was said: it is the beginning of a statement from Allah, exalted is He. And ishrak (association) is to believe that there is another originator alongside Him. The discussion of the etymology of "al-Masih" has already passed in (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 88 and what follows.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

(And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 73–74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ That is, one of three. It is not permissible to apply tanwin (nunation) to it, according to al-Zajjaj and others. There is another position among the Arabs, who say "rabi' thalathah" (the fourth of three), and according to this it is permissible to use the genitive and the accusative, because its meaning is the one who makes the three into four by being one of them. Likewise, when you say "thalith ithnayn" (the third of two) with tanwin, it is permissible. This is the saying of the sects of the Christians: the Melkites (al-Malikiyyah), the Nestorians (al-Nusturiyyah) and the Jacobites (al-Ya'qubiyyah), because they say "Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God," and they do not say "three gods," and that is the meaning of their doctrine; they only refuse the expression, while the expression is binding upon them. Whatever is like this is correctly reported with the binding expression, and that is because they say: "The Son is God, and the Father is God, and the Holy Spirit is God." The discussion of this has already been presented in (al-Nisa') [see p. 23 and following of this part]. So Allah declared them disbelievers by this saying of theirs, [and He said]: ﴿And there is no god except one God﴾, that is, that God is not plural, while they are bound to the statement of three gods as already explained, even if they do not state it explicitly. The meaning of "one" has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [see vol. 2, p. 190]. And "min" (from) is superfluous (za'idah). In other than the Qur'an it is permissible to read "ilahan wahidan" (one God) as an exception. Al-Kisa'i permitted the genitive as a substitution (badal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they do not desist﴾, that is, if they do not refrain from saying the Trinity, ﴿a painful punishment will surely afflict them﴾ in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿Will they not then repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ This is an affirmation and a rebuke; that is, let them repent to Him and ask Him to cover their sins. What is meant is the disbelievers among them. The disbelievers were singled out for mention because they are the ones who say this, not the believers.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 73–74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three."﴾ That is, one of three. It is not permissible to apply tanwin (nunation) to it, according to al-Zajjaj and others. There is another position among the Arabs, who say "rabi' thalathah" (the fourth of three), and according to this it is permissible to use the genitive and the accusative, because its meaning is the one who makes the three into four by being one of them. Likewise, when you say "thalith ithnayn" (the third of two) with tanwin, it is permissible. This is the saying of the sects of the Christians: the Melkites (al-Malikiyyah), the Nestorians (al-Nusturiyyah) and the Jacobites (al-Ya'qubiyyah), because they say "Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God," and they do not say "three gods," and that is the meaning of their doctrine; they only refuse the expression, while the expression is binding upon them. Whatever is like this is correctly reported with the binding expression, and that is because they say: "The Son is God, and the Father is God, and the Holy Spirit is God." The discussion of this has already been presented in (al-Nisa') [see p. 23 and following of this part]. So Allah declared them disbelievers by this saying of theirs, [and He said]: ﴿And there is no god except one God﴾, that is, that God is not plural, while they are bound to the statement of three gods as already explained, even if they do not state it explicitly. The meaning of "one" has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [see vol. 2, p. 190]. And "min" (from) is superfluous (za'idah). In other than the Qur'an it is permissible to read "ilahan wahidan" (one God) as an exception. Al-Kisa'i permitted the genitive as a substitution (badal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they do not desist﴾, that is, if they do not refrain from saying the Trinity, ﴿a painful punishment will surely afflict them﴾ in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿Will they not then repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ This is an affirmation and a rebuke; that is, let them repent to Him and ask Him to cover their sins. What is meant is the disbelievers among them. The disbelievers were singled out for mention because they are the ones who say this, not the believers.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger; messengers had passed away before him﴾ is a mubtada' and khabar (subject and predicate). That is, ﴿the Messiah﴾ is the subject and the rest of the sentence is the predicate. The meaning is: the Messiah, even though signs appeared at his hands, brought them only as the messengers before him brought theirs. If he is a god, then every messenger should be a god. This is a refutation of their claim and an argument against them. Then he went further in the argument and said: ﴿and his mother was a truthful woman﴾, which is a mubtada' and khabar. ﴿They both used to eat food﴾, i.e., he was a born and nurtured being. Whoever was born of women and ate food is a created, originated being like all other creatures, and none of them has denied this. So how could the nurtured be fit to be a lord? As for their saying that he ate food in his humanity (nasut, the human nature) and not in his divinity (lahut, the divine nature), this is a move by them toward mixing (ikhtilat, the blending of natures). A god cannot be conceived as mixing with a non-god. If the eternal (qadim) could mix with the originated (muhdath), it would be possible for the eternal to become originated. And if this held true of Jesus, it would hold true of anyone else, so that one could say: divinity mixes with every originated thing.

Some exegetes, on his saying ﴿they both used to eat food﴾, said it is a euphemism for defecation and urination. This indicates that both of them were humans. Whoever argued that Mary, peace be upon her, was not a prophetess used the saying ﴿and his mother was a truthful woman﴾ as evidence. I say: there is room for scrutiny in this, since it is possible for her to be a truthful woman while also being a prophetess, like Idris, peace be upon him. What was mentioned in "Al 'Imran" [[see vol. 4, p. 82 and following]] indicates this. And God knows best. She was called a truthful woman because of her great affirmation of the signs of her Lord and her affirmation of her son in what he informed her of, according to al-Hasan and others. And God knows best.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them﴾ means the proofs (al-dalalat).

(Then look how they are turned away) means how they are diverted from the truth after this clarification. It is said: afakahu, yafikuhu, when he turned him away. In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyya (advocates of human free will against divine predestination) and the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school).

Qur'an 5:76: "Say: Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?"

This is an addition for clarification and the establishment of proof against them [from the versions of ʿAlī and Kūfī, i.e., a marginal variant], meaning: you yourselves acknowledge that ʿĪsā was a fetus in the womb of his mother, possessing no power to harm or benefit anyone. And since you have acknowledged that ʿĪsā, at one stage of his existence, did not hear, did not see, did not know, and neither benefited nor harmed, how then have you taken him as a god?

"And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." That is, He has always been All-Hearing and All-Knowing, possessing the power to harm and to benefit. Whoever has this attribute is truly God. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 77:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth﴾ That is, do not go to extremes as the Jews and the Christians went to extremes concerning Jesus. The excess of the Jews was their saying about Jesus that he was not a child of lawful marriage [[Walad rishdah (with the kasra on the ra, though it may also be fatha): that is, a child of a lawful marriage.]], and the excess of the Christians was their saying that he is God. Al-ghuluw (excess) is going beyond the limit, and its explanation has already been given in (al-Nisa') [[See part 2, p. 21.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people﴾ Al-ahwa' is the plural of hawa (desire), and it has already been discussed in (al-Baqarah) [[See part 2, p. 24 and what follows.]].

Hawa was so named because it plunges its companion into the Fire. ﴿Who have gone astray before﴾ Mujahid and al-Hasan said: this refers to the Jews.

﴿And led many astray⦆ That is, they led many people astray.

﴿And strayed from the right way﴾ That is, they strayed from the aim of the way of Muhammad (ﷺ). The repetition of "strayed" conveys that they went astray before and went astray after, and what is meant are the forebears who established misguidance and acted upon it from among the leaders of the Jews and the Christians.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, the son of Mary.﴾ In this there is one issue: the permissibility of cursing disbelievers even if they are from among the offspring of prophets, and that the nobility of lineage does not prevent applying the curse to them. The meaning of "upon the tongue of David and Jesus, the son of Mary" is that they were cursed in the Psalms (al-Zabur) and the Gospel (al-Injil), for the Zabur is the tongue of David and the Injil is the tongue of Jesus; that is, Allah cursed them in these two books. Their derivation has already been discussed.

Mujahid, Qatadah and others said: "He cursed them" means He transformed them into apes and swine. Abu Malik said: Those who were cursed upon the tongue of David were transformed into apes, and those who were cursed upon the tongue of Jesus were transformed into swine. Ibn Abbas said: Those who were cursed upon the tongue of David were the people of the Sabbath, and those who were cursed upon the tongue of Jesus were those who disbelieved after the descent of the Table (al-Ma'idah). Something similar has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It has also been said: the predecessors and the successors among those who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) were cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus, because the two of them informed that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a prophet who would be sent, so they cursed whoever would disbelieve in him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾ "That" (dhalika) is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), meaning: that curse is because of what they disobeyed, that is, because of their disobedience. It is also permissible that it be in the position of an implied subject, meaning: the matter is that. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative position, meaning: We did that to them because of their disobedience and transgression.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not forbid one another﴾, meaning, none of them forbade another. ﴿Certainly evil was what they used to do﴾ is a condemnation of their abandoning of forbidding, and likewise whoever comes after them is condemned for doing their deed. Abu Dawud related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first thing that entered deficiency upon the Children of Israel was that a man would meet another man and say, 'O such-and-such, fear Allah and leave off what you are doing, for it is not lawful for you.' Then he would meet him the next day and that would not prevent him from being his eating companion, his drinking companion and his sitting companion. When they did that, Allah struck their hearts, one against another. Then He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed by the tongue of David and Jesus, son of Mary. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾, up to His saying: ﴿defiantly disobedient﴾." Then he said: "No, by Allah, you must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and you must take hold of the hand of the wrongdoer and turn him onto the truth, and you must confine him to the truth, or Allah will strike your hearts, one against another, and He will curse you as He cursed them." [Al-Tirmidhi also related it. The meaning of "la-ta'turunnahu" is "la-taruddunnahu" (you must turn him back).]

The second: Ibn Atiyyah said: There is consensus that forbidding wrong is an obligation upon whoever is able to do it and is safe from harm to himself and to the Muslims. If he fears harm, he should disapprove in his heart and shun the one committing the wrong and not mix with him. The scholars of expertise said: It is not a condition for the one forbidding to be free of sin; rather, sinners forbid one another. Some of the jurists said: It was obligatory upon those who indulge in the cups to forbid one another, and they took evidence from this verse, saying: because His saying, "They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed," requires that they shared in the act and that He condemned them for abandoning mutual forbidding. The verse is also evidence for prohibiting sitting with criminals and for commanding that they be abandoned and shunned. He reinforced this with His saying in rebuking the Jews: ﴿You see many of them making allies of those who disbelieve﴾. The "mā" in His saying "mā kānū" may be in the accusative position, with what follows it serving as its qualifier, the sense being: "Evil is a thing they used to do." Or it may be in the nominative position, meaning "alladhī" (that which).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You see many of them﴾, i.e., of the Jews. It was said: [they were] Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions. Mujahid said: he means the hypocrites. (They take as allies those who disbelieve), i.e., the polytheists, and they were not upon their religion.

(Evil is what their souls have put forward for them), i.e., their souls made it seem fair and adorned it. It was also said: the meaning is, "Evil is what they put forward for their souls and their return."

(That Allah has become wrathful with them): "That" (an) is in the position of the nominative, by implying a subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), as when you say: "Zayd is a wretched man" (bi'sa rajulan Zaydun). It was also said: it is a substitute (badal) for "what" (ma) in His saying "evil is" (labi'sa), on the basis that "what" is indefinite (nakirah), so it is also in the nominative. It is permissible that it be in the accusative position, with the meaning of "because Allah became wrathful with them." (And in the punishment they will abide forever): a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar, the predicate of a nominal sentence).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if they had believed in Allah, and in the Prophet, and in what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies﴾. This indicates that whoever takes a disbeliever as an ally is not a believer, if he holds his belief and approves of his actions.

﴿But many of them are defiant transgressors﴾: that is, they have departed from faith in their Prophet because of their distortion (of his message), or from faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) because of their hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 82:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews﴾. The lam is the lam of oath, and the nun (of emphasis) entered upon it according to the opinion of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, to distinguish between the present and the future. "ʿadawatan" (enmity) is in the accusative as a specification (al-bayan), and likewise ﴿and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward the believers those who say, "Indeed, we are Christians"﴾. This verse was revealed concerning the Negus (al-Najashi) and his companions when the Muslims came to them during the first migration (al-hijra al-ula), as is well known in the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq and others, fearing the polytheists and their persecution, and they were a large group. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated to Madinah after that, and they were unable to reach him, as war stood between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Battle of Badr took place and Allah killed in it the chieftains of the disbelievers, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Your vengeance is in the land of Abyssinia. Send gifts to the Negus and send to him two men of your judgment; perhaps he will give you those who are with him, and you will kill them in return for those of yours who were killed at Badr." So the disbelievers of Quraysh sent ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs and ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Rabiʿah with gifts. The Prophet (ﷺ) heard of this, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent ʿAmr ibn Umayyah al-Damri and wrote a letter with him to the Negus. He arrived before the Negus, who read the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then he summoned Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib and the emigrants, and sent for the monks and priests and gathered them. Then he ordered Jaʿfar to recite the Qur'an to them, and he recited Surah Maryam, and they stood up with tears flowing from their eyes. They are the ones concerning whom Allah revealed "And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward the believers those who say, 'Indeed, we are Christians'" and he recited up to "the witnesses." Abu Dawud narrated it. He said: Muhammad ibn Salamah al-Muradi narrated to us, he said: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, he said: Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab, from Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, and from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, and from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, that the first migration was the migration of the Muslims to the land of Abyssinia, and he related the hadith in full. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned from Ibn Ishaq, he said: Twenty men came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in Makkah, or near that, from the Christians, when news of him reached them from Abyssinia. They found him in the mosque [[In (j), (k), (h), (ʿ): in the assembly.]], so they spoke with him and questioned him, and men of Quraysh were in their clubs around the Kaʿbah. When they finished asking the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) what they wished, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and recited the Qur'an to them. When they heard it, their eyes flowed with tears, then they responded to him, believed in him and confirmed him, and they recognized from him what had been described to them in their Scripture concerning his matter. When they stood up from his presence, Abu Jahl confronted them with a group of Quraysh and said: "May Allah disappoint you, what a caravan! Those behind you from the people of your religion sent you to seek information for them, and you come to them with news of the man. Your sitting with him has not shown (anything), until you have abandoned your religion and confirmed what he told you. We know of no caravan more foolish than you"—or as he said to them. They said: "Peace be upon you. We do not seek ignorance from you. For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. We will not fall short in what is good for ourselves." It is said that the group were Christians from the people of Najran. It is also said that these verses were revealed concerning them: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ [al-Qasas: 52] up to His saying: ﴿we do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. It is also said that Jaʿfar and his companions came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with seventy men wearing woolen garments, among them sixty-two from Abyssinia and eight from the people of Syria, and they were Bahira [[Bahira al-Rahib: like Amir, with a long vowel; in one narration with the alif maqsurah.]] the monk, Idris, Ashraf, Abrahah, Thumamah, Qutham, Duraid, and Ayman [[The originals are corrupted in the naming of the names and were corrected from (al-Bahr) and (Ruh al-Maʿani). In (j), (k), (ʿ): Tamam: Nashim instead of Abrahah and Qutham.]], and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to them Surah "Ya Sin" to its end, and they wept when they heard the Qur'an and believed, and they said: "How similar this is to what was revealed to ʿIsa." Then there was revealed concerning them: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah, and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward the believers those who say, "Indeed, we are Christians"﴾, meaning the delegation of the Negus, and they were people of the monasteries (ṣawāmiʿ). Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: Allah also revealed concerning them: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ [al-Qasas: 52] up to His saying ﴿those will be given their reward twice﴾ [al-Qasas: 54] to the end of the verse. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: They were forty men from the people of Najran from the Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, and thirty-two from Abyssinia, and sixty-eight from the people of Syria. Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning some people of the People of the Book who were upon a law of truth brought by ʿIsa, and when Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) they believed in him, so Allah praised them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks (ruhban)﴾. The singular of "qissisin" is qass and qissis, as said by Qutrub. The qissis is the scholar, and its origin is from qassa, meaning to trace a thing and seek it out. The rajiz said:

They awake, turning away from the slander of harm, heedless.

And "tqassasat aswatuhum bil-layl" means I listened to them. And al-qass is slander (namimah). Al-qass is also a leader among the leaders of the Christians in religion and knowledge, and its plural is qusus; likewise qissis is like al-shar and al-shirrir. So the qissisun are those who follow the scholars and the worshippers. It is said of the broken plural of qissis: qasawisah [[Thus in the originals, and it agrees with what is in (al-Qamus), and with it becomes clear his later saying: (one of the two sins was replaced by waw). In (al-Lisan): qasaqisah on the pattern of mahalibah. It is understood from the commentary of (al-Qamus) that it has both plurals.]], one of the two sins replaced by a waw, and qasawisah also, like mahalibah. The original is qasasisah, and they replaced one of the sins with a waw because of their frequency. The word qissis is either Arabic, or in the language of the Romans, but the Arabs mixed it into their speech so it became part of their language, since there is nothing in the Book that is not from the language of the Arabs, as has passed. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: My father narrated to us, Nasr ibn Dawud narrated to us, Abu ʿUbayd narrated to us, he said: I was told from Muʿawiyah ibn Hisham, from Nusayr al-Ta'i, from al-Salt, from Hamiyah ibn Rabab [[Thus in the originals; in Ibn Kathir: Jathimah ibn Ri'ab.]], he said: I said to Salman, "that among them are qissisin and ruhban," and he said: Leave the qissisin in the monasteries and the sanctuary; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it to me as "that among them are siddiqin and ruhban." ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr said: The Christians lost the Injil, and they introduced into it what is not from it, and the ones who altered it were four men: Luqas, Marqus, Yahnas, and Maqbus [[Thus in all the originals; perhaps the correct is Matyus, that is Matthew, for the four reliable Gospels are those of Luke, Mark, John and Matthew.], and there remained a qissis upon the truth and upright conduct; whoever was upon his religion and guidance is a qissis.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and monks (ruhban)﴾. Ruhban is the plural of rahib, like rukban and rakib. Al-Nabighah said: "Had she appeared to a white-haired monk, a worshipper of God who was celibate..."

We would have been captivated by her sight and the beauty of her speech, and we would have thought him rightly guided, though he was not rightly guided.

The verb from it is rahiba Allah, yarhabuhu, meaning he feared Him, with rahban, rahaban, and rahbah. Al-rahbaniyyah and al-tarahhub mean worship in a hermitage (sawma'ah). Abu ʿUbayd said: Ruhban may be used for both the singular and the plural. Al-Farra' said: Ruhban, when it is singular, is pluralized as rahabinah and rahabin, like qurban and qarabin. Jarir said in the plural:

The monks of Madyan, if they saw you, would descend, and the mountain goats from the cliffs of the peaks, the pregnant (ones)...

Al-fadir is the aged one among the wild goats. It is also said: the great one; likewise al-fadur, its plural fudr and fudur, and its place is al-mafdarah, said al-Jawhari. Another said in tawhid:

Had she seen the monks of a monastery in the mountain, the monks would have hurried down, running and praying.

From prayer (salat). Al-rahabah, on the pattern of al-sahabah, is a bone in the chest projecting over the belly like the tongue. This praise is for those among them who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), not for those who persisted in their disbelief; for this reason He said: (and that they are not arrogant), meaning, from submitting to the truth.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 83:

The Most High said: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾, i.e., with tears (bi-l-damʿ). It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and likewise ﴿they say﴾. Imru' al-Qays said:

fafāḍat dumūʿu l-ʿayni minnī ṣabābatan ... ʿalā l-naḥri ḥattā ball damʿī miḥmalī [[al-miḥmal (on the pattern of mirjal) is the strap of the sword.]]

A report that is mustafid is one that has become widespread and spread abroad, like the overflowing of water from abundance. These are the states of the scholars: they weep but do not swoon, they ask but do not shriek, and they grieve but do not die. As the Most High said: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent and repeated; the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it, then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 248.]] [Az-Zumar: 23]. And He said: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾. The explanation of this meaning will come in (Surat al-Anfal), if Allah the Most High wills [[See vol. 7, p. 365.]]. In these verses Allah, glory be to Him, has made clear that the most intense of the disbelievers in rebellion, arrogance and enmity toward the Muslims are the Jews, and the polytheists resemble them; and He made clear that the nearest of them in affection are the Christians. And Allah knows best.

The Most High said: ﴿So inscribe us among the witnesses﴾, i.e., among the community of Muhammad ﷺ who bear witness to the truth, from the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle community, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 153.]] [Al-Baqarah: 143], related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jurayj. Al-Hasan said: those who bear witness to faith. Abu ʿAli said: those who bear witness to the confirmation of Your Prophet and Your Book. The meaning of ﴿fa-uktubna﴾ is "make us (ijʿalna)", so it takes the place of what has been written and decreed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 84:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth?﴾ This shows their insight into the religion, i.e., they say, "And why should we not believe?" meaning, "And what is it for us, abandoning faith?" So "nu'min" (we believe) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

(﴿And we hope that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people﴾) i.e., along with the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), by the evidence of His words: ﴿That the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya':105], meaning the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). There is an implied element in the speech, i.e., "we hope that our Lord will admit us to Paradise." It has also been said that "naṭma'u" (we hope) carries the meaning of "fi" (in), just as "fi" is used with the meaning of "ma'a" (with), as you say: "I was among those who met the amir," i.e., with those who met the amir. The verb ṭam'a (to hope/covet) may be used both in its basic form and in its doubled/intensified form; it is said: ṭami'a fīhi ṭam'an, wa ṭamā'atan, wa ṭamā'iyatan, and the form with the basic verb is ṭami'a, so he is ṭami' (covetous/hopeful).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 85–86:

Allah's saying: ﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said with gardens﴾ is evidence of the sincerity of their faith and the truthfulness of their words. Allah answered their request and fulfilled their hope. Likewise, whoever's faith is sincere and whose certainty is true, his reward is Paradise. Then He said: (And those who disbelieved) among the Jews and the Christians and the polytheists (and denied Our signs, they are the companions of the Hellfire). Al-Jahim (the Hellfire) is the fiercely blazing fire. It is said: Jahama fulan al-nar, meaning he intensified its kindling. It is also said of the eye of a lion: jahmah, because of its intense blazing. This is also said of war, the poet said:

And war does not leave, for its lions (jihaha), imagination and swaggering,
except the youth who is patient in the moments of courage, and the horse that is hard-hoofed (al-waqah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 85–86:

Allah's saying: ﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said with gardens﴾ is evidence of the sincerity of their faith and the truthfulness of their words. Allah answered their request and fulfilled their hope. Likewise, whoever's faith is sincere and whose certainty is true, his reward is Paradise. Then He said: (And those who disbelieved) among the Jews and the Christians and the polytheists (and denied Our signs, they are the companions of the Hellfire). Al-Jahim (the Hellfire) is the fiercely blazing fire. It is said: Jahama fulan al-nar, meaning he intensified its kindling. It is also said of the eye of a lion: jahmah, because of its intense blazing. This is also said of war, the poet said:

And war does not leave, for its lions (jihaha), imagination and swaggering,
except the youth who is patient in the moments of courage, and the horse that is hard-hoofed (al-waqah).

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress.﴾ In it are five issues.

**The first issue:** al-Tabari traced back, through a chain to Ibn Abbas, that the verse was revealed concerning a man who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, when I eat meat, I become aroused and my desire overtakes me, so I have forbidden meat to myself." So Allah revealed this verse. It was also said that it was revealed concerning a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, among them Abu Bakr, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abdullah ibn Umar, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, Salim the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, Salman al-Farisi and Ma'qil ibn Muqarrin, may Allah be pleased with them all, who gathered in the house of Uthman ibn Maz'un and agreed that they would fast by day, stand in prayer by night, not sleep on beds, not eat meat or *al-wadak* [[al-wadak: al-dasm (fat, grease).]], not approach women or perfume, wear coarse wool garments, renounce the world, wander across the earth, live as monks, and castrate themselves. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. Reports with this meaning are numerous, even if they do not mention the occasion of revelation. They include:

**The second issue:** Muslim transmitted from Anas that a number of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked the wives of the Prophet ﷺ about his practice in private. Some of them said, "I will not marry women." Others said, "I will not eat meat." Others said, "I will not sleep on a bed." So he praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "What is the matter with people who say such and such? But I pray and I sleep, I fast and I break my fast, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me."

Al-Bukhari also transmitted it from Anas, and its wording is: Three men came to the houses of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ asking about his worship. When they were informed, they considered it little, and said: "Where are we in relation to the Prophet ﷺ? Allah has forgiven him his past and future sins." One of them said: "As for me, I will pray all night forever." Another said: "As for me, I will fast the whole year and not break my fast." Another said: "As for me, I will keep away from women and never marry." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and said: "Are you the ones who said such and such? By Allah, I am the one among you who fears Allah most and is most conscious of Him, but I fast and I break my fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me."

Both (Muslim and al-Bukhari) also transmitted from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: Uthman ibn Maz'un wanted to abstain completely (*yatabattal*) from women, but the Prophet ﷺ forbade him. Had he permitted him that, we would have castrated ourselves.

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah be pleased with him, transmitted in his Musnad, saying: Abu al-Mughirah narrated to us, saying: Mu'an ibn Rifa'ah narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Yazid narrated to me, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: We went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on one of his expeditions. He said: A man passed by a cave in which there was some water, so he resolved to stay in that cave, where the water in it would sustain him and he could eat the herbs growing around it, and he would withdraw from the world. He said: "If only I went to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him. If he permits me, I will do it, and if not, I will not do it." So he came to him and said: "O Prophet of Allah, I passed by a cave in which there is water and herbs that would sustain me, and my soul has urged me to stay there and withdraw from the world." He said: The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "I was not sent with Judaism or Christianity, but I was sent with the upright, tolerant monotheism (*al-hanifiyyah al-samhah*). By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, a morning's journey or an evening's journey in the way of Allah is better than the world and all that is in it, and the standing of one of you in the row (in battle) is better than his prayer for sixty years."

**The third issue:** Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said that this verse and what resembles it, and the hadiths that come with a similar meaning, are a refutation of the extreme ascetics (*ghulat al-mutazahhidin*) and of the idle among the Sufis (*ahl al-batalah min al-mutasawwifin*), since each group has departed from its path and deviated from its verification. Al-Tabari said: It is not permitted for any Muslim to forbid himself anything of what Allah has made lawful for His believing servants, of good foods, clothing and marriage, if by making it lawful for himself he fears some hardship and difficulty. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ rejected Ibn Maz'un's abstention, and so it is established that there is no merit in abandoning anything that Allah has made lawful for His servants. Merit and righteousness lie only in doing what He has recommended to His servants, what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ practised, established as a Sunnah for his community, and what the rightly guided Imams followed in his path, since the best guidance is the guidance of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Given this, it becomes clear that the error is in one who prefers wearing hair and wool over wearing cotton and linen when he is able to wear such things lawfully, and who prefers eating coarse food and abstaining from meat and other things out of fear of the need for women arising. Al-Tabari said: If someone supposes that the excellence lies in something other than what we have said, because of the hardship on the self in wearing coarse clothing and eating coarse food, and the diversion of the difference in value between them to those in need, then he has erred. That is because what is most fitting for a person is the soundness of his self and assisting it in obeying its Lord. Nothing harms the body more than bad food, because it corrupts the intellect and weakens the faculties that Allah has made a means to His obedience.

A man came to al-Hasan al-Basri and said: "I have a neighbour who does not eat *al-faludhaj* [[a sweet made of starch, honey and other ingredients]]." He said: "And why?" He said: "He says, 'I cannot render its thanks.'" Al-Hasan said: "Does he drink cold water?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Your neighbour is ignorant. Allah's blessing upon him in cold water is greater than His blessing upon him in *al-faludhaj*."

Ibn al-Arabi said: Our scholars said: This applies when religion is sound and wealth is not unlawful. But when religion has corrupted among people and the unlawful has become widespread, then abstention is better, and leaving pleasures is preferable. When the lawful is found, however, the state of the Prophet ﷺ is more excellent and higher.

Al-Muhallab said: The Prophet ﷺ only forbade abstention and monasticism because he would outnumber the nations through his community on the Day of Resurrection, and because in this world he fights with them against groups of disbelievers, and at the end of time they will fight the Dajjal. So the Prophet ﷺ wanted the offspring to increase.

**The fourth issue:** His words, the Exalted: ﴿and do not transgress.﴾ It was said: the meaning is, do not transgress by making lawful what Allah has forbidden. On this view the two prohibitions together encompass both extremes, i.e. do not be strict and forbid what is lawful, and do not be lax and make lawful what is forbidden. This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri. It was also said: its meaning is an emphasis on His words "do not forbid," said by al-Suddi, Ikrimah and others, i.e. do not forbid what Allah has permitted and legislated. The first view is preferable, and Allah knows best.

**The fifth issue:** Whoever forbids to himself food, drink or a female slave of his, or anything else that Allah has made lawful, there is nothing upon him, and there is no expiation (*kaffarah*) for any of that according to Malik, except that if he intends by forbidding the slave-girl her manumission, she becomes free and it becomes unlawful for him to have intercourse with her except by a new marriage contract after her manumission. Likewise, if he says to his wife, "You are forbidden to me (*anti 'alayya haram*)," she is divorced from him three times. That is because Allah the Exalted has permitted him to forbid his wife to himself by divorce, explicitly and by implication, and "forbidden" is among the implicit expressions of divorce. What the scholars hold concerning this will come in Surah (al-Tahrim) [[See vol. 18, p. 177.]], if Allah the Exalted wills.

Abu Hanifah said: whoever forbids something makes it forbidden to himself, and if he consumes it he incurs expiation. This is far-fetched, and the verse refutes him. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the "futile oath" (*laghw al-yamin*) is the forbidding of what is lawful, and this is the meaning of al-Shafi'i's view, as will come.

The Qur'an verse on the Quranic word for eating: ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾. There is one issue here. Here, "eating" (al-akl) is an expression for enjoying food, drink, clothing, riding and similar benefits. Eating is singled out for mention because it is the greatest of these purposes and the most essential of the benefits a person gains. The rulings on eating, drinking and clothing will come in "al-A'raf" (see vol. 7, p. 189), God willing. [From manuscripts J, K and ʿ.]

As for craving pleasurable things and the soul's pull toward seeking appealing kinds of food, people differ on whether to indulge the soul in them. Some hold that it is better to turn the soul away from them and restrain it from following its desires, so that its reins become submissive and its stubbornness becomes easier to bear, for when a person grants the soul what it wants, it becomes a captive of its desires and is led by them. It is related that Abu Hazim would pass by fruit, desire it, and then say: "Your appointment is Paradise."

Others say that indulging the soul in its pleasures is preferable, because it brings the soul delight and vigour through the fulfilment of its will. Still others say that moderation in this matter is preferable, since granting the soul this at one time and withholding it at another combines both approaches, and that is the fair middle path without blame.

The meaning of transgression (al-i'tida') and of provision (al-rizq) has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" (see vol. 1, p. 177 on "provision" and p. 432 on "transgression" in the same volume). And praise be to God.

In it are forty-seven issues.

**First:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle (*lagh*, meaningless) oaths in your oaths﴾. The meaning of *lagh* has already been discussed in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 3, p. 99 onward.]]. The meaning of "in your oaths" is "from your oaths." *Al-Aymān* is the plural of *yamīn* (oath). It is said that *yamīn* is a form (*faʿīl*) from *al-yumn*, which means blessing. Allah named it so because it protects rights. *Yamīn* may be masculine or feminine, and its plurals are *aymān* and *aymun*. Zuhayr said:

*"So the oaths (aymun) of us and of you are gathered, / with a sworn pledge over which blood flows."* [[The second half of the verse: "bi-muqsamatin tamūru bihā al-dimāʾ."]]

**Second:** There is disagreement about the occasion of revelation of this verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its occasion was the people who forbade for themselves the good foods, clothing and marriage, and swore to that. When it was revealed, "Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you," they said: "What shall we do about our oaths?" So this verse was revealed.

According to this view, the meaning is: when you swear an oath and then make it *lagh*, that is, you nullify its ruling by expiation (*takfīr*) and you expiate it, then Allah will not hold you accountable for that. He will only hold you accountable for what you bound yourselves to and did not nullify, that is, you did not expiate it. Thus it is clear that an oath does not make something unlawful. This is the proof of al-Shafiʿi that an oath cannot make the lawful unlawful, and that declaring the lawful unlawful is *lagh*, just as declaring the unlawful lawful is *lagh*, like the saying of one who says: "I have made the drinking of wine permissible." So the verse, according to this view, indicates that Allah made the prohibition of the lawful *lagh* in that it has no effect. He said: "Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths," that is, for making the lawful unlawful.

It is related that ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha had orphans and a guest. He returned from his work after a part of the night had passed. He said: "Have you fed my guest?" They said: "We were waiting for you." He said: "No, by Allah, I will not eat it tonight." The guest said: "I will not eat either." The orphans said: "We will not eat either." When he saw that, he ate, and they ate. Then he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said to him: "You obeyed the Merciful and disobeyed Satan." Then the verse was revealed.

**Third:** Oaths in the Sharia are of four kinds: two kinds in which there is expiation, and two kinds in which there is no expiation. Al-Daraqutni recorded in his *Sunan*: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz narrated to us; Khalaf ibn Hisham narrated to us; ʿAbthar narrated to us, from Layth, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from ʿAlqama, from ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud), who said: The oaths are four: two that are expiated and two that are not expiated. The two that are expiated are: a man who swears, 'By Allah, I will not do such and such,' and then does it; and a man who says, 'By Allah, I will certainly do such and such,' and then does not do it.
