The two that are not expiated are: a man who swears, 'By Allah, I did not do such and such,' when he did it; and a man who swears, 'Indeed I did such and such,' when he did not do it."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: Sufyan al-Thawri mentioned it in his *Jamiʿ*, and al-Marwazi also related it from him. Sufyan said: The oaths are four: two that are expiated, namely that a man says, "By Allah, I will not do it," and then does it, or says, "By Allah, I will certainly do it," and then does not do it. And two that are not expiated, namely that a man says, "By Allah, I did not do it," when he did, or says, "By Allah, I did it," when he did not.

Al-Marwazi said: As for the first two, there is no disagreement among the scholars concerning them, as Sufyan stated. As for the other two, the people of knowledge have disagreed about them. If the one swearing swore that he had not done such and such, or that he had done such and such, while in his own mind he was truthful, believing that it was as he swore, then there is no sin on him and no expiation on him, according to the view of Malik, Sufyan al-Thawri, and the people of opinion (*ahl al-raʾy*). Ahmad and Abu ʿUbayd also said likewise. Al-Shafiʿi said: there is no sin on him, but he owes expiation. Al-Marwazi said: al-Shafiʿi's view on this is not strong. He said: If the one swearing swore that he had not done such and such, when he had done it, deliberately lying, then he is sinful, and there is no expiation on him according to the view of the majority of scholars: Malik, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of opinion, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr and Abu ʿUbayd. Al-Shafiʿi used to say that he must expiate. He said: It has been related from some of the Successors (*tabiʿun*) a view like that of al-Shafiʿi. Al-Marwazi said: I incline to the view of Malik and Ahmad.

He said: As for the idle oath (*yamin al-lagh*), on which the majority of scholars agree that it is idle, it is the statement of a man: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," in his speech and talk, which does not bind an oath, nor does he intend it. Al-Shafiʿi said: This happens during heated argument, anger and haste.

**Fourth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But He will hold you accountable for what you have firmly bound by oaths﴾. *Muʿaqqadtum* is with the *qāf* lightened, from *al-ʿaqd* (binding). *Al-ʿaqd* is of two kinds: sensory, like tying a rope, and legal, like a contract of sale. The poet said [[The verse is by al-Hutayʾa, praising a people who bound a covenant for their neighbour and fulfilled it and did not break it. Its explanation was given earlier on the margin of p. 32 of this part.]]:

*"A people who, when they bind a covenant for their neighbour, / tie the knot and tie the tie above it."*

So the binding oath (*al-yamin al-munʿaqida*) is passive from *al-ʿaqd*, and it is the binding of the heart concerning the future: that one does not do something and then does it, or that he will certainly do something and then does not do it, as has been mentioned. These are the oaths that exception (*istithnaʾ*) and expiation dissolve, as will come.

It is read *ʿāqadtum* with an *alif* after the *ʿayn*, on the pattern *fāʿala*, and that is mostly not done except by two. The second may be the one for whose sake the oath was sworn in a speech that took place with him, or the meaning is: "what the oaths have bound you to," because *ʿāqada* is close in meaning to *ʿāhada* (to covenant), so it was made transitive with a preposition, since it has the meaning of *ʿāhada*. And *ʿāhada* takes two objects, the second of which takes a preposition. Allah said: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant with Allah﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 277.]] [al-Fath 48:10]. This is like when you make *nādaytum* (you called) transitive with *ilā* (to), "you called to prayer," whose original form is "nādaytu Zaydan," but since it has the meaning of *daʿawtu* (I invited), it was made transitive with *ilā*. Allah said: ﴿Who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 359.]] [Fussilat 41:33]. Then the usage was broadened in His saying, "ʿāqadtum ʿalayhi al-aymān" (you bound with it the oaths), so the preposition was dropped, and the verb reached the object, becoming *ʿāqadtumūhu* (you bound it), then the *hāʾ* was dropped, as it was dropped in His saying: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 61.]] [al-Hijr 15:94]. Or *fāʿala* may have the meaning of *faʿala*, as He said: ﴿Allah fights them﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 116.]] [al-Tawbah 9:30], meaning "Allah kills them." The *mufāʿala* form sometimes comes from one party in Arabic without the meaning of *fāʿaltu*, as in their saying: *safartu* (I travelled) and *ẓāhartu* (I supported).

It is also read *ʿaqqadtum* with the *qāf* doubled. Mujahid said: its meaning is *taʿammadtum*, that is, you intended, you aimed. It is related from Ibn ʿUmar that the doubling implies repetition, so expiation is not obligatory unless the oath is repeated. But this is refuted by what is related, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, if Allah wills, I will not swear an oath, and then see something other than it as better, but that I will do what is better and expiate for my oath." [In this, he mentioned the obligation of expiation for an oath that was not repeated.] Abu ʿUbayd said: doubling implies repetition, time after time, and I am not sure that whoever reads with this reading must hold that no expiation is due for a single oath unless he repeats it many times. And this is a view contrary to consensus. Nafiʿ related that when Ibn ʿUmar broke an oath without emphasizing it, he would feed ten needy persons, but when he emphasized the oath, he would free a slave. It was asked of Nafiʿ: "What is the meaning of emphasizing the oath?" He said: That one swears about a matter many times.

**Fifth:** There is disagreement about the perjurious oath (*al-yamin al-ghamus*), whether it is a binding oath or not. The view of the majority is that it is an oath of deceit, trickery and lying, so it is not binding and there is no expiation for it. Al-Shafiʿi said: it is a binding oath, because it is an act of the heart, bound by a report, linked with the name of Allah, and in it there is expiation. The correct view is the first. Ibn al-Mundhir said: This is the view of Malik ibn Anas and those who follow him from the people of Medina. It was also said by al-Awzaʿi and those who agreed with him from the people of Syria. It is the view of al-Thawri and the people of Iraq. Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Abu ʿUbayd, the people of hadith and the people of opinion from Kufa also said so. Abu Bakr said: The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath and sees something other than it as better, let him do what is better and let him expiate for his oath," and his saying: "Let him expiate for his oath and do what is better," indicate that expiation is only obligatory for one who swears to do a future act and does not do it, or to not do a future act and does it. There is a second view on this issue, namely that one must expiate even if he sins and deliberately swears falsely by Allah. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi. Abu Bakr said: We know of no report that supports this view, while the Book and the Sunnah support the first view. Allah said: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths, that you should be righteous and fear Allah and make peace between people﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:224].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 89 (part 2 of 6):

[Al-Baqarah: 224] Ibn Abbas said: It refers to the man who swears that he will not maintain the ties of kinship with his relative. Allah has provided him a way out through expiation (kaffarah), and commanded him not to use Allah as a pretext, but to make expiation for his oath. The reports indicate that the oath by which a man takes unlawful property is greater than that the expiation for an oath could atone for it. Ibn al-Arabi said: The verse came with two kinds of oath, the vain oath (lagha) and the binding oath (mun'aqida), and it went according to what is common in people's oaths. So leave aside what follows, it would be a hundred oaths, for no expiation is attached to it. I say: al-Bukhari related from Abdullah ibn Amr who said: A Bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what are the major sins (al-kaba'ir)?" He said: "Associating partners with Allah." He said: "Then what?" He said: "Disobedience to one's parents." He said: "Then what?" He said: [The perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus)]. I said: "And what is the perjurious oath?" He said: [The one by which a person takes the property of a Muslim man while he is lying in it]. Muslim related from Abu Umamah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: ["Whoever takes the right of a Muslim man by his oath, Allah has made the Fire obligatory for him and forbidden Paradise to him."] A man said: "Even if it is a small thing, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: ["Even if it is a twig of arak-wood."] And from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: ["Whoever swears an oath of coercion (yamin sabr)" [The oath of sabr is an oath imposed on a person and compelled upon him. Sabr means coercion; it is said: the judge made so-and-so swear an oath of sabr, meaning he compelled him.] by which he takes the property of a Muslim man while he is a wrongdoer in it, will meet Allah while He is angry with him."] Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77] to the end of the verse, and it does not mention expiation. If we were to make expiation obligatory for him, his sin would be dropped, and he would meet Allah while He is pleased with him, and he would not deserve the threat that was threatened against him. And how could that not be so, when this swearer has combined lying, making lawful the property of another, treating the oath by Allah lightly and carelessly, and preferring the world? He has demeaned what Allah has exalted, and exalted what Allah has belittled, and that is enough for you. For this reason it was said: the perjurious oath was named "ghamus" only because it immerses its doer (taghmisu sahibaha) in the Fire.

The sixth issue: The one who swears that he will not do something, when it is a matter of righteousness (burr), and he has not done it, then if he does it he breaks his oath (hanitha) and expiation becomes binding on him because of the violation from him. The same applies if he says: "If I do it." And if he swears that he will certainly do something, then he is immediately in breach (hinth) because of the violation; if he does it, he has fulfilled (barra). The same applies if he says: "If I do not do it."

The seventh issue: The swearer's saying "I will certainly do it, if I do not do it" is equivalent to a command, and his saying "I will not do it, if I do it" is equivalent to a prohibition. In the first case he does not fulfil the oath until he does the whole of what was sworn upon. For example: "I will certainly eat this loaf," and he eats part of it; he does not fulfil the oath until he eats all of it, because every part of it is what was sworn upon. But if he says, "By Allah, I will certainly eat," without restriction, then he fulfils it with the smallest part of what the name applies to, because the essence of eating is brought into existence. As for the prohibition, he breaks the oath by the smallest amount to which the name applies, because its requirement is that no single instance of what is forbidden should come into existence. If he swears that he will not enter a house and he puts one of his legs in, he has broken the oath. The evidence for this is that we find the Lawgiver made the direction of prohibition stringent by the first part of the name, in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married﴾ [An-Nisa': 22]. So whoever contracts marriage with a woman and has not consummated it, she becomes forbidden to his father and his son. But in the direction of permission he did not suffice with the first part of the name, so he said: [No, until she tastes his honey (ʿusayla)].

The eighth issue: The one sworn by is Allah, the Glorified, and His Most Beautiful Names, such as al-Rahman, al-Rahim, al-Sami', al-'Alim, al-Halim, and similar of His names and His exalted attributes, such as His might (izza), His power (qudra), His knowledge ('ilm), His will (irada), His greatness (kibriya'), His majesty ('azama), His covenant ('ahd), His pact (mithaq), and all the attributes of His essence, because it is an oath by the Eternal, the uncreated; so the one who swears by them is like the one who swears by the Essence. Al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others related that when Jibril (peace be upon him) looked at Paradise and returned to Allah, the Exalted, he said: "By Your might, no one who hears of it will fail to enter it." Likewise he said of the Fire: "By Your might, no one who hears of it will fail to enter it." Al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i and others also related from Ibn Umar who said: The oath of the Prophet ﷺ was [No, by the Turner of hearts (Muqallib al-Qulub)], and in another narration [No, by the Director of hearts (Musarrif al-Qulub)]. The scholars have agreed that whoever swears, saying "By Allah," or "Billah," or "Tallah," and breaks the oath, then expiation is upon him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Ubayd, Abu Thawr, Ishaq and the companions of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) used to say: Whoever swears by one of the names of Allah and breaks the oath, then expiation is upon him; and by this we say, and I know of no disagreement on that. I say: It has been transmitted (in the chapter on mentioning swearing by the Qur'an), and Ya'qub said: Whoever swears by al-Rahman and breaks it, there is no expiation upon him. I say: al-Rahman is among His names, glorified is He; it is agreed upon and there is no disagreement about it.

The ninth issue: They differed regarding "wa-haqqi Allah" (by the right of Allah), "wa-'azamati Allah" (by the greatness of Allah), "wa-qudrati Allah" (by the power of Allah), "wa-'ilmi Allah" (by the knowledge of Allah), "wa-la'amri Allah" (by the life of Allah), and "wa-ayman Allah" (by the oaths of Allah). Malik said: all of these are oaths for which expiation is required. Al-Shafi'i said: "wa-haqqi Allah," "wa-jalali Allah," "wa-'azamati Allah," and "wa-qudrati Allah" are an oath if he intended by them an oath; and if he did not intend an oath, then it is not an oath, because it could mean "the right of Allah is binding" and "the power of Allah is in force." He said regarding "amanati Allah" (the trust of Allah): it is not an oath; and "la'amri Allah" and "ayman Allah," if he did not intend an oath by them, then they are not an oath. The companions of opinion said: if he says "wa-'azamati Allah," "wa-'izzati Allah," "wa-jalali Allah," "wa-kibriya'i Allah," or "wa-amanati Allah," and breaks it, then expiation is upon him. Al-Hasan said regarding "wa-haqqi Allah": it is not an oath, and there is no expiation for it; and this is the statement of Abu Hanifa, related from him by al-Razi. Likewise "'ahd Allah" (the covenant of Allah), "mithaq Allah" (the pact of Allah) and "amanat Allah" (the trust of Allah) are not oaths. Some of his companions said: they are an oath. Al-Tahawi said: it is not an oath, and likewise if he says "wa-'ilmi Allah," it is not an oath according to the statement of Abu Hanifa; but his companion Abu Yusuf disagreed and said: it is an oath. Ibn al-Arabi said: What led him to this is that knowledge ('ilm) may refer to the known (ma'lum), which is created, so it is not an oath. He overlooked that power (qudra) refers to the thing empowered (maqdur), so every statement he made about the empowered is our proof concerning the known. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: [By the oaths of Allah, he was indeed worthy of leadership (al-imara)] in the story of Zayd and his son Usama. Ibn Abbas used to say "wa-ayman Allah," and likewise Ibn Umar said it. Ishaq said: if by "ayman Allah" he intends an oath, it is an oath by intention and resolve of the heart.

The tenth issue: They differed regarding swearing by the Qur'an. Ibn Mas'ud said: there is an oath for every verse. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibn al-Mubarak said the same. Ahmad said: I know of nothing that repels it. Abu Ubayd said: it is one oath. Abu Hanifa said: there is no expiation upon him. Qatadah used to swear by the mushaf (the codex). Ahmad and Ishaq said: we do not dislike that.

The eleventh issue: An oath is not binding if it is by other than Allah, His names or His attributes. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: if he swears by the Prophet ﷺ, his oath is binding, because he swore by something without which faith is not complete, so expiation is obligatory upon him, just as if he had sworn by Allah. This is refuted by what is established in the two Sahihs and others from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he came upon 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in a riding party while 'Umar was swearing by his father, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called out to them: [Indeed Allah forbids you to swear by your fathers. Whoever is swearing, let him swear by Allah or let him keep silent]. This is a restriction to not swearing by anything other than Allah, His names and His attributes, as we have mentioned. And among what confirms this is what Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: [Do not swear by your fathers, nor by your mothers, nor by the rivals (al-andad), and do not swear except by Allah, and do not swear by Allah except when you are truthful]. Then it is refuted by one who says: "And Adam and Ibrahim," for there is no expiation upon him, though he has sworn by something without which faith is not complete.

The twelfth issue: The imams related, and the wording is Muslim's, from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: [Whoever among you swears and says in his oath "By al-Lat," let him say "There is no god but Allah." And whoever says to his companion, "Come, I will gamble with you," let him give charity]. Al-Nasa'i related from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd from his father who said: We used to mention some matter, and I was recently converted from the Jahiliyyah, so I swore by al-Lat and al-'Uzza. Some of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "What an evil thing you have said!" And in another narration: "I said something wrong (hujran)." So I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and he said: [Say: There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner. To Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things powerful. And spit three times to your left, and seek refuge in Allah from Satan, then do not return to it]. The scholars said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded whoever uttered that to say after it "There is no god but Allah," as an expiation for that utterance, a reminder from heedlessness, and a completion of the blessing. He specified al-Lat for mention because it was the most common of what was on their tongues, and the ruling for its like among the names of their gods is the same as its ruling, since there is no difference between them. Likewise whoever says to his companion "Come, I will gamble with you, then let him give charity": the ruling concerning it is like the ruling concerning al-Lat, because they had become accustomed to gambling (muqamara), and it is among the consuming of property falsely (akl al-mal bil-batil).

The thirteenth issue: Abu Hanifa said regarding a man who says: "He is a Jew, or"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 89 (part 3 of 6):

"A Christian," or "free of Islam," or "free of the Prophet," or "free of the Qur'an," or "I associate partners with Allah," or "I disbelieve in Allah": this is an oath that requires expiation (kaffarah), but it does not require it if he says, "By Judaism, by Christianity, by the Prophet, by the Kaaba," even if it is in the form of oaths. Its proof is what al-Daraqutni narrated from Abu Rafi': that his mistress wanted to separate him from his wife, so she said, "She is a Jew one day and a Christian another day, every slave of hers is free, all her wealth is for the cause of Allah, and it is incumbent upon her to walk to the House of Allah if she does not separate them." So he asked Aisha, Hafsa, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas and Umm Salamah, and all of them said to her, "Do you want to be like Harut and Marut?" and they commanded her to make expiation for her oath and to let them be. He also narrated from him, who said: My mistress said, "I will certainly separate you from your wife, and all her wealth is in the treasury (ritaj) of the Kaaba, and she is a Jew one day, a Christian another day, and a Magian another day, if I do not separate you from your wife." He said: So I went to the Mother of the Believers, Umm Salamah, and said, "My mistress wants to separate me from my wife." She said, "Go to your mistress and say to her: This is not lawful for you." He said: So I returned to her. He said: Then I came to Ibn Umar and informed him, and he came until he reached the door and said, "Here are Harut and Marut!" She said, "I have dedicated all my wealth to the treasury of the Kaaba." He said, "Then what do you eat with?" She said, "And I also said, 'I am a Jew one day, a Christian another day, and a Magian another day.'" He said, "If you become a Jew, you will be killed; if you become a Christian, you will be killed; if you become a Magian, you will be killed." She said, "What do you command me?" He said, "Make expiation for your oath, and unite your male and female servants (or: your young man and young woman)."

The scholars agreed that if the one swearing says, "I swear by Allah," it is an oath. They differed if he says, "I swear" or "I testify that such-and-such will happen" without saying "by Allah." According to Malik, it is an oath if he intended "by Allah," and if he did not intend "by Allah," it is not an oath requiring expiation. Abu Hanifa, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: it is an oath in both cases. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not an oath until he mentions the name of Allah Most High; this is the narration of al-Muzani from him. Al-Rabi' narrated from him a view like that of Malik.

The fourteenth issue: If he says, "I adjure you (aqsamtu 'alayka) that you will certainly do it," then if he intends a request, there is no expiation in it and it is not an oath. If he intends an oath, then what we mentioned earlier applies.

The fifteenth issue: Whoever swears by something attributed to Allah Most High that is not an attribute, such as his saying, "By the creation of Allah, His provision, and His house," there is nothing upon him, because these are impermissible oaths and an oath by other than Allah Most High.

The sixteenth issue: When an oath is concluded, it is dissolved either by expiation (kaffarah) or by the exception (istithna'). Ibn al-Majishun said: the exception is a substitute for expiation and is not a dissolution of the oath. Ibn al-Qasim said: it is a dissolution of the oath. Ibn al-Arabi said: this is the view of the jurists of the cities and it is the sound view. Its condition is that it be connected and spoken aloud, based on what al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever swears and then makes an exception, if he wills, he may proceed, and if he wills, he may leave it, without breaking the oath." So if he intends it without uttering it, or cuts it off without an excuse, it will not benefit him. Muhammad ibn al-Mawwaz said: the exception must accompany the oath in intention, even with the last letter. He said: if he finishes the oath and then makes an exception, that does not benefit him, because the oath was concluded without an exception, so its subsequent occurrence does not affect it, like a delay. But this is refuted by the hadith, "Whoever swears and then makes an exception," and the particle "fa" (then) indicates sequence, and this is the view of the majority of the people of knowledge. Also, that would lead to an oath that began being contracted never being dissolved, and that is invalid.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: Our companions differed about when one makes an exception in his mind to specify what he swore about. Some of our companions said: his exception is valid, though he has wronged the one to whom he swore. Some of them said: it is not valid until he makes the one to whom he swore hear it. Some of them said: it is valid if he moves his tongue and lips with it, even if the one to whom he swore does not hear. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: We only said that his exception in himself is valid because oaths are judged by intentions. And we only said that it is not valid unless he moves his tongue and lips with it, because whoever does not move his tongue and lips with it is not speaking, and an exception to speech occurs only through speech and not otherwise. And we only said that it is not valid in any case because that is a right of the one to whom he swore, and it takes effect according to what the judge enforces for him. Since the oath was not under the swearer's choice but was enforced upon him, it must be that he has no ruling in it.

Ibn Abbas said: the exception reaches the oath after a year. Abu al-Aliyah and al-Hasan followed him in this, and he relied on the words of Allah Most High: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god besides Allah﴾ [al-Furqan 25:68], to the end of the verse. When a year had passed, the verse ﴿except one who repents﴾ [Maryam 19:60] was revealed. Mujahid said: whoever says "in shā' Allāh" after two years, it suffices him. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: if he makes the exception after four months, it suffices him. Tawus said: he may make the exception as long as he remains in his gathering. Qatadah said: if he makes the exception before he stands up or speaks, then he has his exception. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ishaq said: he may make the exception as long as he is still in that matter. Ata' said: he has that for the duration of milking a plentiful she-camel.

The seventeenth issue: Ibn al-Arabi said: As for what Ibn Abbas relied on from the verse, he has no basis in it, because the two verses were connected in the knowledge of Allah Most High and in His Preserved Tablet, and their revelation was only delayed for a wisdom that Allah knew in it. However, a good branch is built upon this: if the swearer says, "By Allah, I will not enter the house, and you are divorced if you enter the house," and he makes an exception in his first oath, "if Allah wills," in his heart, and in the second oath he also makes in his heart an exception suitable for the kind that lifts the oath for a period, a cause, or someone's will, and he shows no part of the exception out of intimidation of the one to whom he swore, then that benefits him and the two oaths are not concluded against him. This applies to divorce as long as the evidence (bayyinah) is not present. [Note in another manuscript: "the intention; if the intention is present..." etc.] If evidence is present, his claim of exception is not accepted from him, and that benefits him only if he comes asking for a legal opinion (mustaftiyan).

I say: The reason for the exception is that Allah Most High made the first verse manifest and concealed the second. Likewise, the swearer who swears in intimidation and conceals the exception. And Allah knows best.

Ibn al-Arabi said: Abu al-Fadl al-Maraghi (a nisba to al-Maraghah, a well-known town in the lands of Azerbaijan) used to study in the City of Peace (Baghdad). It is said it was named so because the Tigris is called the Valley of Peace, and it is said al-Mansur named it so optimistically for safety. It is also called the House of Peace, in comparison with Paradise (Mu'jam al-Buldan). Books would come to him from his town, and he would place them in a chest and would not read a single one of them, for fear that he might look into something that would disturb him and cut him off from his pursuit. When five years had passed and he had accomplished a purpose of the quest and resolved to depart, he tied up his saddlebag, brought out his books, and took out those letters. He read in them what, if any one of them had been read by him after his arrival, he would not have been able to acquire a single letter of knowledge afterward. So he praised Allah, and he mounted his animal with his household goods (qamash: household property) and went out to the Halabah Gate, the road to Khurasan. The hired-animal owner (al-kari) had gone ahead with the animal, and he remained behind with a baker (fami: here, a baker) to buy his provisions (sufrah: food prepared by the traveler). While he was trying that with him, he heard him say to another baker, "Did you not hear the scholar (i.e., the preacher) say that Ibn Abbas permits the exception even after a year? My mind has been occupied with that since I heard it, and I have remained pondering it. If that were correct, Allah would not have said to Ayyub: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle of grass and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ [Sad 38:44]. And what prevents him from saying, 'Say: in shā' Allāh!'?" When he heard him say that, he said: "A city in which the bakers have this share of knowledge and this rank, I will leave it for al-Maraghah? I will never do that!" He followed the trail of the hired-animal owner, released him from the rent, and stayed there until he died.

**The eighteenth issue:** The exception (*istithna'*, saying "if Allah wills") only cancels an oath sworn by Allah the Exalted, because it is a concession (*rukhsah*) from Allah, and there is no disagreement on this. They differed about the exception in an oath sworn by other than Allah. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah said: the exception applies to every oath, such as divorce, manumission and others, just as it applies to an oath by Allah the Exalted. Abu 'Umar said: "What they agreed upon is the truth, and the textual provision (*tawqif*) for the exception was only revealed for an oath by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and not for anything else."

**The nineteenth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so its expiation﴾. The scholars differed over whether the expiation (*kaffarah*) is valid if it is given before breaking the oath (*hinth*), after they agreed that breaking the oath before the expiation is permissible and good, and that it is preferable for them. There are three opinions:

First: it is valid without restriction. This is the view of fourteen of the Companions and the majority of jurists, and it is the well-known position of Malik.

Abu Hanifah and his companions said: it is not valid in any way. This is also a narration from Ashhab, from Malik.

The argument for validity is what Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, if Allah wills, I will never swear an oath and then see something other than it to be better, except that I expiate for my oath and do what is better." Abu Dawud recorded it.

On the basis of meaning: the oath is the cause of the expiation, by His saying: ﴿That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn﴾. He attributed the expiation to the oath, and meanings are attributed to their causes. Also, the expiation is a substitute for fulfilling the oath (*birr*), so it is permissible to give it before breaking the oath.

The argument for prohibition is what Muslim narrated from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something other than it to be better, let him do what is better." An-Nasa'i added: "and let him expiate for his oath."

On the basis of meaning: the expiation is only for lifting sin, and as long as he has not broken the oath, there is nothing to lift, so there is no point in performing it. The meaning of His saying: ﴿when you have sworn﴾ is: when you have sworn and broken [the oath]. Also, every act of worship performed before it becomes obligatory is not valid, by analogy with the prayers and all other acts of worship.

Al-Shafi'i said: it is valid with feeding, freeing (a slave) and clothing, but it is not valid with fasting, because physical action is not established before its time. Otherwise, giving the expiation in advance is valid, and this is the third opinion.

**The twentieth issue:** Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in the expiation three alternatives and gave a choice among them. When none is available, He followed with fasting. He began with feeding, because it was the best option in the lands of the Hijaz, due to the strong need for it and their lack of food. There is no disagreement that the expiation for an oath is by choice. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "What I think is that it depends on the circumstances. If you know someone is in need, then feeding is better, because when you free a slave you do not meet their need, and you add an eleventh needy person to them. Clothing is next to it. Since Allah knew the need, He began with what is most important."

**The twenty-first issue:** His saying: ﴿feeding ten needy persons﴾. According to us and according to al-Shafi'i, it is necessary to give the needy ownership of what is given to them and to hand it over to them, until they take ownership of it and dispose of it, by His saying: ﴿He feeds but is not fed﴾ [6:14]. In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the grandfather a sixth (of the inheritance)." Also, because it is one type of expiation, so nothing is valid in it except ownership transfer, like clothing.

Abu Hanifah said: if he gives them lunch and dinner, it is valid. This is the view chosen by Ibn al-Majishun from our scholars. Ibn al-Majishun said: "Enabling them to eat is feeding. Allah says: ﴿and they give food, despite love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive﴾ [76:8]. So in whatever way he feeds him, he is included in the verse."

**The twenty-second issue:** His saying: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾. It has already been mentioned in (al-Baqarah) that *al-wasat* means "the highest and best." Here it means a position between two positions and a midpoint between two extremes. From this is the hadith: "The best of matters is their middle path." Ibn Majah recorded: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us; 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us; Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, from Sulayman ibn Abi al-Mughirah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man used to provide his family with a spacious sustenance, and a man used to provide his family with a restricted sustenance. So the verse was revealed: ﴿from the average of what you feed your families﴾." This indicates that *al-wasat* is what we have mentioned, namely what lies between two things.

**The twenty-third issue:** Feeding, according to Malik, is one *mudd* (a measure, about a handful less than a *ratl*) for each of the ten needy persons, if it is in the city of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Shafi'i and the people of Medina also said this. Sulayman ibn Yasar said: "I met people who, when they gave in the expiation for an oath, gave one *mudd* of wheat by the smaller *mudd*, and they considered that sufficient for them." This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn Thabit, and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah also said this.

There is disagreement if it is in other places. Ibn al-Qasim said: one *mudd* suffices everywhere. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: Ibn Wahb issued a ruling in Egypt for one and a half *mudds*, and Ashhab for one and a third *mudds*. He said: "A *mudd* and a third is indeed the average of the living standards of the cities for lunch and dinner."

Abu Hanifah said: one gives half a *sa'* (a measure) of wheat, and a full *sa'* of dates or barley, based on the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Tha'labah ibn Su'ayr, from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood to deliver a sermon and commanded the zakat of breaking the fast: a *sa'* of dates, or a *sa'* of barley, for each head, or a *sa'* of wheat between two persons." Sufyan and Ibn al-Mubarak adopted this, and it was narrated from 'Ali, 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab also said this, and it is the view of most jurists of Iraq, based on what Ibn 'Abbas narrated, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made expiation with a *sa'* of dates and commanded the people to do the same; whoever does not find [dates], then half a *sa'* of wheat [for each person]." [The addition "from the average of what you feed your families" is not found in Ibn Majah in this hadith.] Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan.

**The twenty-fourth issue:** It is not permissible to feed a rich person, nor a relative whose maintenance is obligatory upon him. If the person is one whose maintenance is not obligatory upon him, Malik said: "I do not like feeding him, but if he does so and the person is poor, it suffices him." If he feeds a rich person unknowingly about his wealth, then in *al-Mudawwanah* and elsewhere it is not valid, while in *al-Asadiyyah* it is valid.

**The twenty-fifth issue:** A man gives from what he eats. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Here a group of scholars has erred, saying: if he eats barley while people eat wheat, then let him give from what people eat. This is a clear mistake, because the person making expiation, if he can only afford barley for himself, is not required to give anything else to others. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'a *sa'* of food, a *sa'* of barley,' distinguishing between them so that each person gives his obligation from what he eats. This is not obscure at all."

**The twenty-sixth issue:** Malik said: if he gives lunch and dinner to ten needy persons, it suffices him. Al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible to feed them all at once, because they differ in eating, but he should give each needy person one *mudd*. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that feeding the ten with one meal does not suffice, meaning lunch without dinner, or dinner without lunch, until he feeds them lunch and dinner. Abu 'Umar said: this is the view of the leading jurists in the cities.

**The twenty-seventh issue:** Ibn Habib said: bread alone (*qafar*, without any condiment) does not suffice, but he should give with it its condiment, oil, *kashk* or *kamakh* (a kind of condiment, arabicized), or whatever is available. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "I do not consider this obligatory. However, it is recommended for him to feed them sugar with the bread, yes, and meat. As for specifying a condiment for the food, there is no way to it, because the wording does not include it." I say: the revelation of the verse about the average implies bread with oil or vinegar, and what is similar to them such as cheese and *kashk*, as Ibn Habib said. And Allah knows best. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Vinegar is an excellent condiment." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: if he feeds them bread and meat, or bread and oil, once a day until they are satisfied, it suffices him. This is also the view of Ibn Sirin, Jabir ibn Zayd and Makhul, and it was narrated from Anas ibn Malik.

**The twenty-eighth issue:** According to us, it is not permissible to give the expiation to a single needy person, and al-Shafi'i said the same. The companions of Abu Hanifah prohibit giving the whole to one person in a single instalment, and they differ about whether it is valid if he gives the whole amount on one day in different instalments. Some of them permitted it, and said that when the act is repeated, it is valid to say about the second act that it is not prevented from the one to whom it was first given, since the name "needy person" applies to him. Others said: it is permissible to give that amount to him over several days, since multiple days stand in place of the number of needy persons. Abu Hanifah said: it suffices him, because the purpose of the verse is to specify the quantity of what is fed, so if he gives that amount to one person, it suffices him.

Our proof is Allah's explicit text specifying ten, so it is not permissible to deviate from them. Also, it involves providing for a group of Muslims and sustaining them for one day, so that they may devote themselves to worshipping Allah, blessed and exalted is He, and to His supplication, and so He forgives the one making expiation because of that. And Allah knows best.

**The twenty-ninth issue:** His saying: ﴿so its expiation﴾. The pronoun, according to grammatical rules, refers to (*bi-ma*, "by what"). In this position it may mean "the one which," and it may be a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*). Or it refers to the sin of breaking the oath, even though no explicit mention of it has preceded, but the meaning requires it.

**The thirtieth issue:** His saying: ﴿ahlikum (your families)﴾. It is the sound plural of *ahl*. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq read: *ahaliikum*, and this is a broken plural. Abu al-Fath said: *ahali* is like *layali* (nights); its singular is *ahlat* and *laylat*, and the Arabs say: *ahl* and *ahlah*. The poet said [this is Abu al-Tamhan al-Qayni; he means: many a person deserving of affection whom I have shown my love to, and to whom I have given all my effort and my gift. In al-Taj: "my giving and my gift." In al-Lisan: "in praise my effort and my gift"]:

*"And people worthy of affection, whose love I have made clear to them,
and I have tested them in hardship with my praise and my gifts."*

He says: "I sought their affection," as Ibn al-Sikkit reported.

**The thirty-first issue:** Allah's words, ﴿or their clothing﴾. It is read with a kasra and with a damma on the kaf (*kiswatuhum* and *kusbatuhum*). Both are dialect forms, like *iswa* and *uswa* (example, model).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn al-Sumaygha al-Yamani read: "or like their clothing" (*aw ka-iswatihim*), meaning "like the clothing of your family."

For men, *kiswa* (clothing) means one garment that covers the whole body. For women, the minimum that suffices for prayer is the *dir* (long shirt) and the *khimar* (headscarf). The same ruling applies to children. Ibn al-Qasim said in *al-Utbiyya*: "A young girl is clothed with the clothing of a grown woman, and a young boy with the clothing of a grown man, by analogy with food."

Al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: the minimum that falls under the name is one garment. In a narration of Abu al-Faraj from Malik, and this is also the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Mughira, the minimum is what covers the whole body, on the basis that prayer is not valid in less than that.

It is related from Salman (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The best garment is the *tubban*" (*al-tubban* [[A small pair of trousers, about a span in size, that covers the primary private parts.]]). Al-Tabari transmitted it with a chain of narrators.

Al-Hakam ibn Utayba said: a turban with which one wraps the head is sufficient. This is also the view of al-Thawri.

Ibn al-Arabi said: "How I wish someone would say that only clothing that protects from the harm of heat and cold is acceptable, just as the food required must satisfy hunger. I would hold that view. But as for the view that one single wrapper suffices, I do not know of it. May Allah open up knowledge for me and for you by His help."

I say: some scholars have taken into account the customary dress and the clothing commonly worn. Some of them said: one garment is not sufficient unless it is of a kind that can be wrapped around the body, such as a cloak or a large wrap (*milhafa*) [[In the copy J: "with which one covers oneself"; in copy A: "with which one wraps oneself."]].

Abu Hanifa and his companions said: in the expiation for an oath, each poor person is given a garment: a robe and a waist-wrap, or a mantle, or a shirt, or a *qaba'* (long coat), or a blanket.

It is related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that he ordered that two garments be given for each person on his behalf. This was also the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin. This is the meaning of what Ibn al-Arabi chose, and Allah knows best.

**The thirty-second issue:** Giving the monetary value (*qima*) instead of food or clothing is not valid. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said it is valid. He argued: the value is valid in zakat, so how much more so in expiation! Ibn al-Arabi said: the basis of his position is that the purpose is to fill the need and remove the hardship, so the value suffices for this. We say: if you look at filling the need, where is the act of worship? And where is the explicit text of the Qur'an on the three specific items, and the shift in the explanation from one kind to another?

**The thirty-third issue:** If one gives the clothing to a *dhimmi* (non-Muslim under protection) or to a slave, it is not valid. Abu Hanifa said it is valid, because he is a poor person (*miskin*), covered by the word *maskana* (poverty), and the general wording of the verse includes him.

We reply: this is restricted by the statement that it is a portion of wealth that must be paid out to the poor, so it may not be given to a disbeliever. Its root is zakat. We agree that it may not be given to an apostate. So every evidence that restricts it for the apostate is our evidence regarding the *dhimmi*. A slave is not a poor person, since he is supported by his master's maintenance, so he is not given it, like a wealthy person.

**The thirty-fourth issue:** Allah's words, ﴿or the freeing of a slave﴾. *Tahrir* means releasing from slavery. It is also used for captivity, hardships, the toil of this world, and similar things. From this is the saying of Maryam's mother: "I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one devoted [*muharraran*]" [Al 'Imran: 35], meaning freed from the troubles of this world and similar things [[See vol. 4, p. 65.]].

From this is also the saying of al-Farazdaq ibn Ghalib:

*O Banu Ghudana, I have freed you,*
*so I gave you as a gift to Atiyya ibn Ji'al.*

That is: I freed you from satire (*hija'*).

The verse singles out the *raqaba* (neck) of a person, because it is the part on which the shackle and the bond are usually placed among living beings. So it is the place of ownership, and the freeing is attributed to it.

**The thirty-fifth issue:** According to us, it is not valid except to free a neck that is a complete believer, with no share in it belonging to someone else, and no partial freeing, and no freeing deferred to a term, and no *kitaba* (contract of self-purchase) and no *tadbir* (freeing upon the master's death). It must not be an *umm walad* (a slave woman who has borne her master's child), nor one who would be freed by the one who owns him, and it must not have such old age or chronic illness as would harm its earning ability. It must be whole and free from defects. This is in contrast to Dawud, who permitted freeing a defective slave.

Abu Hanifa said: freeing a disbelieving woman is permitted, because the unqualified wording requires it.

Our evidence is that it is an obligatory act of devotion, so a disbeliever is not a valid recipient of it, like zakat. Also, every unqualified instance of this in the Qur'an refers back to the qualified case of freeing a slave in the case of accidental killing.

We said: it must not have any share belonging to another, because of Allah's words: ﴿so the freeing of a slave﴾ [An-Nisa': 92]. Part of a neck is not a neck. We said there must be no contract of freedom in it, because *tahrir* requires an initial freeing, not the immediate execution of a previously arranged freeing. We said: it must be whole, because of His words, ﴿the freeing of a slave﴾. The unqualified wording requires freeing a complete neck, and a blind person is incomplete.

In the authentic collections it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No Muslim frees a Muslim man but that his release from the Fire is in exchange for every limb of his for a limb of the freed man, even the private part for the private part." [This is an explicit text. There are two opinions in the school regarding the one-eyed slave, and likewise regarding the deaf and the castrated.]

**The thirty-sixth issue:** If someone sets aside money to free a slave for an expiation, and the money is lost, the expiation remains due upon him. This is unlike the one who sets aside zakat money to give to the poor, or to buy a slave, and it is lost: he is not obliged to pay anything else, since he has fulfilled the command.

**The thirty-seventh issue:** Scholars differed about the expiation when the one who swore dies. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: expiations for oaths are paid out of the deceased's estate before the inheritance is divided. Abu Hanifa said: it comes from the third (of the estate that may be bequeathed). Malik said the same, if he made a bequest for it.

**The thirty-eighth issue:** Whoever swears while wealthy, and does not pay the expiation until he becomes poor; or breaks his oath while poor, and does not pay until he becomes rich; or breaks his oath while a slave, and does not pay until he is freed: in all these cases the consideration is the time of paying the expiation, not the time of breaking the oath.

**The thirty-ninth issue:** Muslim reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, for one of you to persist in his oath concerning his family [[(concerning his family) i.e., in cutting off relations with them, like swearing not to speak to them. Mentioning the family in this context is for emphasis. See the explanation of the hadith in the margin of the Istanbul edition of Muslim, vol. 5, p. 88.]] is more sinful for him before Allah than giving the expiation which Allah has prescribed." *Lijaj* (persistence) in an oath means carrying out its requirement even if this entails hardship or difficulty, or abandoning something beneficial, immediate or later. If any of that is the case, it is better for him to break his oath and perform the expiation. He should not use the oath as an excuse, as we have mentioned regarding Allah's words: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ [Al-Baqara: 224] [[See vol. 3, p. 96.]].

The Prophet (peace be upon him) also said: "Whoever swears to an oath, then sees something other than it to be better, let him expiate his oath and do what is better." [That is, what is more beneficial.]

**The fortieth issue:** Muslim reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The oath is according to the intention of the one who makes the other person swear." The scholars said: its meaning is that whoever is obliged to swear an oath concerning a right, and swears while intending something else, his intention does not benefit him, and he is not freed from the sin of that oath. This is the meaning of his words in another hadith: "Your oath is according to what your companion accepts from you." Another version reads: "What your companion accepts from you," also transmitted by Muslim.

Malik said: whoever swears to the claimant regarding a right that the claimant has against him, and makes an exception in his oath, or moves his tongue or lips, or speaks it, his exception does not benefit him, because the intention is that of the one to whom the oath is sworn, since the oath is his right. It is fulfilled according to what the judge takes from him, not according to the swearer's choice, since it is exacted from him.

That is the summary of his school and his view.

**The forty-first issue:** Allah's words, ﴿whoever does not find﴾ mean: does not find in his possession any of these three, namely feeding, clothing, or freeing a slave. This is by consensus. When he lacks these three, he fasts.

Lack has two forms: either the wealth is absent from him, or he has none. The first is when it is in another land. If he finds someone who will lend it to him, fasting does not suffice for him. If he does not find anyone to lend to him, opinions differ. It is said he should wait until he returns to his land. Ibn al-Arabi said: this is not required of him. Rather, he expiates by fasting, because the obligation has been established on his account, and the condition of lack has been realized. So there is no reason to delay the matter. He should expiate on the spot, since he is unable to perform the three kinds, based on Allah's words: ﴿whoever does not find﴾.

It is also said: whoever has no surplus beyond his capital, by which he lives, is the one who does not find. It is also said: he is the one who has nothing but the food of his day and night, and has no surplus with which to feed others. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, chosen by al-Tabari, and it is the school of Malik and his companions.

It is related from Ibn al-Qasim that whoever has a surplus beyond the daily sustenance of his day, does not fast. Ibn al-Qasim said in the book of Ibn Muzayn: if the one who broke the oath has a surplus beyond the food of his day, he must feed (others), unless he fears hunger, or he is in a land where no one is kind to him.

Abu Hanifa said: if he does not have the minimum amount that is subject to zakat (*nisab*), he is considered unable to find.

Ahmad and Ishaq said: if he has the food for a day and a night, he feeds the surplus beyond that.

Abu Ubayd said: if he has the food of his day and night, and his dependents', and clothing that suffices for them, and beyond that he possesses the amount for the expiation, then in our view he is considered able to find. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Abu Ubayd's view is good.

**The forty-second issue:** Allah's words: ﴿consecutive days﴾. Ibn Mas'ud read it as *mutatabi'at* (consecutive), and the unqualified is restricted by it. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri, one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, and it is chosen by al-Muzani, by analogy with fasting in the expiation for *zihar*, and by reference to the reading of Abd Allah.

Malik and al-Shafi'i in his other opinion said: separating the days is permitted, because consecutiveness is an attribute that is only obligatory by explicit text or by analogy to an explicit text, and neither is present here.

**The forty-third issue:** Whoever breaks the fast on one day of the fasting days by forgetting: Malik said he must make up the day, and al-Shafi'i said there is no making up on him, according to what was explained earlier regarding fasting in *al-Baqara*.

The forty-fourth issue: this expiation (kaffarah) that God has specified is obligatory for a free Muslim by consensus (ijma'). The scholars differed over what a slave must do if he breaks an oath. Sufyan al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i and the Ashab al-Ra'y (the people of opinion) said: he must only fast, and nothing else suffices for him. Malik's position on this is reported in different versions. Ibn Nafi' related from him that he said: a slave does not expiate by manumission, because he cannot possess wala' (the right of patronage over a freed person), but he may expiate by giving charity if his master permits him, and the most correct of these is that he fasts. Ibn al-Qasim related from him that he said: "If he feeds or clothes [others] with the master's permission, that is not clear to me, and there is something in my heart about it."

The forty-fifth issue: God's words ﴿That is the expiation of your oaths﴾. Kaffarah means covering or concealing your oaths, as in "kaffartu al-shay'" (I covered and concealed the thing), which has been mentioned before. There is no disagreement that this expiation applies to oaths sworn by God, although some of the Successors (tabi'un) held that the expiation for an oath is doing the good deed that one swore to abandon.

Ibn Majah entered in his Sunan a chapter heading: "Whoever says its expiation is abandoning it." He narrated to us 'Ali ibn Muhammad, who narrated to us 'Abd Allah ibn Numayr, from Haritha ibn Abi al-Rijal, from 'Amra, from 'A'isha, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears to sever family ties or to do what is not right, his piety is not to fulfil it." [Footnote in the margin of Ibn Majah: Its apparent meaning is that it is piety in the sense of the Sharia, so there is no need with it for another expiation. But the well-known hadiths indicate the obligation of expiation, so the hadith, if authentic, is taken to mean that it has the status of piety in being something legally required.]

He also cited from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something other than it as better, let him abandon it, for abandoning it is its expiation." I say: This is supported by the story of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may God be pleased with him, when he swore that he would not eat the food, and his wife swore that she would not eat it until he ate it, and the guest (or guests) swore that he would not eat it or that they would not eat it until he ate it. Abu Bakr said: "This was from Satan." He then called for the food, and he ate and they ate. al-Bukhari recorded it. Muslim added: He said: "In the morning he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, they kept their oath and I broke mine.' He informed him, and he said: 'Rather, you are the most pious of them and the best of them.'" He said: "No expiation reached me."

The forty-sixth issue: The scholars differed concerning the expiation for oaths other than an oath by God, the Mighty and Majestic. Malik said: whoever swears by giving away his wealth in charity must give away a third of it. al-Shafi'i said: he is liable for the expiation of an oath, and this was also the view of Ishaq and Abu Thawr, and it was related from 'Umar and 'A'isha, may God be pleased with them both. al-Sha'bi, 'Ata' and Tawus said: he is not liable for anything.

As for swearing by walking to Makkah, he must fulfil it according to Malik and Abu Hanifa. According to al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abu Thawr, the expiation for an oath suffices for him. Ibn al-Musayyib and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: he is not liable for anything. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Most of the people of knowledge in Madina and elsewhere require for the oath of walking to Makkah an expiation like the expiation for an oath by God, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is the view of a group of the Companions and Successors and the majority of the jurists of the Muslims. Ibn al-Qasim issued this as a legal opinion to his son 'Abd al-Samad, and he mentioned to him that it was the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd. The well-known position of Ibn al-Qasim is that there is no expiation in his view for walking to Makkah except by walking, for whoever is able to do so, and this is the view of Malik.

As for one who swears by manumission (freeing a slave), he is liable to free the one he swore to free, according to Malik, al-Shafi'i and others. It was related from Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha that he expiates with the expiation for an oath and is not obliged to free anyone. 'Ata' said: he gives something in charity. al-Mahdawi said: The scholars whose statements are relied upon agreed that divorce is binding on one who swears by it and breaks the oath.

The forty-seventh issue: God's words ﴿And guard your oaths﴾, meaning: by hastening to fulfil the expiation that becomes binding on you if you break them. It was also said: meaning by abandoning swearing, for if you do not swear, these obligations do not fall upon you.

(﴿so that you may be grateful﴾). The meaning of gratitude (shukr) and of (la'alla, perhaps/so that) has been discussed before in Surat al-Baqara. [Footnote: See vol. 1, p. 226 and following for (la'alla), and p. 397 and following for (shukr).] And praise be to God.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 5, verses 90–92 (part 1 of 2)**

In this passage there are seventeen issues (masa'il).

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. This is an address to all the believers to abandon these things, since they were desires and habits that they had engaged in during the Jahiliyyah (the time of ignorance before Islam), and which had dominated their souls, so that some of them remained in the souls of many believers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: From this category is the passion for augury by birds (zajr bi-l-tair), and seeking omens in books (fa'l fi-l-kutub), and similar things that people practise today. As for wine (khamr), it had not yet been prohibited, and its prohibition was revealed in the third year after the Battle of Uhud. The Battle of Uhud took place in Shawwal in the third year after the Hijrah.

As for al-azlam (divining arrows), they are the arrows (qidah), and the discussion of them has passed at the beginning of the surah. It is said that they were in the House (the Ka'bah) with the custodians of the House and the attendants of the idols. A man would come when he wanted to undertake some matter, and he would draw one of them; if it bore "My Lord has commanded me," he would go out to his affair as he loved or disliked.

The first thing revealed concerning it was: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both is great sin and some benefit for people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], meaning in their trade. When this verse was revealed, some people gave it up and said: "We have no need of that in which there is great sin." Others did not give it up and said: "We will take its benefit and leave its sin." He said: I ate and drank with them. He said: Then I mentioned the Ansar and the Muhajirun in their presence, and I said: "The Muhajirun are better than the Ansar." He said: Then a man took the jawbone of a camel and struck me with it, and it cut my nose — and in another narration, "it split it," and Sa'd's nose was split. The hadith of Hamza is clear about this, when he split the flanks of the two she-camels of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and cut off their humps. 'Ali informed the Prophet ﷺ of this, so he came to Hamza, and Hamza said to the Prophet ﷺ words of rudeness, contrary to what was obligatory upon him of honouring, reverencing and supporting the Prophet ﷺ. This indicates that Hamza's mind had been taken away by something intoxicating, and therefore the narrator said: "So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that he was drunk." Then the Prophet ﷺ did not denounce Hamza nor rebuke him, neither during his intoxication nor after it. Rather, he turned back when Hamza said: "Are you not but slaves of my father?" — backing away — and left him. Therefore it is obligatory to prevent everything that removes it or disturbs it. However, the hadith of Hamza may suggest that he did not intend by his drinking to become intoxicated, but he was quick to it and it overcame him. And Allah knows best.

He said: "Had it been impure, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, would not have done that, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have forbidden it, as he forbade defecating in the roads." The answer is that the Companions did that because they had no pits (surub) underground nor wells in which to pour it, for generally their homes did not have latrines (kunuf). Also, it was possible to avoid them, for the roads of Medina were wide, and wine was not so abundant as to become a river covering the whole road; rather it flowed only in small places that could be avoided. Moreover, there was the benefit of publicising its spilling in the roads of Medina, so that acting upon the requirement of its prohibition — by destroying it and that it is not benefited from — would spread, and people would follow and agree upon that. And Allah knows best.

We reply: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿rijs﴾ indicates its impurity, for rijs in the language means impurity (najasah). Furthermore, if we were to hold that we may not rule on any matter unless we find an explicit text for it, the Shari'ah would be rendered void, for explicit texts in it are few. Which explicit text is found declaring urine, excrement, blood, carrion and other things impure? Rather, there are only apparent indications (zawahir), general terms ('umumat), and analogies (aqyisah). What will clarify this meaning, if Allah wills, will come in Surah al-Hajj [See vol. 12, p. 53].

He said: "No." He said: Then he whispered to a man, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "What did you whisper to him?" He said: "I ordered him to sell it." He said: "Indeed, the One who prohibited its drinking has prohibited its sale." He said: Then he opened the waterskin until what was in it was gone. This hadith indicates what we have mentioned, for if there had been in it any permissible benefit, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have explained it, as he said concerning the dead sheep: "Why did you not take its hide, tan it, and benefit from it?" — the hadith [in full].

**The eighth issue:** The Muslims have agreed on the prohibition of selling wine and blood, and in that there is evidence for the prohibition of selling excrement and all other impurities and what is not lawful to eat. For this reason — and Allah knows best — Malik disliked the sale of animal dung (zibl al-dawabb), while Ibn al-Qasim permitted it because of the benefit in it. The analogy is what Malik said, and it is the position of al-Shafi'i. And this hadith is evidence for the soundness of that.

**Ninth issue:** Most jurists hold that it is not permissible for anyone to make wine into vinegar (*takhlil*). This is the view of a group of scholars from the people of hadith and of opinion (*ra'y*), and Sahnun ibn Said inclined to it.

And success is from Allah.

If that is so, then the prohibition on making it into vinegar at that time, and the command to pour it out, do not prevent eating it once it has become vinegar.

This report was mentioned by Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam in his book. But the correct view is what Malik said in the narration of Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb: it is not lawful for a Muslim to treat wine until he makes it vinegar, nor to sell it, but he should pour it out.

**Tenth issue:** There has been no difference of statement between Malik and his companions that if wine turns into vinegar by itself, eating that vinegar is lawful. This is also the view of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, Qabisa, Ibn Shihab, Rabiʿa, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafiʿi, and it is the established position of his school according to most of his companions.

**Eleventh issue:** Ibn Khuwayz Mandad mentioned that it may be owned, and he based that on the fact that choking can be relieved with it and a fire can be extinguished with it. But this is a report not known from Malik. Rather, this is derived from the view of those who hold that wine is pure. And if its ownership were permissible, the Prophet ﷺ would not have ordered it to be poured out. Also, ownership is a kind of benefit, and it has been nullified by pouring it out. And praise be to Allah.

**Twelfth issue:** This verse indicates the prohibition of playing backgammon (*nard*) and chess (*shatranj*), whether for gambling or not. For when Allah, exalted is He, prohibited wine, He informed of the meaning that is in it, saying: "O you who believe, wine and gambling..." [the verse]. Then He said: "Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you..." [the verse]. So every frivolous pastime whose small amount leads to a large amount, which casts enmity and hatred among those devoted to it, and which turns one away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer, is like drinking wine, and it is necessarily forbidden like it.

If it is said: drinking wine produces intoxication, so one cannot pray while under its influence, and this meaning is not present in playing backgammon and chess. It is answered: Allah has combined wine and gambling in the prohibition, and He described both of them as causing enmity and hatred among people, and turning them away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer. It is known that if wine intoxicates, gambling does not intoxicate. Yet the difference between them in that respect does not prevent, in Allah's sight, equating them in prohibition because of what they share in meanings. Also, a small amount of wine does not intoxicate, just as playing backgammon and chess does not intoxicate, yet a small amount of wine is forbidden just like a large amount. So it is not to be denied that playing backgammon and chess may be forbidden just like wine, even though they do not intoxicate. Also, the beginning of play produces heedlessness, and that heedlessness which takes control of the heart stands in place of intoxication. If wine was forbidden only because it intoxicates and thereby turns one away from the prayer, then playing backgammon and chess should be forbidden, because it causes heedlessness and distraction and thereby turns one away from the prayer. And Allah knows best.

**Thirteenth issue:** The narration of Mahdi al-Rawiya [[So in manuscripts J, ʿ, W, Y, H; in K: "This narration indicates..." etc. The original wording is probably: "The hadith of Mahdi al-Rawiya..." etc.]] indicates that the abrogating ruling (*al-nasikh*) had not reached him, and he was adhering to the earlier permission. This is evidence that a ruling is not cancelled by the mere existence of the abrogating text, as some of the jurists of legal theory (*usul*) say, but rather by its reaching the person, as this hadith indicates, and this is the correct view. For the Prophet ﷺ did not rebuke him but explained the ruling to him. Also, he was addressed to act on the first ruling, such that if he abandoned it he would be disobedient without any disagreement, even though the abrogating ruling had already come into existence. This is like what happened to the people of Quba' [[Quba' is a village two miles from Medina.]], who used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis until the one who came to them informed them of the abrogating ruling, and so they turned toward the Kaʿba. This was mentioned earlier in *Surat al-Baqara* [[See vol. 2, p. 148 and what follows.]], praise be to Allah, and the mention of wine, its derivation, and gambling was mentioned earlier there [[See vol. 2, p. 51 and what follows.]]. And the discussion of the idols (*ansab*) and the arrow-divining (*azlam*) has passed at the beginning of this surah [[See p. 57 and what follows of this part.]]. Praise be to Allah.

**Fourteenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾, [the verse]. Allah informed His servants that Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among us because of wine and other things, so He warned us against them and forbade them to us. It is related that two tribes of the Ansar drank wine and became intoxicated, and some of them played with others. When they became sober, some of them saw in the faces of others the traces of what they had done. They had been brothers with no rancor in their hearts, but one of them [[In manuscripts J and ʿ: "a man."]] began to say: "If my brother had been merciful to me, he would not have done this to me." So resentments arose among them, and Allah revealed: "Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you..." [the verse].

**Fifteenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer﴾. It means: when you are intoxicated, you do not remember Allah and do not pray; and if you pray, you become confused, as happened to ʿAli, and it is also related of ʿAbd al-Rahman, as was mentioned earlier in *al-Nisa'* [[See vol. 5, p. 200.]]. ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUmar said: al-Qasim ibn Muhammad was asked about chess: is it gambling? And about backgammon: is it gambling? He said: "Everything that turns one away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer is gambling." Abu ʿUbayd said: He interpreted the statement of Allah, exalted is He: "and turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer."

**Sixteenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ When ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, knew that this was a severe threat beyond the meaning of "desist," he said: "We have desisted." The Prophet ﷺ ordered his herald to proclaim in the lanes of Medina: "Verily, wine has been prohibited!" So the jars were broken, and the wine was poured out until it flowed through the lanes of Medina.

**Seventeenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware﴾ is a confirmation of the prohibition, an intensification of the threat, a call to comply with the command, and a restraint from what is forbidden. The conjunction "and obey Allah" is well placed because the preceding statement carried the sense of "desist." He repeated "and obey" with regard to the Messenger for emphasis. Then He warned against opposing the command and threatened the one who turns away with the punishment of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, you oppose, ﴿then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only to deliver clearly﴾ regarding the prohibition of what he was commanded to prohibit. And it is for the Sender to punish or reward according to whether He is disobeyed or obeyed.

He said: "Had it been impure, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, would not have done that, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have forbidden it, as he forbade defecating in the roads." The answer is that the Companions did that because they had no pits (surub) underground nor wells in which to pour it, for generally their homes did not have latrines (kunuf). 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: They were disgusted at building latrines inside the houses, and carrying them outside Medina involved hardship and difficulty, and it would entail delaying what was obligatory immediately. Also, it was possible to avoid them, for the roads of Medina were wide, and wine was not so abundant as to become a river covering the whole road; rather it flowed only in small places that could be avoided. And Allah knows best.

If it is said: "Making impure is a legal ruling, and there is no explicit text for it, and it does not follow that what is prohibited is impure, for many things prohibited in the law are not impure." We reply: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿rijs﴾ indicates its impurity, for rijs in the language means impurity (najasah). Furthermore, if we were to hold that we may not rule on any matter unless we find an explicit text for it, the Shari'ah would be rendered void, for explicit texts in it are few. What will clarify this meaning, if Allah wills, will come in Surah al-Hajj [See vol. 12, p. 53].

He said: "No." He said: Then he whispered to a man, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "What did you whisper to him?" He said: "I ordered him to sell it." He said: "Indeed, the One who prohibited its drinking has prohibited its sale." He said: Then he opened the waterskin until what was in it was gone. This hadith indicates what we have mentioned, for if there had been in it any permissible benefit, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have explained it, as he said concerning the dead sheep: "Why did you not take its hide, tan it, and benefit from it?" — the hadith [in full].

For when Allah, exalted is He, prohibited wine, He informed of the meaning that is in it, saying: "O you who believe, wine and gambling..." [the verse]. Then He said: "Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you..." [the verse]. It is known that if wine intoxicates, gambling does not intoxicate. Yet the difference between them in that respect does not prevent, in Allah's sight, equating them in prohibition because of what they share in meanings. Also, a small amount of wine does not intoxicate, just as playing backgammon and chess does not intoxicate, yet a small amount of wine is forbidden just like a large amount. So it is not to be denied that playing backgammon and chess may be forbidden just like wine, even though they do not intoxicate. Also, the beginning of play produces heedlessness, and that heedlessness which takes control of the heart stands in place of intoxication. If wine was forbidden only because it intoxicates and thereby turns one away from the prayer, then playing backgammon and chess should be forbidden, because it causes heedlessness and distraction and thereby turns one away from the prayer. And Allah knows best.

So resentments arose among them, and Allah revealed: "Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you..." [the verse].

Abu ʿUbayd said: He interpreted the statement of Allah, exalted is He: "and turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer."

So the jars were broken, and the wine was poured out until it flowed through the lanes of Medina.
