Then He warned against opposing the command and threatened the one who turns away with the punishment of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, you oppose, ﴿then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only to deliver clearly﴾ regarding the prohibition of what he was commanded to prohibit. And it is for the Sender to punish or reward according to whether He is disobeyed or obeyed.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 5, verses 90–92 (part 1 of 2)**

In this passage there are seventeen issues (masa'il).

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. This is an address to all the believers to abandon these things, since they were desires and habits that they had engaged in during the Jahiliyyah (the time of ignorance before Islam), and which had dominated their souls, so that some of them remained in the souls of many believers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: From this category is the passion for augury by birds (zajr bi-l-tair), and seeking omens in books (fa'l fi-l-kutub), and similar things that people practise today. As for wine (khamr), it had not yet been prohibited, and its prohibition was revealed in the third year after the Battle of Uhud. The Battle of Uhud took place in Shawwal in the third year after the Hijrah.

Its etymology has already been mentioned [See vol. 3, pp. 51–52]. As for "al-maysir" (gambling), the discussion of it has already passed in al-Baqarah [See vol. 3, pp. 51–52]. As for al-ansab (idols/stone altars), it is said that they are idols. It is also said that they are backgammon and chess; their explanation will come in Surah Yunus at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus: 32] [See vol. 8, p. 335]. As for al-azlam (divining arrows), they are the arrows (qidah), and the discussion of them has passed at the beginning of the surah. It is said that they were in the House (the Ka'bah) with the custodians of the House and the attendants of the idols. A man would come when he wanted to undertake some matter, and he would draw one of them; if it bore "My Lord has commanded me," he would go out to his affair as he loved or disliked.

**The second issue:** The prohibition of wine came gradually and through many occurrences, for they were devoted to drinking it. The first thing revealed concerning it was: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both is great sin and some benefit for people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], meaning in their trade. When this verse was revealed, some people gave it up and said: "We have no need of that in which there is great sin." Others did not give it up and said: "We will take its benefit and leave its sin." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] [See vol. 5, p. 191]. Some people gave it up and said: "We have no need of what distracts us from prayer." Others drank it at times other than the times of prayer, until the verse was revealed: "O you who have believed, indeed wine, gambling, the stone altars, and divining arrows are an abomination" — the verse — and so it became forbidden to them, to the point that some of them would say: "Allah has not prohibited anything more severe than wine."

Abu Maysarah said: It was revealed on account of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, for he mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ the defects of wine and what befalls people because of it, and he supplicated Allah concerning its prohibition, saying: "O Allah, make clear to us a healing explanation regarding wine." Then these verses were revealed, and 'Umar said: "We have ceased, we have ceased." Its discussion has passed in al-Baqarah [See vol. 3, pp. 51–52] and al-Nisa' [See vol. 5, p. 191].

Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated" [al-Nisa': 43], and "They ask you about wine and gambling" [al-Baqarah: 219] were abrogated (nasakhat) by the verse in al-Ma'idah: "Indeed wine, gambling, and the stone altars..."

In Sahih Muslim, from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, that he said: Verses of the Qur'an were revealed concerning me, and in it he said: I came upon a group of the Ansar, and they said: "Come, we will feed you and give you wine to drink," and that was before wine was prohibited. He said: I went to them in a hush (hush) — and the hush is the orchard — and there was the roasted head of a camel [with them] [the addition is from Sahih Muslim] and a skin of wine. He said: I ate and drank with them. He said: Then I mentioned the Ansar and the Muhajirun in their presence, and I said: "The Muhajirun are better than the Ansar." He said: Then a man took the jawbone of a camel and struck me with it, and it cut my nose — and in another narration, "it split it," and Sa'd's nose was split. So I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed concerning me — meaning himself — the matter of wine: "Indeed wine, gambling, the stone altars, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it."

**The third issue:** These hadiths indicate that the drinking of wine was at that time permissible, practised and well known among them, to the extent that it was not denounced nor changed, and that the Prophet ﷺ approved it. This is something on which there is no disagreement. The verse of al-Nisa', "Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated," indicates it, as already mentioned.

This indicates that Hamza's mind had been taken away by something intoxicating, and therefore the narrator said: "So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that he was drunk." Then the Prophet ﷺ did not denounce Hamza nor rebuke him, neither during his intoxication nor after it. Rather, he turned back when Hamza said: "Are you not but slaves of my father?" — backing away — and left him. This is contrary to what the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun) said and related, for they said: Intoxication is prohibited in every law, because the laws are for the welfare of the servants, not their harm, and the root of welfare is the intellect, just as the root of harm is its loss. Therefore it is obligatory to prevent everything that removes it or disturbs it. So every frivolous pastime whose small amount leads to a large amount, which casts enmity and hatred among those devoted to it, and which turns one away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer, is like drinking wine, and it is necessarily forbidden like it.

If it is said: drinking wine produces intoxication, so one cannot pray while under its influence, and this meaning is not present in playing backgammon and chess. It is answered: Allah has combined wine and gambling in the prohibition, and He described both of them as causing enmity and hatred among people, and turning them away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer. It is known that if wine intoxicates, gambling does not intoxicate. Yet the difference between them in that respect does not prevent, in Allah's sight, equating them in prohibition because of what they share in meanings. Also, a small amount of wine does not intoxicate, just as playing backgammon and chess does not intoxicate, yet a small amount of wine is forbidden just like a large amount. So it is not to be denied that playing backgammon and chess may be forbidden just like wine, even though they do not intoxicate. Also, the beginning of play produces heedlessness, and that heedlessness which takes control of the heart stands in place of intoxication. If wine was forbidden only because it intoxicates and thereby turns one away from the prayer, then playing backgammon and chess should be forbidden, because it causes heedlessness and distraction and thereby turns one away from the prayer. And Allah knows best.

**Thirteenth issue:** The narration of Mahdi al-Rawiya [[So in manuscripts J, ʿ, W, Y, H; in K: "This narration indicates..." etc. The original wording is probably: "The hadith of Mahdi al-Rawiya..." etc.]] indicates that the abrogating ruling (*al-nasikh*) had not reached him, and he was adhering to the earlier permission. This is evidence that a ruling is not cancelled by the mere existence of the abrogating text, as some of the jurists of legal theory (*usul*) say, but rather by its reaching the person, as this hadith indicates, and this is the correct view. For the Prophet ﷺ did not rebuke him but explained the ruling to him. Also, he was addressed to act on the first ruling, such that if he abandoned it he would be disobedient without any disagreement, even though the abrogating ruling had already come into existence. This is like what happened to the people of Quba' [[Quba' is a village two miles from Medina.]], who used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis until the one who came to them informed them of the abrogating ruling, and so they turned toward the Kaʿba. This was mentioned earlier in *Surat al-Baqara* [[See vol. 2, p. 148 and what follows.]], praise be to Allah, and the mention of wine, its derivation, and gambling was mentioned earlier there [[See vol. 2, p. 51 and what follows.]]. And the discussion of the idols (*ansab*) and the arrow-divining (*azlam*) has passed at the beginning of this surah [[See p. 57 and what follows of this part.]]. Praise be to Allah.

**Fourteenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾, [the verse]. Allah informed His servants that Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among us because of wine and other things, so He warned us against them and forbade them to us. It is related that two tribes of the Ansar drank wine and became intoxicated, and some of them played with others. When they became sober, some of them saw in the faces of others the traces of what they had done. They had been brothers with no rancor in their hearts, but one of them [[In manuscripts J and ʿ: "a man."]] began to say: "If my brother had been merciful to me, he would not have done this to me." So resentments arose among them, and Allah revealed: "Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you..." [the verse].

**Fifteenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer﴾. It means: when you are intoxicated, you do not remember Allah and do not pray; and if you pray, you become confused, as happened to ʿAli, and it is also related of ʿAbd al-Rahman, as was mentioned earlier in *al-Nisa'* [[See vol. 5, p. 200.]]. ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUmar said: al-Qasim ibn Muhammad was asked about chess: is it gambling? And about backgammon: is it gambling? He said: "Everything that turns one away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer is gambling." Abu ʿUbayd said: He interpreted the statement of Allah, exalted is He: "and turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer."

**Sixteenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ When ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, knew that this was a severe threat beyond the meaning of "desist," he said: "We have desisted." The Prophet ﷺ ordered his herald to proclaim in the lanes of Medina: "Verily, wine has been prohibited!" So the jars were broken, and the wine was poured out until it flowed through the lanes of Medina.

**Seventeenth issue:** His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware﴾ is a confirmation of the prohibition, an intensification of the threat, a call to comply with the command, and a restraint from what is forbidden. The conjunction "and obey Allah" is well placed because the preceding statement carried the sense of "desist." He repeated "and obey" with regard to the Messenger for emphasis. Then He warned against opposing the command and threatened the one who turns away with the punishment of the Hereafter, saying: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, you oppose, ﴿then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only to deliver clearly﴾ regarding the prohibition of what he was commanded to prohibit. And it is for the Sender to punish or reward according to whether He is disobeyed or obeyed.

It contains nine issues.

**The first:** Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and Anas ibn Malik said: when the prohibition of wine (khamr) was revealed, some of the Companions said: "What about those among us who died while drinking it and consuming gambling (maysir), and the like?" Then this verse was revealed. Al-Bukhari narrated from Anas, who said: "I was the one serving the drink to the people at the house of Abu Talha. Then the prohibition of wine was revealed, so [the Prophet ﷺ] ordered a caller to call out. Abu Talha said: 'Go out and see what this sound is!' So I went out and said: 'It is a caller calling out: Indeed, wine has been prohibited.' He said: 'Go and pour it out.' The wine was made from fadikh [a drink of crushed dates]." He said: "It flowed through the alleys of Madinah. Some of the people said: 'People have been killed while it was in their stomachs.' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, to the end of the verse."

**The second:** This verse and this hadith are similar to their question about those who died while the first qiblah was still in place, and then [Allah] revealed: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143]. Whoever does what is permitted to him until he dies upon that act, there is neither a reward nor a punishment for him: no sin, no accountability, no blame, no reward and no praise, because the permissible (mubah) is equal on both sides with respect to the Shari'ah. In light of this, it should not have been feared, nor should one ask about the state of one who died while wine was in his stomach at the time it was permitted. Either that speaker was unaware of the evidence of permissibility and it did not occur to him, or, out of his overwhelming fear of Allah the Exalted and his compassion for his fellow believers, he imagined a sanction and punishment for the earlier drinking of wine. So Allah removed that imagining by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, to the end of the verse.

**The third:** This hadith about the occasion of revelation is clear evidence that date wine (nabidh al-tamr), when it intoxicates, is khamr. This is a textual matter (nass) and it is not permissible to object to it, because the Companions, may Allah have mercy on them, were people of the language (ahl al-lisan). They understood that their drink was khamr, since they had no other drink in Madinah at that time. The poet al-Hakami said:

"We have wine, but not the wine of the vineyard,
but from the produce of the lofty palms;
Noble, they rise high into the sky,
and the hands of the pickers miss their fruits."

And among the clear evidence on this is what al-Nasa'i narrated: Al-Qasim ibn Zakariyya informed us, 'Ubayd Allah informed us, from Shayban, from al-A'mash, from Muharib ibn Dithar, from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Raisins and dates—that is khamr."

It is also established by sound transmission that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him—and sufficient is he as a scholar of the language and the Shari'ah—delivered a sermon from the pulpit of the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O people, indeed the prohibition of wine was revealed on the day it was revealed, and it is from five things: from grapes, dates, honey, wheat and barley. And khamr is whatever covers the intellect (khamara al-'aql)." This is the clearest statement of the meaning of khamr: 'Umar delivered it in Madinah from the pulpit in the presence of a group of Companions, and they are people of the language, and they did not understand from khamr anything other than what we have mentioned. Once this is established, the position of Abu Hanifah and the Kufans is refuted; they hold that khamr is only from grapes, and what is from other than grapes is not called khamr and is not covered by the name khamr, but is called nabidh. The poet said:

"I have abandoned nabidh for the people of nabidh,
and I have become an ally of whoever disparages it:
A drink that defiles the honour of the young man
and opens the doors of evil to him."

**The fourth:** Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Mazari said: The majority of scholars from the early generations (salaf) and others hold that whatever its kind intoxicates is forbidden to drink, whether little or much, raw or cooked, and there is no difference between what is extracted from grapes or from other things. Whoever drinks any of it is subject to the hadd (prescribed punishment). As for the intoxicating extract of grapes, there is consensus (ijma') on the prohibition of its little and its much, even a single drop of it. As for what is other than that, the majority holds it to be prohibited. The Kufans disagreed regarding what is little of what is other than what has been mentioned, which does not reach intoxication, and regarding cooked extract of grapes. A group from Basra held that the prohibition is restricted to the pressed juice of grapes and the steeped raisin liquid (naqi' al-zabib) when raw; as for the cooked form of both, and the raw and cooked forms of anything other than them, they are permissible so long as intoxication does not occur. Abu Hanifah held that the prohibition is restricted to the pressed extract of the fruits of palms and grapes, with detail: he holds that the sulafah [pure juice] of grapes is forbidden in both little and much unless it is boiled until two-thirds of it is reduced. As for the steeped liquid of raisins and dates, its cooked form is permissible even if fire touches it only slightly, without considering a limit; but its raw form is forbidden. However, even though it is forbidden, it does not necessitate the hadd. All of this applies so long as intoxication does not occur; if intoxication occurs, all of them are equal.

Our shaykh, the jurist and imam Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, said: It is strange that the dissenters in this issue say that a little of the wine extracted from grapes is forbidden like its much, and this is agreed upon. So if they are asked: why is a little wine forbidden when it does not remove reason? They must say: because it leads to the much, or it is for the sake of worship (ta'abbud). Then it is said to them: everything you have ascribed to a little wine is found in exactly the same way in a little nabidh, so it is also forbidden, since there is no difference between them except the mere name, if that is granted. This analogy (qiyas) is the highest type of analogy, because the derivative (far') is equal to the original (asl) in all its attributes, like what they say regarding the analogy of the female slave to the male slave in the spread of manumission. Then strange is the position of Abu Hanifah and his companions, may Allah have mercy on them! They go deep into qiyas and give it preference over solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad), and yet they have abandoned this clear analogy, which is supported by the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus of the early leaders of the Ummah, in favour of hadiths none of which is authentic according to what the hadith scholars have clarified in their books regarding their defects, and none of them is in the Sahih.

The complete discussion of this issue will come in Surah al-Nahl [cf. vol. 10, p. 127], God willing.

**The fifth:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ṭa'imū﴾ [they ate]. The original sense of this word is eating. One says: "ṭa'ima al-ṭa'ām" (he ate the food) and "shariba al-sharāb" (he drank the drink). But it has been used figuratively in this sense, so one says: "lam aṭ'am khubzan wa-lā māʾan wa-lā nawman" (I did not taste bread, nor water, nor sleep). The poet said:

"Ostriches at Wajrah [a place between Makkah and Basra; the poet says: they are fasting from it, not tasting it. It is narrated in al-Lisan as 'not tasting water', and he said: this is because ostriches do not come to water nor taste it. Before it:
As for the sons of 'Amir, by the fire,
on the morning they met us, they were ostriches—
Yellow of cheeks, they do not taste sleep
except as fasting."

The matter was discussed in al-Baqarah [cf. vol. 3, p. 252] regarding His saying: ﴿And whoever does not taste it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:249], with what suffices.

**The sixth:** Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: This verse includes the permissibility of pleasures and the enjoyment of every delicious thing—of food, drink and marriage—even if one goes to excess in it and exceeds in its price. This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:87], and similar to His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants, and the good provisions?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:32].

**The seventh:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, and then fear Allah and believe, and then fear Allah and do good, and Allah loves the good-doers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:93]. Regarding this there are four views.
The first: there is no repetition in the mention of taqwa (God-consciousness). The meaning is: "they feared [Allah regarding] drinking it, and believed in its prohibition." The second meaning: their fear of Allah and their faith persisted. The third is in the sense of excelling in taqwa.
The second: they feared Allah before the prohibition in respect of other forbidden things; then they feared Allah after its prohibition regarding drinking it; then they feared Allah in the rest of their deeds, and did good deeds.
The third: they feared shirk (associating partners with Allah) and believed in Allah and His Messenger. The second meaning: then they feared the major sins, and increased in faith. The meaning of the third: then they feared the minor sins and did good, i.e. they performed voluntary acts.
Muhammad ibn Jarir said: The first taqwa is fear of Allah by receiving the command of Allah with acceptance, affirmation, submission to it and acting upon it. The second taqwa is fear of Allah by steadfastness upon affirmation. The third is fear of Allah by excellence and drawing near through voluntary acts.

**The eighth:** His saying: ﴿Then fear Allah and do good, and Allah loves the good-doers﴾ is evidence that the God-fearing one who does good is better than the God-fearing believer who does righteous deeds; He favoured him with the reward of excellence (ihsan).

**The ninth:** This verse was interpreted by Qudamah ibn Maz'un al-Jumahi, one of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. He was among those who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia with his two brothers, 'Uthman and 'Abd Allah; then he emigrated to Madinah, witnessed Badr, and lived a long life ['umirra: lived a long time]. He was the brother-in-law (khatan) of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, the maternal uncle of 'Abd Allah and Hafsah. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab appointed him over Bahrain, then removed him on the testimony of al-Jarud, chief of 'Abd al-Qays, against him for drinking wine.

Al-Daraqutni narrated, saying: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Muhammad al-Misri told us, Yahya ibn Ayyub al-'Allaf told us, Sa'id ibn 'Ufayr told me, Yahya ibn Fulayh ibn Sulayman told me, Thawr ibn Zayd told me, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: that the drinkers were beaten during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with hands, sandals and sticks, until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died. Then in the caliphate of Abu Bakr there were more of them than in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Abu Bakr would flog them forty lashes until he died. Then 'Umar, after him, would flog them likewise forty, until a man from the early emigrants was brought to him, who had drunk, and he ordered that he be flogged. The man said: "Why are you flogging me? Between me and you is the Book of Allah!" 'Umar said: "And in which Book of Allah do you find that I should not flog you?" He said: "Indeed Allah, Exalted, says in His Book: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, to the end of the verse. So I am among those who believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good; I witnessed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ Badr, Uhud, the Trench and all the battles." 'Umar said: "Will you not answer him on what he says?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "These verses were revealed as an excuse for those who had passed away and as a proof against the people, because Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine and gambling﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:90], to the end of the verse, then he recited until he completed the other verse: ﴿If he is among those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, to the end of the verse. Indeed Allah has forbidden him to drink wine." 'Umar said: "You have spoken the truth. What do you think?" 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, when he drinks he becomes intoxicated; and when he becomes intoxicated he talks nonsense; and when he talks nonsense he slanders; and the slanderer deserves eighty lashes." So 'Umar ordered him to be flogged eighty lashes.

Al-Humaydi mentioned from Abu Bakr al-Barqani [al-Barqani (with a fatha on the ba' and sukun on the ra'): this nisba refers to a village in the region of Khwarazm that was ruined and became a farm].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 93 (part 2 of 2):

(al-Ansab) by al-Sam'ani.]] On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When al-Jarud came from Bahrain, he said: "O Commander of the Faithful, Qudamah ibn Maz'un has drunk an intoxicant, and when I see a right from the rights of Allah, it is incumbent upon me to report it to you." 'Umar said: "Who will bear witness to what you say?" He said: "Abu Hurayrah." So 'Umar summoned Abu Hurayrah and said: "On what do you testify, O Abu Hurayrah?" He said: "I did not see him when he drank, but I saw him drunk, sakran yaqi (يقي)." 'Umar said: "You have gone to extremes (tanatta'ta) in testimony," [[Tana''ta fi al-kalam: he went to excess and exaggerated.]] Then 'Umar wrote to Qudamah, who was in Bahrain, ordering him to come to him. When Qudamah and al-Jarud arrived in Medina, al-Jarud spoke to 'Umar, saying: "Establish the Book of Allah upon him." 'Umar said to al-Jarud: "Are you a witness or an adversary?" al-Jarud said: "I am a witness." He said: "You had already given the testimony." Then he said to 'Umar: "I adjure you by Allah!" 'Umar said: "By Allah, you will either restrain your tongue or I will harm you!" al-Jarud said: "By Allah, that is not the truth: that the cousin of yours should drink and that you should harm me!" So 'Umar threatened him. Abu Hurayrah, who was sitting, said: "O Commander of the Faithful, if you are in doubt about our testimony, then ask the daughter of al-Walid, the wife of Ibn Maz'un." So 'Umar sent for Hind, adjuring her by Allah, and Hind testified against her husband. 'Umar said: "O Qudamah, I am going to flog you." Qudamah said: "By Allah, even if you had drunk, as they say, it would not be lawful for you to flog me, O 'Umar." He said: "And why, O Qudamah?" He said: "Because Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾ up to ﴿the good-doers﴾." 'Umar said: "You have misinterpreted it, O Qudamah. If you fear Allah, you avoid what Allah has forbidden." Then 'Umar turned to the people and said: "What do you think about flogging Qudamah?" The people said: "We do not think you should flog him while he is ill [[wajaʿ: sick.]]." So 'Umar refrained from flogging him. Then one day he rose and said to his companions: "What do you think about flogging Qudamah?" The people said: "We do not think you should flog him while he is ill." 'Umar said: "By Allah, for me to meet Allah under the whip is more beloved to me than to meet Allah while he is around my neck! By Allah, I will flog him. Bring me a whip!" His freedman Aslam came with a thin, small, soft whip, and 'Umar took it, wiped it with his hand, and said to Aslam: "The ways of your family (diqrarah) have taken hold of you! Bring me a whip other than this." [[al-Diqrarah (pl. al-daqarir): falsehoods and bad habits. He meant the bad habit that is the habit of your people, which is turning away from the truth and inclining toward falsehood (????), and it came to you and you acted upon it. Aslam was a Bajawi (Berber-type) slave.]] He said: Then Aslam brought him a full-sized whip, and 'Umar ordered Qudamah to be flogged. Qudamah became angry with 'Umar and boycotted him. They performed the Hajj while Qudamah was shunning 'Umar, until they returned from their pilgrimage. 'Umar stopped at al-Suqya [[al-Suqya (with a damma): a place between Medina and Wadi al-Safra.]] and slept there. When 'Umar awoke, he said: "Hurry to me with Qudamah! Go and bring him to me, for by Allah, I saw in my sleep that a visitor came to me and said: 'Reconcile with Qudamah, for he is your brother.'" When they came to Qudamah, he refused to come to him, so 'Umar ordered that Qudamah be dragged to him until 'Umar spoke with him and asked forgiveness for him. That was the first reconciliation between them. Ayyub ibn Abi Tamima said: "None of the people of Badr was flogged for wine except him."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: This shows you the interpretation of the verse. As for what is mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas in the hadith of al-Daraqutni, and 'Umar in the hadith of al-Barqani, it is sound. Its explanation is that if whoever drank wine and feared Allah in other matters were not punished for wine, then no one would have been flogged for wine. So this is one of the most corrupt interpretations. It was hidden from Qudamah, but it was known to those whom Allah granted success, such as 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The poet said:

"Indeed, I do not see anyone weeping through time over his sorrow, except that I weep over 'Umar."

It is also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that some people drank in Syria and said: "It is lawful for us," and they interpreted this verse. So 'Ali and 'Umar agreed that they should be asked to repent; if they repented, well and good, otherwise they should be killed. This was mentioned by Ilkiya al-Tabari.

**First issue: the verse and its occasion.** There are eight issues in this verse. The first concerns Allah's words ﴿Allah will surely test you﴾, meaning He will surely try you, and *al-ibtila'* (testing) is *al-ikhtibar* (examination). Hunting was one of the livelihoods of the *al-'Arab al-'Ariba* (the original pure Arabs) and was widespread and very common among all of them. So Allah tested them concerning it while they were in the state of *ihram* (ritual consecration for pilgrimage) and in the *Haram* (the sacred precinct), just as He tested the Children of Israel in not transgressing on the Sabbath. It is said that the verse was revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. Some of the people had entered the state of ihram with the Prophet (ﷺ) and some had not. Whenever game appeared, their circumstances and actions differed, and the rulings on it became unclear to them. So Allah revealed this verse to explain the rulings on their circumstances and actions and the prohibitions of their Hajj and 'Umrah.

**Second issue:** The scholars differed over who is addressed by this verse, on two views. The first is that they are the *muhillun* (those not in ihram), as Malik said. The second is that they are the *muhrimun* (those in ihram), as Ibn 'Abbas said. Those who held this view relied on Allah's words ﴿He will test you﴾, since the obligation of abstaining, through which the testing is realized, is specifically in the state of ihram. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this does not necessarily follow, because the obligation is realized in the *mahall* (the place, i.e. the non-ihram state) through the conditions set for hunting and the manner of hunting prescribed for it. The correct view is that the address in the verse is to all people, both those not in ihram and those in ihram, based on Allah's words ﴿He will test you﴾, meaning He will impose obligations upon you. All obligation is a test, even though it varies in its magnitude and smallness, and differs in its ease and difficulty.

**Third issue:** Allah's words ﴿with something of the game﴾ mean with some of the game. The *min* is for partition (*tab'idh*), and it refers specifically to land game. It does not cover all game, since there is game in the sea, as al-Tabari and others said. By *al-sayd* (game) here is meant *al-masid* (the thing hunted), based on His words ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾.

**Fourth issue:** Allah's words ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾ explain the ruling on small game and large game. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read *yanaluhu* with a *ya'* dotted from below. Mujahid said: hands reach the chicks and the eggs and whatever cannot flee, and spears reach large game. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach﴾. Everything a person reaches with his hand, or with his spear, or with some of his weapons, and kills, is game, as Allah the Exalted said.

**Fifth issue:** Allah the Exalted specifically mentioned the hands because they are the main instrument of control in hunting, and into them enter trained hunting animals, snares, and what is worked by hand, such as traps and nets. He specifically mentioned the spears because they are the main means by which game is wounded, and into them enters the arrow and the like. The discussion of what is hunted with trained animals and arrows has already passed at the beginning of the surah, with what is sufficient, and praise be to Allah.

**Sixth issue:** What falls into a trap or a snare belongs to its owner. If someone drives the game into it, and without him it could not have been caught, then the owner of the trap is his partner in it. What falls into a *jabh* (a beehive in a mountain cleft; the word is pronounced with a *jim* and a silent *ba'*, and its plural is *ajbuh*, *juboh* and *jibah*) of honeybees set in a mountain is like the snare and the trap. Pigeon-coops' birds are returned to their owners if this can be done, and likewise the bees of a *jibah*; this is narrated from Malik. But some of his companions said: whoever comes into possession of pigeons or bees is not obliged to return them. If dogs drive game so that it enters someone's house or dwelling, it belongs to the hunter who sent the dogs, not to the owner of the house. If it entered the house without the dogs compelling it, then it belongs to the owner of the house.

**Seventh issue:** Some people argued from this verse that the game belongs to the one who catches it, not to the one who startles it, because the one who startled it had not yet reached it with his hand or his spear. This is the view of Abu Hanifah.

**Eighth issue:** Malik disliked hunting the game of the People of the Book but did not prohibit it, based on Allah's words ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾, meaning the people of faith, based on His words at the beginning of the verse ﴿O you who believe﴾. So the People of the Book are excluded. The majority of scholars disagreed with him, based on Allah's words ﴿The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:5], and it (the game) is among their slaughtered animals in their view. Our scholars answered that the verse only includes eating their food, and hunting is a different category, so it is not included in the generality of "food" and the bare wording does not cover it. I (al-Qurtubi) say: this is based on the premise that hunting is not prescribed among them, so it is not part of their food, and this objection falls away from us. But if it is prescribed in their religion, then it is incumbent upon us to eat it, since the wording covers it, for it is part of their food. And Allah knows best.

**Part 1 of 5.** There are thirty issues (masa'il) in this verse.

**First issue:** Allah's words ﴿O you who believe﴾ are a general address to every Muslim, male and female. This prohibition is the trial mentioned in His words ﴿Surely Allah will test you with something of the game﴾ and the rest of the verse. It is narrated that Abu al-Yasar, whose name is Amr ibn Malik al-Ansari [[As in the original; his name in (al-Tahdhib) and elsewhere is Ka'b ibn Amr... etc.]], was in a state of ihram (ritual consecration for pilgrimage) during the year of al-Hudaybiyah, performing 'umrah. He killed a wild ass, and so the verse was revealed about him: ﴿Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾.

**Second issue:** Allah's words ﴿Do not kill game﴾. Killing (qatl) is every act that causes the soul to depart. It takes several forms, including slaughtering, cutting the throat, strangling, crushing, and the like. Allah therefore forbade the one in ihram every act that causes the game to die.

**Third issue:** Whoever kills game, or slaughters it and then eats from it, is liable for one compensation (jaza') for the killing alone, not for the eating. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: he is liable for the compensation for what he ate, meaning its value. His two companions disagreed with him and said: nothing is owed except seeking forgiveness (istighfar), because he has consumed carrion, just as if he had consumed other carrion. For this reason, if another person in ihram ate it, he would owe only istighfar.

The argument of Abu Hanifa is that he has consumed what his ihram forbids, since killing it was among the prohibitions of ihram. It is known that the purpose of killing is consumption. If that which leads to the purpose, namely the act whose ihram forbids it, obligates compensation, then the purpose itself is more deserving of it.

**Fourth issue:** According to us, it is not permissible for the one in ihram to slaughter game, because Allah, glorified is He, forbade the one in ihram from killing it. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa. Al-Shafi'i said: the slaughter (dhabh) of the one in ihram for game is a valid ritual slaughter (dhakah). He relied on the argument that it is a slaughter that proceeds from one who is qualified to perform it, namely a Muslim, and that it is applied to its proper object, namely the livestock, so it brings about its intended result of making the eating lawful. Its basis is the slaughter of one who is not in ihram.

We reply: your statement that it is a slaughter proceeding from one who is qualified means that the one in ihram is not qualified to slaughter game, since qualification (ahliyyah) cannot be acquired

Al-Qurtubi's Commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 5, Verse 95 (Part 2 of 5):

...rational faculty, rather the Law (al-shar') confers it, namely by His permission to slaughter, or negates it, namely by His prohibition from slaughtering. The one in ihram is forbidden from slaughtering game, due to His saying: "Do not kill game," so the capacity (al-ahliyyah) is negated by the prohibition. As for your statement that it (slaughter) yields its intended effect, we agree that when the one in ihram slaughters game, it is not lawful for him to eat it, and according to you, only others may eat from it. So if slaughter does not make it lawful for the slaughterer, it is all the more fitting and more appropriate that it should not make it lawful for another, because the branch follows the root in its rulings, and so it is not valid that the branch should acquire what the root does not acquire.

The fifth issue: His Exalted saying: ﴿al-sayd﴾ (game) is a verbal noun (masdar) treated as a noun, so it is applied to the animal that is hunted. The word "sayd" here is general, covering every land and sea game, until the saying of the Exalted came: ﴿And the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96], so He permitted sea game with an absolute permission, as will be explained in the verse after this, God willing, Exalted is He.

The sixth issue: The scholars differed concerning the exclusion of predatory beasts (al-siba') from land game and their being specified from it. Malik said: Every animal that does not attack (ya'du) among the predators, such as the domestic cat, the fox, the hyena, and what resembles them, the one in ihram shall not kill it, and if he kills it, he must pay its compensation (fidyah). He said: I do not think the one in ihram should kill young wolves; if he kills them, he must pay their compensation, and they are like the young of crows. There is no harm in killing whatever attacks people generally, such as the lion, the wolf, the panther, and the leopard. Likewise, there is no harm for him in killing snakes, scorpions, the mouse, the crow, and the kite. Isma'il said: That is only due to his (peace be upon him) saying: "Five are wicked creatures that may be killed in the sanctuary and outside it," (the hadith), so he named them "wicked" (fussaq) and described them by their actions, because the wicked one is the doer of wickedness, and the young have no actions; and he described the dog as "the biting one" (al-'aqur), and its offspring do not bite, so they do not enter under this description. Al-Qadi Isma'il said: The biting dog is among those whose harm to people is great. He said: Among these is the snake and the scorpion, because they are feared, and likewise the kite and the crow, because they snatch meat from people's hands. Ibn Bukayr said: Permission to kill the scorpion was given only because it has a sting (hummah) [[The hummah: the poison, or the stinger with which the scorpion and the wasp and the like strike.]], and the mouse because it gnaws the waterskin (siqa') [[The siqa': the water skin.]] and the shoes, by which the traveller's sustenance is secured. And the crow because it alights on the back (zahr) [[The zahr: the camels which are carried upon and ridden.]] and pecks at its flesh. It has been narrated from Malik that he said: The crow and the kite are not to be killed unless they cause harm. Al-Qadi Isma'il said: The wasp has been disputed; some likened it to the snake and the scorpion. He said: Were it not that the wasp does not initiate attack, it would be more harmful to people than the snake and the scorpion, but it does not have in its nature the hostility that the snake and the scorpion have; the wasp only becomes aggressive when provoked. He said: If a wasp approaches a person and he repels it from himself, there is no blame on him for killing it. It is established from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he permitted killing the wasp. Malik said: The killer shall feed something (to the poor), and Malik said the same concerning one who kills the flea, the gnat, the ant, and the like. The Companions of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: There is nothing upon the killer of all of these. Abu Hanifah said: The one in ihram shall not kill any predator except the biting dog and the wolf specifically, whether they initiate attack or he initiates it against them, and if he kills other predators, he must pay compensation. He said: If other predators than these initiate attack and he kills them, there is nothing upon him. He said: There is nothing upon him for killing the snake, the scorpion, the crow, and the kite. This is the sum of the position of Abu Hanifah and his companions, except Zufar, and it was also the view of al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan. They argued that the Prophet (ﷺ) specified certain animals by name and granted the one in ihram leave to kill them on account of their harm, so there is no basis for adding to them, unless they agree upon something, in which case it enters into their meaning. I say: It is strange that Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, extends the wheat-rule to dust by the cause of measure, yet does not extend the aggressive beasts to the dog by the cause of wickedness and biting, as Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them, did! Zufar ibn al-Hudhayl said: Only the wolf alone may be killed, and whoever kills other than it while in ihram owes compensation, whether it initiated attack or not, because it is a dumb creature (ajma'), so his act is void (hadar); but this is a rejection of the hadith and an opposition to it. Al-Shafi'i said: Whatever its meat is not eaten, the one in ihram may kill it, and its young and its adult are alike, except the sim'a, which is the offspring between the wolf and the hyena. He said: There is nothing in the rakhamah (vulture), the beetles, the ticks, the hulam [[The hulam, with the vowel of ḥarakah, is the plural of (ḥalmah), which is the small tick. It is also said: the large one among them.]], and whatever its meat is not eaten. This is because these are not game, due to His saying: "And the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in ihram," so this shows that the game which is forbidden to them is that which was lawful to them before the ihram. Al-Muzani and al-Rabi' related this entire position from him. If it is said: Why is the louse subject to compensation when it causes harm and is not eaten? It is said to him: It is only subject to compensation as is the case with compensation for hair, nails, and wearing what one is not permitted to wear, because in casting off the louse there is removal of harm from oneself when it is on one's head and beard, so it is as if he removed some of his hair. But when it appears and is killed, it does not cause harm. The position of Abu Thawr in this matter is like that of al-Shafi'i, as Abu 'Umar stated.

The seventh issue: The Imams narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Five of the creatures there is no blame upon the one in ihram for killing: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse, and the biting dog." The wording is that of al-Bukhari, and this is the view of Ahmad and Ishaq. In the Book of Muslim, from 'A'ishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Five are wicked creatures that may be killed in the sanctuary and outside it: the snake, the white-bellied crow (al-abqa'), the mouse, the biting dog, and the kite." A group of the people of knowledge also held this view, and they said: Of the crows only the white-bellied one may be killed, specifically, because this is a restriction of an absolute. In the Book of Abu Dawud, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "He may throw at the crow but not kill it." This is also the view of Mujahid. The majority of scholars act upon the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and Allah knows best. In the narration of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi: "and the aggressive predator," and this is an indication of the reason (ʿillah).

The eighth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you are in ihram﴾ is general to both categories, men and women, free and slaves. It is said: a man is ḥaram and a woman is ḥaram, and the plural of that is ḥurum, like their saying: qadhāl and qudhul. And "ahrama al-rajul" means he entered the sacred state, as it is said: "ashhala" means he entered the easy ground. This word encompasses time, place, and the state of ihram by shared meaning, not by general application. It is said: a man is ḥaram when he has entered the sacred months or the sanctuary, or has clothed himself in ihram. However, the sanctity of time has by consensus been excluded from being considered, and the sanctity of place and the state of ihram remain on the basis of legal obligation (al-taklif). This was stated by Ibn al-'Arabi.

The ninth issue: The sanctity of place is of two kinds: the sanctuary of Madinah and the sanctuary of Makkah. Al-Shafi'i added al-Ta'if. So according to him it is not permissible to cut its trees, nor to hunt its game, and whoever does so owes no penalty. As for the sanctuary of Madinah, hunting in it is not permissible for anyone, nor is cutting its trees, as in the sanctuary of Makkah. If one does so, he sins, but there is no penalty upon him according to Malik, al-Shafi'i, and their companions. Ibn Abi Dhi'b said: He owes the penalty. Sa'd said: His penalty is that his spoils be taken; this is also narrated from al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: The game of Madinah is not forbidden, and likewise the cutting of its trees. Some of those who followed his school argued for this with the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever you find hunting within the boundaries of Madinah or cutting its trees, take his spoils." Sa'd took the spoils of whoever did so. He said: The jurists have agreed that the spoils of one who hunts in Madinah are not taken, which shows that it has been abrogated. Al-Tahawi also argued for their position with the hadith of Anas: "What did the little bird (al-nughayr) do?" — and he did not disapprove of its hunting and keeping. All of this has no proof in it. As for the first hadith, it is not strong; and even if it were sound, the abrogation of one ruling regarding spoils would not nullify what is established of the sanctity of Madinah, for many a person in ihram has no worldly penalty upon him. As for the second hadith, it is possible that the bird was outside the sanctuary. Likewise the hadith of 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a wild animal which, when it went out, played, grew excited, came and went; but when it sensed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it crouched and did not stir, out of dislike of harming him. Our proof against them is what Malik narrated from Ibn Shihab, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that Abu Hurayrah said: "Had I seen the gazelles grazing in Madinah, I would not frighten them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What lies between its two lava-plains (laabatay) [[The two lava-plains of Madinah are two black rocky tracts that enclose it.]] is sacred." So Abu Hurayrah's saying "I would not frighten them" is evidence that it is not permissible to startle game within the sanctuary of Madinah, just as it is not permissible to startle it within the sanctuary of Makkah. Likewise, Zayd ibn Thabit's snatching the nughs (a bird) from the hand of Shurahbil ibn Sa'd, which he had hunted in Madinah, is evidence that the Companions understood the intent of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in making the game of Madinah sacred, so they did not permit hunting in it nor possessing what is hunted. The basis of Ibn Abi Dhi'b is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Sahih: "O Allah, Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I make Madinah sacred, like what he made sacred of Makkah, and a like amount along with it, its grass shall not be cut (la yukhla khalaha) [[Khala: tender plants while they are moist; yukhla: is cut.]], its trees shall not be felled, and its game shall not be startled." And because...

He prohibited hunting within it, so the penalty became attached to it, as with the Sacred Precinct (*haram*, the sanctuary) of Makkah. Al-Qadi ʿAbd al-Wahhab said: "This view is, in my judgment, more consistent with our principles, especially since the Madinah is, according to our companions, superior to Makkah, and prayer in it is superior to prayer in the Masjid al-Haram."

Among the arguments of Malik and al-Shafiʿi against imposing a penalty (*jaza'*) or taking the spoils (*salab*) from one who hunts in it, according to the well-known position of al-Shafiʿi, is the general sense of the Prophet's statement ﷺ in the *Sahih*: "Madinah is a sanctuary (*haram*) between ʿAyr and Thawr." [ʿAyr is a mountain in the area of Madinah. As for Thawr, some people of hadith hold that its mention here is a mistake by the narrator, and that it is in fact a mountain in Makkah. The correct version is "from ʿAyr to Uhud," which is a rare narration. Some have estimated that the sanctuary of Madinah is the extent between ʿAyr and Thawr. In *al-Nawawi*, al-Qadi said: most narrators in the *Book of al-Bukhari* mention ʿAyr; as for Thawr, some alluded to it by a term, and others left a blank in its place, because they regarded the mention of Thawr here as an error.]

"Whoever introduces an innovation (*hadath*) in it, or shelters an innovator, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels and all people. Allah will not accept from him on the Day of Resurrection any *sarf* or *ʿadl*." [*Sarf* means repentance and *ʿadl* means ransom. It has been said: *sarf* is supererogatory acts and *ʿadl* is obligatory acts. It has also been said other things.]

So the Prophet ﷺ issued a severe threat and did not mention an expiation (*kaffarah*). As for what is reported from Saʿd, that is a view specific to him, as is reported from him in the *Sahih* that he rode to his estate at al-ʿAqiq and found a slave cutting or stripping trees, so he seized him. When Saʿd returned, the slave's people came to him and asked him to return to their boy, or to them, what he had taken from their boy. He said: "God forbid that I return anything that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave me as a reward (*nafl*)," and he refused to return it to them. So his statement "gave me" (*nafalanihi*) apparently indicates a specific ruling. And Allah knows best.

The tenth matter: the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally﴾. Allah mentioned the intentional killer and did not mention the one who errs or forgets. "Intentional" here means one who aims at a thing while knowing he is in a state of *ihram*. The one who errs is one who aims at something and hits game, and the one who forgets is one who intends to hunt and does not remember his *ihram*. The scholars differed on this in five views.

The first: what al-Daraqutni transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Expiation applies only to the intentional act, and they were made strict in the case of error so that they would not repeat it."

The second: that his words "intentionally" came out in accordance with what is usual, so the rare case was assimilated to it, like the principles of the Sharia.

The third: that there is no penalty for the one who errs or forgets. This was the view of al-Tabari and of Ahmad ibn Hanbal in one of his two narrations, and it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr. Tawus and Abu Thawr also held this, and it is the view of Dawud. Ahmad relied on the argument that when Allah singled out the intentional act with mention, this indicates that other cases are different. He added that the original state is the freedom of the obligation (*baraʾat al-dhimmah*), so whoever claims it is occupied must produce evidence.

The fourth: that one is penalized for intentional, mistaken and forgetful killing. Ibn ʿAbbas said this, and it is reported from ʿUmar, Tawus, al-Hasan, Ibrahim and al-Zuhri. Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Hanifah and their companions also held this. Al-Zuhri said: the penalty for the intentional act is required by the Qurʾan, and for error and forgetfulness it is required by the *Sunnah*. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: if by the *Sunnah* he means the reports from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿUmar, then how excellent they are, and how fine a model they are.

The fifth: that one kills intentionally, intending to kill but forgetting one's *ihram*. This is the view of Mujahid, based on the Exalted's words after this: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾. He said: had he been mindful of his *ihram*, the punishment would have been required on the first occasion. He said: this shows that he intended to kill the game while forgetting his *ihram*. Mujahid said: if he was mindful of his *ihram*, then he has exited the state (*halal*) and has no valid pilgrimage (*hajj*), since he committed a prohibition of his *ihram*, so it is nullified for him, as if he spoke during prayer or broke his ablution in it. He said: whoever errs, that is the one for whom it suffices.

Our evidence against Mujahid is that Allah required the penalty and did not mention invalidation (*fasad*), and there is no difference between being mindful of the *ihram* or forgetting it. The analogy of pilgrimage to prayer is not valid, since they are different. It has been reported from him that there is no ruling against one who kills intentionally, and he seeks forgiveness from Allah, and his pilgrimage is complete. Ibn Zayd also held this.

Our evidence against Dawud is that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the hyena (*duba*), and he said: "It is game," and he made a ram the penalty for a *muhrim* who hunts it, and he did not say "intentionally" or "by mistake."

Ibn Bukayr, one of our scholars, said: the Exalted's words "intentionally" did not intend to excuse error. Rather, he meant "intentionally" to clarify that it is not like the human being, for whose killing no expiation is prescribed for intentional killing, while in hunting there is an expiation. He did not intend to drop the penalty for accidental killing. And Allah knows best.

The eleventh matter: if he kills game repeatedly while in *ihram*, a penalty is imposed each time he kills, according to the view of Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Abu Hanifah and others, because of Allah's words: ﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in *ihram*. Whoever among you kills it intentionally, the penalty is the like of what he killed from the livestock﴾. The prohibition is continuous and persists upon him as long as he is in *ihram*, so whenever he kills it, the penalty is necessarily due from him for that reason.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "He is not judged twice in Islam. He is judged only once. If he returns a second time, he is not judged, and it is said to him: Allah will take retribution from you," based on His words: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾. This was also the view of al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Mujahid and Shurayh.

Our evidence against them is what we have mentioned about the continuation of the prohibition during *ihram*, and the address (*khitab*) being directed at him in the religion of Islam.

The twelfth matter: the words of the Exalted: ﴿then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾. In it there are four readings. "*Fa-jaza'un mithlu*" with *jaza'un* in the nominative and with tanwin, and *mithlu* in apposition as a qualifier, the predicate being implied. The estimate is: "then upon him is a penalty equivalent, obligatory or required, from the livestock." This reading requires that the *mithl* be the penalty itself.

"*Jaza'u*" in the nominative without tanwin, and "*mithlu*" in the construct state (*idafah*), meaning: "then upon him is a penalty of the like of what he killed." Here "*mithlu*" is inserted (*muqhamah*), as in your saying: "I honour the like of you," while you mean "I honour you." A parallel to this is the Exalted's words: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among people like one who is in darkness?﴾ The estimate is "like one who is in the darknesses." And His words: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, meaning "there is nothing like Him." This reading requires that the penalty be other than the like, since a thing is not attributed to itself.

Abu ʿAli said: the obligation is for the penalty for the slain game, not the penalty for the like of the slain game, and the construct state requires the penalty for the like and not the penalty for the slain game. This is also al-Shafiʿi's view, as will come.

His words "from the livestock" (*min al-naʿam*) are a qualifier of *jaza'* in both readings together. Al-Hasan read *min al-naʿm* with a sukun on the ʿayn, and that is a dialect form. ʿAbd al-Rahman read *fa-jaza'un* with *raf'* and tanwin and *mithla* with *nasb*. Abu al-Fath said: *mithla* is in the accusative governed by the penalty itself, and the meaning is that the like of what he killed is to be given as penalty. Ibn Masʿud and al-Aʿmash read *fa-jaza'uhu mithlu* with the *ha'* made explicit, and it may refer either to the game or to the hunter who killed it.

The thirteenth matter: the penalty is required only by killing the game, not merely by taking it, as the Exalted said. In the *Mudawwana*: whoever hunts a bird, plucks its feathers, then holds it until its feathers grow back and it flies away, he said: there is no penalty upon him. [He said: and likewise, if he cuts off the wing of game, or its leg, or any part of its limbs, and its life is spared and it recovers and joins the game, then there is nothing upon him. It has been said: upon him is a part of the penalty proportionate to what he diminished. If it escapes and he does not know what became of it, then upon him is its penalty. If the game is disabled and does not join the game, or he leaves it in a frightening state, then upon him is its full penalty.]

The fourteenth matter: two kinds of game are subject to penalty: land animals and birds. For land animals, the penalty is the counterpart in form and appearance. For the ostrich there is a camel (*badanah*), for the wild ass and the wild cow there is a cow, and for the gazelle there is a sheep. This is also al-Shafiʿi's view. The least that suffices according to Malik is what is affordable from the offering (*hady*), which should be fit as a sacrifice (*udhiyyah*), such as a six-month-old lamb (*jadhaʿ*) of sheep and a two-year-old of other species. If its penalty does not reach that, then there is feeding (*itʿam*) or fasting (*siyam*).

For all pigeons, the penalty is its value, except the pigeons of Makkah, for in a pigeon of Makkah there is a sheep, following the early authorities in this matter. The *dubsi* (a type of ring-dove), the *fawakhit*, the *qumri* and the ones with collars are all pigeons. Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam related from Malik that in the pigeons of Makkah and their young there is a sheep. He said: and likewise the pigeons of the Sacred Precinct. He said: and in the pigeons of the non-sacred area (*hill*) there is an assessment (*hukumah*).

Abu Hanifah said: the likeness is considered only in value, not in form. So the game is valued in dirhams at the place where it was killed, or at the nearest place to it if game is not sold at the place of killing. Then he buys with that value an offering if he wishes, or buys food with it and feeds the poor, giving each poor person half a *sa'* of wheat, or a *sa'* of barley, or a *sa'* of dates.

As for al-Shafiʿi, he holds that the likeness is from livestock, and then the likeness is valued, as in the case of destroyed property, where the likeness is valued and the value of the likeness is taken like the value of a thing, since the likeness is the original in the obligation. This is clear, and the reading with the construct state (*fa-jaza'un mithlu*) is interpreted accordingly.

Abu Hanifah argued: if resemblance in form were required, then for the ostrich there would be a camel, for the ass a cow, and for the gazelle a sheep, and He would not have made it subject to the judgment of two just men, because that is known, so it would not need deliberation and consideration. The judgment of two just men and consideration is needed only where the situation is unclear and the path of reasoning about it is confused.

Our evidence against him is the Exalted's words: ﴿then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾, to the end of the verse. The word *mithl* by its apparent meaning requires the likeness in outward creation and form, not in meaning. Then He said "of the livestock," which specifies the kind of likeness. Then He said: ﴿judged by two just men among you﴾, and this pronoun refers to a likeness from livestock, since no other thing had been mentioned to which the pronoun could refer. Then He said: ﴿as an offering to reach the Kaʿbah﴾, and what can be conceived as an offering is a likeness of the slain livestock. As for value, it cannot be conceived as an offering, and it has no mention in the verse itself. So what we have mentioned is correct. And praise belongs to Allah.

As for their statement: "if resemblance were required, He would not have made it subject to two just men," the answer is that the requirement of two just men is due only to the examination of the state of the game, whether young or old, and of what has no kind among what has a kind. Extending what has no explicit text to what does have an explicit text is what is at issue.

The fifteenth matter: If someone in a state of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage) in Makkah shuts the door of his house on pigeon chicks so that they die, he must pay a sheep for each chick. Malik said: For young game the same as for adult game is due, and this is the view of Ata'. According to Malik, nothing is redeemed with an 'anaq (a female kid of goats) or a jafrah (a weaned kid)·· [The 'anaq is a female young of goats. The jafrah is a young goat.] Malik said: That is like blood-money (diyah), where the young and the old are alike. For the dabb (spiny-tailed lizard) and the yarbu' (jerboa) he holds that their value is due as food. Some of the people of Madinah differ with him regarding young game and regarding the consideration of the jadha' (a six-month-old kid) and the thani (a two-year-old), and they say what 'Umar said: For the hare an 'anaq is due, and for the yarbu' a jafrah is due. Malik transmitted this as a statement of 'Umar (mawquf). Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: For the dab' (hyena) that a muhrim kills there is a ram; for the zabi (gazelle) a sheep; for the hare an 'anaq; and for the yarbu' a jafrah. [He said: The jafrah is one that has grazed.] In another route, I said to Abu al-Zubayr: What is the jafrah? He said: The one that has been weaned and grazed. Al-Daraqutni recorded it. Al-Shafi'i said: For the ostrich a camel (badanah) is due; for its chick a young camel (fasil); for the wild ass a cow; and for its young (sakhl) a calf. This is because Allah Most High ruled with equivalence in form, and young and old differ, so the young and the old must be considered in it as in all other destroyed things. Ibn al-Arabi said: This is correct, and it is the choice of our scholars. They said: If the game is one-eyed, lame, or broken, the equivalent would be in the same condition, so that equivalence is realized, and the destroyer is not obligated beyond what he destroyed. Our proof is the words of Allah Most High: ﴿Then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾, and He did not distinguish between young and old. His saying "hadyan" (as an offering) requires what the name hady (offering) covers, by the rule of unrestricted application, and that requires a complete offering. And Allah knows best.

The sixteenth matter: For ostrich eggs, according to Malik, a tenth of the price of a camel is due. For eggs of the Makkan pigeon, according to him, a tenth of the price of a sheep is due. Ibn al-Qasim said: It is the same whether or not there is a chick in it, as long as the chick has not cried out after breaking out of the shell. If it cried out, the full penalty is due, like the penalty for the adult of that bird. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: It is determined by the judgment of two just men. Most scholars hold that for the eggs of every bird the value is due. Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas, from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled concerning an ostrich egg that a muhrim had broken that the penalty is its price in measure. Al-Daraqutni recorded it. It is also related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: For every ostrich egg there is a day's fast or feeding a poor person [.

The seventeenth matter: As for what has no equivalent, such as sparrows and elephants, its penalty is the value of its meat or its equivalent in food, not what is intended for it of other uses, because what is taken into account in what has an equivalent is that its equivalent is obligatory, and if the equivalent is absent, the value stands in its place, as in usurpation and other cases. And because people are of two views: one that considers value for all game, and one that restricts value to what has no equivalent among livestock. So this entails consensus on taking value into account in what has no equivalent. As for the elephant, it was said: For it a camel (badanah) of the large Hijan camels that have two humps is due, which are white Khurasani camels. If none of these camels is found, then its value in food is considered, and that is what is due. The procedure for it is that the elephant is placed in a boat, and the point to which the boat sinks in the water is marked. Then the elephant is taken out and food is placed in the boat until it sinks to the same mark where it sat with the elephant. That is its equivalent in food. As for considering its value, it would have a great price because of its bulk and tusks, so the food would become excessive, and that is harmful.

The eighteenth matter: Allah Most High says: ﴿Judged by two just men among you﴾. Malik narrated from Abd al-Malik ibn Qurayb, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, that a man came to Umar ibn al-Khattab and said: I and a companion of mine ran two horses racing toward a mountain pass (thaghrat thaniyyah) (a path climbing a mountain), and we struck a gazelle while we were both in ihram. What do you think? 'Umar said to a man beside him: Come, let you and me judge it. They judged against him a she-goat. The man turned away saying: This is the Commander of the Believers, who cannot judge about a gazelle until he calls a man to judge with him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab heard the man's words, so he summoned him and asked him: Do you recite Surah al-Ma'idah? He said: No. He asked: Do you know the man who judged with me? He said: No. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If you had told me you recite Surah al-Ma'idah, I would have beaten you severely. Then he said: Allah, glorified is He, says in His Book: "Judged by two just men among you, as an offering reaching the Ka'bah," and this is Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf.

The nineteenth matter: If the two judges agree, the judgment is binding. This is also the view of al-Hasan and al-Shafi'i. If they disagree, another is considered. Muhammad ibn al-Mawwaz said: One does not adopt the higher of their two opinions, because that is acting without an arbitration. Likewise, one does not shift from the equivalent in form to food once they have judged by it, because it is a matter already binding, said Ibn Sha'ban. Ibn al-Qasim said: If he commissioned them to judge by the equivalent of the penalty and they did so, and then he wished to shift to food, it is permitted. Ibn Wahb, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-'Utbiyyah: It is part of the Sunnah that the two judges give the one who struck the game the option, just as Allah gave him the option to offer "an offering reaching the Ka'bah, or expiation: feeding the poor, or the equivalent of that in fasting." If he chooses the offering, the two judge against him with what they consider a counterpart to what he destroyed, between that and the equivalent of a sheep, since a sheep is the least of offerings. If it does not reach a sheep, they judge it in food, and then he is given the option either to feed it, or to fast one day for each mudd (a measure of grain). Malik said the same in al-Mudawwanah.

The twentieth matter: The judgment is to be renewed in every case where a judgment has or has not been given. Yet it would be good to rely on the judgment of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, concerning what they judged regarding the penalty for game. It is related from Malik that everything other than the pigeons of Makkah, the wild ass, the gazelle, and the ostrich requires a judgment, and for these four one may rely on the judgment of the earlier generations, may Allah be pleased with them.

The twenty-first matter: The wrongdoer may not be one of the two judges. This is the view of Abu Hanifah. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said that the wrongdoer may be one of the two judges. This is a laxity on his part, for the apparent meaning of the verse requires a wrongdoer and two judges. Dropping part of the number destroys the apparent meaning and corrupts the sense, because a man's judgment in his own case is not permitted. Had it been permitted, he would have been self-sufficient and needed no one else, since it is a judgment between him and Allah Most High. So the addition of a second man to him is evidence for the requirement of judgment by two men.

The twenty-second matter: If a group of muhrims share in killing a game animal, Malik and Abu Hanifah said: Each one owes a full penalty. Al-Shafi'i said: They all owe one expiation together, based on the judgment of 'Umar and Abd al-Rahman. Al-Daraqutni narrated that the clients (mawali) of Ibn al-Zubayr entered ihram, and when a hyena passed by them they struck it with their staffs and hit it. It weighed on their minds, so they went to Ibn 'Umar and told him. He said: All of you owe a ram. They said: Or does each one of us owe a ram? He said: You are too numerous for that (inna-kum la-mu'azzaz bi-kum), so all of you owe one ram. [Linguists said: la-mu'azzaz bi-kum means "strictly bound to you," i.e., "severely burdened by you."] [The clients had earlier asked Ibn 'Umar's companion, who issued a separate expiation to each of them; then they asked Ibn 'Umar and told him the ruling of the one who had given them the verdict, and he said: "You are too numerous for that..." etc.] It is also related from Ibn Abbas concerning a people who killed a hyena: he said: They owe a ram, which they share among themselves. [Yatakharajuh means each takes his share of its price.] Our proof is the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever among you kills it intentionally, then a penalty equal to what he killed of the livestock﴾, and this is an address to every killer. Each of those who kill the game is a full killer of a soul, by the evidence of the killing of a group for one person. Had it not been so, retaliation (qisas) would not be obligatory for them, and we have said that it is obligatory by consensus between us and them, so what we have said is established.

The twenty-third matter: Abu Hanifah said: If a group kills game in the sacred territory, all of them being in a non-ihram state, they owe one penalty. This differs from the case where muhrims kill it in the non-sacred area and in the sacred area, for that does not differ. Malik said: Each one of them owes a full penalty, based on the principle that a man becomes a muhrim by entering the sacred territory just as he becomes one by pronouncing the talbiyah for ihram, and each of the two acts has attached to him a status to which a prohibition is attached, so he violates it in both states. The proof of Abu Hanifah is what the judge Abu Zayd al-Dabusi mentioned: He said: The secret of it is that the offense in ihram is against the act of worship, and each of them committed what his ihram forbids. When non-muhrims kill game in the sacred territory, they have destroyed a sacred creature, in the same position as if a group destroyed an animal, for each of them is a killer of an animal, and they share in its value. Ibn al-Arabi said: Abu Hanifah is stronger than us, and this argument our scholars belittle, yet it is hard for us to refute.

The twenty-fourth matter: Allah Most High says: ﴿As an offering reaching the Ka'bah﴾. The meaning is that if the two judges rule with an offering, it is treated as an offering is treated, by marking it (ish'ar) and garlanding it (taqlid), and it is sent from the non-sacred area to Makkah, and it is slaughtered and given in charity there, because of His saying "an offering reaching the Ka'bah." He did not mean the Ka'bah itself, for the offering does not reach it, since it is in the mosque. He meant the sacred territory (al-haram), and there is no disagreement on this. Al-Shafi'i said: The offering does not need to be sent from the non-sacred area, on the basis that the small offering is due for small game, and it is bought in the sacred territory and offered there.

**The twenty-fifth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: "(or as expiation, the feeding of needy people)". The *kaffarah* (expiation) applies only to game, not to the *hady* (sacrificial offering). Ibn Wahb said: Malik said, "The best I have heard concerning one who kills game and is judged for it is that he values the game he killed, and considers how much it is worth in food, and then feeds each needy person one *mudd* (a measure of about a handful and a half), or fasts one day in place of each *mudd*." Ibn al-Qasim reported from him: "If he values the game in dirhams and then values the dirhams as food, that suffices him, but the first is correct." Abdullah ibn Abd al-Hakam said the same, and he added: "He has a choice among these three, and whichever he does suffices him, whether he is wealthy or poor." Ata' and the majority of jurists said this as well, because "or" (*aw*) indicates choice. Malik said: "Everything in the Book of God concerning expiations that says 'this or that', its bearer has a choice in it, and he does whichever he wishes."

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "If the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) kills a gazelle or the like, he must sacrifice a sheep to be slaughtered in Makkah. If he does not find one, then he must feed six needy persons. If he does not find that, he must fast three days. If he kills a wild goat (*iyal*) or the like, he must sacrifice a cow. If he does not find one, he feeds twenty needy persons. If he does not find that, he fasts twenty days. If he kills an ostrich or a wild ass, he must sacrifice a camel, and if he does not find one, he feeds thirty needy persons, and if he does not find that, he fasts thirty days. The food is one *mudd* for each of them, for their satiety." [Editor's note: *iyal* is said to be pronounced with three vowelings, and the correct form is with a kasra; it is the male of the wild goats (*awwal*).] [Editor's note: in some manuscripts: "then he must give in its place food, thirty needy persons."]

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Hammad ibn Salamah said: the meaning of "or as expiation, the feeding of [needy people]" is if he does not find the *hady*. Al-Tabari related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "When the muhrim hunts game, he is judged for its equivalent. If he finds its equivalent, he slaughters it and gives it in charity. If he does not have its equivalent, its equivalent is valued in dirhams, then the dirhams are valued in wheat, and then he fasts one day for every half *sa'* (a measure)." He said: "The purpose of mentioning food is to clarify the matter of fasting, so whoever does not find food, he finds its equivalent." He also traced this to al-Suddi. This view is objected to on the apparent wording of the verse, for it contradicts it.

**The twenty-sixth issue:** The scholars differed about the time at which the destroyed property is considered. Some said: the day of the destruction. Others said: the day of the judgment. Others said: the destroyer is obliged to pay the higher of the two values, from the day of the destruction until the day of the ruling. Ibn al-Arabi said: "Our scholars differed as the others did. The correct view is that the value is owed on the day of the destruction, and the proof of that is that the existence [of the thing] was a right of the one whose property was destroyed. So when the destroyer annihilated it, he became obliged to restore it with its like, and that is at the time of its non-existence."

**The twenty-seventh issue:** As for the *hady*, there is no disagreement that it must be in Makkah, because of His saying, Exalted is He: "as an offering reaching the Ka'bah." As for feeding, the opinion of Malik differed on whether it is in Makkah or at the place of the offence. Al-Shafi'i held that it is in Makkah. Ata' said: whatever is of blood or food is in Makkah, and he may fast wherever he wishes, and this is Malik's view concerning fasting, and there is no disagreement about it.
