The Qadi Abu Muhammad Abd al-Wahhab said: it is not permissible to give any part of the penalty for game outside the Haram, except fasting. Hammad and Abu Hanifah said: one makes expiation at the place of the offence, without restriction. Al-Tabari said: one makes expiation wherever he wishes, without restriction. As for the view of Abu Hanifah, it has no basis in reasoning and no support in narration. As for those who said he may fast wherever he wishes, it is because fasting is an act of worship specific to the one who fasts, so it is valid in every place, like the fasting of all other expiations and other things. As for the basis of the view that the food must be in Makkah, it is because it is a substitute for the *hady* or its counterpart, and the *hady* is a right of the needy of Makkah, so its substitute or counterpart must be in Makkah. As for those who said it may be in any place, they reason by analogy with every food and *fidyah* (ransom), since these are permissible in any place. And God knows best.

**The twenty-eighth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾. *Al-'adl* and *al-'idl*, with the vowel of the letter *ayn* either fatha or kasra, are two dialects, and both mean "the like", as said by al-Kisai. Al-Farra' said: *'idl* of a thing with a kasra on the *ayn* means its like of the same kind, and with a fatha on the *ayn* means its like of a different kind. This view is transmitted from al-Kisai. You say: "I have the equivalent of your dirhams in dirhams," and "I have the equivalent of your dirhams in garments." The sound report from al-Kisai is that they are two dialects, and this is the view of the Basrans. It is not valid that fasting should resemble food in a way closer than in number. Malik said: one fasts a day for every *mudd*, even if that exceeds two or three months, and al-Shafi'i said likewise. Yahya ibn Umar, one of our companions, said: "It is said: how many men would be satisfied by this game? The number is known. Then it is said: how much food would satisfy that number? If he wishes, he gives that food, and if he wishes, he fasts the number of his *mudds*." This is a good view, one in which caution is exercised, for the value of the game in food may be small, and by this consideration the feeding becomes more. Among the people of knowledge are those who do not allow the fasting of the penalty to exceed two months, saying: "for it is the highest of the expiations." Ibn al-Arabi chose this view. Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, said: one fasts a day for every two *mudds*, by analogy with the ransom for harm (*fidyat al-adha*).

**The twenty-ninth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾. "Taste" (*dhawq*) here is used figuratively, as in His saying: "Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble" [Surah al-Dukhan 44:49], and His saying: "So God caused them to taste the garment of hunger and fear" [Surah al-Nahl 16:112]. The literal meaning of tasting is in the sense of the tongue, and in all of this it is figurative. From it is the hadith: "Whoever is content with God as Lord has tasted the flavour of faith..." [the hadith continues]. *Al-wabal* means evil consequence. The *mar'a al-wabil* (noxious pasture) is that which one suffers from after eating it. A food is *wabil* if it is heavy, and from it is the saying [of the poet, the verse of Tarafah, whose first half is: "So she passed by like a doe with a ridge of mane" ]:
"A noble lady of an old man, like a heavy burden, quarrelsome." [Editor's note: *yalandad* means very contentious.]
He expressed "his affair" to mean his whole state.

**The thirtieth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God has pardoned what has passed﴾. This means in your pre-Islamic time, from your killing of game, as said by Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and a group with him. It is also said: before the revelation of the expiation.

(﴿And whoever returns﴾), meaning to what was forbidden, (﴿God will take retribution from him﴾), that is, by the expiation. It is also said: the meaning of "God will take retribution from him" is in the Hereafter, if he regards it as lawful, and he is disbelieving in outward judgment. Shurayh and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he is judged for it the first time, and if he returns, he is not judged for it again, and it is said to him: "Go, God will take retribution from you," meaning your sin is too great to be expiated, just as the false oath has no expiation according to most of the people of knowledge, because of the greatness of its sin. Those who are scrupulous guard against retribution by making expiation. It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas: "His back shall be filled with lashes until he dies." It is narrated from Zayd ibn Abi al-Mu'alla that a man killed game while in the state of ihram, and he was pardoned for it, then he returned, and God, Mighty and Majestic, sent down fire from the sky and it burned him. This is a lesson for the community and a deterrent for transgressors from disobedience.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God is Mighty, Owner of retribution﴾. "Mighty" means invincible in His dominion, and nothing He wills is withheld from Him. "Owner of retribution" against whoever disobeys Him, if He wills.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 96 (part 1 of 2):

There are thirteen issues in this verse.

The First: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾. This is a ruling permitting the game of the sea, which is everything that is caught of its fish. Here "game" (ṣayd) refers to what is caught (al-maṣīd), and it is attributed to the sea because it comes from the sea by means of it. The discussion of "the sea" has already passed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 388], and all praise is due to God. And "as an enjoyment" (matāʿan) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: you are given enjoyment by it as an enjoyment.

The Second: His saying, exalted is He: (wa-ṭaʿāmuhu) "and its food." Ṭaʿām (food) is a homonymous term (lafẓ mushtarak). It is applied to everything that is eaten, and it is applied to a specific edible, such as water alone, wheat alone, dates alone, or milk alone. It may also be applied to sleep, as has been mentioned previously. Here it is an expression for what the sea casts up and what floats upon it. Al-Daraqutni transmitted with a chain (asnada) from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding the words of God, mighty and majestic: "Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as an enjoyment for you and for the travelers" (the verse), that "its game is what is caught, and its food is what the sea casts up" [the addition in brackets is from al-Daraqutni's version of Ibn ʿAbbas's report]. The same is related from Abu Hurayrah, and it is the view of a great many of the Companions and the Followers. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "its food is its carrion," and this has the same meaning. It is further related from him that he said: "Its food is what is salted of it and remains," and a group held this view along with him. Some people said: "Its food is its salt, which forms from its water, and all other things in it of plants and the like."

The Third: Abu Hanifah said: the floating fish is not eaten, while other fish are eaten, and no animal of the sea is eaten except fish. This is also the view of al-Thawri in the transmission of Abu Ishaq al-Fazari from him. Al-Hasan disliked eating floating fish. It is related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, that he disliked it; and it is also related from him that he disliked eating the jirri [the jirri is a kind of fish with a long back and a wide mouth, having no bone except the jaw bones and the spine], but it is also related from him that he permitted eating all of it, and this is more sound. ʿAbd al-Razzaq mentioned it from al-Thawri, from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, from ʿAli, who said: "Locusts and fish are slaughtered (dhakī)." Thus the report from ʿAli differs regarding eating floating fish, whereas there is no disagreement that Jabir [in one manuscript: Ibn Zayd] disliked it. This is also the view of Tawus, Muhammad ibn Sirin, and Jabir ibn Zayd. They argued from the generality of God's saying: "Forbidden to you is carrion" [al-Ma'idah 5:3]. They also cited what Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni transmitted from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Eat what the sea recedes from (ḥasara), what it casts up, and what you find dead or floating upon the water, do not eat." Al-Daraqutni said: ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn ʿUbayd Allah alone transmitted it from Wahb ibn Kaysan from Jabir, and ʿAbd al-ʿAziz is weak and is not to be used as proof. Sufyan al-Thawri transmitted from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ, something similar. Al-Daraqutni said: none traced it to al-Thawri except Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, and Waki', the two ʿAdanis [the text in the originals reads thus except in one manuscript, where a part has dropped], ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Mu'ammal, Abu ʿAsim, and others opposed him; they transmitted it from al-Thawri as a statement of Jabir (mawqūf), and this is the correct version. Likewise Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Ibn Jurayj, Zuhayr, Hammad ibn Salamah, and others transmitted it from Abu al-Zubayr as mawqūf. Abu Dawud said: this hadith has also been traced through a weak route from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Daraqutni said: it was also transmitted from Isma'il ibn Umayyah and Ibn Abi Dhi'b from Abu al-Zubayr as marfūʿ, but its elevation is not sound; Yahya ibn Sulaym elevated it from Isma'il ibn Umayyah, while others made it stop at the Companion.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Awza'i, and al-Thawri in the transmission of al-Ashja'i said: every animal in the sea is eaten, whether fish or other creatures and all other sea animals, whether it was hunted or found dead. Malik and those who followed him argued with his saying, upon him be blessings and peace, concerning the sea: "Its water is pure, and its carrion is lawful." The most sound of what is transmitted on this subject in terms of chain is the hadith of Jabir concerning the fish called al-ʿAnbar, which is among the most firmly established hadiths; the two Sahihs recorded it. In it: "When we came to Medina, we came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and he said: 'It is a provision God brought out for you. Do you have any of its flesh, so that you may feed us?' We sent him some of it, and he ate it." This is the wording of Muslim. Al-Daraqutni transmitted with a chain from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "I bear witness concerning Abu Bakr that he said: 'A floating fish is lawful for whoever wishes to eat it.'" He also transmitted from him: "I bear witness concerning Abu Bakr that he ate floating fish upon the water." He also transmitted from Abu Ayyub that he boarded the sea with a company of his companions, and they found a fish floating upon the water, and asked him about it; he said: "Is it good, has it not changed?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then eat it and set aside my share of it," and he was fasting. He also transmitted from Jabalah ibn ʿAtiyyah that the companions of Abu Talhah found a floating fish, and asked Abu Talhah about it, and he said: "Send it to me as a gift." ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "Fish is slaughtered, and locusts are entirely slaughtered"; al-Daraqutni transmitted this from him. These reports refute the view of those who disliked it, and they specify the generality of the verse. It is a proof for the majority. However, Malik used to dislike the sea-swine on account of its name, but did not forbid it, and he said: "You call it a swine!" Al-Shafi'i said: "There is no harm in the sea-swine." Al-Layth said: "There is no harm in the carrion of the sea." He said: "Likewise the sea-dog and the sea-horse." He said: "The sea-man and the sea-swine are not eaten."

The Fourth: The scholars differed concerning an animal that lives both on land and in the sea: is its game lawful for the one in ihram or not? Malik, Abu Mijlaz, ʿAta, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others said: every creature that lives on land and has life in it is game of the land; if the one in ihram kills it, he must pay compensation (yaduhu). Abu Mijlaz added to this frogs, tortoises, and crabs. The frog and its kinds are forbidden according to Abu Hanifah, and there is no disagreement from al-Shafi'i that it is not permissible to eat frog; his view differed concerning what has a resemblance on land among the things not eaten, such as the swine and the dog and other things. The sound view is that all of that is eaten, because he expressly permitted the eating of the swine, and it has a resemblance on land to what is not eaten. According to him, the crocodile is not eaten, nor the qirsh [the qirsh is a predatory creature of the salt sea; the dolphin, with a dammah on the dal, is a sea creature that rescues the drowning, and the common people say: "al-Durfil"], nor the dolphin, nor anything that has fangs, because of his peace and blessings being upon him forbidding the eating of every animal with fangs. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: among these are kinds that never leave the water, so they are without doubt game of the sea; and on this basis Malik's answer concerning frogs was derived in the Mudawwanah, for he said: "Frogs are of the game of the sea." It is related from ʿAta ibn Abi Rabah the opposite of what we have mentioned, namely that the greater part of the animal's life is taken into account. He was asked about the water-son (ibn al-ma'), whether it is game of the land or game of the sea, and he said: "Wherever it is most, it belongs to it, and wherever it breeds, it belongs to it," and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. The correct view concerning the water-son is that it is game of the land, as it grazes and eats grain. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: the sound view regarding an animal that lives on land and in the sea is to prohibit it, because two evidences conflict concerning it: the evidence of permission and the evidence of prohibition, so the evidence of prohibition is given precedence out of caution. And God knows best.

**Fifth issue:** His words, exalted is He: ﴿And for the traveller﴾. There are two opinions on this. The first is that it refers to both the resident and the traveller, as in the hadith of Abu Ubayda, that they ate it while they were travelling, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ate it while he was resident. So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that it is lawful for the resident just as He made it lawful for the traveller. The second is that the *sayyara* (caravan or travelling party) are those who ride on it, as in the hadith of Malik and al-Nasa'i: a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), "We ride the sea and carry with us a little water. If we perform ablution with it we become thirsty. Shall we perform ablution with seawater?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Its water is pure, and its dead animals are lawful." Ibn al-Arabi said: "Our scholars said: If the Prophet (ﷺ) had said 'Yes' [in answer to the question], it would only have been permissible to perform ablution with it when there is fear of thirst, because the answer is tied to the question, and so it would have been restricted to that. But the Prophet (ﷺ) began by laying down the principle and explaining the Law, and said: 'Its water is pure, and its dead animals are lawful.'" I say: The answer would have been limited to them and would not extend to others, were it not for the established principle of the Law that its ruling on one person is its ruling on all, except what is explicitly specified, such as his saying to Abu Burda concerning the young goat: "Sacrifice it, but it will not suffice for anyone other than you."

**Sixth issue:** His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the hunting of land game is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾. Prohibition is not a property of physical things; it applies to actions. So the meaning of "the hunting of land game is forbidden to you" is the act of hunting, that is, the prohibition of hunting. Alternatively, *al-sayd* can mean the thing hunted, by naming the object with the verbal noun, as has already been explained. The first is more apparent, because the scholars agree that it is not permissible for one in ihram to accept game given to him as a gift, nor to buy it, nor to hunt it, nor to acquire ownership of it in any way whatsoever. There is no disagreement among the scholars of the Muslims on this, based on the general wording of His words, exalted is He: "The hunting of land game is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram," and on the hadith of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama, as will come.

**Seventh issue:** The scholars differed regarding what a muhrim (one in ihram) may eat of game. Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions, Ahmad, and a view reported from Ishaq, and what is authentically reported from Uthman ibn Affan, hold that there is no harm in the muhrim eating game if it was not hunted for his sake and not on his behalf. They rely on what al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni narrated from Jabir, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The game of land is lawful for you as long as you do not hunt it or have it hunted for you." Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is the best hadith on the subject." Al-Nasa'i said: "Amr ibn Abi Amr is not strong in hadith, though Malik narrated from him." If he eats from game that was hunted for his sake, he must pay compensation (fidya). This is also the view of al-Hasan ibn Salih and al-Awza'i. Malik's position differed regarding game hunted for a specific muhrim. The well-known position in his school is that the muhrim does not eat what was hunted for a specific muhrim or for an unspecified one. He did not adopt the view of Uthman when meat of game was brought to his companions while he was in ihram; Uthman said: "Eat, for you are not like me, since it was hunted for my sake." This is also the view of a group of the people of Madina, and it is reported from Malik. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: eating game is permissible for the muhrim in every circumstance if it was hunted by a non-muhrim, whether or not it was hunted for his sake, based on the apparent wording of His words, exalted is He: "Do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram," which forbids the muhrim to hunt or kill it, but not what others have hunted. They argued with the hadith of al-Bahzi, whose name is Zayd ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning a wild ass that was wounded (al-'aqir), that he commanded Abu Bakr and he divided it among the companions on the journey, narrated by Malik and others. And with the hadith of Abu Qatada from the Prophet (ﷺ), in which he said: "It is only a provision which Allah has provided for you." This is also the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab, and of Uthman ibn Affan in one narration from him, and of Abu Hurayra, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Mujahid, Ata', and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It is reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar that it is not permissible for the muhrim to eat game in any circumstance, whether it was hunted for his sake or not, based on the general wording of His words, exalted is He: "The hunting of land game is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram." Ibn Abbas said: "It is unspecified (mubhama)." This is also the view of Tawus, Jabir ibn Zayd Abu al-Sha'tha'; it is reported from al-Thawri, and Ishaq also held it. They argued with the hadith of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama al-Laythi, that he gave the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a wild ass while he was at al-Abwa' or Waddan, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned it to him. He said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw what was on my face, he said: 'We did not return it to you except that we are in ihram.'" The imams narrated it, and the wording is Malik's. Abu Umar said: Ibn Abbas narrated, through Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Miqsam, Ata' and Tawus from him, that al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama gave the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the meat of a wild ass. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said in his narration: "the haunch of a wild ass, and he returned it dripping blood, as if it had been hunted at that very time." Miqsam said in his narration: "the leg of a wild ass." Ata' said in his narration: "He gave him the forelimb of game, and he did not accept it and said: 'We are in ihram.'" Tawus said in his narration: "a piece of meat of game." Ismail narrated it from Ali ibn al-Madini [[This nisba refers to the city of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); his origin was from there, and he settled in Basra. (al-Ansab).]], from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Jurayj, from al-Hasan ibn Muslim, from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas, except that some of them make it from Ibn Abbas, from Zayd ibn Arqam. Ismail said: "I heard Sulayman ibn Harb interpret this hadith as meaning that the game was hunted for the sake of the Prophet (ﷺ), and were it not for that, eating it would have been permissible." Sulayman said: "Among what shows that it was hunted for the sake of the Prophet (ﷺ) is their saying in the hadith: 'he returned it dripping blood, as if it had been hunted at that very time.'" Ismail said: "Sulayman only interpreted this hadith because it needs interpretation. As for Malik's narration, it does not need interpretation, because the muhrim may not keep a live animal of game without slaughtering it." Ismail said: "According to Sulayman ibn Harb's interpretation, all the hadiths traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) are free of contradiction [in them], if Allah the Exalted wills."

**Eighth issue:** If one enters ihram while holding game in his hand, or while it is in his house with his family, Malik said: if it is in his hand, he must release it; if it is with his family, he is not obliged to release it. This is also the view of Abu Hanifa and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said: whether it is in his hand or in his house, he is not obliged to release it. This is also the view of Abu Thawr, and it is reported from Mujahid and Abd Allah ibn al-Harith the same, and it is reported from Malik. Ibn Abi Layla, al-Thawri, and al-Shafi'i in his other opinion said: he must release it, whether it is in his house or in his hand; if he does not release it, he is liable. The argument for the view of releasing it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the hunting of land game is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾, and this is general regarding ownership and all disposal. The argument for the view of keeping it is that it is a matter which does not prevent the beginning of ihram, so it does not prevent the continuation of ownership of it; its root is marriage.

**Ninth issue:** If a non-muhrim hunts game within the non-sacred area (al-hill) and brings it into the sacred area (al-haram), it is permissible for him to dispose of it in any way, by slaughtering it or eating its meat. Abu Hanifa said: it is not permissible. Our proof is that it is an action performed on game, so it is permissible within the sacred area for a non-muhrim, like keeping it, or buying it, and there is no disagreement about these.

**Tenth issue:** If a muhrim points out game to a non-muhrim (hill) and the non-muhrim kills it, there is disagreement. Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: there is nothing owed by him. This is also the view of Ibn al-Majishun. The Kufans, Ahmad, Ishaq, and a group of the Companions and the Successors said: he owes the compensation (jaza'), because the muhrim, by his ihram, committed himself to abstaining from interfering [with game], so he is liable by pointing it out, like the depositary who points a thief to a theft.

**Eleventh issue:** They differed regarding a muhrim who points out game to another muhrim. The Kufans and Ashhab, among our companions, went to the view that each of them owes a compensation. Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: the compensation is on the muhrim who kills, because of His words, exalted is He: "And whoever of you kills it intentionally," so He tied the obligation of compensation to the killing, which indicates its absence through other than it; and because he is one who points out, so he is not liable for a penalty by his pointing, as if a non-muhrim in the sacred area pointed to game in the sacred area. The Kufans and Ashhab relied on the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Qatada: "Did you point it out or assist in it?" This indicates the obligation of compensation. The first view is more correct. And Allah knows best.

**Twelfth issue:** If a tree grows in the non-sacred area while its branch is in the sacred area, and game which is on it is struck, there is compensation for it, because it was taken within the sacred area. If its root is in the sacred area and its branch is in the non-sacred area, our scholars differed regarding what was taken from it, on two views: compensation, looking to the root; and its negation, looking to the branch.

**Thirteenth issue:** His words, exalted is He: ﴿And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered﴾. This is an emphasis and a reminder after this permitting and forbidding, then He reminded them of the matter of the gathering and the Resurrection, in exaggeration of the warning. And Allah knows best.

There are five issues in this passage.

The first issue concerns the words of Allah, ﴿Allah made the Kaʿbah﴾. Here "made" (jaʿala) carries the sense of "created," and this has been discussed earlier. The Kaʿbah was named "Kaʿbah" because it is square, whereas most Arab houses are round. It is also said that it was named Kaʿbah for its protrusion and prominence, since every protruding, prominent thing is called a kaʿb, whether it is round or not. From this comes kaʿb al-qadam (the ankle bone) and kuʿūb al-qanāh (the joints of a spear). A woman's breast is said to have kaʿaba when it appears prominent on her chest. The house (bayt) is so called because it has a roof and walls, and this is the true meaning of "house," even if no one dwells in it. Allah named it "sacred" (ḥarām) because He prohibited it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Makkah was made sacred by Allah, and people did not make it sacred." Most of this has been fully treated earlier, and all praise is due to Allah.

The second issue concerns the words of Allah, ﴿a means of standing for the people﴾. This means a means of wellbeing and livelihood, because people are secure through it. According to this, "qiyaman" means "by which they stand," that is, they establish themselves by it. It is also said that "qiyaman" means that they stand by its laws. Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim read "qiyaman" as "qiyaman" (with a different vowelling), and both forms derive from the root with a waw, so the waw was changed to a yāʾ because of the kasra before it. It has also been said that the form is "qiwām." The scholars said: The wisdom behind Allah making these things a means of standing for the people is that Allah, glorified is He, created creatures with the natural disposition of human beings, which includes envy, rivalry, severing of ties, turning away from one another, plundering, raiding, killing and vengeance. In the divine wisdom and the primordial will, there was therefore no escape from a restraining force that keeps the present state lasting, and a controlling authority through which the outcome is praiseworthy. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed I am placing a successor (khalīfah) on the earth﴾ (al-Baqarah: 30). So Allah commanded them to have a successor, and placed their affairs in the hands of one person who restrains them from disputing, leads them to unity rather than severance, turns the oppressor away from the oppressed, and keeps every hand in control of what it governs. Ibn al-Qāsim narrated, saying: Mālik told us that ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "The ruler restrains more than the Qur'an restrains." Abū ʿUmar, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned this. The tyranny of a ruler for one year is less harmful than people being in chaos for a single moment. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, established the caliphate for this benefit, so that affairs proceed according to his judgment, and through him Allah restrains the aggression of the masses. Allah, glorified is He, thus magnified the Sacred House in their hearts, placed its awe in their souls, and made its sanctity great among them. Whoever sought refuge in it was protected by it, and whoever was persecuted was safeguarded by being in it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not see that We have made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ (al-ʿAnkabūt: 67). The scholars said: Since it was a specific place that not every oppressed person could reach, and not every fearful person could attain, Allah made the sacred month another refuge. This leads to the third issue.

The third issue: "the sacred months" is a generic noun, and the intended meaning is the four months, by consensus of the Arabs. Allah established their sanctity in their hearts, so they did not terrorize anyone (sirban, meaning a soul) during them, did not seek blood in them, and did not expect vengeance in them. A man would meet the killer of his father, son or brother and would not harm him. They set aside a third of the year, and they joined three of them consecutively, as a respite, a rest, and an opportunity for travel in security and ease. They made one of them stand alone in the middle of the year as a means of showing respect, and this is the month of Rajab, which is called al-Aṣamm and also called Muḍar. It was called Rajab al-Aṣamm because no sound of iron was heard in it, and it is also called Munṣil al-Asinnah, because they would remove the spear-heads from their spears during it. It was the month of Quraysh, and ʿAwf ibn al-Aḥwaṣ said about it:

"The month of the Banū Umayyah, and the offerings, when they are driven, their blood-stained..."

The Prophet (ﷺ) called it "the month of Allah," meaning the month of the family of Allah, and the people of the sacred precinct used to be called "the family of Allah." It may also mean "the month of Allah," because Allah strengthened and reinforced it, since many Arabs did not recognize it. The names of the months will come later in Surat Barāʾah, if Allah wills. Then Allah facilitated for them inspiration, and through the tongues of the noble messengers, legislated the offerings (hadī) and the garlands (qalāʾid). This is the fourth issue: when they took a camel, they would mark it with blood, or hang a sandal on it, or a man would do this to himself by garlanding (taqlīd), as explained earlier at the beginning of the surah. No one would frighten him wherever they met him, and the decisive matter between him and whoever pursued or wronged him was that sanctity. This continued until Allah brought Islam, and made the truth clear through Muḥammad, peace be upon him. Then the religion was arranged in its proper order, and the truth returned to its rightful place. Leadership (imāmah) was then ascribed to him, and its obligation became binding on creation toward him, as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ (al-Nūr: 55), and so on. The rulings on leadership have already passed in al-Baqarah, so there is no point in repeating them.

The fifth issue concerns the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That is so that you may know﴾. "That" refers to Allah's making these matters a means of standing. The meaning is: Allah did that so that you would know that Allah knows the details of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, and knows your interests, O people, both before and after. So look at His kindness toward His servants despite their state of disbelief.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is a warning (takhwif), and ﴿and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a giving of hope (tarjiyah). This meaning has already been discussed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 99:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey (the message)﴾. That is, he does not possess guidance and success (tawfiq), nor the reward; rather, his duty is only the conveying (al-balagh). In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, as has already been mentioned.

Its origin is al-balagh, which is al-bulugh (balagh), meaning arrival and reaching. One says balagha yablughu bulughan, abla-ghahu ibla-ghan, tabalagha tabalugh-an, balagha-hu mubalaghatan, and ballagha-hu tablighan. From this comes al-balagha (eloquence), because it is the conveying of meaning to the soul in a beautiful form of expression. And "tabalagha al-rajul" means when a man affects eloquence while not being eloquent (bali;gh). In this context, "balagh" means sufficiency, because it reaches the measure of need.

(﴿And Allah knows what you reveal﴾) That is, what you make apparent. It is said: "al-sirr bada" and its owner "abda-hu, yubdihi" (he disclosed it).

(﴿and what you conceal﴾) That is, what you keep secret and hide in your hearts of disbelief and hypocrisy.

The Qur'an commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on surah 5, verse 100:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "The impure and the pure are not equal"﴾. On this there are three issues.

The first: al-Hasan said, "the impure and the pure" refers to the lawful and the unlawful. Al-Suddi said it refers to the believer and the disbeliever. It was also said it refers to the obedient and the disobedient, and it was said it refers to the bad and the good, but this is by way of example. The sound view is that the wording is general across all matters: it applies to earnings and deeds, to people, and to forms of knowledge and other things. So the impure in all of these does not prosper and does not yield good, and its outcome is not good however much of it there is, whereas the pure, though little, is beneficial and has a good outcome. Allah, Exalted is He, says: "And the good land brings forth its vegetation by the permission of its Lord, and that which is impure does not come forth except sparsely" (al-A'raf: 58). [[In manuscript j: "beneficial, praiseworthy, beautiful", etc.]] [[See vol. 7, p. 231.]]

A parallel to this verse is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds the same as the corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous the same as the wicked?﴾ (Sad: 28), and His saying: "Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?" (al-Jathiyah: 21). So the impure is not equal to the pure in quantity, in expenditure, in place, or in going. The pure takes the direction of the right, and the impure takes the direction of the left. The pure is in Paradise, and the impure is in the Fire. This is clear. [[See vol. 15, p. 191.]] [[See vol. 16, p. 165.]]

The real meaning of equality (al-istiwa') is persistence in one direction. Similar to it is uprightness (al-istiqamah), and its opposite is crookedness (al-i'wijaj). [[In manuscripts b, j, k, h, and ' : "a single direction" is written as "sanctity".]]

When this has been established, the second issue: some of our scholars said that an invalid sale (al-bay' al-fasid) is annulled and is not enforced, whether by the passage of time in the market or by a change in the body of the item. It is not equal to a valid sale in being enforced; rather it is annulled permanently. The price is returned to the buyer if he has taken it, and if it is destroyed in his possession he is liable for it, because he did not take it as a trust, but rather took it on the basis of a defective contract. It was also said that it is not annulled, out of consideration that if a sale is annulled and returned after the item has been lost, the seller suffers harm and loss: the commodity may be worth one hundred and be returned to him when it is worth twenty, and there is no punishment in property. The first view is more correct because of the generality of the verse, and because of the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our matter, it is rejected." 

I say: when this meaning of non-equality is traced through legal questions, they multiply and become numerous. Among them is the usurper (al-ghasib). This is the third issue: if he builds or plants on the usurped plot, he must remove that building and planting, because it is impure, and return the land. This differs from Abu Hanifah, who said it is not removed and the owner takes its value. What refutes this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is no right for an unjust root." [[The narration "'irq" is with tanwin, which implies an omitted noun: "for the owner of an unjust root," so the root itself is described as unjust and the right belongs to its owner. Or the unjust may describe the owner of the root. If it is narrated as the construct "'irq," then the unjust is the owner of the root and the right belongs to the root, which is one of the roots of a tree.]] (Ghayat al-Nihayah.)

Hisham said: the unjust root is when a man plants in another's land in order to claim it by that means. Malik said: the unjust root is anything that is taken, dug up, and planted without right. Malik said: whoever usurps land and cultivates it, or usurps a house and lives in it, or rents it out, and then its owner claims it back, the usurper owes the rent for what he lived in and must return what he took as rent. His view varied when he did not live in it or did not cultivate the land and left it idle. The well-known position of his school is that he owes nothing for this, but it has also been narrated from him that he owes the rent for all of that. This was chosen by al-Waqqar [[he is Zakariyya ibn Yahya al-Misri]], and it is the school of al-Shafi'i, on the basis of the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is no right for an unjust root."

Abu Dawud narrated from Abu al-Zubayr that two men brought a dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): one of them had planted palm trees in the land of the other. He ruled for the owner of the land with his land and ordered the owner of the palm trees to remove his palms from it. He said: "I saw them, and they were being struck at their roots with axes until they were removed from it, and they were full-grown palm trees ('umm)." [[Umm: that is, complete, in height and in their thickness. Its singular is 'amimah, and its root is 'amam, which was softened and assimilated.]] This is an explicit text. Ibn Habib said: the ruling in this is that the owner of the land has a choice regarding the wrongdoer. If he wishes, he may keep that in his land by paying its value as if it were uprooted; and if he wishes, he may pull it out of his land, and the cost of removal is on the usurper.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from Aisha, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever builds on the dwellings [[rubā' (plural of rab'), meaning a dwelling]] of people with their permission, he has the value; and whoever builds without their permission, he has the materials (al-naqd)." Our scholars said: he has only the value because he built on a place whose benefit he owns. This is like one who builds or plants on a doubtful basis, who has a right: if the owner of the property wishes, he may pay him its value as it stands; and if he refuses, it is said to the one who built or planted: pay the owner the value of the land as bare ground (baraḥ) [[al-barah: the open land that has no crops or trees]]. If he refuses, the two become partners. Ibn al-Majishun said: the explanation of their partnership is that the land is valued as bare, and then valued with its improvements; whatever its value increases by reason of the improvements over its value as bare, the worker becomes a partner with the owner of the land in it. If they wish, they divide it, or they keep it as it is. Ibn al-Jahm [[in manuscript k: Abu al-Jahm]] said: if the owner of the land pays the value of the improvements and takes back his land, he is entitled to its rent for the years that have passed.

It has been narrated from Ibn al-Qasim and others that if a man builds on another man's land with his permission, and then the other becomes entitled to remove it, he gives him the value of his building as uprooted. The first view is more correct, on the basis of the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "then he has the value," and most jurists hold this view.

The fourth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And even if the abundance of the impure impresses you﴾. It was said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is his community, for the Prophet (ﷺ) is not impressed by the impure. It was also said: the intended meaning is the Prophet (ﷺ) himself, and his being impressed means that it became a source of wonder to him, because of what he witnessed of the multitude of disbelievers and unlawful wealth, and the scarcity of believers and lawful wealth.

(So fear Allah, O people of understanding, that you may prosper.) Its meaning has already been mentioned.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 5, verses 101–102 (part 1 of 2)**

There are ten issues concerning it.

**The first issue:**

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related, and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from Anas who said: A man said, "O Prophet of Allah, who is my father?" He said, "Your father is so-and-so." [Variant: "He said."] Then the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾, to the end of the verse.

He also narrated from Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, and in it: "By Allah, you will not ask me about anything except that I will inform you of it as long as I am in this place of mine." A man stood up and said, "Where is my place of entry, O Messenger of Allah?" He said, "The Fire." 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah then stood up and said, "Who is my father, O Messenger of Allah?" He said, "Your father is Hudhafah." And he mentioned the hadith.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah embraced Islam early, emigrated to the land of Abyssinia in the second emigration, and witnessed Badr. He had a sense of humour (*al-da'abah*: jesting). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent him to Khosrow with the letter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When he said, "Who is my father, O Messenger of Allah?" and he said, "Your father is Hudhafah," his mother said to him, "I have never heard of a son more undutiful than you. Are you not afraid that your mother committed what the women of the Jahiliyyah committed, so that she would be disgraced before people's eyes!"

He replied, "By Allah, if he had attributed me to a black slave, I would have been attributed to him."

Al-Tirmidhi and al-Daraqutni related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: When this verse was revealed: ﴿And for Allah is the pilgrimage to the House, a duty upon the people for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:97] (see vol. 4, p. 137), they said, "O Messenger of Allah, is it every year?" He remained silent, and they said, "Every year?" He said, "No. Had I said yes, it would have become obligatory." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: "O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you," to the end of the verse.

There are seven issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God did not appoint﴾. Here *ja'ala* (appoint) means *sammā* (name), as in His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an" [Az-Zukhruf: 3], meaning, "We have named it." The meaning of this verse is that God did not name these, nor did He establish them as a ruling, nor did He prescribe them as an act of worship in the Law. Rather, He decreed them in His knowledge and brought them into existence by His power and will as creation, for God is the Creator of everything, whether good or evil, beneficial or harmful, obedience or disobedience. [See vol. 16, p. 61.]

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾. The *min* (of) here is superfluous. *Bahirah* is a form of *fa'ilah* in the sense of *maf'ulah* (passive), and it follows the pattern of *nati'ah* (an animal killed by a blow) and *dhabihah* (a slaughtered animal). In the Sahih it is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: the *bahirah* is the one whose milk was withheld for the idols (*tawaghit*), so that no one among the people would milk her. As for the *sa'ibah*, it is the one that they would let loose for their gods.

It was also said: the *bahirah* linguistically is the she-camel whose ear is split. It is said, "I slit the ear of the she-camel" (*baharat udhn al-naqah*), meaning I split it widely, and the she-camel is called *bahirah* and *mabhurah*. Slitting the ear was a sign of her being set free. Ibn Sidah said: it is said that the *bahirah* is the one that was left unattended without a herder. It is also said of a prolific she-camel that she is a *bahirah*.[[Ibn Atiyyah said: I think the *bahirah* is one that is well-fed and fattened, and whose milk is abundant, so she is likened to the abundant (sea) by being called a *bahr* (sea).]]

Ibn Ishaq said: the *bahirah* is the daughter of the *sa'ibah*, and the *sa'ibah* is the she-camel that gives birth to ten females in succession with no male among them. Her back was not ridden, her wool was not shorn, and none drank her milk except a guest. Whatever she bore after that female, its ear was split and it was let go with its mother. Its back was not ridden, its wool was not shorn, and none drank its milk except a guest, just as had been done to its mother. So she is the *bahirah*, the daughter of the *sa'ibah*.

Al-Shafi'i said: when a she-camel bears five offspring that are all females, her ear is slit and she becomes forbidden. He said:

*"Forbidden: no one eats her flesh,*
*and we are not in anything like the bahair (forbidden ones)."*

Ibn Uzayz [[So in ج، وا، وك. Perhaps this is Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Uzayz al-Sijistani, author of Gharib al-Qur'an, but it is corrected to be "Uzayr" with a *zay* and *ra'* (unpointed), as in ى، وب، وز. The Taj (under the root *ʿazz*) attributes this definition to Ibn Arafah, from al-Azhari.]] said: the *bahirah* is the she-camel that bears five offspring. If the fifth is a male, they slaughter it, and men and women eat it. If the fifth is a female, they slit its ear, that is, they split it, and its flesh and milk became forbidden to women. This was said by Ikrimah. When she died, it became lawful for women.

The *sa'ibah* is the camel let loose because of a vow that a man would make, that if God delivered him from an illness, or brought him to his home, he would do this. It was not to be kept from pasture or water, and no one would ride it. This is what Abu Ubayd said. The poet said:

*"And a sa'ibah for God that grows fat [[Namat al-naqah: she became fat.]] in thanks,*
*if God restores 'Amir or Mujashi'."*

They may also let loose animals other than the she-camel. When they let loose a slave, he had no *wala'* (right of patronage) owed to him. It was also said: the *sa'ibah* is the one left free with no tether upon her and no herder for her. It is an active participle used in the sense of a passive one, like *'ishatin radiyah* (a pleasing life), meaning *mardiyyah* (pleasing). It comes from *sabat al-hayyah wa-insabat* (the snake slid away and slipped off). The poet said:

*"You slaughtered a she-camel that belonged to my Lord,*
*and a sa'ibah; so rise up for the punishment."*

As for the *wasilah* and the *ham*, Ibn Wahb said that Malik said: the people of the Jahiliyyah would free camels and sheep, letting them loose. As for the *ham*, it was from camels: when a stallion had finished its mating, they would put upon it some of the peacock's feathers and let it loose. As for the *wasilah*, it was from sheep: when they bore female after female, they let them loose. Ibn Uzayz said: the *wasilah* is among sheep. He said: when a ewe bore seven litters, they looked: if the seventh was a male, it was slaughtered and men and women ate of it; if it was a female, it was left among the sheep; and if it was a male and a female together, they said, "She has joined (*wasalat*) her brother," so it was not slaughtered on her account. Its flesh was forbidden to women, and the milk of the female was forbidden to women, unless one of them died, and then men and women ate it.

The *hami* is the stallion when it has been ridden to produce offspring from its offspring. The poet said:

*"Abu Qabus protected her in the might of his kingdom,*
*as the stallion protects the offspring of its offspring."*

It is said: when ten litters were born from its loins, they said, "Its back has been protected," so it is not ridden and is not prevented from pasture or water.

Ibn Ishaq said: the *wasilah* is the ewe that bears ten females in succession over five litters with no male among them. They said, "She has joined," so whatever she bore after that was for the males among them only, not the females, unless one of them died, in which case their males and females shared in eating it.

**The third issue:** Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw Amr ibn Amir al-Khuza'i dragging his *qusb* [[al-Qusb: the intestine.]] in the Fire, and he was the first to let loose the *sawa'ib*." [And in another narration:] "Amr ibn Luhay ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif, brother of the Banu Ka'b, dragging his intestines in the Fire."

Abu Hurayrah also narrated: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to Aktham ibn al-Jawn: "I saw Amr ibn Luhay ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif dragging his intestines in the Fire, and I have never seen a man more like a man than you are like him, nor he like you." Aktham said: "O Messenger of God, I fear that his resemblance will harm me." He said: "No, you are a believer and he is a disbeliever. He was the first to change the religion of Isma'il, to slit the ears of the *bahirah*, to let loose the *sa'ibah*, and to protect the *hami*." [In another narration:] "I saw him, a short man, hairy, with a long forelock [[al-Wafrah: hair of the head that reaches the earlobe.]], dragging his *qudub* in the Fire." [In a narration of Ibn al-Qasim and others, from Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata ibn Yasar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said:] "He will harm his people in the Fire by his stench." This is a *mursal* narration, mentioned by Ibn al-Arabi.

It was also said that the first to innovate that was Junadah ibn Awf. And God knows best. The Sahih suffices. Ibn Ishaq narrated that the cause of setting up the idols and changing the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him) was that Amr ibn Luhay went out from Makkah to Syria. When he arrived at Ma'ab [[Ma'ab (with a fatha on the hamzah and an alif after it): a town at the edge of Syria, in the region of al-Balqa'.]]

...(Mu'jam Yaqut)]] from the land of al-Balqa'. At that time the 'Amaliq, the sons of 'Imliq (also said 'Imlaq), son of Lawadh, son of Sam, son of Nuh, lived there. He saw them worshipping idols and said to them: "What are these idols that I see you worshipping?" They said: "These are idols through which we seek rain and are given rain, and through which we seek victory and are given victory." He said to them: "Will you not give me one of them, that I may take it to the land of the Arabs so that they worship it?" So they gave him an idol called (Hubal). He came with it to Makkah and set it up, and the people began to worship it and venerate it. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), Allah revealed to him: ﴿Allah did not ordain any bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released to roam), sa'iba (a beast released for idols or for vows), wasila (a she-camel or sheep that gave twin females), or ham (a stallion camel released after a number of covers)﴾ [5:103]. "But those who disbelieve," meaning the Quraysh, Khuza'a and the polytheistic Arabs, "fabricate lies against Allah" by saying that Allah had commanded their prohibition. They claimed that they did this to please their Lord and out of obedience to Allah, but obedience to Allah is known only from His word, and they had no word from Allah concerning this. So it was among the things they fabricated against Allah. They also said: ﴿What is in the bellies of these cattle is exclusively for our males﴾ [6:139], meaning the offspring and the milk, ﴿and forbidden to our wives; but if it is born dead, then they share in it﴾ [6:139], meaning if it is born dead, both men and women share in it. This is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are partners in it. He will repay them for their description﴾ [6:139], meaning for their lying, with punishment in the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed, He is Wise and Knowing﴾ [6:139], meaning in prohibition and permission. [[See vol. 7, p. 95.]] And He revealed to him: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made from it what is unlawful and lawful? Say: Did Allah permit you, or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 354.]] [10:59]. And He revealed to him: ﴿Eight pairs﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 95.]] [6:143], and He revealed to him: ﴿And cattle over which the name of Allah is not mentioned, fabricating against Him﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 95.]] [6:138], and the rest of the verse.

The fourth issue: Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, relied, in forbidding endowments (ahbas, sing. habs, meaning waqf) and rejecting awqaf (charitable endowments), on the fact that Allah, the Exalted, criticised the Arabs for what they did, namely releasing animals, protecting them, and withholding their benefits from them. He analogised this to the bahira and the sa'iba. But the difference is clear. If a man intended a plot of land of his and said: "This shall be an endowment, its fruit shall not be picked, its land shall not be cultivated, and no benefit shall be derived from it," it would be permissible to liken this to the bahira and the sa'iba. 'Alqama said to one who asked him about these matters: "Why do you want something that was among the practices of the people of ignorance and has passed away?" Ibn Zayd said something similar.

The majority of scholars hold the view that endowments and awqaf are permissible, except Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf and Zufar. This is also the view of Shurayh, except that Abu Yusuf retracted Abu Hanifa's view on this when Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to him from Ibn 'Awn, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to give his share at Khaybar in charity, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Retain the principal and give its fruit in charity." [[That is, make it a waqf, and permit its fruit to whoever you endow it to.]] Every one who permits endowments uses this as evidence, and Abu 'Umar said it is a sound hadith. Also, the matter is a consensus (ijma') of the Companions, for Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, 'A'isha, Fatima, 'Amr ibn al-'As, Ibn al-Zubayr and Jabir all made awqaf, and their endowments in Makkah and Madinah are well known and widely reported. It is related that Abu Yusuf said to Malik in the presence of al-Rashid: "Endowment is not permissible." Malik said to him: "These endowments are the endowments of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Khaybar and Fadak, and the endowments of his Companions." As for the verse that Abu Hanifa cited, there is no proof in it, because Allah, glorified is He, only criticised them for acting by their own minds without a law addressed to them, or an obligation imposed on them, by cutting off the path of benefit, removing the blessing of Allah, the Exalted, and eliminating the benefit that the servants have in those camels. It is for this reason that these matters differ from the ahbas and awqaf.

Among the evidence that Abu Hanifa and Zufar relied on is what 'Ata' narrated from Ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "I asked Shurayh about a man who made his house an endowment for the last of his children." He said: "There is no endowment against the obligations (fara'id) of Allah." They said: "This is Shurayh, the judge of 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and he ruled in this way." He also cited what Ibn Lahi'a narrated from his brother 'Isa, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, after Surat al-Nisa' was revealed, and Allah had revealed in it the obligatory shares of inheritance: 'He forbids endowment (habs).'" Al-Tabari said: The charity that a donor carries out during his lifetime, in accordance with what Allah permitted through His Prophet and what the Rightly Guided Imams, may Allah be pleased with them, acted upon, is not from the endowment that goes against the obligations of Allah. There is no proof in the words of Shurayh, nor in the words of anyone who contradicts the Sunnah and the practice of the Companions, who are the proof over all creation. As for the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, it was narrated by Ibn Lahi'a, who was a man whose mind became confused in the last part of his life, and his brother is not known, so there is no proof in it. Ibn al-Qassar said this.

If it is asked: How is it permissible for land to be removed by an endowment from the ownership of its owners without passing into the ownership of a owner? Al-Tahawi said: It is said to them: What is objectionable about this, when you and your opponent agree on land that its owner makes a mosque for the Muslims and leaves it open to them, and it has thereby passed from one ownership to no owner, but to Allah, the Exalted? Likewise with water-distribution points, bridges and causeways. Whatever you impose on your opponent as proof against him applies to you in all of this. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: Those who permit endowments differ regarding what the endower may do with it. Al-Shafi'i said: "The endower is forbidden to own it, just as he is forbidden to own the person of a slave, except that it is permissible for him to supervise his charity, and it may remain in his hand to distribute it and spend it on what he designated it for, because 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, continued to supervise his charity, as far as we have been told, until Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, took him." He said: "Likewise 'Ali and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with them both, supervised their charities." Abu Yusuf also held this view. Malik said: "If someone endows land, a palm grove or a house for the needy, and it remains in his hand, he cultivates it, rents it out and distributes it among the needy until he dies while the endowment is still in his hands, it is not an endowment, unless someone other than him approves it, and it becomes an inheritance. Property such as houses, orchards and land is not valid as an endowment, and its taking possession (hawz) is not completed, until someone other than the one who endowed it manages it. This is unlike horses and weapons." This is the summary of his school according to the majority of his followers. Ibn Abi Layla also held this view.

The sixth issue: It is not permissible for the endower to benefit from his endowment, because he has dedicated it to Allah and cut it off from his ownership. Therefore, benefiting from any part of it is a retraction of his charity. He may benefit from it only if he stipulated this in the endowment, or if the endower, or his heirs, become poor, in which case it is permissible for them to eat from it. Ibn Habib narrated from Malik, who said: "If someone endows a property whose yield goes to the needy, his children are given from it when they become poor, whether they were rich or poor on the day he endowed it, but they are not given the whole yield, lest the endowment be obliterated. Instead, a share of it remains for the needy so that the name of endowment remains upon it, and a document is written for the children stating that they are only given from it what they receive on the basis of need, and not as a right to them to the exclusion of the needy."

The seventh issue: Freeing a sa'iba (a slave freed without a guardian relationship, called 'itq al-sa'iba) is permissible. It means that a master says to his slave: "You are free," intending manumission, or says: "I have freed you as a sa'iba." According to the well-known view of Malik's school among the majority of his followers, his walā' (the right of inheritance and patronage) belongs to the community of Muslims, and his manumission is valid. Thus Ibn al-Qasim, Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Ashhab and others narrated from him, and Ibn Wahb also held this view. But Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, who said: "No one should free a sa'iba, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the sale of walā' and its gift." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "This, according to all who hold his view, is interpreted only as disapproval of freeing a sa'iba, and no more. If it occurs, it takes effect, and the ruling on it is what we have mentioned." Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim also narrated from Malik that he said: "I dislike freeing a sa'iba and forbid it. If it occurs, it takes effect, and it becomes an inheritance for the community of Muslims, and its blood money is upon them." Asbagh said: "There is no harm in freeing a sa'iba from the outset," following the well-known view of Malik's school. Isma'il al-Qadi (from k) ibn Ishaq adopted this view and held it as his doctrine. Among his arguments for this is that freeing a sa'iba is widespread in Madinah, and no scholar denies it, and that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and others among the early generations freed slaves as sa'iba. It was also narrated from Ibn Shihab, Rabi'a, Abu al-Zinad, and this is the view of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Abu al-'Aliya, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar and others.

I say: Abu al-'Aliya al-Riyahi al-Basri al-Tamimi (in the originals: al-Taymi; the correct form is what I have recorded), may Allah be pleased with him, was among those freed as a sa'iba. A freedwoman of his from the Banu Riyah freed him as a sa'iba for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, and took him around the circles of the mosque. His name was Rufay' ibn Mihran. Ibn Nafi' said: "There is no sa'iba in Islam today. Whoever frees a sa'iba, his walā' belongs to him." This is also the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Ibn al-Majishun, and Ibn al-'Arabi inclined to it. They based their view on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever frees a sa'iba, his walā' belongs to him," and his saying: "Walā' belongs only to the one who frees." Thus he negated that walā' could belong to anyone other than the one who frees. They also based it on Allah's saying: ﴿Allah did not ordain any bahira or sa'iba﴾, on the hadith "There is no sa'iba in Islam," and on what Abu Qays narrated from Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil, who said: A man said to 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud): "I have freed a boy of mine as a sa'iba. What do you think about him?" 'Abd Allah said: "The people of Islam do not release (yusayyibun) in this way. Only the people of ignorance used to release. You are his heir and the patron of his benefit."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon."﴾ The verse... Its meaning has already been mentioned, and the discussion of it occurred in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 2, p. 210 and what follows.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

There are four issues concerning this.

The first: Our scholars said: the connection of this verse with what precedes it is the warning against what must be guarded against, namely the condition of those whose description has preceded, from among those who relied in their religion upon the imitation (taqlid) of their fathers and forebears. The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that enjoining good and forbidding evil (al-amr bil-ma'ruf wal-nahy 'anil-munkar) is not obligatory when a person is upright, and that no one is held to account for the sin of another, were it not for what has been transmitted of its interpretation in the Sunnah and the sayings of the Companions and the Successors, as we shall mention, God willing.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guard your own souls﴾. Its meaning: guard your souls from sins. You say "'alayka Zaydan" meaning "keep to Zayd" (ilzam Zaydan). It is not permissible to say "'alayhi Zaydan"; rather, this usage occurs in address only with three expressions: "'alayka Zaydan," meaning "take Zayd" (khudh Zaydan); "'indaka 'Amran," meaning "Amr is present with you" (hadarak); and "duunaka Zaydan," meaning "bring Zayd close to you" (qarrib min-ka). He recited:

"O you who draw water, my bucket is for you (dunaka)..."

[[The mani' is the one who goes down to the bottom of the well when its water has run low, so as to fill the bucket. Its completion is:

"Indeed I have seen people praising you."]]

As for his saying "'alayhi rajulan layasnee," it is anomalous (shadhdh).

The third: Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Qays, who said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, addressed us and said: "You recite this verse and interpret it other than its proper interpretation: ﴿O you who believe, guard your own souls; he who strays cannot harm you if you are guided﴾. Indeed I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'When people see the wrongdoer and do not take hold of his hands, Allah will soon envelop them with a punishment from Him.'" Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. Ishaq ibn Ibrahim said: I heard 'Amr ibn 'Ali say: I heard Waki' say: "Nothing is authentically transmitted from Abu Bakr from the Prophet ﷺ, not even a single hadith." I said: "Nor (is there) Isma'il from Qays?" He said: "Isma'il narrated from Qays only as a mawquf (halting at the Companion)." [Note: in one manuscript: Ibn Rahawayh; it is Ibn Ibrahim.]

Al-Naqqash said: this is an excess (ifraat) on Waki's part. Shu'bah narrated it from Sufyan, and Ishaq from Isma'il, marfu'an (traced to the Prophet ﷺ). Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Abu Umayyah al-Sha'bani, who said: I came to Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani and said to him: "How do you deal with this verse?" He said: "Which verse?" I said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, guard your own souls; he who strays cannot harm you if you are guided﴾. He said: "By Allah, you have asked about it one who is well informed. I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he said: 'Rather, enjoin good and forbid evil, until you see stinginess obeyed, desire followed, the world preferred, and every person pleased with his own opinion. Then keep to your own self and leave aside the affair of the common people, for behind you are days in which patience is like grasping a live coal; the one who acts therein will have the reward of fifty men who act like your deeds.'" In another narration it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, the reward of fifty of us, or of them?" He said: "Rather, the reward of fifty of you." Abu 'Isa said: this is a hasan gharib hadith. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: his saying "Rather, of you" — some narrators have omitted this phrase and did not mention it, and it has already been mentioned.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "You are in a time in which whoever abandons a tenth of what he is commanded to do perishes; then there will come a time in which whoever acts upon a tenth of what he is commanded to do is saved." He said: this is a gharib hadith.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "This is not the time of this verse. Speak the truth as long as it is accepted from you; but when it is rejected from you, then (guard) your own souls."

It was said to Ibn 'Umar, at some time of trials: "If you were to leave off speaking in these days, not commanding and not forbidding?" He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: 'Let the one who is present convey (it) to the one who is absent.' We were present, so it is incumbent upon us to convey it to you. And a time will come when, if the truth is spoken in it, it will not be accepted." In a narration from Ibn 'Umar, after his saying "Let the one who is present convey it to the one who is absent," he added: "We were the witnesses and you are the absent ones; but this verse is for peoples who will come after us: if they speak, it will not be accepted from them."

Ibn al-Mubarak said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Guard your own souls﴾ is addressed to all believers, meaning: "Guard the religion of you all," like His saying, Exalted is He: "And do not kill your own souls." It is as if He said: let some of you enjoin others, and let some of you forbid others. So it is evidence for the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil, and "he who strays cannot harm you" refers to the error of the polytheists, the hypocrites and the People of the Book. This is because enjoining good applies to Muslims among the disobedient, as has preceded. A similar meaning has been related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: the meaning of the verse is: "he who strays cannot harm you if you are guided" after enjoining good and forbidding evil.

Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: the verse includes the occupation of a person with his own self, his leaving off probing the faults of people and searching into their conditions, for they do not ask about his condition, so he does not ask about theirs. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: "Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned" [al-Muddaththir 74:38], and "No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another" [al-An'am 6:164]; and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Be a sitter in your house (kun jalisa baytika) and keep to your own self." It is also possible that it refers to the time in which enjoining good and forbidding evil is impossible, so one disapproves in his heart and occupies himself with reforming himself.

I say: there has come a strange hadith narrated by Ibn Lahi'ah: he said: Bakr ibn Sawadah al-Judhami narrated to us from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When it is the head of two hundred, do not enjoin good and do not forbid evil, and keep to your own self."

Our scholars said: the Prophet ﷺ said this only because of the change of the times, the corruption of conditions, and the scarcity of helpers.

Jabir ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse: "O you who believe" — from among the sons of those who slit the ears of the baheera and loosed the sawaib — "guard your own souls in steadfastness upon the religion; the error of the forebears cannot harm you if you are guided." He said: when a man embraced Islam, the disbelievers would say to him: "You have foolished your fathers and misguided them, and you did such and such," so Allah revealed the verse on account of that.

It was also said: the verse concerns the people of desires who are not benefited by admonition. When you know that a people will not accept, but rather mock and show contempt, then keep silent about them.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning the captives whom the polytheists tortured until some of them apostatized; so it was said to those who remained upon Islam: "Guard your own souls; the apostasy of your companions cannot harm you."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it concerns the People of the Book. Mujahid said: it concerns the Jews and Christians and those like them, who hold that the meaning is: the disbelief of the People of the Book cannot harm you if they pay the jizyah.

It was also said: it is abrogated by the command to enjoin good and forbid evil; this was said by al-Mahdawi. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is weak, and its proponent is not known. I say: it has come from Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam that he said: there is no verse in the Book of Allah Exalted that combines the abrogating and the abrogated except this verse. Another said: its abrogating part is His saying: "if you are guided"; and the guidance here is enjoining good and forbidding evil. And Allah knows best.

The fourth: Enjoining good and forbidding evil is obligatory whenever acceptance is hoped for, or whenever there is hope of turning back the wrongdoer, even by force, so long as the one enjoining does not fear harm befalling him personally, or a strife that he would bring upon the Muslims, either by splitting the community or by harm reaching a group of people. When this is feared, then "Guard your own souls" is muhkam (definitive) and obligatory to stop at. And it is not a condition for the one forbidding that he be just, as has preceded; and on this is a group of the people of knowledge. So understand it.

**Part 1 of 5. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 106–108**

There are twenty-seven issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** Makki (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "These three verses are, according to the scholars of meanings, among the most difficult verses of the Qur'an in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), meaning, and ruling." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is the statement of one who has not found the satisfaction (thalj) in its tafsir," and this is clear from his book, may Allah have mercy on him. [[Thalajat al-nafs bi-al-shay' thaljan: the soul was content with a thing and felt reassured by it. It is also said: it recognised it and was delighted by it.]]

I say: What Makki (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned was also mentioned earlier by Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas. I know of no disagreement that these verses were revealed concerning Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada'.

Al-Bukhari, al-Daraqutni and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada' [[in some copies: "from"]] used to travel to Makkah. A young man from Banu Sahm went out with them, and he died in a land where there was no Muslim. He made them his executors, so they handed his estate to his family, but they withheld a silver cup (jam) inlaid with gold. [[Al-Jam: a vessel of silver. Jam makhus: covered with gold sheets like palm fronds.]] The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear: "You have neither concealed nor appropriated anything." Then the cup was found in Makkah, and they said: "We bought it from 'Adi and Tamim." Two men from the heirs of the Sahmi came and swore that this cup belonged to the Sahmi, and that "our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed." He said: So they took the cup, and this verse was revealed concerning them. This is the wording of al-Daraqutni.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Tamim al-Dari concerning this verse, "O you who believe, the testimony between you...", that people were absolved of it except for me and 'Adi ibn Bada'. Both were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. They arrived in Syria with their merchandise, and a client (mawla) of Banu Sahm called Budayl ibn Abi Maryam came to them with merchandise, carrying a silver cup that he intended to present to the king, and it was the greatest part of his trade. He fell ill and made them his executors, and instructed them to deliver what he had left to his family. Tamim said: When he died we took that cup and sold it for a thousand dirhams, then divided the proceeds between me and 'Adi ibn Bada'. When we came to his family we handed over what we had with us, but they missed the cup and asked us about it. We said: "He left nothing but this, and he did not hand over anything else to us." Tamim said: When I embraced Islam after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah, I felt guilty about this, so I went to his family and told them the story, and I paid them five hundred dirhams, and I informed them that my companion had an equal amount. They brought the matter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who asked them for evidence, but they could not produce any. He instructed them to make the other party swear by that which is most sacred to their religion (yuqta' [[yuqta': he magnifies, honours]] bihi 'ala ahl dinihi). So he swore, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "O you who believe, the testimony between you..." up to His words "after their oath." Then 'Amr ibn al-'As and another man from among them stood up and swore, and the five hundred were taken from the hands of 'Adi ibn Bada'.

Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a gharib hadith, and its chain is not sound.

Al-Waqidi mentioned that the three verses were revealed concerning Tamim and his brother 'Adi, who were both Christians, and whose trade was with Makkah. When the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah, Ibn Abi Maryam, client of 'Amr ibn al-'As, came to Madinah intending to go to Syria as a merchant. He went out with Tamim and his brother 'Adi, and he mentioned the hadith.

Al-Naqqash mentioned: It was revealed concerning Budayl ibn Abi Maryam, client of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. He had set out as a traveller by sea to the land of the Negus, and with him were two Christian men, one called Tamim, who was from Lakhm, and 'Adi ibn Bada'. Budayl died while they were on the ship, so he was thrown into the sea. He had written his will and placed it among the goods, and he said: "Deliver these goods to my family." When Budayl died, the two took the money and took from it whatever pleased them. Among what they took was a silver vessel weighing three hundred mithqal, engraved and overlaid with gold. He mentioned the hadith. Sunayd also mentioned it and said: When they reached Syria, Budayl fell ill, and he was a Muslim... the hadith.

**The second issue:** The Almighty's words, ﴿The testimony between you﴾ [5:106]. The word "shahida" (to witness) occurs in the Book of Allah with various different meanings. Among them is His words, ﴿And call to witness two witnesses from among your men﴾ [2:282]. It is said that its meaning is "bring them to be present." Among them is "shahida" meaning "decided," i.e., "knew," as said by Abu 'Ubaydah, as in His words, ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [3:18]. [[See vol. 4, p. 40.]] Among them is "shahida" meaning "acknowledged," as in His words, ﴿But the angels bear witness﴾ [4:166]. [[See vol. 6, p. 19.]] Among them is "shahida" meaning "judged," as in His words, ﴿And a witness from among her family testified﴾ [12:26]. [[See vol. 9, p. 172.]] Among them is "shahida" meaning "swore," as in the case of li'an (mutual oath-cursing). Among them is "shahida" meaning "bequeathed," as in His words, ﴿O you who believe, the testimony between you...﴾.

It has also been said that its meaning here is "presence for the bequest," as one says: "I witnessed the bequest of so-and-so," meaning "I was present for it."

Al-Tabari held that testimony here means oath, so the meaning would be: the oath between you is that two swear. He argued that this is different from the testimony given to the one in whose favour it is made, since there is no ruling of Allah requiring an oath from the witness. Al-Qaffal chose this view. The oath was called testimony because a ruling is established by it just as it is established by testimony.

Ibn 'Atiyyah chose that the testimony here is the testimony that is preserved and then delivered, and he rejected its meaning as presence or oath.

**The third issue:** The Almighty's words, "between you" (baynikum). It has been said that the meaning is "what is between you," so "ma" was deleted, and "testimony" was attributed to the adverbial noun (zarf). It was used as a noun in its literal sense, and this is what grammarians call the object (maf'ul) by extension (al-sa'ah), as the poet said:

*A day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir...*

He meant: "we witnessed in it." [[This is the first half of a line by a man from Banu 'Amir; the second half is: "Few besides me are the spear-thrusts, its additions (nawafiluhu)." Sulaym and 'Amir are two tribes of Qays 'Aylan.]]
