And the Almighty said, ﴿But rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [34:33], meaning "your plotting in them."

And he recited:

*You shake hands with one whom I have met as an enemy, a handshake, while my resentment is withdrawn between your eyes.*

He intended "what is between the two of you" and omitted it, as in His saying ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [Al-Kahf 18:78], meaning "what is between me and you."

The Fourth point: His saying ﴿when death approaches﴾ means when it is about to arrive, for if death has actually arrived, the dying person does not call witnesses. This is like His saying ﴿When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [An-Nahl 16:98], and His saying ﴿When you divorce women, divorce them﴾ [At-Talaq 65:1], and there are many similar examples. The element governing "idha" (when) is the verbal noun "shahadah" (testimony).

The Fifth point: His saying ﴿at the time of the bequest, two﴾. "Hin" (at the time of) is an adverb of time, and the element governing it is "hadara" (approached). His saying "ithnan" (two) by its unrestricted meaning implies two persons, and could mean two men. However, when He said afterwards "dhawa 'adl" (persons of justice), it made clear that He meant two men, because this word applies only to males, just as "dhawatan" [Ar-Rahman 55:48] applies only to females. "Ithnan" is in the nominative as the predicate of the subject "shahadah." Abu 'Ali said: "Shahadah" is nominative as the subject, and the predicate is in His saying "ithnan." The meaning is: the testimony among you concerning your bequests is the testimony of two, so the genitive noun was omitted and the noun in the genitive was placed in its position, as in His saying ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 33:6], meaning "like their mothers." It is also permissible for "ithnan" to be nominative governed by "shahadah," the meaning being: "and among what has been revealed to you" or "let there be among you" that two bear witness, or "let two establish the testimony."

The Sixth point: His saying ﴿persons of justice from among you﴾. "Dhawa 'adl" is a qualifier of "ithnan," and "minkum" is a qualifier following another qualifier. His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ means "or the testimony of two others from other than you," so "min ghayrikum" is a qualifier of "akharan" (two others). This separation is the difficult point in this verse, and the correct treatment is to say that the scholars differed on it in three opinions.

The first opinion: the "ka" and "mim" in His saying "minkum" refer to the Muslims, while "aw akharan min ghayrikum" refers to the disbelievers. On this view, the testimony of People of the Book against Muslims is permissible during travel when it concerns a bequest. This is the most likely reading according to the context of the verse, together with what has been established in the hadiths. This is the view of three Companions who witnessed the revelation: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, 'Abdullah ibn Qays [the text in the original editions reads "Ibn Qays is Abu Musa, and perhaps the correct reading is 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, as is inferred from Ahkam al-Jassas"], and 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas. According to this view, the meaning of the verse from beginning to end is that Allah, exalted is He, informed that His ruling concerning testimony on the testator, when death approaches, is that it should be the testimony of two just persons. If he is on a journey, which is traveling in the land, and no believer is with him, then he should call two witnesses from among those present who are of the disbelievers. When they return and render testimony concerning his bequest, they swear after the prayer [the text in some manuscripts reads "after the testimony"] that they did not lie, did not alter, and that what they testified to is true, that they did not conceal any testimony, and judgment is given on their testimony. If it is afterwards discovered that they lied or betrayed, or committed something similar that is sinful, then two men from among the heirs of the testator swear during the journey, and the two witnesses are obliged to pay what was proven against them. This is the meaning of the verse according to the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, Ibrahim, Shurayh, 'Abidah al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ibn 'Abbas, and others. Among the jurists, Sufyan al-Thawri held this view, and Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam inclined to it because of the number of those who held it. Ahmad ibn Hanbal chose it and said: "The testimony of the dhimmis is permissible against Muslims during travel when no Muslims are present." They all say that "minkum" means from among the believers, and "min ghayrikum" means the disbelievers. Some of them said: this verse was revealed concerning an incident in which there was no believer except in Medina, and they used to travel for trade in the company of People of the Book, idolaters, and various kinds of disbelievers. The verse is considered muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) according to the view of Abu Musa, Shurayh, and others.

The second opinion: His saying, exalted is He, "or two others from other than you" is abrogated (mansukh). This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Nakha'i, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, and other jurists, except that Abu Hanifah differed from them and said: the testimony of disbelievers against one another is permissible, but it is not permissible against Muslims. They argued with His saying ﴿of those whom you find acceptable as witnesses﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:282] and His saying ﴿and call to witness two persons of justice from among you﴾ [At-Talaq 65:2]. They claimed that the verse on debt is among the last revealed, and that it contains "of those whom you find acceptable as witnesses," so it abrogates the earlier ruling. Islam at that time existed only in Medina, so the testimony of its People of the Book was permissible, but today Islam has spread across the earth, so the testimony of disbelievers has lapsed. The Muslims have agreed that the testimony of sinners is not permissible, and disbelievers are sinners, so their testimony is not permissible.

I say: what you have mentioned is correct, but we maintain its implication, namely that this is permissible in the testimony of dhimmis against Muslims concerning a bequest during travel only, out of necessity, when no Muslim is present. When a Muslim is present, it is not permissible. What you claim as abrogation has not come from anyone among those who witnessed the revelation. Three Companions held the first view, and there is no such view from anyone else. Departing from the Companions in favour of others is repugnant to the people of knowledge. This is reinforced by the fact that Surat al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, to the extent that Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and others said: there is no abrogation (naskh) in it. What they claim as abrogation is not valid, for abrogation requires establishing the abrogating text in a manner that makes the two rulings incompatible, with the abrogating text coming later. What they have mentioned cannot be abrogating, because it concerns a different case from the case of the bequest, arising from need and necessity, and it is not impossible for a ruling to differ in cases of necessity. Moreover, a disbeliever may sometimes be trustworthy in the eyes of a Muslim and acceptable to him in a case of necessity. Therefore there is no abrogation in what they have stated.

The third opinion: the verse contains no abrogation. This was said by al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah. According to this view, the meaning of His saying "minkum" is "from among your tribe and your kinsmen," because they are more retentive, more precise, and less prone to forgetting.

The meaning of His words, ﴿or two others from among other than you﴾, is: from outside your kinship and tribe. Al-Nahhas said: This rests on a subtle point of the Arabic language. The sense of "ākhar" (other) in Arabic is of the same kind as the first. You say, "I passed by a noble man and another noble man (karīm ākhar)." The word "ākhar" indicates that the second is of the same kind as the first. According to the people of Arabic (ahl al-ʿarabiyya, the grammarians), it is not permissible to say "I passed by a noble man and a base man ākhar," nor "I passed by a man and a donkey ākhar." From this it follows that the meaning of His words, "or two others from among other than you," is "two just men (ʿadlān)." Unbelievers are not just, so on this reading the view of those who say "from other than you" means from outside your clan among the Muslims is sound. This is a good reading from the standpoint of the language. It may be cited as evidence for Mālik and those who follow his view, since for them the meaning is "from other than you," that is, from other than your tribe. However, this view has been countered by the fact that at the beginning of the verse is ﴿O you who believe﴾, so the address is to the community of believers.

Seventh: Abū Ḥanīfa used this verse as evidence for the admissibility of testimony by unbelievers from among the protected people (ahl al-dhimma, non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule) in matters among themselves. He said: The meaning of "or two others from among other than you" is from among people other than your own religion, which indicates that some of them may testify against others. It is said to him: You do not hold to the implication of this verse, because it was revealed concerning the acceptance of the testimony of the protected people against Muslims, and you do not hold to that, so your argument from it is not valid. If it is said: This verse indicates, by its explicit wording, the admissibility of the testimony of the protected people against Muslims, and by implication (tanbīh) the admissibility of their testimony against the protected people, because if their testimony is accepted against Muslims, it is all the more fitting that it be accepted against the protected people; then the evidence established the invalidity of their testimony against Muslims, so their testimony against the protected people remains as it was. This is not a valid argument, because the acceptance of the testimony of protected people against protected people is a branch (farʿ) of the acceptance of their testimony against Muslims. So when their testimony against Muslims, which is the root (aṣl), is invalidated, it is all the more fitting that their testimony against the protected people, which is its branch, be invalidated. And God knows best.

Eighth: His words, ﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾, mean: if you journey. The sentence contains an omission; its full sense is: "If you are travelling in the land, and ﴿the calamity of death befalls you﴾, then you make a bequest to two just men in your estimation, and you hand over to them what wealth you have with you. Then you die, and the two go to your heirs with the estate, and they doubt their conduct and accuse them of betrayal. The ruling is that you detain them after the prayer," that is, you secure them (tastawthiqū minhumā). God Most High called death in this verse a calamity (muṣība). Our scholars said: Although death is a great calamity and a supreme disaster, greater than it is heedlessness of it, turning away from remembering it, neglecting to reflect upon it, and failing to act for it. In death alone there is a lesson for whoever takes lessons, and a reflection for whoever reflects. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) [that he said:] [[from manuscript ʿ.]] "If animals knew of death what you know, you would not eat any of them fat." It is related that a Bedouin was riding a camel of his, and the camel fell dead. The Bedouin dismounted and began circling it, reflecting upon it and saying: "What is wrong with you that you do not stand? What is wrong with you that you do not rise? These limbs of yours are complete, and your joints are sound. What is your condition? What was carrying you? What was driving you? What felled you? What prevented you from movement?" Then he left it and went away reflecting upon its condition, amazed at its state.

Ninth: His words, ﴿you detain them﴾. Abū ʿAlī said: "tahbisūnahumā" is an adjective (ṣifa) of "ākhar ān" (two others), and a clause has been inserted between the adjective and the qualified noun, namely "in antum" (if you are). This verse is a foundation for detaining anyone who is owed a right. Rights are of two kinds: some can be fulfilled promptly, and others cannot be fulfilled except in deferred form. If the debtor is left free, he disappears and conceals himself, the right is lost and the wealth is gone (tawā al-māl: the wealth has perished and is no longer expected to be recovered). Then there is no alternative to securing the debt against him. This is done either by a material equivalent for the right, which is called a pledge (rahn), or by a person who stands in his place in the demand and in liability, who is the guarantor (ḥamīl, surety, that is, the kafīl). The second is inferior to the first, because he may vanish just as the debtor did and become unavailable just as the debtor became unavailable. But no more than this can be done. If both are impossible, nothing remains but to secure the debtor by detaining him until he fulfils what he owes, or until his poverty becomes evident.

Tenth: If the right is bodily and does not admit of substitution, such as the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) and retaliation (qiṣāṣ), and it cannot be fulfilled promptly, then there is nothing for it but to secure the person by imprisoning him. For this wisdom imprisonment was prescribed. Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and others narrated from Bahz ibn Ḥakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) detained a man on a charge. Abū Dāwūd also narrated from ʿAmr ibn al-Sharīd, from his father, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who said: "The delay of the one who is able to pay makes his honour and his punishment permissible." Ibn al-Mubārak said: "His honour is made permissible" means he is treated harshly, and "his punishment" means he is imprisoned. Al-Khaṭṭābī said: Detention is of two kinds: detention as punishment (ḥabs ʿuqūba) and detention for verification (ḥabs istiẓhār). Punishment is applied only for a proven obligation, whereas detention on a charge is only for verification, in order to uncover what lies beyond it. It is related that he detained a man on a charge for an hour of the day and then released him. Maʿmar narrated from Ayyūb, from Ibn Sīrīn, who said: When Shurayḥ (the judge) ruled against a man in a matter of right, he would order him detained in the mosque until he stood up; if he gave the right, well and good, otherwise he would order him sent to prison.

Eleventh: His words, ﴿after the prayer﴾, mean the afternoon prayer (ʿaṣr). This is said by the majority of scholars, because the adherents of the religions (ahl al-adyān) revere that time and avoid lying and false oaths at it. Al-Ḥasan said: it is the noon prayer (ẓuhr). It is said: any prayer whatever. It is said: after their prayer, on the basis that they are unbelievers, as al-Suddī said. It is also said: the purpose of stipulating "after the prayer" is to magnify the time and to instil awe through it, since the angels witness that time. In the authentic collection: "Whoever swears a false oath after the afternoon prayer will meet God while He is angry with him."

Twelfth: This verse is a foundation for the aggravation of oaths (taghlīẓ al-aymān). Aggravation occurs in four ways. The first is time, as we have mentioned. The second is place, such as the mosque and the pulpit (minbar). This differs from Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, who say: no one is required to take an oath at the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ), nor between the Corner (al-rukn) and the Station (al-maqām), neither in small matters nor in great ones. Al-Bukhārī, may God have mercy on him, held this view when he titled a chapter: "Chapter: the defendant swears wherever the oath becomes obligatory upon him and it is not transferred from one place to another." Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said: in the oaths of the qasāma (the procedure of oaths in cases of homicide), whoever belongs to the districts of Mecca is brought to Mecca and swears between the Corner and the Station; whoever belongs to the districts of Medina is brought to Medina and swears at the pulpit. The third is the state of the swearer. Muṭarrif, Ibn al-Mājishūn and some of al-Shāfiʿī's companions narrated that he swears standing, facing the qibla, because that is more effective in restraint and deterrence. Ibn Kināna said: he swears seated. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: My view is that he swears in the same posture in which judgment is given against him: if standing, then standing; if seated, then seated, since no tradition or reasoning has been established requiring standing or sitting to be taken into account.

I say: Some scholars have deduced standing from his words in the hadith of ʿAlqama ibn Wāʾil, from his father: [so he set off to swear] — and God knows best. Muslim narrated it. The fourth is aggravation by wording. One group held that one swears only by God and nothing more, based on His words, ﴿they both swear by God﴾, and His words, ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord﴾ [[see vol. 8 p. 351]] (Yūnus 10:53), and ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ [[see vol. 11 p. 296]] (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:57), and his peace be upon him saying: "Whoever is swearing, let him swear by God or let him keep silent," and a man's saying: "By God, I will not add to them." Mālik said: He swears by God, the One besides whom there is no god, that he owes him no right, and that what he claims against me is false. The evidence for him is what Abū Dāwūd narrated: Musaddad related to us, saying: Abū al-Aḥwaṣ related to us, saying: ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib related to us, from Abū Yaḥyā, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, meaning to a man whom he made swear: "Swear by God, the One besides whom there is no god, that he has nothing of yours." Meaning to the claimant. Abū Dāwūd said: Abū Yaḥyā's name is Ziyād [[he is Abū Yaḥyā Ziyād al-Aʿraj, client of the Anṣār]]; he is a Kufan, trustworthy and reliable. The Kufans said: he swears by God alone; if the judge suspects him, he aggravates the oath against him, so he makes him swear by God, the One besides whom there is no god, the Knower of the unseen and the visible, the Compassionate, the Merciful, who knows what is secret as He knows what is open, who knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. The followers of al-Shāfiʿī added aggravation by the Muṣḥaf (the copy of the Qurʾān). Ibn al-ʿArabī said: This is an innovation (bidʿa); none of the Companions ever mentioned it. Al-Shāfiʿī claimed that he saw Ibn Māzin, judge of Ṣanʿāʾ, swearing by the Muṣḥaf and ordering his companions to do so, and that he related it from Ibn ʿAbbās, but it is not authenticated. I say: In the book al-Muhadhdhab: if he swears by the Muṣḥaf and what is in it of the Qurʾān, al-Shāfiʿī related from Muṭarrif that Ibn al-Zubayr used to make people swear on the Muṣḥaf. He said: I saw Muṭarrif in Ṣanʿāʾ making people swear on the Muṣḥaf. Al-Shāfiʿī said: It is good. Ibn al-Mundhir said: They agreed that it is not fitting for the judge to make a person swear by divorce, manumission, or the Muṣḥaf [[in some copies: or the Muṣḥaf]]. I say: It has already been mentioned in the chapter on oaths that Qatāda used to swear by the Muṣḥaf. Aḥmad and Isḥāq said: that is not disliked; Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted this from them.

Thirteenth: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī differed in this chapter concerning the amount of property for which an oath is taken to settle a claim (maqṭaʿ al-ḥaqq, the cutting off of a dispute). Mālik said: an oath in settling a claim is not valid for less than three dirhams, by analogy with theft (qaṭʿ), and every amount for which the hand is cut off and by which the sanctity of the limb is forfeited is a substantial amount. Al-Shāfiʿī said: the oath in this matter is not valid for less than twenty dinars, by analogy with zakat; and likewise at the pulpit of every mosque.

Fourteenth: His words, ﴿then they swear by God﴾. The fāʾ in "fayuqsimān" is conjunctive, linking one clause to another, or it is the answer to a conditional, because "tahbisūnahumā" means "detain them," that is, for the oath. It is therefore a response to the command which the sentence implies, as if he said: "When you detain them, the two shall swear." Dhū al-Rumma said:

"The pupil of my eye drains the water once,
then it appears, and at other times it overflows and drowns."

Its estimate according to them: "if it becomes apparent (that they have lied)." The Fifteenth: It has been disputed who is meant by His saying, "then two others shall swear" (fa-yuqsimani)? It was said: they are the two executors (al-wasiyyan) when doubt arises concerning their statement. It was also said: they are the two witnesses when they are not trustworthy and the judge doubts their statement, so he makes them swear. Ibn al-Arabi, refuting this view, said: "What I have heard, and it is an innovation, from Ibn Abi Layla is that the claimant is made to swear with his two witnesses that what they testified to is true, and then judgment is given to him in accordance with the truth. My interpretation of this, in my view, is that when the judge doubts the taking of possession, he makes [the claimant] swear that it remains [in his possession]. As for other than that, it is not to be heeded. This concerns the claimant; so how can the witness be imprisoned or made to swear?! This is not to be heeded." I say: It has already been mentioned in al-Tabari's statement that there is no known divine ruling by which an oath is obligatory upon the witness. It has also been said: the two witnesses were made to swear only because they had become defendants against whom the heirs claimed that they had betrayed the property.

The Sixteenth: His saying, Exalted is He, "if you doubt" (in ertabtum) is a condition, and the swearing of the two witnesses is not directed except by it; whenever no doubt or disagreement arises, there is no oath. Ibn Atiyyah said: What is evident from the ruling of Abu Musa concerning the making of the dhimmis swear is that by the oath their testimony is completed and the bequest is enforced for its beneficiaries. Abu Dawud narrated from al-Sha'bi that a man from among the Muslims was approaching death at Daquqa [[Daquqa (with a fatha on its first letter, a damma on its second, after the waw a qaf, then a long alif, and it is shortened): a well-known city between Irbil and Baghdad, which has mention in reports and conquests, and in which there was also a battle with the Kharijites (Mu'jam al-Buldan).]] (this is as it stands in the originals, and it seems there is an omission here; let it be considered), and he did not find anyone from among the Muslims present to witness his bequest, so he called two men from the People of the Book to witness. They came to Kufa and went to al-Ash'ari and informed him, and they brought his estate and his bequest. Al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that did not happen after what happened in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." So he made them swear after the afternoon prayer: "By God, they have not betrayed, nor lied, nor altered, nor concealed, nor changed; and indeed it is the bequest of the man and his estate," and he then enforced their testimony. Ibn Atiyyah said: This doubt, according to those who do not hold the verse to be abrogated, is to be applied in cases of betrayal and of accusation of inclining toward some of the beneficiaries over others; and the oath in such cases is, in his view, also imposed. As for those who hold the verse to be abrogated, no oath is imposed except where the doubt concerns betrayal or transgression in some form of transgression; the oath then, in their view, is according to the claim against a denier, not as a completion of the testimony. Ibn al-Arabi said: The oath of doubt and suspicion is of two kinds. The first: that in which doubt arises after the right has been established and the claim has been directed; there is no disagreement about the obligation of the oath. The second: general suspicion in rights and penalties, which has its details explained in the books of jurisprudence; and here the claim has been realized and strengthened, as mentioned in the reports.

The Seventeenth: The condition in His saying, "if you doubt," is connected to His saying, "you shall detain them" (tahbisunahuma), not to His saying "then they shall swear" (fa-yuqsimani), because this detention is the cause of the oath.

The Eighteenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will not barter it for any price, even if it be (to) a near kinsman﴾. That is, they say in their oath: "We will not exchange our oath for any consideration that we take in place of what was bequeathed, nor will we hand it over to anyone, even if the one for whom we swear is a near kinsman of ours." The omission of the saying is frequent, as in His saying: "And the angels enter upon them from every gate: 'Peace be upon you'" (al-Ra'd: 23–24), meaning they say, "Peace be upon you." The purchasing (ishtira') here does not mean selling but obtaining.

The Nineteenth: The lam in His saying, "we will not barter" is the answer to His saying, "then they shall swear," because the verb of swearing (aqsama) takes what the oath takes: "la" and "ma" in negation, and "inna" and the lam in affirmation. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the name of God, Exalted is He, as it is the nearest mentioned; the meaning is: "We will not sell our share from God with this commodity." It may also refer to the testimony, which is mentioned in the sense of the saying, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and God," where he returned the pronoun [[from k.]] to the sense of "supplication" (da'wah), which is "du'a'." This has been mentioned previously in Surat al-Nisa' [[see vol. 5 p. 50, where it reads: (fa-innahu laysa baynahu), referring to the witness; and all the originals read (baynaha), so there is no evidence in it.]].

The Twentieth: His saying, "a price" (thamanan). The Kufans said: the meaning is "possessor of a price," that is, "a commodity of price," so the qualified noun is omitted and the qualifier is put in its place. According to us and many scholars, the price may itself be the commodity, since the price in our view is also something bought, just as the priced item is bought; so each of the two exchanged items is both price and priced good, and the sale revolves around goods and cash, or two goods, or two cash items. On this principle a question is built: if the buyer goes bankrupt and the seller finds his goods, is he more entitled to them? Abu Hanifa said: he is not more entitled to them, and he built this on this principle, saying that its owner is on equal footing with the creditors. Malik said: he has a better right to it in bankruptcy but not in death. Al-Shafi'i said: its owner has a better right to it in both bankruptcy and death. Abu Hanifa held to what we have mentioned, and to the general principle that the debt is in the liability of the bankrupt and the dead, and what is in their hands is the place of payment, so all the creditors share in it in proportion to their capitals; there is no difference in this between whether the goods themselves exist or not, since they have left the ownership of their seller and their prices became due to them as a liability by consensus; so they have only their prices or what is found of them. Malik and al-Shafi'i made an exception to this rule by reports transmitted on this subject, which the imams, including Abu Dawud and others, narrated.

The Twenty-first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of God﴾, that is, the testimony God has made known to us. There are seven readings concerning it; whoever wants them will find them in (al-Tahsil) [[which is Tahsil al-Manafi' 'ala Kitab al-Durar al-Lawami', in the reading of Nafi' and others.]].

The Twenty-second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then if it is discovered that the two have deserved sin﴾. 'Umar said: this verse is the most difficult of the rulings in this surah. Al-Zajjaj said: the most difficult thing in the Qur'an in terms of i'rab is His saying: "from among those upon whom the two nearest have a claim" (min alladhina istahagga 'alayhimu al-awlayan). 'Athara 'ala kadha means he came upon it, it is said: "I came upon a betrayal from him" (athartu minhu 'ala khiyanah), meaning I discovered it, and "I made another come upon it" (a'thartu ghayri 'alayhi), and from this is His saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾ (al-Kahf: 21), because they were seeking them while their location was hidden from them. The root of 'uthur is falling upon and striking something; from it comes the saying: "the man stumbled ('athara al-rajulu ya'thiru 'uthuran) when his toe struck something and was hit and fell upon it," and "the toe of so-and-so stumbled over such-and-such" when it struck it and fell upon it. The horse stumbled ('athara al-faras 'ithara), al-A'sha said:
With a she-camel of strength (lawth), 'afarnatah, when she stumbles, the ruin is nearer to her than my saying "la'a" (may she be well).
The 'athir is the rising dust, because it falls upon the face; and the 'athir is a faint trace, because it is fallen upon from concealment. The pronoun in "annahuma" refers to the two executors mentioned in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: "two" (ithnan), according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also said it refers to the two witnesses, according to Ibn 'Abbas. "Istahaqqa" means they became deserving of "sin" (ithman), meaning by betrayal and taking what is not theirs, or by a false oath, or by false testimony. Abu 'Ali said: "sin" here is the name of the thing taken, because its taker is sinful by taking it, so it is called "sin," just as what is taken without right is called "injustice" (maẓlimah). Sibawayh said: "maẓlimah" is the name of what is taken from you, so likewise this taken thing was named by the name of the verbal noun, which is "jam'."

The Twenty-third: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then two others shall stand in their place﴾, meaning in the oaths or in the testimony. He said "two others" according to the fact that the heirs were two. "Two others" (akharan) is in the nominative by an implied verb. "Stand" (yaqumani) is in the position of a qualifier. "In their place" (maqamahuma) is a verbal noun, and its estimate is: "a standing like their standing," then the qualifier was put in place of the qualified, and the verbal noun in place of its genitive.

The Twenty-fourth: His saying, Exalted is He: (from among those upon whom [[the reading of Nafi' is with the passive voice, which is the reading of the majority.]] the two nearest have a claim). Ibn al-Sarri said: the meaning is "upon whom the bequest has been claimed." Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best things said about it, because one letter is not made a substitute for another; al-Nahhas preferred it, and Ibn al-Arabi chose it. Also, the interpretation follows it, since according to the people of tafsir the meaning is: "from among those upon whom the bequest has been claimed." "The two nearest" (al-awlayan) is an apposition to His saying "two others," as Ibn al-Sarri said; al-Nahhas preferred it, and it is apposition of a definite noun to an indefinite one, which is permitted. It was also said: an indefinite noun, once its mention has preceded and it is then mentioned again, becomes definite, as in His saying: "like a niche in which is a lamp" (al-Nur: 35), then He said: "the lamp is in a glass" (al-Nur: 35), then He said: "the glass" (al-Nur: 35). It was also said: it is an apposition to the pronoun in "yaqumani," as if He had said: "then the two nearest shall stand," or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: "then two others shall stand in their place; they are the two nearest." Ibn 'Isa said: "al-awlayan" is the object of "istahagga" with an omitted noun, meaning: "the sin of the two nearest has been claimed against them and because of them," so "upon them" (alayhim) carries the sense of "concerning them," like "over the kingdom of Solomon" (al-Baqarah: 102), meaning "concerning the kingdom of Solomon." The poet said:
Whenever you deny them, you will know them: upon their horizons is a clot, freshly flowing.

That is, in its regions. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and Hamza read *al-awwalina*, the plural of *awwal*, as a substitute (*badal*) for *alladhina* or for the *ha'* and *mim* in *alayhim*. Hafs read *istahagga*, with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'*. It is also narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and its subject is *al-awlayani*, with the object omitted. The implied meaning is: "from among those against whom the two nearest of kin (*al-awliya'*) were entitled, through the deceased, to his bequest which he had made." It was also said: "the two nearest of kin were entitled against them to the return of the oaths." It is narrated from al-Hasan: *al-awwalani*, and from Ibn Sirin: *al-awwalayni* [[Ibn 'Atiyya said: "in the dual of *awwal*; the accusative is on the assumption of *al-awwalayni*, and the first in rank."]] Al-Nahhas said: "Both readings are ungrammatical (*lahn*). One does not say *muthannan* as the dual of *muthanna*, except that it has been narrated from al-Hasan, *al-awwalani*."

The twenty-fifth issue: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Then they both shall swear by God﴾. That is, the other two, who stand in the place of the two witnesses, will swear: "What our companion said in his bequest is true, and the property he bequeathed to you two was more than what you brought us, and this vessel is indeed from the property of our companion, which he took with him on his journey, and which he recorded in his bequest, and you two have betrayed [him]." That is His saying: ﴿Surely our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾, that is, our oath is more worthy than their oath. Thus it is established that *shahada* (testimony) may have the meaning of *yamin* (oath). From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 182.]] (Surah al-Nur 24:6). Ma'mar narrated from Ayyub, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, who said: "Two men from among the heirs of the deceased stood up and swore." ﴿Surely our testimony is more worthy﴾ is a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). His saying: ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾, that is, we have not exceeded the truth in our oath.
﴿Indeed then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾: that is, if we had sworn to a falsehood and taken what was not ours.

The twenty-sixth issue: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿That is more suitable﴾ is a subject and predicate. ﴿That﴾ (*an*) is in the accusative position. ﴿They bring﴾ (*ya'tu*) is in the accusative governed by *an*. ﴿Or they fear﴾ (*yakhafu*) is coordinated with it. ﴿That oaths be returned﴾ (*an turadda*) is in the accusative position, governed by *yakhafu*. ﴿Oaths after their oaths﴾. It was said: the pronoun in *ya'tu* and *yakhafu* refers to the two who were entrusted with the bequest, and this is the most fitting for the context of the verse. It was also said: what is meant is people in general, that is, people are more likely to beware of betrayal and therefore testify to the truth, for fear of disgrace in having the oath returned upon the claimant. And God knows best.

The twenty-seventh issue: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And fear God and listen﴾ is an imperative, and for this reason the *nun* is dropped from it. That is: listen to what is said to you, accepting it, obeying God's command in it.
﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾. *Fasaqa*, *yafsiqu* and *yafsuqu* mean to leave obedience for disobedience. This has been discussed before [[See vol. 1, p. 245.]]. And God knows best.

**Part 1 of 5. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 106–108**

There are twenty-seven issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** Makki (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "These three verses are, according to the scholars of meanings, among the most difficult verses of the Qur'an in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), meaning, and ruling." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is the statement of one who has not found the satisfaction (thalj) in its tafsir," and this is clear from his book, may Allah have mercy on him. [[Thalajat al-nafs bi-al-shay' thaljan: the soul was content with a thing and felt reassured by it. It is also said: it recognised it and was delighted by it.]]

I say: What Makki (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned was also mentioned earlier by Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas. I know of no disagreement that these verses were revealed concerning Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada'.

Al-Bukhari, al-Daraqutni and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada' [[in some copies: "from"]] used to travel to Makkah. A young man from Banu Sahm went out with them, and he died in a land where there was no Muslim. He made them his executors, so they handed his estate to his family, but they withheld a silver cup (jam) inlaid with gold. [[Al-Jam: a vessel of silver. Jam makhus: covered with gold sheets like palm fronds.]] The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them swear: "You have neither concealed nor appropriated anything." Then the cup was found in Makkah, and they said: "We bought it from 'Adi and Tamim." Two men from the heirs of the Sahmi came and swore that this cup belonged to the Sahmi, and that "our testimony is more worthy than their testimony, and we have not transgressed." He said: So they took the cup, and this verse was revealed concerning them. This is the wording of al-Daraqutni.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Tamim al-Dari concerning this verse, "O you who believe, the testimony between you...", that people were absolved of it except for me and 'Adi ibn Bada'. Both were Christians who used to travel to Syria before Islam. They arrived in Syria with their merchandise, and a client (mawla) of Banu Sahm called Budayl ibn Abi Maryam came to them with merchandise, carrying a silver cup that he intended to present to the king, and it was the greatest part of his trade. He fell ill and made them his executors, and instructed them to deliver what he had left to his family. Tamim said: When he died we took that cup and sold it for a thousand dirhams, then divided the proceeds between me and 'Adi ibn Bada'. When we came to his family we handed over what we had with us, but they missed the cup and asked us about it. We said: "He left nothing but this, and he did not hand over anything else to us." Tamim said: When I embraced Islam after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah, I felt guilty about this, so I went to his family and told them the story, and I paid them five hundred dirhams, and I informed them that my companion had an equal amount. They brought the matter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who asked them for evidence, but they could not produce any. He instructed them to make the other party swear by that which is most sacred to their religion (yuqta' [[yuqta': he magnifies, honours]] bihi 'ala ahl dinihi). So he swore, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "O you who believe, the testimony between you..." up to His words "after their oath." Then 'Amr ibn al-'As and another man from among them stood up and swore, and the five hundred were taken from the hands of 'Adi ibn Bada'.

Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a gharib hadith, and its chain is not sound.

Al-Waqidi mentioned that the three verses were revealed concerning Tamim and his brother 'Adi, who were both Christians, and whose trade was with Makkah. When the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah, Ibn Abi Maryam, client of 'Amr ibn al-'As, came to Madinah intending to go to Syria as a merchant. He went out with Tamim and his brother 'Adi, and he mentioned the hadith.

Al-Naqqash mentioned: It was revealed concerning Budayl ibn Abi Maryam, client of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. He had set out as a traveller by sea to the land of the Negus, and with him were two Christian men, one called Tamim, who was from Lakhm, and 'Adi ibn Bada'. Budayl died while they were on the ship, so he was thrown into the sea. He had written his will and placed it among the goods, and he said: "Deliver these goods to my family." When Budayl died, the two took the money and took from it whatever pleased them. Among what they took was a silver vessel weighing three hundred mithqal, engraved and overlaid with gold. He mentioned the hadith. Sunayd also mentioned it and said: When they reached Syria, Budayl fell ill, and he was a Muslim... the hadith.

**The second issue:** The Almighty's words, ﴿The testimony between you﴾ [5:106]. The word "shahida" (to witness) occurs in the Book of Allah with various different meanings. Among them is His words, ﴿And call to witness two witnesses from among your men﴾ [2:282]. It is said that its meaning is "bring them to be present." Among them is "shahida" meaning "decided," i.e., "knew," as said by Abu 'Ubaydah, as in His words, ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [3:18]. [[See vol. 4, p. 40.]] Among them is "shahida" meaning "acknowledged," as in His words, ﴿But the angels bear witness﴾ [4:166]. [[See vol. 6, p. 19.]] Among them is "shahida" meaning "judged," as in His words, ﴿And a witness from among her family testified﴾ [12:26]. [[See vol. 9, p. 172.]] Among them is "shahida" meaning "swore," as in the case of li'an (mutual oath-cursing). Among them is "shahida" meaning "bequeathed," as in His words, ﴿O you who believe, the testimony between you...﴾.

It has also been said that its meaning here is "presence for the bequest," as one says: "I witnessed the bequest of so-and-so," meaning "I was present for it."

Al-Tabari held that testimony here means oath, so the meaning would be: the oath between you is that two swear. He argued that this is different from the testimony given to the one in whose favour it is made, since there is no ruling of Allah requiring an oath from the witness. Al-Qaffal chose this view. The oath was called testimony because a ruling is established by it just as it is established by testimony.

Ibn 'Atiyyah chose that the testimony here is the testimony that is preserved and then delivered, and he rejected its meaning as presence or oath.

**The third issue:** The Almighty's words, "between you" (baynikum). It has been said that the meaning is "what is between you," so "ma" was deleted, and "testimony" was attributed to the adverbial noun (zarf). It was used as a noun in its literal sense, and this is what grammarians call the object (maf'ul) by extension (al-sa'ah), as the poet said:

*A day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir...*

He meant: "we witnessed in it." [[This is the first half of a line by a man from Banu 'Amir; the second half is: "Few besides me are the spear-thrusts, its additions (nawafiluhu)." Sulaym and 'Amir are two tribes of Qays 'Aylan.]]

And the Almighty said, ﴿But rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [34:33], meaning "your plotting in them."

And he recited:

*You shake hands with one whom I have met as an enemy, a handshake, while my resentment is withdrawn between your eyes.*

He intended "what is between the two of you" and omitted it, as in His saying ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾ [Al-Kahf 18:78], meaning "what is between me and you."

The Fourth point: His saying ﴿when death approaches﴾ means when it is about to arrive, for if death has actually arrived, the dying person does not call witnesses. This is like His saying ﴿When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [An-Nahl 16:98], and His saying ﴿When you divorce women, divorce them﴾ [At-Talaq 65:1], and there are many similar examples. The element governing "idha" (when) is the verbal noun "shahadah" (testimony).

The Fifth point: His saying ﴿at the time of the bequest, two﴾. "Hin" (at the time of) is an adverb of time, and the element governing it is "hadara" (approached). His saying "ithnan" (two) by its unrestricted meaning implies two persons, and could mean two men. However, when He said afterwards "dhawa 'adl" (persons of justice), it made clear that He meant two men, because this word applies only to males, just as "dhawatan" [Ar-Rahman 55:48] applies only to females. "Ithnan" is in the nominative as the predicate of the subject "shahadah." Abu 'Ali said: "Shahadah" is nominative as the subject, and the predicate is in His saying "ithnan." The meaning is: the testimony among you concerning your bequests is the testimony of two, so the genitive noun was omitted and the noun in the genitive was placed in its position, as in His saying ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 33:6], meaning "like their mothers." It is also permissible for "ithnan" to be nominative governed by "shahadah," the meaning being: "and among what has been revealed to you" or "let there be among you" that two bear witness, or "let two establish the testimony."

The Sixth point: His saying ﴿persons of justice from among you﴾. "Dhawa 'adl" is a qualifier of "ithnan," and "minkum" is a qualifier following another qualifier. His saying ﴿or two others from other than you﴾ means "or the testimony of two others from other than you," so "min ghayrikum" is a qualifier of "akharan" (two others). This separation is the difficult point in this verse, and the correct treatment is to say that the scholars differed on it in three opinions.

The first opinion: the "ka" and "mim" in His saying "minkum" refer to the Muslims, while "aw akharan min ghayrikum" refers to the disbelievers. On this view, the testimony of People of the Book against Muslims is permissible during travel when it concerns a bequest. This is the most likely reading according to the context of the verse, together with what has been established in the hadiths. This is the view of three Companions who witnessed the revelation: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, 'Abdullah ibn Qays [the text in the original editions reads "Ibn Qays is Abu Musa, and perhaps the correct reading is 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, as is inferred from Ahkam al-Jassas"], and 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas. According to this view, the meaning of the verse from beginning to end is that Allah, exalted is He, informed that His ruling concerning testimony on the testator, when death approaches, is that it should be the testimony of two just persons. If he is on a journey, which is traveling in the land, and no believer is with him, then he should call two witnesses from among those present who are of the disbelievers. When they return and render testimony concerning his bequest, they swear after the prayer [the text in some manuscripts reads "after the testimony"] that they did not lie, did not alter, and that what they testified to is true, that they did not conceal any testimony, and judgment is given on their testimony. If it is afterwards discovered that they lied or betrayed, or committed something similar that is sinful, then two men from among the heirs of the testator swear during the journey, and the two witnesses are obliged to pay what was proven against them. This is the meaning of the verse according to the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Mijlaz, Ibrahim, Shurayh, 'Abidah al-Salmani, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ibn 'Abbas, and others. Among the jurists, Sufyan al-Thawri held this view, and Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam inclined to it because of the number of those who held it. Ahmad ibn Hanbal chose it and said: "The testimony of the dhimmis is permissible against Muslims during travel when no Muslims are present." They all say that "minkum" means from among the believers, and "min ghayrikum" means the disbelievers. Some of them said: this verse was revealed concerning an incident in which there was no believer except in Medina, and they used to travel for trade in the company of People of the Book, idolaters, and various kinds of disbelievers. The verse is considered muhkam (definitive, not abrogated) according to the view of Abu Musa, Shurayh, and others.

The second opinion: His saying, exalted is He, "or two others from other than you" is abrogated (mansukh). This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Nakha'i, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, and other jurists, except that Abu Hanifah differed from them and said: the testimony of disbelievers against one another is permissible, but it is not permissible against Muslims. They argued with His saying ﴿of those whom you find acceptable as witnesses﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:282] and His saying ﴿and call to witness two persons of justice from among you﴾ [At-Talaq 65:2]. They claimed that the verse on debt is among the last revealed, and that it contains "of those whom you find acceptable as witnesses," so it abrogates the earlier ruling. Islam at that time existed only in Medina, so the testimony of its People of the Book was permissible, but today Islam has spread across the earth, so the testimony of disbelievers has lapsed. The Muslims have agreed that the testimony of sinners is not permissible, and disbelievers are sinners, so their testimony is not permissible.

I say: what you have mentioned is correct, but we maintain its implication, namely that this is permissible in the testimony of dhimmis against Muslims concerning a bequest during travel only, out of necessity, when no Muslim is present. When a Muslim is present, it is not permissible. What you claim as abrogation has not come from anyone among those who witnessed the revelation. Three Companions held the first view, and there is no such view from anyone else. Departing from the Companions in favour of others is repugnant to the people of knowledge. This is reinforced by the fact that Surat al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, to the extent that Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and others said: there is no abrogation (naskh) in it. What they claim as abrogation is not valid, for abrogation requires establishing the abrogating text in a manner that makes the two rulings incompatible, with the abrogating text coming later. What they have mentioned cannot be abrogating, because it concerns a different case from the case of the bequest, arising from need and necessity, and it is not impossible for a ruling to differ in cases of necessity. Moreover, a disbeliever may sometimes be trustworthy in the eyes of a Muslim and acceptable to him in a case of necessity. Therefore there is no abrogation in what they have stated.

The third opinion: the verse contains no abrogation. This was said by al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah. According to this view, the meaning of His saying "minkum" is "from among your tribe and your kinsmen," because they are more retentive, more precise, and less prone to forgetting.

The meaning of His words, ﴿or two others from among other than you﴾, is: from outside your kinship and tribe. Al-Nahhas said: This rests on a subtle point of the Arabic language. The sense of "ākhar" (other) in Arabic is of the same kind as the first. You say, "I passed by a noble man and another noble man (karīm ākhar)." The word "ākhar" indicates that the second is of the same kind as the first. According to the people of Arabic (ahl al-ʿarabiyya, the grammarians), it is not permissible to say "I passed by a noble man and a base man ākhar," nor "I passed by a man and a donkey ākhar." From this it follows that the meaning of His words, "or two others from among other than you," is "two just men (ʿadlān)." Unbelievers are not just, so on this reading the view of those who say "from other than you" means from outside your clan among the Muslims is sound. This is a good reading from the standpoint of the language. It may be cited as evidence for Mālik and those who follow his view, since for them the meaning is "from other than you," that is, from other than your tribe. However, this view has been countered by the fact that at the beginning of the verse is ﴿O you who believe﴾, so the address is to the community of believers.

Seventh: Abū Ḥanīfa used this verse as evidence for the admissibility of testimony by unbelievers from among the protected people (ahl al-dhimma, non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule) in matters among themselves. He said: The meaning of "or two others from among other than you" is from among people other than your own religion, which indicates that some of them may testify against others. It is said to him: You do not hold to the implication of this verse, because it was revealed concerning the acceptance of the testimony of the protected people against Muslims, and you do not hold to that, so your argument from it is not valid. If it is said: This verse indicates, by its explicit wording, the admissibility of the testimony of the protected people against Muslims, and by implication (tanbīh) the admissibility of their testimony against the protected people, because if their testimony is accepted against Muslims, it is all the more fitting that it be accepted against the protected people; then the evidence established the invalidity of their testimony against Muslims, so their testimony against the protected people remains as it was. This is not a valid argument, because the acceptance of the testimony of protected people against protected people is a branch (farʿ) of the acceptance of their testimony against Muslims. So when their testimony against Muslims, which is the root (aṣl), is invalidated, it is all the more fitting that their testimony against the protected people, which is its branch, be invalidated. And God knows best.

Eighth: His words, ﴿If you are travelling in the land﴾, mean: if you journey. The sentence contains an omission; its full sense is: "If you are travelling in the land, and ﴿the calamity of death befalls you﴾, then you make a bequest to two just men in your estimation, and you hand over to them what wealth you have with you. Then you die, and the two go to your heirs with the estate, and they doubt their conduct and accuse them of betrayal. The ruling is that you detain them after the prayer," that is, you secure them (tastawthiqū minhumā). God Most High called death in this verse a calamity (muṣība). Our scholars said: Although death is a great calamity and a supreme disaster, greater than it is heedlessness of it, turning away from remembering it, neglecting to reflect upon it, and failing to act for it. In death alone there is a lesson for whoever takes lessons, and a reflection for whoever reflects. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) [that he said:] [[from manuscript ʿ.]] "If animals knew of death what you know, you would not eat any of them fat." It is related that a Bedouin was riding a camel of his, and the camel fell dead. The Bedouin dismounted and began circling it, reflecting upon it and saying: "What is wrong with you that you do not stand? What is wrong with you that you do not rise? These limbs of yours are complete, and your joints are sound. What is your condition? What was carrying you? What was driving you? What felled you? What prevented you from movement?" Then he left it and went away reflecting upon its condition, amazed at its state.

Ninth: His words, ﴿you detain them﴾. Abū ʿAlī said: "tahbisūnahumā" is an adjective (ṣifa) of "ākhar ān" (two others), and a clause has been inserted between the adjective and the qualified noun, namely "in antum" (if you are). This verse is a foundation for detaining anyone who is owed a right. Rights are of two kinds: some can be fulfilled promptly, and others cannot be fulfilled except in deferred form. If the debtor is left free, he disappears and conceals himself, the right is lost and the wealth is gone (tawā al-māl: the wealth has perished and is no longer expected to be recovered). Then there is no alternative to securing the debt against him. This is done either by a material equivalent for the right, which is called a pledge (rahn), or by a person who stands in his place in the demand and in liability, who is the guarantor (ḥamīl, surety, that is, the kafīl). The second is inferior to the first, because he may vanish just as the debtor did and become unavailable just as the debtor became unavailable. But no more than this can be done. If both are impossible, nothing remains but to secure the debtor by detaining him until he fulfils what he owes, or until his poverty becomes evident.

Tenth: If the right is bodily and does not admit of substitution, such as the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) and retaliation (qiṣāṣ), and it cannot be fulfilled promptly, then there is nothing for it but to secure the person by imprisoning him. For this wisdom imprisonment was prescribed. Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and others narrated from Bahz ibn Ḥakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) detained a man on a charge. Abū Dāwūd also narrated from ʿAmr ibn al-Sharīd, from his father, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who said: "The delay of the one who is able to pay makes his honour and his punishment permissible." Ibn al-Mubārak said: "His honour is made permissible" means he is treated harshly, and "his punishment" means he is imprisoned. Al-Khaṭṭābī said: Detention is of two kinds: detention as punishment (ḥabs ʿuqūba) and detention for verification (ḥabs istiẓhār). Punishment is applied only for a proven obligation, whereas detention on a charge is only for verification, in order to uncover what lies beyond it. It is related that he detained a man on a charge for an hour of the day and then released him. Maʿmar narrated from Ayyūb, from Ibn Sīrīn, who said: When Shurayḥ (the judge) ruled against a man in a matter of right, he would order him detained in the mosque until he stood up; if he gave the right, well and good, otherwise he would order him sent to prison.

Eleventh: His words, ﴿after the prayer﴾, mean the afternoon prayer (ʿaṣr). This is said by the majority of scholars, because the adherents of the religions (ahl al-adyān) revere that time and avoid lying and false oaths at it. Al-Ḥasan said: it is the noon prayer (ẓuhr). It is said: any prayer whatever. It is said: after their prayer, on the basis that they are unbelievers, as al-Suddī said. It is also said: the purpose of stipulating "after the prayer" is to magnify the time and to instil awe through it, since the angels witness that time. In the authentic collection: "Whoever swears a false oath after the afternoon prayer will meet God while He is angry with him."

Twelfth: This verse is a foundation for the aggravation of oaths (taghlīẓ al-aymān). Aggravation occurs in four ways. The first is time, as we have mentioned. The second is place, such as the mosque and the pulpit (minbar). This differs from Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, who say: no one is required to take an oath at the pulpit of the Prophet (ﷺ), nor between the Corner (al-rukn) and the Station (al-maqām), neither in small matters nor in great ones. Al-Bukhārī, may God have mercy on him, held this view when he titled a chapter: "Chapter: the defendant swears wherever the oath becomes obligatory upon him and it is not transferred from one place to another." Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said: in the oaths of the qasāma (the procedure of oaths in cases of homicide), whoever belongs to the districts of Mecca is brought to Mecca and swears between the Corner and the Station; whoever belongs to the districts of Medina is brought to Medina and swears at the pulpit. The third is the state of the swearer. Muṭarrif, Ibn al-Mājishūn and some of al-Shāfiʿī's companions narrated that he swears standing, facing the qibla, because that is more effective in restraint and deterrence. Ibn Kināna said: he swears seated. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: My view is that he swears in the same posture in which judgment is given against him: if standing, then standing; if seated, then seated, since no tradition or reasoning has been established requiring standing or sitting to be taken into account.

I say: Some scholars have deduced standing from his words in the hadith of ʿAlqama ibn Wāʾil, from his father: [so he set off to swear] — and God knows best. Muslim narrated it. The fourth is aggravation by wording. One group held that one swears only by God and nothing more, based on His words, ﴿they both swear by God﴾, and His words, ﴿Say: Yes, by my Lord﴾ [[see vol. 8 p. 351]] (Yūnus 10:53), and ﴿By God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ [[see vol. 11 p. 296]] (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:57), and his peace be upon him saying: "Whoever is swearing, let him swear by God or let him keep silent," and a man's saying: "By God, I will not add to them." Mālik said: He swears by God, the One besides whom there is no god, that he owes him no right, and that what he claims against me is false. The evidence for him is what Abū Dāwūd narrated: Musaddad related to us, saying: Abū al-Aḥwaṣ related to us, saying: ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib related to us, from Abū Yaḥyā, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, meaning to a man whom he made swear: "Swear by God, the One besides whom there is no god, that he has nothing of yours." Meaning to the claimant. Abū Dāwūd said: Abū Yaḥyā's name is Ziyād [[he is Abū Yaḥyā Ziyād al-Aʿraj, client of the Anṣār]]; he is a Kufan, trustworthy and reliable. The Kufans said: he swears by God alone; if the judge suspects him, he aggravates the oath against him, so he makes him swear by God, the One besides whom there is no god, the Knower of the unseen and the visible, the Compassionate, the Merciful, who knows what is secret as He knows what is open, who knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. The followers of al-Shāfiʿī added aggravation by the Muṣḥaf (the copy of the Qurʾān). Ibn al-ʿArabī said: This is an innovation (bidʿa); none of the Companions ever mentioned it. Al-Shāfiʿī claimed that he saw Ibn Māzin, judge of Ṣanʿāʾ, swearing by the Muṣḥaf and ordering his companions to do so, and that he related it from Ibn ʿAbbās, but it is not authenticated. I say: In the book al-Muhadhdhab: if he swears by the Muṣḥaf and what is in it of the Qurʾān, al-Shāfiʿī related from Muṭarrif that Ibn al-Zubayr used to make people swear on the Muṣḥaf. He said: I saw Muṭarrif in Ṣanʿāʾ making people swear on the Muṣḥaf. Al-Shāfiʿī said: It is good. Ibn al-Mundhir said: They agreed that it is not fitting for the judge to make a person swear by divorce, manumission, or the Muṣḥaf [[in some copies: or the Muṣḥaf]]. I say: It has already been mentioned in the chapter on oaths that Qatāda used to swear by the Muṣḥaf. Aḥmad and Isḥāq said: that is not disliked; Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted this from them.

Thirteenth: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī differed in this chapter concerning the amount of property for which an oath is taken to settle a claim (maqṭaʿ al-ḥaqq, the cutting off of a dispute). Mālik said: an oath in settling a claim is not valid for less than three dirhams, by analogy with theft (qaṭʿ), and every amount for which the hand is cut off and by which the sanctity of the limb is forfeited is a substantial amount. Al-Shāfiʿī said: the oath in this matter is not valid for less than twenty dinars, by analogy with zakat; and likewise at the pulpit of every mosque.

Fourteenth: His words, ﴿then they swear by God﴾. The fāʾ in "fayuqsimān" is conjunctive, linking one clause to another, or it is the answer to a conditional, because "tahbisūnahumā" means "detain them," that is, for the oath. It is therefore a response to the command which the sentence implies, as if he said: "When you detain them, the two shall swear." Dhū al-Rumma said:

"The pupil of my eye drains the water once,
then it appears, and at other times it overflows and drowns."

Its estimate according to them: "if it becomes apparent (that they have lied)." The Fifteenth: It has been disputed who is meant by His saying, "then two others shall swear" (fa-yuqsimani)? It was said: they are the two executors (al-wasiyyan) when doubt arises concerning their statement. It was also said: they are the two witnesses when they are not trustworthy and the judge doubts their statement, so he makes them swear. Ibn al-Arabi, refuting this view, said: "What I have heard, and it is an innovation, from Ibn Abi Layla is that the claimant is made to swear with his two witnesses that what they testified to is true, and then judgment is given to him in accordance with the truth. My interpretation of this, in my view, is that when the judge doubts the taking of possession, he makes [the claimant] swear that it remains [in his possession]. As for other than that, it is not to be heeded. This concerns the claimant; so how can the witness be imprisoned or made to swear?! This is not to be heeded." I say: It has already been mentioned in al-Tabari's statement that there is no known divine ruling by which an oath is obligatory upon the witness. It has also been said: the two witnesses were made to swear only because they had become defendants against whom the heirs claimed that they had betrayed the property.

The Sixteenth: His saying, Exalted is He, "if you doubt" (in ertabtum) is a condition, and the swearing of the two witnesses is not directed except by it; whenever no doubt or disagreement arises, there is no oath. Ibn Atiyyah said: What is evident from the ruling of Abu Musa concerning the making of the dhimmis swear is that by the oath their testimony is completed and the bequest is enforced for its beneficiaries. Abu Dawud narrated from al-Sha'bi that a man from among the Muslims was approaching death at Daquqa [[Daquqa (with a fatha on its first letter, a damma on its second, after the waw a qaf, then a long alif, and it is shortened): a well-known city between Irbil and Baghdad, which has mention in reports and conquests, and in which there was also a battle with the Kharijites (Mu'jam al-Buldan).]] (this is as it stands in the originals, and it seems there is an omission here; let it be considered), and he did not find anyone from among the Muslims present to witness his bequest, so he called two men from the People of the Book to witness. They came to Kufa and went to al-Ash'ari and informed him, and they brought his estate and his bequest. Al-Ash'ari said: "This is a matter that did not happen after what happened in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." So he made them swear after the afternoon prayer: "By God, they have not betrayed, nor lied, nor altered, nor concealed, nor changed; and indeed it is the bequest of the man and his estate," and he then enforced their testimony. Ibn Atiyyah said: This doubt, according to those who do not hold the verse to be abrogated, is to be applied in cases of betrayal and of accusation of inclining toward some of the beneficiaries over others; and the oath in such cases is, in his view, also imposed. As for those who hold the verse to be abrogated, no oath is imposed except where the doubt concerns betrayal or transgression in some form of transgression; the oath then, in their view, is according to the claim against a denier, not as a completion of the testimony. Ibn al-Arabi said: The oath of doubt and suspicion is of two kinds. The first: that in which doubt arises after the right has been established and the claim has been directed; there is no disagreement about the obligation of the oath. The second: general suspicion in rights and penalties, which has its details explained in the books of jurisprudence; and here the claim has been realized and strengthened, as mentioned in the reports.

The Seventeenth: The condition in His saying, "if you doubt," is connected to His saying, "you shall detain them" (tahbisunahuma), not to His saying "then they shall swear" (fa-yuqsimani), because this detention is the cause of the oath.

The Eighteenth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will not barter it for any price, even if it be (to) a near kinsman﴾. That is, they say in their oath: "We will not exchange our oath for any consideration that we take in place of what was bequeathed, nor will we hand it over to anyone, even if the one for whom we swear is a near kinsman of ours." The omission of the saying is frequent, as in His saying: "And the angels enter upon them from every gate: 'Peace be upon you'" (al-Ra'd: 23–24), meaning they say, "Peace be upon you." The purchasing (ishtira') here does not mean selling but obtaining.

The Nineteenth: The lam in His saying, "we will not barter" is the answer to His saying, "then they shall swear," because the verb of swearing (aqsama) takes what the oath takes: "la" and "ma" in negation, and "inna" and the lam in affirmation. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the name of God, Exalted is He, as it is the nearest mentioned; the meaning is: "We will not sell our share from God with this commodity." It may also refer to the testimony, which is mentioned in the sense of the saying, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and God," where he returned the pronoun [[from k.]] to the sense of "supplication" (da'wah), which is "du'a'." This has been mentioned previously in Surat al-Nisa' [[see vol. 5 p. 50, where it reads: (fa-innahu laysa baynahu), referring to the witness; and all the originals read (baynaha), so there is no evidence in it.]].

The Twentieth: His saying, "a price" (thamanan). The Kufans said: the meaning is "possessor of a price," that is, "a commodity of price," so the qualified noun is omitted and the qualifier is put in its place. According to us and many scholars, the price may itself be the commodity, since the price in our view is also something bought, just as the priced item is bought; so each of the two exchanged items is both price and priced good, and the sale revolves around goods and cash, or two goods, or two cash items. On this principle a question is built: if the buyer goes bankrupt and the seller finds his goods, is he more entitled to them? Abu Hanifa said: he is not more entitled to them, and he built this on this principle, saying that its owner is on equal footing with the creditors. Malik said: he has a better right to it in bankruptcy but not in death. Al-Shafi'i said: its owner has a better right to it in both bankruptcy and death. Abu Hanifa held to what we have mentioned, and to the general principle that the debt is in the liability of the bankrupt and the dead, and what is in their hands is the place of payment, so all the creditors share in it in proportion to their capitals; there is no difference in this between whether the goods themselves exist or not, since they have left the ownership of their seller and their prices became due to them as a liability by consensus; so they have only their prices or what is found of them. Malik and al-Shafi'i made an exception to this rule by reports transmitted on this subject, which the imams, including Abu Dawud and others, narrated.

The Twenty-first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of God﴾, that is, the testimony God has made known to us. There are seven readings concerning it; whoever wants them will find them in (al-Tahsil) [[which is Tahsil al-Manafi' 'ala Kitab al-Durar al-Lawami', in the reading of Nafi' and others.]].

The Twenty-second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then if it is discovered that the two have deserved sin﴾. 'Umar said: this verse is the most difficult of the rulings in this surah. Al-Zajjaj said: the most difficult thing in the Qur'an in terms of i'rab is His saying: "from among those upon whom the two nearest have a claim" (min alladhina istahagga 'alayhimu al-awlayan). 'Athara 'ala kadha means he came upon it, it is said: "I came upon a betrayal from him" (athartu minhu 'ala khiyanah), meaning I discovered it, and "I made another come upon it" (a'thartu ghayri 'alayhi), and from this is His saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found﴾ (al-Kahf: 21), because they were seeking them while their location was hidden from them. The root of 'uthur is falling upon and striking something; from it comes the saying: "the man stumbled ('athara al-rajulu ya'thiru 'uthuran) when his toe struck something and was hit and fell upon it," and "the toe of so-and-so stumbled over such-and-such" when it struck it and fell upon it. The horse stumbled ('athara al-faras 'ithara), al-A'sha said:
With a she-camel of strength (lawth), 'afarnatah, when she stumbles, the ruin is nearer to her than my saying "la'a" (may she be well).
The 'athir is the rising dust, because it falls upon the face; and the 'athir is a faint trace, because it is fallen upon from concealment. The pronoun in "annahuma" refers to the two executors mentioned in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: "two" (ithnan), according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also said it refers to the two witnesses, according to Ibn 'Abbas. "Istahaqqa" means they became deserving of "sin" (ithman), meaning by betrayal and taking what is not theirs, or by a false oath, or by false testimony. Abu 'Ali said: "sin" here is the name of the thing taken, because its taker is sinful by taking it, so it is called "sin," just as what is taken without right is called "injustice" (maẓlimah). Sibawayh said: "maẓlimah" is the name of what is taken from you, so likewise this taken thing was named by the name of the verbal noun, which is "jam'."

The Twenty-third: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then two others shall stand in their place﴾, meaning in the oaths or in the testimony. He said "two others" according to the fact that the heirs were two. "Two others" (akharan) is in the nominative by an implied verb. "Stand" (yaqumani) is in the position of a qualifier. "In their place" (maqamahuma) is a verbal noun, and its estimate is: "a standing like their standing," then the qualifier was put in place of the qualified, and the verbal noun in place of its genitive.

The Twenty-fourth: His saying, Exalted is He: (from among those upon whom [[the reading of Nafi' is with the passive voice, which is the reading of the majority.]] the two nearest have a claim). Ibn al-Sarri said: the meaning is "upon whom the bequest has been claimed." Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best things said about it, because one letter is not made a substitute for another; al-Nahhas preferred it, and Ibn al-Arabi chose it. Also, the interpretation follows it, since according to the people of tafsir the meaning is: "from among those upon whom the bequest has been claimed." "The two nearest" (al-awlayan) is an apposition to His saying "two others," as Ibn al-Sarri said; al-Nahhas preferred it, and it is apposition of a definite noun to an indefinite one, which is permitted. It was also said: an indefinite noun, once its mention has preceded and it is then mentioned again, becomes definite, as in His saying: "like a niche in which is a lamp" (al-Nur: 35), then He said: "the lamp is in a glass" (al-Nur: 35), then He said: "the glass" (al-Nur: 35). It was also said: it is an apposition to the pronoun in "yaqumani," as if He had said: "then the two nearest shall stand," or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: "then two others shall stand in their place; they are the two nearest." Ibn 'Isa said: "al-awlayan" is the object of "istahagga" with an omitted noun, meaning: "the sin of the two nearest has been claimed against them and because of them," so "upon them" (alayhim) carries the sense of "concerning them," like "over the kingdom of Solomon" (al-Baqarah: 102), meaning "concerning the kingdom of Solomon." The poet said:
Whenever you deny them, you will know them: upon their horizons is a clot, freshly flowing.

That is, in its regions. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and Hamza read *al-awwalina*, the plural of *awwal*, as a substitute (*badal*) for *alladhina* or for the *ha'* and *mim* in *alayhim*. Hafs read *istahagga*, with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'*. It is also narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and its subject is *al-awlayani*, with the object omitted. The implied meaning is: "from among those against whom the two nearest of kin (*al-awliya'*) were entitled, through the deceased, to his bequest which he had made." It was also said: "the two nearest of kin were entitled against them to the return of the oaths." It is narrated from al-Hasan: *al-awwalani*, and from Ibn Sirin: *al-awwalayni* [[Ibn 'Atiyya said: "in the dual of *awwal*; the accusative is on the assumption of *al-awwalayni*, and the first in rank."]] Al-Nahhas said: "Both readings are ungrammatical (*lahn*). One does not say *muthannan* as the dual of *muthanna*, except that it has been narrated from al-Hasan, *al-awwalani*."

The twenty-fifth issue: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Then they both shall swear by God﴾. That is, the other two, who stand in the place of the two witnesses, will swear: "What our companion said in his bequest is true, and the property he bequeathed to you two was more than what you brought us, and this vessel is indeed from the property of our companion, which he took with him on his journey, and which he recorded in his bequest, and you two have betrayed [him]." That is His saying: ﴿Surely our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾, that is, our oath is more worthy than their oath. Thus it is established that *shahada* (testimony) may have the meaning of *yamin* (oath). From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So the testimony of one of them is four testimonies﴾ [[See vol. 12, p. 182.]] (Surah al-Nur 24:6). Ma'mar narrated from Ayyub, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, who said: "Two men from among the heirs of the deceased stood up and swore." ﴿Surely our testimony is more worthy﴾ is a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*). His saying: ﴿and we have not transgressed﴾, that is, we have not exceeded the truth in our oath.
﴿Indeed then we would be among the wrongdoers﴾: that is, if we had sworn to a falsehood and taken what was not ours.

The twenty-sixth issue: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿That is more suitable﴾ is a subject and predicate. ﴿That﴾ (*an*) is in the accusative position. ﴿They bring﴾ (*ya'tu*) is in the accusative governed by *an*. ﴿Or they fear﴾ (*yakhafu*) is coordinated with it. ﴿That oaths be returned﴾ (*an turadda*) is in the accusative position, governed by *yakhafu*. ﴿Oaths after their oaths﴾. It was said: the pronoun in *ya'tu* and *yakhafu* refers to the two who were entrusted with the bequest, and this is the most fitting for the context of the verse. It was also said: what is meant is people in general, that is, people are more likely to beware of betrayal and therefore testify to the truth, for fear of disgrace in having the oath returned upon the claimant. And God knows best.

The twenty-seventh issue: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And fear God and listen﴾ is an imperative, and for this reason the *nun* is dropped from it. That is: listen to what is said to you, accepting it, obeying God's command in it.
﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾. *Fasaqa*, *yafsiqu* and *yafsuqu* mean to leave obedience for disobedience. This has been discussed before [[See vol. 1, p. 245.]]. And God knows best.

**Part 1 of 5. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 106–108**

There are twenty-seven issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** Makki (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "These three verses are, according to the scholars of meanings, among the most difficult verses of the Qur'an in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), meaning, and ruling." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is the statement of one who has not found the satisfaction (thalj) in its tafsir," and this is clear from his book, may Allah have mercy on him.
