Muslim and others transmitted it. And from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The angels send blessings upon a man as long as his table is laid." [Transmitted by the trustworthy narrators.] It has been said: The ma'ida is anything that is extended and spread, like a cloth or a napkin. It ought to have been spelled with a doubled dal, but they made one of the two dals a ya', so it was called ma'ida, while the verb acts upon it, so it ought to be mamdudah (extended). But in the language it was constructed in the pattern of fa'il, as they say: "sirr katim" (a concealed secret), though it is maktum, and "'ishah radiyah" (a pleasant life), though it is mardiyyah. Likewise, in the language, what is fa'il has been constructed in the pattern of maf'ul, as they say: "rajul mash'um" (an ill-omened man), though he is sha'im, and "hijab mastur" (a veil that is concealed), though it is satir. He said: So the khiwan is what is raised above the ground on its legs; the ma'ida is what is extended and spread; and the sufra is what reveals what is in its interior, because it is folded by its fastenings. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: Eating upon the khiwan is the practice of kings, eating upon the napkin is the practice of non-Arabs, and eating upon the sufra is the practice of the Arabs, and it is the Sunnah. [And Allah knows best.]

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 5, verse 116:**

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two deities besides Allah'?"﴾ Scholars differ about the time of this statement. Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, and most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: it will be said to him this on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Suddi and Qutrub said: He said this to him when He raised him to the heavens, and the Christians said what they said about him. They argued with His saying: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:118], since "idh" (when) in the speech of the Arabs refers to the past. The first view is more correct, as indicated by what precedes it, His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:109], and the verse, and what follows it: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:119]. On this view, "idh" carries the meaning of "idha" (when), as in His saying: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified﴾ [Saba' 34:51], meaning "idha fazi'u" (when they were terrified). Abu al-Najm said:

*Then may Allah reward him on my behalf, when He rewards [him] with the gardens of Eden in the highest heavens.*

meaning "idha jaza" (when He rewards). Al-Aswad ibn Ja'far al-Azdi said:

*So now, when I jest with them, they say: "Has the old man not gone his way?"*

meaning "idha hazaltuhunna" (when I jest with them). Here he expressed the future with a past form, because this is to confirm the matter and make its proof manifest, as if it had already occurred. In the Revelation there is also: ﴿The companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf 7:50], and there are many like it, some of which have already been mentioned. The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about the meaning of this question. It is not a true question, though it takes the form of one, according to two views. The first: He asked him about this as a rebuke to those who claimed it about him, so that His denial after the question would be more emphatic in refuting them and more severe in rebuke and reproach. The second: By this question He intended to inform him that his people had changed after him and had attributed to him what he had not said. If it is said: The Christians did not take Mary as a god, so how does He say this about them? It is answered: Since it was part of their doctrine that she did not bear a human but bore a god, it followed for them that they must say she was, by virtue of bearing him, a partner in his divinity, so when this was binding upon them, they became in the position of those who say it.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿He will say, "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to. If I had said it, You would have known it.﴾ Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah who said: Jesus received his argument, and Allah inspired him in His saying: "And when Allah says, 'O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, Take me and my mother as two deities besides Allah?'" Abu Hurayrah said, from the Prophet (ﷺ): [So Allah inspired him] "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to," the whole verse. Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a hadith that is hasan sahih (good and sound). He began with glorification (tasbih) before the answer for two reasons. One: to declare Him far exalted above what was attributed to Him. The second: in submission to His might and fear of His power. It is also said: When Allah, exalted is He, said to Jesus, "Did you say to the people, Take me and my mother as two deities besides Allah?", he was seized with trembling from that statement, to the point that he heard the sound of his bones within himself, and he said, "Glory be to You," then said, "It is not for me to say what I have no right to," meaning, that I should claim for myself what is not rightfully mine, namely that I am a lord when I am only one who is lordly-served, and a worshipper when I am not one who is worshipped. Then he said, "If I had said it, You would have known it," thus referring the matter to His knowledge, though Allah already knew that he had not said it; but He asked him about it as a rebuke to those who took Jesus as a god. Then he said: (You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Yours), meaning: You know what is in my unseen, and I do not know what is in Your unseen. It was also said: the meaning is, You know what I know, and I do not know what You know. It was said: You know what I conceal, and I do not know what You conceal. It was said: You know what I intend, and I do not know what You intend. It was said: You know my secret, and I do not know Your secret, because the secret has its place in the soul. It was said: You know what happened from me in the worldly life, and I do not know what will happen from You in the Hereafter. I say: The meanings of these statements are close to one another, that is, You know my secret and what my inner self conceals, which You created, and I do not know anything of what You have reserved for Yourself from Your unseen and Your knowledge.

﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen.﴾ (That is) what has been, what will be, what has not been, and what would be if it were.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 117:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ That is, during the world, [enjoining] monotheism.

(An u'budu Allah) "An" (that) has no place in i'rab (grammatical inflection); it is explanatory (mufassirah), like "And the chiefs among them went forth saying: Walk on" (Surah Sad, 38:6). [See vol. 15, p. 151.] It may also be in the accusative position, meaning: I mentioned to them only the worship of Allah. It may also be in the genitive position, meaning: "with [the command] that worship Allah." The damma on the nun is preferable, because they find a kasra followed by a damma heavy; the kasra is permissible according to the original rule for meeting of two sakin (unvowelled letters).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I was a witness over them﴾, that is, a guardian over them with respect to what You commanded them.

(Ma dumtu fihim) "Ma" is in the accusative position, meaning: for the time of my remaining among them.

(Falamma tawaffaytani kunta anta al-raqib 'alayhim) It has been said: this indicates that Allah, exalted and majestic, caused him to die in the sense of raising him. This is not correct, because the reports are consistent that he was raised, that he is alive in the heavens, that he will descend and kill the Dajjal, as will be explained; the meaning is rather: "when You raised me up to heaven." Al-Hasan said: tawaffi in the Book of Allah, exalted and majestic, has three meanings. The death of dying, as in His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ (Surah al-Zumar, 39:42), meaning at the time the term expires. The sleep-death, as Allah the Exalted said: "It is He who takes you back at night" (Surah al-An'am, 6:60), meaning He who puts you to sleep. The death of raising, as Allah the Exalted said: "O Isa, I will take you and raise you" (Surah Al 'Imran, 3:55).

His saying "kunta anta" here: "anta" is for emphasis. "Al-raqib" is the predicate of "kunta," and its meaning is the one who guards over them, the one who knows them, and the witness to their deeds. Its root is al-muraqabah, i.e., observation; from it comes al-marqabah (watchtower), because it stands in the position of the watcher from a high place.

(Wa anta 'ala kulli shay'in shahid) That is, over what I said and what they said. It has also been said: over those who disobey and those who obey. Muslim related from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us giving a sermon and said: "O people, you will be gathered before Allah barefooted, naked and uncircumcised" [as in His saying: "As We began the first creation, We will repeat it; a promise upon Us. Indeed, We will do it" (Surah al-Anbiya, 21:104)]. Indeed, the first of creation to be clothed on the Day of Resurrection will be Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Indeed, some men from my nation will be brought and taken to the left side, and I will say: "O Lord, my companions!" It will be said: "You do not know what they innovated after you." So I will say, as the righteous servant said: "And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them. But when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things. If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise." He said: Then it will be said to me: "Indeed they have not ceased to turn back on their heels since you parted from them."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 118:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ is a conditional clause (shart), and its response (jawab) is "And if You forgive them, indeed You, only You, are the Mighty, the Wise," which is similar to it. Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Dharr who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) stood (in prayer) one night reciting a single verse until morning [[That is, he recited a verse repeating it in his prayer until morning.]], and the verse was: "If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants, and if You forgive them, indeed You, only You, are the Mighty, the Wise."

There has been disagreement about its interpretation (ta'wil). It has been said: he said it in a manner of entreaty for them and compassion towards them, as a master entreats for his servant, and for this reason he did not say, "indeed they have disobeyed You." It has also been said: he said it in a manner of submission to His command and seeking refuge from His punishment, while knowing that a disbeliever will not be forgiven. It has also been said that the pronoun (al-ha' wal-mim) in "If You punish them" refers to those among them who died upon disbelief, and the pronoun in "If You forgive them" refers to those among them who repented before death, and this is good. As for the statement of one who says that Jesus, peace be upon him, did not know that a disbeliever is not forgiven, it is a saying that is audacious against the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because reports from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are not abrogated. It has also been said: it was in Jesus's knowledge that they had introduced sins and acted after him in ways he had not commanded them, though they were still upon the pillar of his religion, so he said: "And if You forgive them" what they introduced after me of sins. And he said: "indeed You, only You, are the Mighty, the Wise," and did not say, "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," in keeping with what the narrative requires of submission to His command and entrusting His judgment. For had he said, "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," it would have implied a supplication for forgiveness for one who died in his polytheism, and that is impossible. So the implied meaning is: if You leave them in their disbelief until they die, then You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You guide them to Your monotheism and obedience, and so forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, whom nothing can prevent from what He wills, the Wise in what He does; You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. A group has recited: "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," but this is not from the codex (al-mushaf). Qadi 'Iyad mentioned this in his book "al-Shifa'." Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Some have criticized the Qur'an by saying that His saying "indeed You, only You, are the Mighty, the Wise" is not consistent with His saying "And if You forgive them," because what would be consistent with forgiveness is "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful." The answer is that it admits only what Allah revealed, and whenever it is transferred to what they transferred it to, its meaning weakens, for "the Forgiving, the Merciful" stands alone with the second condition and has no connection to the first condition. What is revealed by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and upon whose recitation the Muslims have agreed, is linked to both conditions, the first and the last, since its summary is: "If You punish them, indeed You are Mighty, Wise; and if You forgive them, indeed You, only You, are the Mighty, the Wise," in both matters, punishment and forgiveness. Thus "the Mighty, the Wise" is more fitting in this place because of its generality, for it encompasses both conditions, whereas "the Forgiving, the Merciful" is not suitable, as it does not bear the generality that "the Mighty, the Wise" bears, and what testifies to the glorification of Allah, His justice, and praise of Him throughout the whole verse, and the two mentioned conditions, is more appropriate and more firmly established in meaning within the verse than what suits only part of the speech and not the rest. Muslim narrated by various chains from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited His saying, the Mighty and Majestic, concerning Abraham: "My Lord, they have indeed led many people astray. Whoever follows me, then he is of me, and whoever disobeys me, then You are indeed Forgiving, Merciful" [[See vol. 9, p. 368.]] [Ibrahim: 36]. And Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants, and if You forgive them, indeed You, only You, are the Mighty, the Wise," then he raised his hands and said: "O Allah, my community," and wept. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "O Jibril, go to Muhammad, and your Lord knows best, and ask him what makes him weep." So Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and asked him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed him of what he had said, and He knows best. Allah said: "O Jibril, go to Muhammad and say to him: Indeed We will satisfy you concerning your community, and We will not grieve you." Some have said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, and its meaning is: "If You punish them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise; and if You forgive them, indeed they are Your servants." But the arrangement of the speech in its order is more preferable, for the reason we have explained. And with Allah is success.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 5, verse 119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah said, "This is a day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful"﴾, meaning: their truthfulness in the world. As for the Hereafter, truthfulness does not benefit anyone there. Their truthfulness in the world may be understood as their sincerity in action for Allah, and it may be understood as their refraining from lying about Him and about His messengers. Truthfulness benefits them on that day even though it benefits them on every day, because the recompense takes place on it.

It was also said: what is meant is their truthfulness in the Hereafter, and that is in testifying for their prophets that they conveyed the message, and in what they testify against themselves regarding their deeds. The way it benefits them is that they will be spared punishment for having concealed the testimony, so they will be forgiven through their acknowledgment to their prophets and against themselves. And Allah knows best.

Nafi' and Ibn Muhaysin read "yawma" (day) with a fatha (accusative). The rest read it with a damma (nominative), and this is the clear reading, on the basis of the subject and predicate: "yawmu yanfa'u" (the day when... benefits) is the predicate of "hadha" (this), and the clause is in the position of an accusative after the verb "qala" (said). As for the reading of Nafi' and Ibn Muhaysin, Ibrahim ibn Humayd reported from Muhammad ibn Yazid that this reading is not permissible, because it is the accusative of the predicate of the inchoative, and building (indeclinability) is not permissible in it. Ibrahim ibn al-Sari said: it is permissible, in the sense of "Allah said to Jesus son of Mary: this [saying], on a day when the truthfulness of the truthful benefits them." So "yawma" is an adverb of time for the saying, and "hadha" is the object of the saying, and the estimated meaning is: Allah said this statement on a day when the truthful benefit. It was also said: the estimated meaning is: Allah, mighty and majestic, said these things will benefit on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: "yawma" is built here on the fatha because it is annexed to something that is not a noun, as you say: "madha yawma'idhin" (it passed on that day). Al-Kisai recited [[The line is by al-Nabigha, and the evidence is the annexation of "hina" (when) to a verb and its being built on fatha with it.]]:

"At the time when I rebuked gray hair for youth, and I said: Would that I were sober, while the gray hair restrains [me]."

Al-Zajjaj said: The Basrans do not permit what the two of them said when you annex the adverb to an imperfect verb; if it is annexed to a perfect verb it is good, as occurred in the line. It is permissible for a verb to be annexed to adverbs of time because the verb has the meaning of a verbal noun.

It was also said: it is permissible for it to be accusative as an adverb, and the predicate of the inchoative, which is "hadha," would be [the predicate], because it refers to an event, and adverbs of time may be used to inform about events. You say: "al-qital al-yawm" (the fighting is today) and "al-khuruj as-sa'ah" (the departure is now), and the clause is in the position of an accusative after the verb "qala." It was also said: it is permissible for "hadha" to be in the position of a nominative as the inchoative, and "yawmu" to be the predicate of the inchoative, with the governing element omitted; the estimated meaning is: Allah said: this which We have related occurs on the day when the truthfulness of the truthful benefits them. There is a third reading: "yawmun yanfa'u" with tanwin, and "as-sadiqina sidquhum" (the truthful, their truthfulness) in the speech has an ellipsis, estimated as "fihi" (in it), like His saying: "And fear a day when no soul will avail another soul in anything" [Al-Baqarah 48; see vol. 1 p. 376]. This is the reading of al-A'mash.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For them are gardens﴾: an inchoative and predicate. "Tajri" (flowing) is in the position of a qualifier. "Min tahtiha" (beneath them) means beneath their chambers and trees, and this has been mentioned before. Then He, may He be exalted, explained their reward and that He is pleased with them with a pleasure after which He will never be angered, and ﴿they are pleased with Him﴾, meaning: with the recompense with which He rewarded them.

﴿That is the great triumph﴾: "i.e., the victory" ﴿the great﴾: i.e., that whose good is immense and abundant, and whose owner's rank is elevated and honored.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [and what is in them]. [[From manuscripts ب, ج, and ك.]] This came after the claim of the Christians concerning ʿĪsā (Jesus), that he is god. So Allah the Exalted informed that the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him alone, not to ʿĪsā and not to the rest of the created beings.

It is also possible that the meaning is: He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth gives the gardens previously mentioned to His obedient servants, may Allah make us among them by His grace and generosity.

The surah of al-Māʾidah is completed, all praise be to Allah the Exalted.
